events.title: CFTC Chair Selig tells CNBC crypto industry is embracing agency rules as legislation hopes fade
events.summary: CFTC Chairman Michael Selig says major crypto exchanges and new entrants are showing interest in using the agency's federal oversight framework. The CFTC published an advance notice on Oct. 5 seeking comment on a framework for retail crypto commodity transactions after the Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act on Sept. 15. Democrats' 2026 congressional gains are expected to bring greater scrutiny of crypto regulation and President Donald Trump's crypto ties in 2027. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is already seeing demand from crypto exchanges planning to opt in to its newly proposed rules governing digital assets, according to Chairman Michael Selig. The commodities regulator in October proposed rules aimed at preventing abuse in crypto markets and codifying crypto transaction rules under a federal rulebook. In the announcement , Selig said the move was a "critical step" in ensuring the United States remains the crypto capital of the world. Speaking this week at Cantor Convergence, an annual FinTech conference held in Miami Beach, Selig told CNBC in an exclusive interview that many of the major crypto exchanges are already registered with the CFTC because they offer financial derivatives, including perpetual futures, on their platforms and would now be able to add spot trading. "We're also getting interest from new entrants who say, 'Look, signing up with 50 different state regimes is tough. We'd rather come to one regulator and get a license at the CFTC' so those new entrants are lining up to come register with us as well," he added. After the Clarity Act, a comprehensive market structure bill that established a regulatory framework for digital assets, stalled in the Senate in September, the CFTC and the SEC moved to establish federal frameworks using their existing statutory authorities. "We need to protect our markets and protect our customers using those markets so we'll continue to do exactly that in the wake of the Clarity Act failing to get the votes it needed to get to the president's desk during the current Congress," Selig said. "Our statute does provide for authority of the agencies to register exchanges that want to offer margined, leveraged, or financed crypto assets or other types of commodity trading so we're utilizing that authority to allow our existing exchanges to begin offering these products under a regulated framework," he said. Selig added that the oversight is opt-in for exchanges that are not currently offering margin leveraged financing, which is not permitted under existing state regimes. But the CFTC's new rules could face new scrutiny and oversight in 2027, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate after the midterms. Selig told CNBC he hopes the U.S. won't see a wave of software developers moving offshore, as many crypto businesses threatened to do under the Biden administration. "I really hope that we learned lessons from the last several years in this space," he said. Crypto firms were at odds with Washington during the Biden administration, asking for clear operating rules, while also facing lawsuits brought by the SEC under former chair Gary Gensler's leadership. That shifted after President Donald Trump's 2024 victory. "I do hope that we can work together with both sides of the aisle to protect software developers who want to do the right thing," Selig said, adding that those looking to commit crimes and engage in fraud should be held accountable. When asked whether he's prepared for increased scrutiny from Congress in 2027, Selig said, "Congress will do its job investigating where it needs to investigate." "I'm happy to answer any questions that Congress has for me just as I would answer Congress' questions today as I've done before hearing committees several times already," he said. Selig has also faced heat from Democrats for his handling of prediction markets. In February, 23 Democratic senators sent a letter to Chairman Selig urging him to reverse the agency's greenlighting of prediction markets. Selig has argued that prediction platforms are federally regulated as more states try to rein them in. The CFTC has sued several states to defend what the agency views as its exclusive jurisdiction to regulate event contracts, which it classifies as swaps. "We're going to fight this up to the Supreme Court if that's where it's going," Selig said. "Our view on the statute is that we have exclusive jurisdiction over these markets, and I will not allow for states to go bring lawsuits against our exchanges, claiming that they're unlicensed gambling." — CNBC's Tanaya Macheel contributed to this report.

events.title: This young startup wants to power floating data centers with the ocean’s heat, and investors are already on board
events.summary: Anyone who has weathered a hurricane can tell you that the oceans — which fuel the storms — contain a tremendous amount of energy. Thanks to global warming, they’re holding more than ever. A new startup wants to harness that energy to power data centers. Drogue , which has kept a low profile until now, is building a system that harvests heat from the ocean to power data centers on board floating vessels. According to co-founder and CEO Sam Sipe, the first prototype should be bobbing around the ocean, crunching bits, less than two years from now. The goal, Sipe said, is to help data center developers deploy servers in AI-friendly timelines. “The data center industry is a real estate game, and so they’re playing on 8- to 10-year timelines, including interoperability with utilities and [independent system operators]” that manage regional power grids, he said. “AI demand has increased 10x in just the last three years. It’s completely incompatible.” Drogue was founded just six months ago in Washington, DC, and the startup told TechCrunch exclusively that it has already raised $20 million, including from XYZ Venture Capital, Toyota Ventures, Tamarack Global, Dream, FDVC, Garuda Ventures, Flexcap, Boost VC, and Slow Ventures, among other investors. In those six months, Drogue has designed a multi-megawatt prototype that will be installed on a traditional ocean-going ship and sent out to sea in early 2028. Future versions will be built on floating structures that more closely resemble offshore oil platforms. To Sipe, the decision to turn to the ocean was obvious. After years flying E-2D Hawkeyes off U.S. Navy aircraft carriers, he had an appreciation for the ocean’s immense power. “Most people think, oh, ocean — hard waves, storms, corrosion, biofouling. And I just see this majestic place and resource that we just ignore,” he said. As the planet warms, the oceans have been absorbing an additional 5.8 million terawatt-hours of energy every year. By comparison, all of human civilization uses about 180,000 terawatt-hours each year. If Drogue were to take some, surely the ocean wouldn’t miss it. The startup’s technology works like a heat pump run in reverse. A heat pump uses electricity to move heat from one place to another; Drogue’s system instead uses a difference in temperature to generate electricity. This approach, known as ocean thermal energy conversion, or OTEC, was first developed in the 1950s. Surface waters are warmer, heated by the sun, while down-deep temperatures are much colder, about 39˚ F on average (4˚ C). “There’s basically no amount of heat we can pull out of that that will collapse that temperature differential,” Sipe said. To leverage the temperature differential, the startup’s system draws in warm surface water, uses it to cool the data centers, and then sends the now-warmer water to boil ammonia, a chemical that turns to gas at -28 °F. That ammonia gas is then sent through a turbine to generate electricity. Once through the turbine, it courses through a condenser, which turns the gas back into a liquid. There, cold water drawn from 1,000 meters deep passes over the condenser’s fins to absorb the heat. The warmed water is then pumped back down to 1,000 meters, where it dissipates into the ocean. The ammonia gets sent back to the start of the sealed loop, and the cycle repeats. The basic idea was tested in the 1980s but tossed aside. “A lot has changed since the ’80s, specifically manufacturing techniques around the pipe and the heat exchangers,” Sipe said. To find out why, Sipe sought out people who had worked on those early efforts. “I just talked to everyone, basically interviewed them and figured out what went wrong, what went right, what would you do next. And everyone was like, dude, this stuff works. It’s just a matter of being able to raise enough capital to build something big enough, because there’s a sweet spot,” he said. There also had to be customers who could use that power while still at sea. Sending power to shore would require lengthy, expensive cables, and manufacturing on board would require similarly expensive shipping of materials and finished goods. Data centers are ideal — the servers are compact relative to other equipment, and shipping data off the platform is incredibly cheap. Each vessel would live at sea for about a decade, Sipe said. Drogue already has “approval in principle,” a preliminary sign-off, from the American Bureau of Shipping, which sets and checks safety standards for ships. Now, it’s in the process of buying its first ship to start building a prototype ready for the open ocean. In many ways, Drogue’s concept is similar to Elon Musk’s plan for orbital data centers : find a cheap source of power, and get the data centers as close to it as possible. Except unlike orbital data centers, Drogue’s don’t need to launch expensive rockets to get there. They can just sail a ship on the ocean, something humanity has been doing for millennia.

events.title: Supreme Court agrees to hear Robinhood challenge to IPO information omission lawsuit
events.summary: The Supreme Court said it will consider an effort by Robinhood to block a lawsuit over the company's omission of interim financial data from its initial public offering in 2021. Robinhood wants the Supreme Court to overturn a ruling by the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals that revived a lawsuit by investors against the company and firms involved with the IPO, including Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan Securities. The Supreme Court on Friday agreed to hear a case in which Robinhood seeks to block a class-action lawsuit over the omission of interim financial data from the online broker's initial public offering in 2021. Robinhood wants the Supreme Court to overturn a ruling by the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals that revived a lawsuit by investors against the company and firms involved with the IPO, including Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan Securities . A San Francisco federal court judge had previously dismissed the lawsuit. The Trump administration and the Securities and Exchange Commission had urged the Supreme Court to hear Robinhood's appeal. "We are pleased the Supreme Court has agreed to hear our case and look forward to presenting our argument," a Robinhood spokesperson said in a statement. CNBC has requested comment from the attorneys representing the plaintiffs in the case. Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling Robinhood's IPO came on the heels of a surge in investor interest during the Covid-19 pandemic of so-called meme stocks, and trading in the crypto asset Dogecoin. In July 2021, Robinhood conducted its IPO, "for which it prepared a registration statement" that "contained only limited information about Robinhood's performance during the second quarter of 2021," the 9th Circuit panel that heard the case noted. "After the initial public offering, Robinhood reported financial results from that second quarter, and its stock price dropped," the panel wrote. The investors who sued Robinhood and the other defendants alleged that the registration statement omitted material information that was legally required to be disclosed.

events.title: How the Microsoft outage impacted courts and governments
events.summary: Courts and governments worldwide felt the impact of this week's Microsoft outage, which sidelined work and stymied communication. Why it matters: When Microsoft's popular workplace software went offline Thursday, it meant an extended lunch break for some offices — but for the courts and governments, it raised questions about the vulnerabilities of the technology underpinning justice and governance. Case in point: The state of Maine's judicial branch warned in a Thursday alert that requests for protection orders filed by email — urgent requests to keep parties safe from harm — may not have been received. Multiple court documents reviewed by Axios show lawyers requesting deadline extensions or alerting judges to the outage impacting their work. That includes DOJ lawyers: Government attorneys asked for an extension in the case brought by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over President Trump 's Kennedy Center takeover , saying the outage prevented them from "completing the necessary coordination." In a separate filing, Beatty's team acknowledged they were impacted as well. Zoom out: The impacts were also felt in courtrooms and offices internationally. The AP reported that a U.K. criminal trial was delayed as a result, with a Manchester judge saying, per BBC's reporting , "We are learning of the dangers of relying on computers and data systems." U.K.-based police forces also urged the public Friday to call first responders for aid, rather than using online forms. The Supreme Court of the Philippines said it, too, was affected by the outage. What they're saying: "We obviously need backup methods to keep the wheels of justice turning," says Gissou Nia, the founder and director of the Atlantic Council's Strategic Litigation Project. She pointed to a prior incident that previewed international reliance on U.S. tech: Though not exposed by an outage, the Trump administration's sanctions on the International Criminal Court prompted the Netherlands-based court to move off of Microsoft software to avoid its work being paralyzed. While court deadlines can be pushed back, service disruption for individuals seeking urgent injunctive relief is more critical, she notes. "If the only way to communicate ... is through these servers, and the request wasn't reached, it can result in somebody having left the country or having moved money out of an account," Nia says. Reality check: Shay Cleary, a National Center for State Courts consultant who specializes in tech and cybersecurity, emphasizes that courts typically have manual back-up plans in place. "Many of the people who work in courts are dedicated public servants, and they can figure out how to do things right," he adds. With Congress back in session, Hill communications were also left in a holding pattern Thursday — with one staffer writing on X, "Hope nobody needs Congress for a little while, your Legislative Branch is currently paralyzed by the Outlook outage." Municipal governments in Austin , Texas, and Jacksonville , Florida, among several others , warned that their emails — and in some cases, phone systems — were impacted. What we're watching: A page providing updates on the suite of Microsoft tech tools said in a Friday morning post that it was seeing "encouraging recovery progress." That statement came some 22 hours after the page first said the company was investigating reports of issues with email access. The bottom line: The very tools that connect us digitally can also divide us when things go wrong — underscoring the importance of preparing old-school backup plans to fill the gaps. events.title: IMF says more progresses needed on Lebanon's banking sector reform
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund on Friday said Lebanon's bank restructuring law remains a key sticking point as Beirut looks to secure a new economic reform programme with the multilateral lender. The fund said progress was made in discussions on the country's banking sector restructuring strategy during a November 11-13 staff-level visit to Lebanon and that further engagement is expected to continue. "However, further work is needed to reach an agreement on a strategy for an effective and durable restructuring of Lebanon’s banking sector, leading to a sound and resilient system," said Ernesto Ramirez Rigo, IMF mission chief to Lebanon. The IMF in particular pointed to the implementation of the Bank Resolution Law and the Financial Stabilisation and Deposits Recovery Law - or the financial gap law - as "essential to restore financial stability and maximise deposits recovery" once they are adopted. Lebanon reached an initial staff-level agreement with the IMF in 2022 after the country's economy collapsed, although the government at the time was slow to implement the fund's recommendations. Lebanon defaulted on its debt for the first time in March 2020, leading to hyperinflation, high unemployment, a surging poverty rate and depositors frozen out of their savings. Its financial collapse generated losses of roughly $70 billion, a figure used in official estimates since 2022, although that number is now expected to be higher. The fund said further talks are needed to maximise deposit repayments while ensuring consistency with the central bank's and the banking sector's liquidity positions, and public debt sustainability and the restoration of the central bank's solvency. The IMF also said it remains critical the Financial Stabilisation and Deposits Recovery Law "upholds the hierarchy of claims in the allocation of losses, thereby maximising protection for depositors". Lebanon's Parliament passed a bank resolution law in August, although President Joseph Aoun appealed it to the Constitutional Council over an amendment concerning the central bank's independence and power. The fund at the time said it would assess any changes to ensure they were consistent with international standards. "The mission looks forward to continuing the engagement with the authorities to make further progress on these fronts in the coming weeks and remains fully committed to supporting Lebanon in its efforts to design and implement a comprehensive economic reform program, in line with the IMF’s policies and mandate," Mr Ramirez Rigo said.

events.title: Nvidia hasn’t selected search firm for permanent Huang replacement, board tells CNBC
events.summary: Nvidia hasn't chosen a search firm to identify potential candidates to replace former CEO Jensen Huang, the company's board told CNBC. Speculation has swirled around who the board will select to permanently succeed Huang. "We have not formally engaged any potential candidates," the board said in a statement. Nvidia hasn't yet selected a search firm to work with in identifying a successor for former CEO Jensen Huang , the company's board told CNBC. "We are in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role," the board said in a Friday statement. "We have not formally engaged any potential candidates." The comments come after speculation has swirled about who might be tapped to replace Huang. Nvidia announced Thursday that Huang would step down as CEO of the chipmaker after multiple reported affairs, including one with a woman purported to be a Chinese spy. Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO and said it will begin a search for a permanent CEO to replace Huang, adding that it will consider both internal and external candidates. The Financial Times reported Friday that Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas in its search for Huang's successor, citing people familiar with the matter. Nvidia's board said, "Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature." Before joining the SoftBank-backed chip company in 2013, Haas spent seven years at Nvidia, serving in a variety of roles including vice president of its computing products business. Nvidia shares fell more than 2% on Friday, dragging the company's market cap below $4 trillion as investors digested the news of Huang's departure, and the specter of ongoing probes into his conduct. On Tuesday, Nvidia said it had retained Wachtell Lipton to investigate allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, following revelations that its then-CEO had an intimate relationship with Alice Huang, who several outlets reported is suspected of working for Chinese intelligence. Three House committees have asked Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 . The Senate Banking Committee has also requested that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify to discuss "serious concerns about our national security," and how the company's top AI chips have reportedly ended up in China. events.title: Pressure grows on Trump's Commerce Secretary Lutnick in fallout from Nvidia scandal
events.summary: How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? Published 13 November 2026, 15:04 GMT US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet. Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions. Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy. Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with. Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months". "But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added. Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said some parts of the administration wanted more controls on trade with Megaspeed Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China. "President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment. There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included. However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia. "The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme , external . "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies? "It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that." Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past. In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, accoprding to US media. How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House Published 7 hours ago How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions Published 1 day ago Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman, Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X. Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips. According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into America for inspection. A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security. "Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said. events.title: After Jensen Huang’s exit, what top financial advisors are doing with Nvidia: Exclusive CNBC poll
events.summary: In a CNBC flash poll of its Financial Advisor 100 and Financial Advisor Council, most respondents said they were holding their Nvidia positions steady; none said they were selling at the time of the poll. AI demand, valuation and Nvidia’s leadership or governance were the most-cited factors that could change respondents’ approach. Advisors said investors should weigh their Nvidia concentration, time horizon and risk tolerance before reacting to short-term volatility. To gauge how wealth managers are responding, CNBC polled members of its Financial Advisor 100 and Financial Advisor Council. Thirty of the 122 firms and professionals contacted responded to the online, multiple-choice flash poll, conducted between 11 a.m. and 5 p.m. EST on Nov. 12. The poll is a snapshot of respondents' views, not a measure of all financial advisors. Most advisors polled are holding steady Most respondents, 19, said they are holding their Nvidia positions steady. Another four said they are increasing their stake, while seven said they do not own the stock. None said they were selling at the time of the poll. "Most of our clients are in a position to hold; the reason is because it makes up a smaller percentage of an overall diversified portfolio," Winnie Sun , managing director and founding partner of Irvine, California-based Sun Group Wealth Partners, said in an interview. Sun is a member of the CNBC Financial Advisor Council. More from CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 Read coverage of CNBC's 2026 Financial Advisor 100 list, including stories featuring ranked firms and their advisors: CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor for 2026 takes a family-office approach CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 FAQ: Who is eligible and how rankings work Roth conversions aren't for everyone. When the 'juice' isn't worth it: Top advisor After Jensen Huang's exit, what top advisors are doing with Nvidia: CNBC poll In open responses, several advisors wrote that they are taking a "wait-and-see" approach before changing their investment strategy with Nvidia and are telling their clients to do the same. "Don't react to short-term headlines," wrote certified financial planner Peyton Jamison, president of Jamison Private Wealth Management in Alpharetta, Georgia. "The company's valuation is extremely attractive, and the focus should remain on its underlying fundamentals and long-term investment potential." His firm is ranked No. 78 on the 2026 CNBC Financial Advisor 100 list. What would change advisors' positions Asked what factors could change their approach to Nvidia, 13 respondents cited the outlook for AI demand, 11 pointed to valuation, and 10 mentioned company leadership or governance. Some said the decision depends on the client, with eight citing risk tolerance and seven mentioning portfolio concentration. Seven said they do not expect to change their approach. Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results Tuesday, after the market close. In poll remarks, advisors said the company's fiscal third-quarter earnings will help determine their course of action. Advisors said that for investors, what to do may depend on how much Nvidia stock they already own, when they expect to need the money and how comfortable they are with volatility. "If this is a company that's going to keep you up at night and you just feel really uncomfortable with these unknown risks, then there was always the option to sell and move that capital to another stock or another portfolio," Sun said. How investors can check Nvidia exposure Nvidia exposure can also come through mutual funds and ETFs . Nvidia's large market value makes it a significant holding in many broad-market funds, including funds that track the S&P 500, as well as target-date funds in retirement-plan options. Investors can check their Nvidia exposure by reviewing the fact sheets for the funds in their 401(k) or brokerage accounts, which typically list a fund's largest holdings. A stock's decline does not translate one-for-one into a fund's decline. However, investors with dedicated technology, semiconductor or growth funds may have more Nvidia exposure than they realize, advisors say. "Nvidia is a big part of virtually everyone's portfolio whether they take an active or passive index approach," wrote Andy Pratt, a partner and director of investment strategy at Burney Wealth Management in Reston, Virginia, which is ranked No. 34 on the 2026 CNBC Financial Advisor 100 list. He said he advises clients not to overreact to short-term news and to let the dust settle before making decisions. — CNBC's Stephanie Dhue contributed reporting to this article.

events.title: AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation
events.summary: Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday. That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago , led by IVP. LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence. With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use. True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well ( case in point is newcomer Mintive ). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce. events.title: Are you team car door or car bonnet? This town's history depends on your answer
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Lightning Ridge opal history dispute plays out on car doors and bonnets Blow the layer of dust off Lightning Ridge and you will find a town as rich in colour as the precious black opal mined here. The stone’s dark undertone is the marriage of carbon and iron oxide, brought together over millennia beneath the earth’s surface. It brings colour to life in a way that no other precious stone can. It is an exceptionally rare find, with more than 90 per cent of the world’s supply located beneath this outback moonscape. Great fortunes have been made and lost here on Yuwaalaraay Country in Northern NSW, where stories have become facts and truth can be just as elusive as the black opal itself. Among the corrugated iron shacks and the long-abandoned mine shafts that pockmark this land, the past is everywhere. Exactly what that history is, however, depends on who's telling it. Barb Moritz is waiting for us in front of an old miner's cottage on the main street. Built in 1932, its warped pinewood beams and lopsided tin roof resemble an abstract painting. It's the headquarters of the Lightning Ridge Historical Society, and the seat from which Barb holds court. She emerges from the shadow of the verandah awning whirring with facts and directions, her dark eyes glowing. Barb cuts a strikingly vibrant figure amid a palette of rusted metal and aging wood. When she smiles, the afternoon sun catches her opal dental filling and it flashes with brilliant greens and blues. Introductions are swift before Barb leaps into her opening stanza, fine tuned over decades of leading tour groups. She points towards the local pool, opened by Dawn Fraser in 1990. The Opal Miners Hall of Fame is further out, just a few minutes' drive from the cottage. Then there's the Lightning Ridge Cemetery, or as Barb refers to it, the "dead end of town". She casts us a deadpan glance and pauses for effect. Barb is a long way from the cornfields of Iowa in the American mid-west, where she grew up. She still isn't quite sure if she chose to move to Lightning Ridge, or if the black opal lured her. "From the very beginning, I feel I was directed to opal," she says, her accent still thick. Barb arrived in Lightning Ridge in the summer of 1990. Three years later, she was working for the historical society. "I met the people who lived here, the old-timers who built this community," she says. It wasn't long before Barb was the society's secretary. Tucked away behind the old miner's cottage is an aging demountable filled to the brim with miners' ledgers and newspaper clippings dating back more than a century. It is the engine room of the historical society. And it's here, among the records, that Barb pieces together a version of Lightning Ridge's opal-mining evolution. In the late 1990s, this history was translated onto a conspicuous canvas unique to the town's identity, the "car door tours". Across the featureless landscape, car doors mark out four colour-coded routes (green, red, yellow and blue) to sites the society deems significant to the town's history. "People lock their car doors because they're afraid maybe one will go missing," Barb says with a glimmer in her eye. The doors have become much more than a tourist attraction for the droves of travellers and grey nomads who pass through. They are now part of the landscape. They're also used by locals and emergency services to help locate people living on claims that are well and truly off the beaten track. The population of Lightning Ridge is a bit of a mystery. Officially, it has about 2,000 residents. Unofficially, it's more like 5,000 because many people move to this outback town to disappear. We follow Barb's car as she navigates the dirt roads, tracing the green car door tour as it winds its way up to McDonald's Six-Mile opal field. Perched on an ironstone ridge above the town, facing the western horizon, it's a moonscape of colourless rock, sheet metal and dozens of deserted mine shafts. You can't miss the monument to Charles Nettleton. Protected by a wire fence, the jagged rectangular stone slab and its plaque look lovingly maintained, but resemble a tombstone. There is pride in Barb's eyes as she takes stock of the monument, pale yellow under the midday sun. It would not be here without her ability to move heaven and earth for her adopted home. "[Charles Nettleton] was the first professional opal miner who came to this country" Barb explains. "And we decided … we needed to have a monument — a historical reserve — to where he had sunk his first shafts for the syndicate of businessmen who hired him.

events.title: The 4 types of people Dario Amodei said he won’t hire — and what Anthropic looks for instead
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said talent and culture "are the most important things" for a company. Bloomberg/Getty Images Dario Amodei said Anthropic doesn't hire jerks or people who can't get along with others. He said talent and culture are the company's top priorities, and he spends 40-50% of his time on it. Amodei said that focus has helped with retention. Don't bother applying for a job at Anthropic if your goal is to be the star of the show. That was one of the first things Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei emphasized on Friday, in a live-streamed interview with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon ahead of the AI startup's hotly anticipated IPO . Amodei said the company has been "very disciplined about turning down people who are deeply technically talented," but don't fit its culture. The company's recent IPO filing stated that its workforce grew from about 940 employees at the end of 2024 to about 5,300 as of late September. "We don't want people who are jerks. We don't want people who try to steal the show and don't work well with others. We don't want people who aren't oriented towards the public benefit," Amodei told Dimon. Amodei, who worked as vice president of research at research at OpenAI and was a senior research scientist at Google Brain, said talent and culture "are the most important things" for a company. He said he now devotes 40% to 50% of his time to focusing on those priorities. 'High-trust, low-ego' The CEO said that talent and culture create technology, and the company's presence and how it's viewed by the public comes from the talent and intentions of the people who build that technology. Amodei said he and his six cofounders decided at the company's founding that talent and culture would be their priority. "If you stick to that consistently, it's painful in the short run. But you get a team where everyone works together, and everyone is on the same side," Amodei said. Anthropic describes itself as a "high-trust, low-ego organization" on its website, and in its IPO filing said that "teams operate in a truth-seeking environment where the best argument wins, not the loudest voice or the most senior title." Amodei told Dimon that he encourages other leaders to demonstrate honesty and trust. He said that every two weeks he holds a "Dario Vision Quest," an all-hands meeting where he said he speaks to the company about what's going on. Amodei said he tries not to hide things from staff and doesn't rely on corporate jargon. That creates an environment where employees can trust leaders and leaders can trust employees, he said. "Everyone feels that we're being honest with them," Amodei said, adding that this carries "enormous value." A focus on retention Amodei told Dimon that the approach works because employees share the same values and a common goal. Whether the task is training a model, meeting a safety objective, building a product, or advancing a policy priority, "the whole company comes together to make it happen," he said. Amodei said that maintaining that kind of environment has helped with retention, which is critical given the company's dependence on senior leaders and key technical team members. Amodei said that all seven cofounders, including himself, are still at the company, along with over three-quarters of its first 100 employees. In its IPO filing, Anthropic said it experienced only about 1% "regrettable attrition" in a 12-month period. Amodei added that it's a "relatively frequent" occurrence for employees to come back after leaving. He said two major product employees left and came back after two weeks. "They said, 'Sorry, we didn't appreciate what we had,'" Amodei said about their return. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process
events.summary: Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse. However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists. Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options. Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds. This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual. This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time. By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI. events.title: Microsoft ‘deeply sorry’ as outage triggers global chaos
events.summary: The US tech company ruled out any malicious “cyber or AI” activity as the cause of the outage and reported a broad recovery across its services. Microsoft on Nov 13 apologised for a global outage that disrupted public services and businesses around the world, as it reported a “broad recovery” for Outlook email and other services. The company ruled out any malicious “cyber or AI” activity as the cause of the outage, which affected several Microsoft products and disrupted health care services, delayed corporate earnings reports and left schools struggling to communicate. “We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners,” Microsoft said on X, adding full services were still being restored after the outage started on Nov 12. “We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services. This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents.” The disruption knocked out Microsoft products in 74 countries and territories, affecting users across the Americas and parts of Europe, Asia and Africa, according to the outage tracker Downdetector. A top UK trade union said the disruptions had a “serious impact” on the country’s health care service. National Health Service staff receiving emergency calls were “unable to refer patient details in the normal way,” creating a massive backlog, said Rachel Harrison, public services head at the GMB union. As the outage dragged on for hours, airlines in India warned that customer queries may not be getting through. IndiGo and Akasa Air both said on X that their email support services had been affected and that they may not be able to receive customers’ emails. Immigration New Zealand said the disruption had forced a halt in the processing of all visa applications. Japan’s economy, trade and industry minister Ryosei Akazawa warned of a “significant impact” of the outage as the Microsoft products were used by a “vast number of people.” In London’s financial district, several people interviewed by AFP said the outage exposed their dependence on Copilot, Microsoft’s AI assistant. “I think one of the biggest things is Copilot not working,” said Yashmit Sharma, 26, an auditor. “I think this was the main bummer. And Outlook as well, of course.” Sheera, 40, a risk manager at a mid-sized bank, said businesses needed to be better prepared for unexpected technology failures. “I think we need to be a little bit more careful,” said Sheera, declining to give her last name. “Anything can happen: you wake up and Outlook is not working and it’s the main communication we use for our global team.” The Australian Computer Society (ACS) called for a national review of sovereign IT risk, with CEO Prins Ralston saying that small businesses may not have a workaround when Outlook fails. “We need to know the systems that keep this country running won’t simply fall over without notice,” Ralston said, according to ACS publication Information Age. On Nov 12, Microsoft attributed the disruption to “elevated load” on its infrastructure. In an updated statement on Friday, it said the “incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change.” “We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.” Reports of problems on Downdetector had begun to decline by 9am GMT (5pm Singapore time). Microsoft initially said it was investigating outage reports “in the Americas,” but later confirmed that the issue apparently affected “Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region.” Microsoft 365 is the company’s cloud-based subscription service that includes popular applications such as Outlook and Teams. events.title: Rip out ugly clutter to help revive UK high streets, says thinktank
events.summary: Exclusive: Report says restricting cars and freeing up pavement space could be a cheap way to entice shoppers The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap? Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing. Central to this, the study says, is trying to banish, or at least tame, motor traffic, because too often urban centres are places “designed to be driven through, not for time to be spent in”. As well as citing a lack of imagination, the report blames planning regulations that favour conformity and clutter and too often treat speeding cars as a given, to which everything else must adjust. “The default high street is engineered for traffic and furnished from a catalogue: a tarmac pavement, guardrails penning people at the kerb, litter bins ordered from a procurement catalogue, a row of plastic planters – public investment that is joyless,” it says. While planners have traditionally focused on car access as a metric for thriving town centres, calculations for the Create Streets report suggest that replacing parking with other kerbside infrastructure, including bike spaces or outside drinking and dining areas, creates more economic value. It found that one parking space in the high street of a market town is typically used by about 3.5 vehicles a day, bringing in just over £73,000 a year in spending to nearby shops. But the same 12 square metres, if used to hold nine share e-bikes, generates an average of 13 trips a day, with over £146,000 a year in spending, even taking into account the lower average spend per person. In a busier city, where share bikes would be used more frequently, the estimated total annual spend rises to more than £300,000. Repurposing the space for outside dining brings less dramatic gains, but in a city centre it can still amount to about £120,000 in extra annual spending. The report, also produced by Cyclehoop, which makes bike storage, calls for a cultural rethink involving low-cost tweaks that rip away ugly and unnecessary street furniture and make better use of kerbsides. Calling use by families “the indicator species of a healthy high street”, the report cites what is known as “the wrist test” – whether it feels safe to let go of a young child’s wrist so they can roam with some freedom. This is best done, it argues, by removing the threat of speeding motor vehicles and not by trying to mitigate their impact. It calls the removal of pedestrian guardrails next to roads “the most cost-effective upgrade for the majority of high streets”, saying they are an eyesore with minimal safety benefits. The report says “the absurdity of modern public realm management” is exemplified by Secured by Design, policy guidelines on cutting neighbourhood crime. These can, critics point out, mean benches and plants are removed on the advice of police, supposedly to discourage antisocial behaviour. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, has pledged to try to reverse the decline of high streets, announcing in September a £210m regeneration fund. However, the bulk of the money will go into buildings: turning old shops into shared workspaces or community cafes, or keeping pubs and clubs in business. The report argues that renovating buildings is pointless if the street outside is unappealing. To reduce clutter, it says, there should be “a presumption of removal where an item cannot be justified”. The effects can be dramatic, the report says, pointing to examples including Altrincham in Cheshire, where the creation of a walkable, car-free urban area helped see retail vacancies fall from over 30% to 7% in less than a decade. Such initiatives do not have to be expensive, it claims, noting the example of an unused patch of land next to a church in Grimsby which was turned into a park for less than £20,000. “Streets that are ugly are not so because councils lack the desire to change them, but because the system is counting the maintenance liabilities, not the benefits,” said David Milner of Create Streets. “What works is cheap: trees in the ground, benches people want to sit on, clutter taken away. “So much of what is built now seems to be temporary, looking more like road works than public realm improvements, so we encourage the concept of permanence; more trees in the ground, not in giant plant pots, for example.” A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “We support local leaders to make decisions on pedestrianisation based on their communities’ needs.

events.title: Lutnick faces questions over Nvidia spy scandal. His sons’ firm has deep ties to the chipmaker
events.summary: Cantor Fitzgerald’s reported Nvidia share count fell by nearly half between September 2025 and March 2026, a CNBC analysis found. That was the period when Axios reported Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faced pressure from administration officials to address suspected smuggling of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China. The Wall Street firm, which Lutnick formerly chaired and is now run by his sons, maintained extensive commercial ties to Nvidia, helping arrange billions of dollars in financing for companies in its AI business universe and repeatedly hosting its top executives. Those relationships have come into sharper focus following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and revelations about Lutnick’s handling of national security concerns involving the chipmaker. There is no evidence that Cantor’s business interests influenced Lutnick’s decisions. In late September, Cantor Fitzgerald hosted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other top executives from the chipmaker for investor meetings in New York, according to a Cantor research report reviewed by CNBC. The Wall Street firm liked what it heard. "We continue to view NVDA as the best risk/reward in our coverage," Cantor analyst C.J. Muse and his colleagues wrote in a research report dated Oct. 3 that maintained a $350 price target and overweight rating on the stock. Yet the firm formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and now led by his sons, Brandon and Kyle, reported a nearly 50% decline in the number of Nvidia shares it held between September 2025 and March 2026 , according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings that excludes options. Nvidia had been one of the largest stock positions reported in Cantor's filings. The decline coincided with White House and U.S. intelligence officials pressing Lutnick to crack down on Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence chips to China . Lutnick repeatedly resisted those efforts, according to Axios . By the time Cantor hosted Huang in New York, Lutnick had also received a classified intelligence warning, according to Axios, about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy and had appeared alongside the CEO at a G20 technology summit in North Carolina. Even as Cantor pared back its Nvidia stake, it continued doing business across the chipmaker's AI empire. A CNBC review of securities filings, corporate announcements and Wall Street research found the firm has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners while maintaining close ties to the chipmaker's leadership. Those ties have drawn fresh scrutiny following Huang's resignation Thursday and Axios' reporting that Lutnick repeatedly resisted a crackdown on companies suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, despite President Donald Trump authorizing new export restrictions on those companies for a third time on Nov. 5. An ethics expert said the relationship between Lutnick and his former firm's investments may raise questions, given what the secretary knew about Nvidia. Richard Painter , the former chief White House ethics lawyer for President George W. Bush and now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota said that while "there's no proof of" Lutnick sharing nonpublic information with Cantor Fitzgerald, "the appearance doesn't look great." "His conversations with his sons better be about publicly available information," Painter told CNBC. There is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of the intelligence concerns, that changes in Cantor's reported holdings were tied to any warnings or that the firm's business interests influenced their father's decisions. "Cantor has to date from time to time had only immaterial stand-alone proprietary positions in Nvidia, unlike the positions reflected in 13F filings which were entered into in the ordinary course of business in connection with client swap transactions, that are common in institutional markets," a Cantor spokesperson told CNBC. Cantor declined to answer CNBC's other questions. The Commerce Department, the White House, Howard Lutnick and his sons did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment or detailed questions about the findings. As scrutiny of Huang intensified, Cantor Chairman Brandon Lutnick was publicly praising the chipmaker's leadership. "Nvidia is one of the great companies on the planet, and they have an amazing leadership team," Brandon Lutnick told Fox Business on Wednesday. Trump is standing by Howard Lutnick. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in the commerce secretary. But cracks in the administration's unity emerged Friday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the Departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months.

events.title: Trump bought Nvidia stock as he helped chipmaker with change to export rule
events.summary: President purchased up to $5m of stock before revoking Biden-era rule that limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to China Donald Trump bought Nvidia stock worth millions of dollars as he made decisions on America’s China policy that would benefit the chipmaker, an analysis has found . In May 2025, Trump’s administration rescinded a Biden-era rule designed to prevent the most advanced US-made AI chips from being exported to China. This rule aimed to strengthen the US’s own chip industry and to protect America from what was widely regarded as a national security threat: the possibility that China might develop superior AI. In the days before he rescinded the rule, Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate that he bought between $1m (£760,000) and $5m worth of Nvidia stock – a purchase noted in an analysis by the anti-corruption group DeKleptocracy. He also bought shares in other tech companies, including Apple, Meta and Microsoft. The diffusion rule would have limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to what has been one of its largest markets: China accounted for about a quarter of the company’s sales between 2010 and 2022. Nvidia’s shares rose in value just after Trump announced the rescission of the rule, and after he had bought the stock. In December 2025 Trump said he would allow Nvidia to sell H200 chips to China, a decision that was greenlit by the Department of Commerce in January 2026. This was a controversial move. H200s were one of the company’s most advanced chips – six times better than what was available in China at the time, said experts. The Council on Foreign Relations suggested selling H200s would “supercharge” China’s future AI factories and strengthen the US’s rival. Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate he made at least three purchases of Nvidia shares in the days after announcing this, all of them between $250,001 and $500,000. These trades are among Trump’s larger purchases of Nvidia stock, although he appears to have made dozens of transactions involving the chipmaker’s shares since taking office. DeKleptocracy wrote in its analysis: “While the country debates how a possible Chinese spy may have manipulated White House policy for one AI company, it must grapple with how Trump’s corruption may have motivated him to deliver the entire AI industry’s technology to China.” Get the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning The US – and the global economy – have been grappling with revelations that Jensen Huang , Nvidia’s former chief executive, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang. Reports have suggested this relationship allowed Alice Huang’s company, Megaspeed, to obtain billions of dollars worth of Nvidia’s chips, even as other companies struggled. Trump was twice briefed by US intelligence officials on their conclusions that Alice Huang was a Chinese asset. He did not act on this assessment. Jensen Huang has been described as a close Trump ally and has met the president a number of times. Nvidia made a $25m contribution to Trump’s ballroom in October 2025, with Huang saying he was “delighted to be a part of it”.

events.title: Hassett expected to depart White House
events.summary: National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett is expected to depart his role at the White House in the coming weeks, three people familiar with his plans told Semafor. Hassett has been inquiring about roles outside the administration since well before this month’s midterm elections, some of the people said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who could hold both jobs, and his counselor, David Zervos, are among those being eyed to replace him. Hassett’s plans haven’t been officially announced and, like much in the Trump administration, there’s always the chance they could change. Neither the White House nor the Treasury Department provided comment for this story. President Donald Trump tapped Hassett, who served in the first Trump administration, to return as his top economic adviser nearly two years ago. Since then, Hassett’s served as the face of everything from the economic fallout from the Iran war to the president’s campaign against former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell. Hassett, who was in the running to replace Powell, saw one of his top priorities advance in February, when the president signed an executive order that sought to expand access to retirement plans for workers whose employers don’t provide one. The order, first reported by Semafor , followed Hassett’s longtime advocacy for recreating the government’s Thrift Savings Plan for private-sector workers — but ultimately took a less ambitious approach, creating a website where workers can shop existing plans. Hassett’s expected departure, while not tied to Republicans’ lackluster midterm results, would be the latest in a series of staffing changes hitting the Trump administration in recent weeks. Hassett’s deputy, Ryan Baasch, left the White House at the end of September . More recently, Trump replaced his then-chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration’s strict immigration policies. Roles under Miller have been shifting in recent weeks, as Semafor reported . Multiple people inside and close to the administration say they expect further staffing changes and departures as the year comes to a close. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is currently in the crosshairs amid scrutiny over his handling of export controls on AI chips.

events.title: Who is Anne Jakrajutatip? Here's what to know about the former Miss Universe CEO
events.summary: Anne Jakrajutatip bought Miss Universe in 2022. Josh Brasted/Getty Images Anne Jakrajutatip became the first woman to own Miss Universe in October 2022.  She said she was inspired by Angela Ponce, who was the first trans woman to compete in the pageant. Jakrajutatip ushered in big changes, including allowing all women 18 or older to compete. Anne Jakrajutatip made history when she purchased Miss Universe in October 2022, making her the first woman to own the organization since it began in 1952. Jakrajutatip brought big changes to the pageant, including allowing all women 18 or older to compete. But her time at the top of the world's biggest pageant was frequently shadowed by controversy, and she ultimately stepped down in June 2025 following an investigation into her company, JKN Global, by Thailand's Securities and Exchange Commission. A Bangkok court issued a warrant for Jakrajutatip's arrest in relation to an ongoing fraud case in November 2025. Jakrajutatip hasn't publicly discussed the allegations and did not respond to Business Insider's repeated requests for comment. Her whereabouts remain unknown. Here's what to know about Jakrajutatip. Anne Jakrajutatip was born and raised in Bangkok, where she struggled with her gender identity from an early age. Anne Jakapong Jakrajutatip was born in Bangkok, Thailand. Courtesy of Miss Universe During a January 2023 interview on "The Journal" podcast , Jakrajutatip said she had known she was "trapped in the wrong body" since age 5. Jakrajutatip also told Them in June 2023 that she was bullied as a child and didn't find her voice until she took a public speaking class in high school. "I wanted to have the weapon that is the microphone to express my attitude and exhibit that leadership to everyone," she said. "No more bullies. You cannot do anything harmful to me because I'm clever and smart and I can be successful." Jakrajutatip attended university in Sydney before returning home to take over her parents' video-rental business. Jakrajutatip is the third richest transgender person in the world. Courtesy of Miss Universe Jakrajutatip graduated with a degree in international relations, paying her tuition with money she earned working at a gas station, according to Them. At this point, Jakrajutatip said she knew she was a transgender woman, but she didn't feel comfortable coming out in Thailand. Jakrajutatip turned her parents' store into a content distribution empire. Hector Vivas/Getty Images Jakrajutatip's first major deal was with the BBC, she told The Guardian in 2023. She said she had spotted the documentary "Walking With Dinosaurs" at her parents' store and offered to distribute the BBC series in Thailand. The outlet reported that she sold a million copies and soon began distributing content from India, Japan, the US, and South Korea as well. Jakrajutatip expanded JKN Global as she launched beauty lines and bought TV channels in Thailand. Jakrajutatip counts Oprah Winfrey as her biggest inspiration. Courtesy of Miss Universe Them reported that Jakrajutatip's profile rose in Thailand as she appeared on the country's version of "Shark Tank" and "Project Runway," and she continued to expand her business portfolio by launching drinks and food supplements. Jakrajutatip previously told The Guardian that Oprah Winfrey served as her main source of inspiration as she pursued a career in media. To this day, Winfrey is the only person that Jakrajutatip follows on Instagram. In 2018, Jakrajutatip launched a nonprofit to support transgender people. Two years later, she underwent gender-affirming surgery. Anne Jakrajutatip has two children. LILLIAN SUWANRUMPHA/AFP via Getty Images According to Them, Jakrajutatip underwent surgery in 2020 and became a mother six months later. She had a second child the following year. Jakrajutatip knew she wanted to own Miss Universe after seeing Miss Spain 2018, Angela Ponce, make history. Miss Spain Angela Ponce during the national costume competition at the 2018 Miss Universe pageant. LILLIAN SUWANRUMPHA/AFP via Getty Images Jakrajutatip told Them that she was in the audience when Ponce became the first transgender woman to compete at Miss Universe. "I stood up and applauded for her. I cried, and she also cried on the stage," Jakrajutatip said. "When I turned back, everyone just stood up after me and applauded her big time." "That moment, I thought, 'This is it. This is a pageant I can turn into a platform, and it must be a women's empowerment platform,'" she added. Jakrajutatip bought Miss Universe for $20 million in October 2022. Jakrajutatip with Miss Universe R'Bonney Gabriel. Roy Rochlin/Getty Images for Empire State Realty Trust Jakrajutatip acquired the Miss Universe brand just weeks after the Miss USA organization descended into chaos as contestants claimed the 2022 pageant had been rigged in favor of R'Bonney Gabriel , who went on to win Miss Universe months later. In a statement sent to Business Insider after the announcement, Jakrajutatip said she was proud to take over the organization. "We seek not only to continue its legacy of providing a platform to passionate individuals from diverse backgrounds, cultures, and traditions, but also to evolve the brand for the next generation," she added. During her first Miss Universe as the owner in January 2023, Jakrajutatip told pageant fans that she was ushering in a new era. "From now on it's going to be run by women, owned by a trans woman, for all women around the world," she said. Jakrajutatip's company filed a "business rehabilitation" petition with Thailand's bankruptcy court in 2023. Jakrajutatip with Miss Universe President Paula Shugart (left) and Miss Universe CEO Amy Emmerich (right) during the Miss Universe Extravaganza in Bangkok on November 7, 2022. LILLIAN SUWANRUMPHA/AFP via Getty Images JKN Global had missed a payment on a multimillion-dollar loan in September 2023. The company said in a letter to Thailand's stock exchange president that its financial liquidity management was "not in line with the expected forecast" and that it intended to restructure its debt. After the news broke, Jakrajutatip told Miss Universe fans on Instagram that the pageant was her "first priority in life." "No matter how joyful or painful it's gonna be…. Our universe must go on, must be great and must stay on top as the legendary Beauty Olympics in the World! I will sacrifice and do everything for the great success of OUR UNIVERSE!" she wrote in the post shared on November 9, 2023, which has since been taken down. Jakrajutatip said diverse contestants "can compete, but they can't win" in an October 2023 video that was later leaked to the press. events.title: Retirees sometimes tap savings for one-off expenses. Here’s what advisors say to consider first
events.summary: Withdrawing money from a traditional 401(k) or individual retirement account is not as simple as taking the amount you need, advisors say. There are tax implications to consider that go beyond owing taxes on the money you withdraw. You may be able to strategize how you tap your nest egg to mitigate the potential tax impact. It's also worth considering other ways to cover your unplanned expense. Retirees facing a large expense that's not in their regular household budget may turn to their traditional 401(k) or individual retirement account balances to cover it. While retirement savings may be the easiest place to turn for the money, financial advisors say there are a few things worth considering before making one-off withdrawals. "Be aware of the fact that it's not as simple as just taking out the amount of money that [covers] what you want it for," said certified financial planner Victoria Trumbower, managing member of Trumbower Financial Advisors in Bethesda, Maryland. The firm ranked No. 19 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026. More from CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 Read coverage of CNBC's 2026 Financial Advisor 100 list, including stories featuring ranked firms and their advisors: CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor for 2026 takes a family-office approach CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 FAQ: Who is eligible and how rankings work Roth conversions aren't for everyone. When the 'juice' isn't worth it: Top advisor After Jensen Huang's exit, what top advisors are doing with Nvidia: CNBC poll At the same time, research shows that many retirees aren't even spending their nest egg . About a third still have 100% or more of their initial assets when they reach their mid-80s, according to a May study by the Employee Benefit Research Institute, a nonpartisan research group. "Retirement savings are meant to be spent," said CFP Alex Canellopoulos, director of wealth and a partner with Vista Capital Partners in Portland, Oregon. "A one-time withdrawal isn't necessarily a bad decision, as long as it fits within a sustainable retirement plan." Unplanned withdrawals often go toward debt In 2025, about 15% of 401(k) owners ages 60 to 72 with balances of at least $100,000 who had left their employer made an ad hoc withdrawal from their account, according to Vanguard's How America Retires 2026 report, which analyzed more than 125,000 ex-plan participants. This age group falls between the onset of penalty-free withdrawals — age 59½ — and the threshold for starting required minimum distributions — currently age 73. RMDs are amounts that retirees must withdraw annually from traditional 401(k)s and IRAs. Not all 401(k) plans allow occasional withdrawals from ex- employees — about 43% did in 2025, up from 16% in 2015, the Vanguard study says. If a plan doesn't offer such ad hoc distributions, a former employee who wants to tap that money would have to withdraw or roll over the entire balance. Typically, they roll it over to an IRA and take withdrawals from there. The most common reasons for retirees taking irregular distributions, based on a 2025 Vanguard survey of 8,000 clients noted in the recent report, are paying off debt , with 31% of respondents citing it; covering unforeseen expenses such as medical care and home repairs, noted by 23%; and discretionary spending, with 22% citing it as a reason. Regardless of why you take the money, advisors say a key consideration is the impact on your tax situation. Distributions from a traditional 401(k) or IRA are generally taxed as ordinary income. If you don't have other means to cover the tax bill, you may have to withdraw extra from your retirement account to compensate — which creates a tricky situation. "It's like a double whammy because you have to pay income tax, but you don't have any money to pay income tax , so you've got to withdraw more money to pay the tax, and then you've got to pay taxes" on the extra amount, Trumbower said. For illustration: If you need $50,000 after taxes and assume a combined federal and state income tax rate of 25%, the math says you would need to withdraw about $66,667. That's because the money withdrawn to cover the tax bill is itself taxable. A $66,667 withdrawal taxed at 25% would result in about $16,667 in taxes, leaving $50,000 after tax. "It's going to cost you a lot more than you think," Trumbower said. There may be an undesirable ripple effect A taxable withdrawal from retirement savings can also trigger additional costs elsewhere. For example, if you're receiving Social Security retirement benefits, the added income could cause a larger portion of that money to become taxable. Depending on how much other income you have, 0%, up to 50%, or up to 85% of your Social Security benefits may be subject to federal income tax . A large retirement-account withdrawal can increase that other income and make more of your benefits taxable.
