events.title: Homes with architectural designs that cost just $1 near completion
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts First Corrimal homes with $1 plans from NSW Pattern Book nearing completion Topic: Housing Construction Industry The four row homes in Corrimal will be the first in the state built using a Pattern Book design. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) A set of row homes in Corrimal will be the first of the NSW government's $1 pattern book designs to be completed. The government has sold more than 25,000 designs from the book, with 22 being built. The opposition says the low numbers show the scheme is a "failure", but builders say it is working. Construction costs might be soaring across the country but on a building site at Corrimal, north of Wollongong, no-one is complaining about the price that was paid for an architect's plans. Builder James Forrest and his team are putting the finishing touches on four new row homes, following designs purchased for just $1 from a pattern book launched by the NSW government in July 2025 . If he meets the November deadline, he will be the first in the state to complete a home under the scheme. Mr Forrest said using the design saved him an extraordinary amount of time, because it included planning controls and a 10-day complying development pathway. "All the rigours of the design work have been done already. It's just matching it to the site, and it's approved," he said. James Forrest aims to complete the project by the end of November. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) The Corrimal development used one of eight low-rise designs available for the nominal fee of $1 in the first six months of the scheme. The program was sold as a way to get more high-quality housing built faster and cheaper. So far, 25,000 designs have been purchased and 22 are being built. Harry Catterns says the designs can be adjusted to different sizes and configurations. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Architect Harry Catterns co-owns the company that designed the row homes. "We thought it would be a more helpful contribution to the housing mix if we could provide small house-like dwellings with their own front door, their own garden, rather than the typical apartment you might see on a site like this," he said. Mr Catterns said the design could be adjusted to one, two or three bedrooms and offered different bathroom configurations. All are two-storey, with balconies and sliding glass doors. The builder is hoping to have the homes ready for tenants, and owners, by Christmas. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Mr Forrest said he hoped to have three homes occupied by Christmas, and the fourth, larger home on the market shortly after. "These will be cheaper for buyers than ordinary builds for a number of reasons, but primarily because of its speed and cost-saving," he said. Mr Forrest estimated the Corrimal build was around $600,000 cheaper than an ordinary project. The Pattern Book now offers 17 designs after nine mid-rise options were added in November 2025. They cost up to $2,500 and do not have the same planning controls or fast-track as the low-rise designs. Tom Forrest says the scheme has been a "dud". ( ABC News: Sam Foster ) The Urban Taskforce's Tom Forrest said the mid-rise developments would still need final development approval from councils and faced the same planning timelines as a typical build. "Nobody is building and it hasn't improved the number of new dwellings brought to the market," he said. So far, the entire Housing Pattern Book program has translated to fewer than 60 applications, with 45 of them approved. The Housing Industry Association does not agree, with NSW chief executive Brad Armitage saying it was working for builders. "When you take those [economic] factors into consideration, so many approvals with this relatively new pattern book is actually quite strong," he said. Brad Armitage says the pattern book is a success. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) The NSW opposition has promised to overhaul the scheme with new designs and review planning controls if it is elected next March, describing it as a "failure". "We want to see a lot more builders like this one at Corrimal rolling out a lot more housing as part of the pattern book and clearly it's not working at the moment," Shadow Housing Minister Chris Rath said. "We need to make it much easier to actually build the pattern book designs. "It's just far too slow and far too restrictive." NSW Planning Minister Paul Scully defended the outcome. "We're seeing challenging economic conditions for new home building, higher interest rates, higher building costs, shortages of skilled labour," he said.

events.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its 'dots' AI agents to make purchases for users
events.summary: OpenAI announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its "dots" AI agents to make purchases on behalf of users. ChatGPT Wallet will initially be available to OpenAI's Pro subscribers in the U.S. who are over 18 years old. OpenAI built ChatGPT Wallet in partnership with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, and it allows those customers to maintain their existing credit card rewards and protections. OpenAI on Friday announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its "dots" artificial intelligence agents to make purchases on behalf of users. The company built ChatGPT Wallet in partnership with American Express , Mastercard and Visa , and it allows cardholders to maintain their existing credit card rewards and protections. Eligible users enter their card information once, prompt their dot to find items to buy and approve each purchase with a security check. OpenAI said its dots agents will never actually access a user's card details. Instead, their payment networks will provide the dot with a "payment token," which contains a scoped card number, security code and expiration date that is specific to a given transaction. "Our goal here is to really focus on merchants and our network partners and start building out a really great foundation that's safe and easy to use," Chaya Nayak, who leads product for monetization and payments at OpenAI, told CNBC in an interview. ChatGPT Wallet comes as a growing number of consumers are exploring how to use personal AI agents to manage their calendars, book travel and complete other day-to-day tasks. OpenAI introduced the dots agents during its annual developer conference in late September, shortly after Meta's Muse offering topped the App Store charts . Purchases made through ChatGPT Wallet could eventually kick-start a new revenue stream for OpenAI, but the company said it is not taking a cut of transactions to start. With the initial launch, OpenAI is working to build relationships with merchants and position itself as a serious platform for shoppers, especially as vendors are beginning to experiment with personal agents. OpenAI has pushed deeper into AI-enabled commerce over the last year, but some of its early attempts failed to take off. The company introduced an " Instant Checkout " feature last fall, which it quickly pivoted away from. By March, it had rolled out a revamped shopping experience that aimed to make it easier for users to find and compare products. Nayak said ChatGPT Wallet builds on OpenAI's previous efforts, particularly around product discovery. "We think that this is the next step, where if someone found something they're really excited to buy, then we want to be able to get them through to that endpoint," she said. Nvidia live updates: CEO Jensen Huang resigns, Colette Kress named interim chief CoreWeave CEO Intrator tells CNBC he has canceled his planned share sale program Meta head of infrastructure will leave and be succeeded by former AWS cloud exec Amazon’s Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses ChatGPT Wallet is initially available to OpenAI's Pro subscribers in the U.S. who are over 18 years old. The limited rollout is intentional, and the "right approach to make sure things are working," said Luke Gebb , executive vice president and global head of innovation at Amex. OpenAI's ChatGPT chatbot supports more than 1.2 billion weekly active users and nearly 100 million paying users as of the end of the third quarter. With such a broad user base, Gebb said OpenAI can decide to "turn up the volume" on ChatGPT Wallet when it wants to. "It just makes sense to watch it, start it in a contained environment, and then keep rolling from there," Gebb told CNBC in an interview. Merchants and vendors are still reckoning with the rise of personal AI agents, and some companies have opted to forgo them entirely. United Airlines said Wednesday that it will block agents from accessing its systems to book tickets, and Amazon prevents the agents from purchasing products on its platform. OpenAI said Friday that agentic commerce is still in its "early days," and it published tools and guidance alongside its ChatGPT Wallet announcement to help businesses start to navigate the transition. The company explained how merchants can make sure their websites aren't inadvertently blocking OpenAI's agents, for instance. "It's going to take time for the ecosystem to build the right infrastructure to be able to make this experience really amazing and seamless across all of their sites," Nayak said. "Really, who we are speaking to here is the networks and the merchants." WATCH: OpenAI raises $15B at a $1.25T valuation, sources say. What it means for the IPO

events.title: Nvidia approached Arm CEO Rene Haas to succeed Jensen Huang, report says
events.summary: Rene Haas spent seven formative years at Nvidia, rising to vice-president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining the British chipmaker as its CEO in 2013. Nvidia’s board has approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang, the Financial Times reported on Nov 13, citing people familiar with the matter. Huang stepped down on Nov 12 after revelations of extramarital affairs , including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, plunging the chipmaker into crisis and sending shockwaves across an AI industry he helped bankroll. Haas’ name has been making the rounds among analysts since Huang’s exit. He spent seven formative years at Nvidia, rising to vice-president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He is among several candidates being considered and there is no guarantee he will be offered the job or accept it, the FT reported. Nvidia’s finance chief Colette Kress is currently interim CEO. Arm declined to comment, while Nvidia did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Reuters could not independently verify the report. Haas became Arm CEO in 2022, overseeing the company’s Nasdaq listing in 2023. Arm designs processor architectures and licences them to other companies that develop chip designs. Historically its strength has been in mobile phones and it is expanding into computers. Arm’s US-listed shares pared losses after the report and were down more than 5%. Nvidia’s shares were down over 3%. Some analysts expect the next CEO to break from Huang’s three-decade reign as the hands-on “chief conductor” who personally steered engineering roadmaps, geopolitical negotiations over China exports and massive investments across the AI ecosystem. A potential shift toward a more institutional leadership structure would come as Nvidia faces heightened regulatory scrutiny and growing consensus among US lawmakers to further restrict the company’s chip exports to China. Insiders and tech titans in the running Analysts view Kress as a steady financial authority, while veteran engineer Ian Buck is seen as a top candidate after leading development of CUDA, the software platform that powers Nvidia’s AI chips. Apart from Haas, external names discussed by analysts include AMD chief Lisa Su, who has navigated the key China market, and Micron chief Sanjay Mehrotra, whose memory chips power Nvidia servers. Other candidates cited by industry watchers include Marvell head Matt Murphy and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who oversaw the iPhone maker’s in-house silicon development. Former Apple chief Tim Cook was floated by US President Donald Trump , as Nvidia’s board evaluates whether to prioritise financial continuity, deep technical expertise, or experience running a global tech heavyweight. events.title: Johnny Depp has reportedly earned $650 million throughout his career. Here's how he makes and spends his money.
events.summary: Johnny Depp. Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images Depp has earned over $650 million in his career, including paydays averaging $20 million per film. He's also been known to spend money on things like an island and $30,000 a month on wine. He reportedly took a smaller payday for his latest movie, "Ebenezer," in exchange for back-end profits. Johnny Depp has been a superstar since the 1980s, and he's been paid like one. From the "Pirates of the Caribbean" franchise, which paid him tens of millions, to a seven-figure deal with Dior, Depp has used his paydays to live a lavish life: He once bought an island in the Bahamas and spent $30,000 a month on wine. Here's a breakdown of Depp's wealth and how he's reportedly spent it. Over a 13-year span, Depp earned $650 million, according to his former management firm. Getty/Atsushi Tomura After finding fame on the hit late-1980s TV series "21 Jump Street," Depp became a bona fide movie star thanks to performances in offbeat Tim Burton movies like"Edward Scissorhands" and "Ed Wood." Depp was paid handsomely for his efforts. According to his former management firm, The Management Group, Depp earned over $650 million in the 13 years they worked together from 1999 to 2016. A large portion of that is paydays he received playing Captain Jack Sparrow in the "Pirates of the Caribbean" franchise. After the success of "Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl," Depp started routinely banking $20 million per movie. Disney The first "Pirates" movie, "Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl," made over $650 million at the box-office worldwide. With that, Depp's asking price soared. On top of taking in $20 million pre-picture in the franchise, he got around 20% of the back end per picture, according to The Hollywood Reporter. So not only was he paid upfront, but Depp was cut another check after the movie broke even. Depp earned more than $40 million on each "Pirates" movie thanks to his back-end deal. Johnny Depp and Captain Jack Sparrow in Disney's "Pirates of the Caribbean." Disney Thanks to the success of the "Pirates" sequels, including 2006's "Dead Man's Chest," which earned over $1 billion worldwide , Depp's earnings from the movies became astronomical. The actor brought in north of $40 million per sequel on the back end of the movies alone, per THR. Again, that doesn't count the $20 million base pay for each. But not all of that went directly into Depp's pocket. His agents got 10%, managers took 5%, and there are deductions for taxes and expenses. However, the paydays only got bigger from there. The back-end deal for "Alice in Wonderland" was even larger: $55 million. Walt Disney Studios Taking a pause from playing Captain Jack in 2010, Depp teamed up with Tim Burton again for the latest adaptation of "Alice in Wonderland." On top of his $20 million base, THR reported that he took in $55 million on the back end thanks to the movie's successful box office run, which brought in over $1 billion . Thanks to the "Pirates" movies, "Alice in Wonderland," and 2014's "Into the Woods," in which he played the Big Bad Wolf, all getting prime home entertainment releases and cable play, Depp took in $25.7 million in residuals in 2016 and 2017 thanks to his profit participation deals on those movies. In 2016, he even landed on Forbes' list of highest-paid celebrities . He reportedly took in $48 million that year. Depp has earned millions as the face of Dior's Sauvage fragrance for men. Dior advertisement featuring Johnny Depp in Milan, Italy in October 2021. Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto/Getty The actor has been the face of Sauvage for years. Depp was reportedly taking in $3 million to $5 million in the deal . In August 2022, Business Insider confirmed that Depp signed a seven-figure, multi-year deal with Dior. Depp was paid $16 million for just one scene in "Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald." Johnny Depp as Gellert Grindelwald in "Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald." Warner Bros. Depp was asked to step down from "Fantastic Beasts 3" days after losing a libel case against the publishers of the UK newspaper, The Sun, over a 2018 article that described him as a "wife beater." However, because he had a "pay-or-play" deal on the movie , meaning he would get paid regardless of if he appeared in it, he was paid his $16 million fee. Depp only filmed one scene as Grindelwald. Mads Mikkelsen took over the role for 2022's "Fantastic Beasts: The Secrets of Dumbledore." Depp bought an island in the Bahamas for $3.6 million. BELGRADE, SERBIA - OCTOBER 19: US actor Johnny Depp attends the promotion of the animated series "Puffins" in Belgrade on October 19, 2021. Srdjan Stevanovic/Getty Images The actor first set eyes on the 45-acre island located 60 miles from Nassau in 2003 while filming "Curse of the Black Pearl." He purchased Little Hall's Pond Cay for $3.6 million in 2004. He's since outfitted the island with solar-powered buildings, including a house with stunning 360-degree views . He spent $5 million to shoot the ashes of his friend, author Hunter S. Thompson, out of a cannon. (L-R) Hunter S. Thompson and Johnny Depp in 1997. Rose Hartman/Archive Photos/Getty Depp befriended famous gonzo journalist Thompson around the time he played him in the 1998 movie "Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas." They stayed friends until Thompson's death in 2005. Thompson had spoken about wanting his funeral to be an extravagant affair involving his ashes shot out of a cannon and a red, white, and blue fireworks show to end the event. Depp said he spent $5 million to fulfill his friend's wishes. Depp had $2 million in monthly bills, including $100,000 a month for addiction issues. Actor Johnny Depp appears in court during his defamation case against ex-wife Amber Heard at the Fairfax County Circuit Court on April 14, 2022. Shawn Thew/Pool via REUTERS Depp had huge daily spending habits to live a lavish lifestyle, which led to him spending $2 million a month on bills, according to his former management firm. Rowling for $27 million ) $30,000 monthly for wine (Although Depp told Rolling Stone this was a conservative estimate.  "It's insulting to say that I spent $30,000 on wine," he said. "Because it was far more.") $100,000 a month for a doctor to treat his addiction issues Depp commented on his spending in 2017, telling the Wall Street Journal , "It's my money." "If I want to buy 15,000 cotton balls a day, it's my thing," he said. events.title: At least 10 killed in Guinea clashes over gold mining ban
events.summary: Guinea banned artisanal gold mining in Siguiri on November 2 due to environmental degradation, causing mass exodus. At least 10 people have been killed and 13 others injured in clashes in northeastern Guinea between protesters and security forces enforcing restrictions on gold mining, the government said. The country’s Ministry of Territorial ‌Administration said late on Thursday that clashes occurred on Wednesday, when defence and security forces were verifying the implementation of a ban on artisanal gold mining. list 1 of 4 Can Nigeria’s drone industry deliver Africa’s defence sovereignty? list 2 of 4 ‘Economic incentives are limited’: What does Russia really offer Africa? list 3 of 4 Ebola death toll in DR Congo passes 5,000 list 4 of 4 Why Guinea-Bissau halted a controversial hepatitis vaccine trial for babies The violence erupted in Balato, in the Siguiri region, during a patrol against illegal and unregulated gold mining. Protesters erected barricades blocking the patrol, as the situation escalated into clashes and exchanges of gunfire, the statement said. It did not specify who opened fire. Ten people, including five foreign nationals whose identities have yet to be established, were among those killed. The injured included civilians and members of the security forces. Two pick-up trucks and a security forces truck were burned, while a firearm and a motorcycle were taken by protesters, the ministry said. Judicial authorities have been tasked with establishing what triggered the violence and determining responsibility. Guinea banned artisanal gold mining in Siguiri on November 2. Authorities said artisanal miners’ failure to comply with regulations had led to environmental degradation, including pollution of agricultural land, rivers and vegetation ⁠cover. Neighbouring Mali said last week that around 100,000 people had arrived in the capital Bamako and nearly 60,000 more in the border town of Kouremale after they ⁠were forced to leave Guinea when the ban on artisanal mining was announced. Burkina Faso said on Friday it had repatriated 45,406 of ⁠its citizens, who were forced to leave Guinea as a result of the ban. Artisanal mining, driven by growing demand ⁠for metals and rising prices, is a common activity across much of West Africa. Artisanal and small-scale gold mining supports the livelihoods of more than 300,000 people in Guinea, according to the UN Environment Programme. But the Guinean government said the restrictions aim to curb environmental damage from mining, including the destruction of farmland by heavy machinery and the pollution of rivers by chemicals. Authorities arrested more than 1,200 people suspected of illegal gold mining in the Siguiri region earlier this month, according to authorities, with the first mass trials opened this week.

events.title: Noelia Voigt was the first Miss USA to give up her crown. Here's what to know about the pageant queen.
events.summary: Noelia Voigt was the first Miss USA to ever relinquish her crown. Courtesy of Miss USA Noelia Voigt won the Miss USA pageant in September 2023. She became the first woman to relinquish her crown when she resigned in May 2024. Voigt has returned to the Miss USA organization since Thom Brodeur replaced Laylah Rose as CEO. Noelia Voigt spent seven years working to become Miss USA . She won first runner-up three times at state pageants before making it to the national stage, where she took the crown in 2023. That made it even more shocking when Voigt became the first Miss USA in the pageant's history to relinquish her title, giving up the crown just months before her reign was set to end in 2024. This is her story. Noelia Voigt began watching pageants at an early age, but her mother didn't allow her to compete as a child. Noelia Voigt of Utah. Courtesy of Miss USA Voigt was born and raised in Sarasota, Florida. Her mother, Jackeline Voigt, is from Venezuela, and her father, Jack Voigt, is an American former Major League Baseball player. He played for the Baltimore Orioles, Oakland A's, Texas Rangers, and Milwaukee Brewers during his 14-year career, according to his website . After winning Miss USA in September 2023, Voigt told Business Insider that she grew up watching pageants with her mother. "My mom is from Venezuela, and over there, pageants are their Super Bowl and Olympics — it's a huge deal," Voigt said. "So I had always wanted to do pageants from a really young age." Voigt said she began asking to compete in pageants before she was 10, but her mother was "really protective" and made her wait. "Depending on the pageant that you're entering at that age, it can be potentially damaging to a young girl if they don't end up winning," Voigt said. "Then they have this negative association with it, and they think that it has something to do with them." "My mom didn't want that for me," she added. "So she waited until I was old enough to understand that, if I didn't win, it's not a reflection of me or who I am." Voigt won her first pageant when she was 16 years old. Vogit volunteering with Smile Train as Miss USA 2023. Courtesy of Miss USA Voigt was named Miss Sarasota Teen USA in 2017. She went on to compete at Miss Florida Teen USA that year and placed first runner-up. Although she found early success in the world of pageants, Voigt said her friends made fun of her newfound passion . "I was really hurt and confused as to why people I thought were my friends were making fun of me for doing something that I was really excited about and that I was doing good things with," Voigt told Business Insider. "At first, it really did sting. But it was clear to me that it was an attempt to steal the joy I had from this accomplishment." Voigt made anti-bullying part of her platform and authored a children's book on the topic called "Maddie the BRAVE." Voigt credited pageants with helping her get out of an abusive relationship in high school. Courtesy of Miss USA Voigt told Business Insider that competing in pageants was an eye-opening experience as she navigated an abusive relationship during her teenage years. "When you're in pageants, you're surrounded by women who are really uplifting of one another," she said. "They all have a really good sense of self-respect, and they know their worth, and a lot of times if you find yourself in an abusive relationship, that might be something that is lacking." "Once I broke into the pageant world and started to get involved in a lot of community service, I started to realize that anybody that was toxic in my life was simply holding me back," she added. "Pageants absolutely helped me realize my worth." Voigt moved to Alabama for school and continued to compete in pageants. Miss USA 2023. Courtesy of Miss Universe Voigt competed in Miss Alabama 2022 and Miss Alabama 2023 , placing first runner-up in both competitions. "A lot of people ask me if it hurt that I kept getting first runner-up, and I just told them the honest truth — that I was really proud of myself for getting that placement," Voigt told Business Insider after her win. "I always felt very honored that the judges still felt I could do the job if something happened and I needed to step in." "Every year that I hadn't won the pageant, it gave me another year of opportunity to do good things for my community, so I really wouldn't have traded it for anything," she added. events.title: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models — uh oh, Jensen!
events.summary: The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims. The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service. While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang. U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff. Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips. White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination. That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch’s data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025. However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed. “If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn’t make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want,” Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer. Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the U.S. and S i ngaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai. In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a “ China problem ” because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law. It detailed Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang’s companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing U.S. chips. Ironically, short-seller Culper’s bet against Nvidia wasn’t driven by the expectation of a U.S. government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government’s response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry. If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they haven’t been cleared for import. Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on U.S.-China technology policy, said he doesn’t buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of U.S. goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips. events.title: ‘People are chucking stuff like gold and Bitcoin’ as rising inflation leads investors to seek yield
events.summary: Bitcoin’s escape from the trenches didn’t last long. The cryptocurrency fell more than 4% on Friday to $68,500, wiping out gains built over the past three months and casting doubt on whether its bear market was ever really over. The asset also faces weaker investor appetite, according to crypto analytics provider CryptoQuant. The firm’s demand indicator recorded its weakest reading since December 2023, while Bitcoin exchange-traded funds became net sellers again. The recent downturn has also extended to other parts of the crypto market. That includes Tether’s USDT, the largest cryptocurrency pegged to the U.S. dollar, whose total value shrank by $7.7 billion over the past two months, according to CryptoQuant, a sign that less cash is available in crypto markets. This time around, inflation has been the main culprit. Tuesday’s Consumer Price Index report showed prices rose 0.4% in October, more than economists expected. Even stripping out food and energy, inflation ran hotter than forecast. Traders now overwhelmingly expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point in December, with some betting on an even bigger increase. “Because these are non-yielding assets, and we expect inflation to rise… people are chucking stuff like gold and Bitcoin to find… government bonds that are going up, providing you [with] income,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at financial technology company IG Group, told Fortune . Bitcoin isn’t alone in its retreat. Gold traded near $3,900 an ounce on Friday, well below its January peak of about $5,600, according to financial data provider Trading Economics. Prices have fallen roughly 5% over the past month and nearly 5% from a year ago. Bitcoin’s bad year Friday’s drop dealt a fresh blow to Bitcoin investors, who had only recently found their footing after months of losses. After Bitcoin hit $58,000 in June, optimism returned in August when the U.S. Treasury announced plans to expand its bond buybacks . The announcement helped spark a rally that carried Bitcoin to $86,000 in September. Since then, though, it has been sliding again. Recent political news has also made Bitcoin’s recovery an uphill battle, though it held its ground until Friday. The midterm elections handed Democrats control of Congress, a setback for a crypto industry that has leaned on Republican allies to advance favorable legislation. Still, Bitcoin initially took the results in stride. That was largely because investors had seen the outcome coming , according to Stephen Coltman, head of macro at crypto asset manager 21Shares. “The midterm results weren’t a surprise, and they don’t change the regulatory interpretations as they stand today… We at least have some regulatory stability for two years,” he said. Inflation and politics aren’t the only forces shaping Bitcoin’s outlook. Analysts say the cryptocurrency is also caught up in the AI boom, which is competing for investors’ money while helping keep the economy strong enough for interest rates to stay high.  Heavy borrowing and spending on AI have created what 21Shares calls an “AI black hole,” drawing money toward the sector and away from assets like Bitcoin and gold. But Bitcoin remains “joined at the hip” with tech stocks, according to Beauchamp. That leaves it in an awkward position: It faces competition for investment dollars when enthusiasm for AI runs high, yet can get dragged down when that enthusiasm fades. The boom also complicates the outlook for interest rates. In Coltman’s view, AI spending is helping prop up an otherwise weak economy, giving the Fed room to keep fighting inflation with higher rates. If rising borrowing costs force AI companies to rein in spending, the economy could weaken enough to push the Fed to change course, potentially giving Bitcoin some breathing room. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
events.summary: Watch: What we know so far about the Microsoft outage Published 13 November 2026, 07:12 GMT A major Microsoft outage has impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world. Services including Teams, Outlook and AI software Copilot, are being restored almost 24 hours since issues first surfaced. Microsoft said the outage was not a cyber-security incident and was caused by a technical issue. It has apologised for the disruption. Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong. Schools, GPs and businesses hit by global Microsoft outage as company scrambles to solve issue Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries. From late on Thursday, customers reported varying levels of access - many were unable to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps. But some users were able to use Teams, messaging and online meeting functions without issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America. The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues". In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels". The company attributed the ongoing outage to an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade. "We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," it said on Friday. Will emails affected by the outage ever arrive? Although services are beginning to resume, Microsoft has warned of continued "intermittent access issues", meaning some users will still struggle to load their inboxes and could experience "delayed email delivery". In other words, it is not quite safe to assume every email you send is going to arrive in its intended recipient's inbox right away. Earlier, Microsoft said it would be extending the "timeout window" to 48 hours "to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up". The email timeout window refers to the amount of time Outlook will wait to receive an email. When they do show up, the timestamp will be when they were delivered rather than when they were sent. Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time. Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues. "What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said. "The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs. "One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in. "You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit." The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online. Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time". He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal. Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences. "Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is. "Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said. In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services." How many people have been affected? More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed. Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services. Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected.

events.title: Nvidia CEO’s exit marks pivotal moment for African AI
events.summary: Alexis’s view Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia could prove to be a turning point in the rollout of AI in Africa. The technology offers the potential to turbocharge economies across the continent, but chips form the backbone of this revolution. And, as our San Francisco Bureau Chief Reed Albergotti put it, “ Huang was Nvidia’s one-man, long-term moat .” Without Huang’s singular vision, there’s uncertainty. The questions swirling in the wake of his exit are a reminder that the development of African compute still relies on hardware and software supplied by US companies. Huang’s resignation raises questions, for example, about the US chipmaker’s relationship with Cassava Technologies: Nvidia last year became an investor in the pan-African digital infrastructure company, which it supplies with chips. The partnership is central to Cassava’s push to expand services in the more than 30 African countries in which it operates. Nvidia’s financial commitment and supply of hardware offered an opportunity for African companies to access the compute needed to train and run their own AI models. If Huang’s successor takes a different approach, the Cassava partnership may not be replicated elsewhere on the continent, limiting the access African firms have to cutting-edge technology. The implications extend to the public sector, too. Only last month, the World Bank named Nvidia and Cassava as partners in an initiative aimed at expanding digital access in Africa to improve services and create jobs. Any change in Nvidia’s strategy would, in the long term, have the biggest implications for South Africa. The continent’s largest economy is home to about 40% of its roughly 160 data centers. So next week’s visit by South African President Cyril Ramaphosa to the US is well-timed. Ramaphosa, who will speak at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event , will be accompanied by a delegation that includes his ministers for finance, trade, and energy. He plans to meet tech executives, researchers, and investors during his trip, which will focus on AI infrastructure. Ramaphosa’s team has described it as an attempt to position South Africa as a “ competitive AI hub ” on the continent — but it’s shaping up to be a first peek at Silicon Valley after the departure of one of its central figures. Notable The proliferation of data centers across Africa is creating new pressure on the continent’s resources, reported Aaliyah Vayez for Al Jazeera.

events.title: Microsoft apologizes for massive outage that caused chaos for businesses
events.summary: Microsoft 365 is suffering an outage affecting services including Outlook and Teams. Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Microsoft's 365 outage entered a second day, affecting services like Teams and Outlook. Microsoft says its services are recovering. The outage disrupted governments, businesses, airlines, and some AI tools. Microsoft has apologized for a massive outage that dragged into a second day and disrupted access to email, Teams, Copilot, and other Microsoft 365 tools. The company said late Friday morning that services were recovering and stabilizing. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," the company said in an X post. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously." The cause of the outage, which disrupted businesses around the world, was "technical" and "not related to cyber or AI / agents," Microsoft added. The company said it has addressed the underlying issue, which stemmed from an earlier network upgrade, and is continuing to restore services. It did not provide a timeline for a full recovery. What happened? Microsoft first flagged the outage on Thursday around midday ET, writing in an X post that users in the Americas were having trouble accessing Exchange Online mailboxes. In a follow-up post, it said the issue could affect users "in any region." Later on Thursday, Microsoft said on X that some of its infrastructure was under elevated load across multiple regions. It said the strain was not caused by an increase in customer traffic, but because a number of servers had unexpectedly become unavailable. By Friday morning, Microsoft's public service status page was still showing "service degradation" for both Microsoft 365 business customers and consumer products. It also had a knock-on effect on some AI tools . Anthropic and OpenAI said in status update pages that their connectors to Microsoft 365 tools had been disrupted. Anthropic said late Friday morning that it was seeing some recovery, but "Microsoft's incident remains open, so errors may return." What was the impact? The outage caused significant disruption for businesses, with many workers unable to use systems such as email or Teams. Downdetector recorded more than 130,000 reports of Outlook problems in the US at the outage's peak on Thursday. That figure reflects user reports, not a confirmed count of affected people or businesses. Other Microsoft services were affected too. It said in its service advisory that the disruption could affect Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, Microsoft Defender, Intune, Power BI, and other Microsoft 365 products that rely on Exchange Online. Reuters reported on Thursday that the US House of Representatives said the outage had affected its users, while electric-truck maker Workhorse Group postponed its quarterly earnings call because of the disruption. Air India said in a Thursday X post that it had rerouted email services, while IndiGo said in an X post on Friday that its email support channel was disrupted. Both airlines said their flight operations were unaffected. AP also reported that government agencies in Singapore, the Philippines, and Japan had reported knock-on effects. Is this unusual? Microsoft and other Big Tech companies have been here before. This outage, however, is unusually long. It lasted more than 22 hours — longer than a major Microsoft 365 disruption in June 2022, which took 16 hours and 27 minutes to recover from, according to a Microsoft service alert , potentially making it the company's longest 365 outage ever. Microsoft also suffered a separate outage for Azure, its cloud service, on September 30 and October 1, affecting customers across several regions. Microsoft said it rolled back a change after some customers had trouble using its cloud networking services. Other cloud providers have faced similar problems. Google said a global Google Cloud and Workspace outage in June 2025 lasted three hours. Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud computing arm, also had a major disruption in Northern Virginia in October 2025. It said it fixed the initial problem in about two and a half hours, though some services took longer to return to normal. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Microsoft apologizes for massive outage that took down Outlook and other 365 services
events.summary: A Microsoft outage on Thursday and Friday affected users of services like Outlook, Teams and 365. The company apologized for the lengthy delay and said it did not suspect malicious activity. Microsoft said it was seeing "encouraging recovery progress" and that email delivery performance was improving. Microsoft issued an apology Friday for a wide-ranging outage that shut down Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products, as the company worked to restore service nearly 24 hours after connectivity problems began. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously," a Microsoft spokesperson said Friday. "We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services." In a statement, Microsoft said the connectivity disruption stemmed from "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade." The software giant said the underlying cause of the outage had been addressed and that they were still working to restore services to some customers. Engineers scrambled to solve connectivity problems that began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday. Email and calendar service Outlook, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, were largely down during the morning hours in the U.S. on Friday and throughout the Asian and European business days. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products were also hit. Users began to regain access to email and other services Friday morning. Nvidia live updates: CEO Jensen Huang resigns, Colette Kress named interim chief CoreWeave CEO Intrator tells CNBC he has canceled his planned share sale program Meta head of infrastructure will leave and be succeeded by former AWS cloud exec Amazon’s Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses In an update around 10:30 a.m. ET, Microsoft noted "encouraging recovery progress" and said that "service availability and email delivery performance [was] improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure" as Outlook and other Microsoft 365 tools began to come back online. In an earlier update Friday morning, Microsoft said that email queues were "approaching normal levels," but that intermittent issues were expected as recovery efforts continue. It had previously given updates by region, with Asia Pacific services among the first to start normalizing. Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online gradually stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages. Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health. The company said it would issue a full report once its assessment of the outage was complete. The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said. Microsoft shares traded largely flat Friday. Governments and businesses review impact Governments and businesses across the U.S., Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption. The U.K.'s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls "may be subject to long waits" as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X. Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage. U.S. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told CNBC's "The Exchange" that he asked for a briefing on the outage. Gottheimer worked at Microsoft prior to serving in Congress. "Is there something that went on that's nefarious here, or is this just something else? These outages occur in a lot of the companies, but the size of it and the length of it and the timing of it," Gottheimer said. Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected.

events.title: Nobody wants to run against Hakeem Jeffries for speaker
events.summary: The movement to prevent House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) from becoming speaker is struggling to get off the ground due to a fatal flaw: Nobody else wants the job. Why it matters: Despite the phone calls and online petitions, the demands from progressive holdouts, Jeffries' ascent has become a self-fulfilling prophecy. The House Democrats most often floated as potential challengers don't appear to be interested: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) told Axios on Thursday his "dream job" is to chair the House Judiciary Committee. "I am not a candidate for speaker in any way. ... I am supporting Hakeem and voting for Hakeem," said Raskin. Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) has privately told colleagues she doesn't want the role despite an online movement seeking to draft her, according to multiple House Democrats who have spoken directly with her. "Congresswoman Pressley is in active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment, and deliver for the people," spokesperson Ricardo Sanchez said in a statement to Axios. "She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership." "He's the only one running," Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.) told Axios on Thursday when asked if she plans to vote for Jeffries as speaker. Said Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.): "I am really encouraging our leadership to make it easy for me to vote for the one person that's running. But as of right now, there's ... no one else that has put their name forward." "As far as I've heard, Jeffries is the only person running," said Rep.-elect Randy Villegas (D-Calif.). Jeffries said in a NY1 interview : "Someone could always emerge in the next week or so, but right now there are no declared challengers, no indication that anyone may put themselves forward." The intrigue: For once it's the Senate, not the House, providing all the drama on Capitol Hill. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) launched his bid to replace Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Thursday night. Yes, but: The progressive grassroots have continued this week to swamp sitting and incoming House Democrats with calls and emails urging them to oppose Jeffries, according to lawmakers and aides. Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) told Axios he has gotten an "avalanche of messages." Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) said she is getting "hundreds" of calls "every day" urging her to oppose Jeffries. A senior House Democrat who is supporting Jeffries told Axios the callers into their office have suggested "like 10" different members as possible alternatives. Jeffries has pushed back on Axios' reporting that members are being flooded with calls, saying in his NY1 interview: "There's no indication that members of Congress have been overwhelmed by any calls." State of play: Jeffries has begun meeting with skeptics ahead of House Democrats' Nov. 18 leadership elections. He is expected to easily win the nomination for speaker, determined by a simple majority vote of the caucus. The real question is whether any House Democrats will oppose him on the House floor on Jan. 3 and deny him the unanimous support he has enjoyed from his caucus since becoming leader in 2022. "We're going to continue to talk to every single member of the House Democratic caucus, both current members and incoming members, about what we all can do together for the American people," Jeffries told reporters at a press conference on Thursday. The Democratic leader said he is "confident that we're on a positive trajectory" but takes "nothing for granted." Between the lines: Several Democratic House members and members-elect predicted that, given the grassroots pressure bearing down on progressives right now, at least a handful are likely to openly oppose him. What they're saying: Leonard told Axios he sat down with Jeffries on Wednesday and shared what he has heard from callers, including "that the Democratic establishment brand is in the toilet and that the leader's name is synonymous with the Democratic establishment." Ramirez said she has "begun conversations" with Jeffries and intends to "have more next week." Asked if Jeffries has met with the Jeffries-skeptic "Bloc" of incoming progressives, she said: "It is my understanding that that they're scheduling time to meet with them." Reps.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.) and LaKesha Womack (D-N.C.) said Jeffries met Wednesday with members of the North Carolina delegation, many of whom are holdouts in the speaker election. "We're still having conversations, we're still listening ... at the end of the day, we're going to all sit together, we're going to listen to everything and we're going to move forward like that," said Ojeda. The bottom line: "I mean, right now, I don't even know if there's anybody that's stepping up against him," Ojeda added.

events.title: Eisenkot slams Netanyahu’s ‘racist’ campaign against Palestinian Israelis
events.summary: Prime ministerial hopeful calls attempts to marginalise and smear Palestinian citizens of Israel ‘an anti-state act’. Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot has accused caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of fuelling a “racist and violent” campaign against Palestinian citizens of Israel during the elections. Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming Israel’s new government , posted a lengthy social media update on recent developments in Israel on Friday. list 1 of 3 Can Netanyahu launch a strike on Iran before he leaves? list 2 of 3 Will Democrats try to strip US-Israel initiative from Pentagon funding? list 3 of 3 UK accused of ‘silencing’ pro-Palestine voices through entry bans “Arab citizens of Israel make up 21 percent of the total population. Since the start of the election campaign, they have faced a racist and violent campaign of delegitimisation fuelled by the outgoing prime minister and his circle for political reasons,” Eisenkot wrote on X. “The prime minister of Israel is the prime minister of all citizens, including those who did not vote for him,” he said. “Arab citizens of Israel are part of the Israeli story. The attempt to marginalise them and smear them as a group is an anti-state act.” In Israel’s October 27 elections , Eisenkot’s four-party alliance won 48 seats, while Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc secured 53, leaving both short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority. Arab-led parties, representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, won a record 19 seats. Netanyahu repeatedly made unproven allegations of electoral fraud by Arab-majority parties – claims Israel’s own electoral authorities have rejected. The caretaker leader has also repeatedly criticised Arab-led parties for refusing to describe Hamas as a “terror group” following the attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, despite all of the parties’ leaders condemning the Hamas-led assault. “One can disagree with the representatives of the Arab parties, and one can even feel deep revulsion toward some of them, but one cannot, should not, and I will not allow an entire sector to be slandered,” Eisenkot said. Arab-led parties have endorsed Eisenkot to replace Netanyahu. However, Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with those parties, which would give him a 67-seat bloc. Winning the backing of the two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats. On efforts to form an emergency government, Eisenkot reiterated that he wants to fulfil the mandate as soon as possible, adding “it would be a grave mistake not to do so”. Netanyahu weighs renewed strikes on Iran Eisenkot, who ran as Netanyahu’s main rival, has six weeks to form a new government. While Netanyahu may be politically weakened, the prime minister is reported to be weighing military action against Iran , despite a lack of enthusiasm from the United States, his own military establishment, and Eisenkot, who has demanded that Netanyahu avoid any new escalation unless it is critical. In Friday’s update, Eisenkot said he had met with Netanyahu and his military secretary on Thursday to discuss the security situation but provided no details. Earlier in the week, Eisenkot said that he was open to including Netanyahu in his coalition. Eisenkot suggested Netanyahu’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich was also welcome to join. Eisenkot led Israel’s military from 2015 to 2019 and sat as an observer in Netanyahu’s war cabinet for the first eight months of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023.

events.title: Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch
events.summary: (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.) Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question. First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago. The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began. Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area: The uptrend line extending from the early 2025 low through the early 2026 low. The 38.2% Fibonacci retracement of the entire 2025-2026 rally. The former 2025 highs, which represented resistance before becoming a key breakout zone earlier this year. This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline. For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse. The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025. Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights). The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective. The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now. That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market? One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses. Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend. We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed. The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off. From here, it's all about the follow through. We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum. events.title: My Dubai Salary: 'I said goodbye to two husbands to focus on my business'
events.summary: Madiha Abaida came to Dubai for a holiday. She ended up buying a property , opening a factory and never leaving. That was in 2018. She had been living in Monaco for a decade before that – a resident for tax reasons , as she puts it plainly – but after her marriage ended, she wanted a fresh start somewhere new. It was not straightforward, though. She launched a fashion brand in Dubai in 2020 and then the pandemic cancelled everything. So, she opened her own textile factory instead. She brought in staff, bought the machinery and worked 16-hour days. The fashion brand – originally conceived in Milan – became a Dubai operation born of necessity. Since then, she has pivoted again. Pink Madi, her beauty salon in Dubai, opened recently. Before that, she spent years building a real estate portfolio across the UAE and Spain's Golden Mile in Marbella, where she buys old homes, renovates them and sells them for $2 million to $3 million. She counts more than 25 properties in total. Today, she describes herself, without hesitation, as a millionaire . And she wants to go to Mars. What was your first job and first salary? When I was 16 or 17, I was selling Coca-Cola and noodles in order to study. People see me as a woman with power, but they don't know the price I paid. I was very hard-working from the beginning. I was a model first, when I was 17. And I studied to be a lawyer because my mother, she was married to a judge. I wanted to make my mother happy. But honestly, I never wanted to be a lawyer. I don't have this kind of personality. One day I said, “OK, I'm sorry – I need to do what I really believe I'm good at.” Then I started my fashion brand, and it was a big success in Milano. I had over 17 magazine covers. My first ever salary was €200. Then at 22, I also opened salons in Marbella – I had three salons there. And now? Now I have my real estate and my Dubai salon. My salon opened only recently – but I bought the salon seven months before that. I believe in energy. I do Reiki. When I entered the salon, it was all blue, and I didn't like the energy. I said, “I need a full renovation.” It took me six months. I was paying my staff throughout that whole time. It's the first salon, but not the last one. I am honestly very hard-working. I don't sleep. That is my secret – I sleep three hours a night. Because I need to watch everything. I'm very picky. Living in Monaco, I learnt luxury. Living in Miami, too, I learnt a lot. I travelled the whole world. With my experience in the fashion industry, I try to create something unique for women. What do you invest in? I have bought very good homes, old homes, in great locations in Marbella. I give them facelifts because I'm good at renovation. I sell them for $2 million or $3 million. I have over 25 properties total. Over six in the UAE. I also invest in stocks, crypto – all of this. That's also why I don't sleep. Money doesn't sleep. Do you have any debt? No, no, no. I always work with my own money. I don't take any credit from the bank. I calculate everything because the interest is high, and I don't like to pay interest. That's also why I divorced twice. When my two exes made me choose between them and my business, I said, "Habibi, bye bye." Madiha Abaida Growing up, were you taught how to handle money? No. My mother, she's very traditional. But I believe when you want something, today we have the platforms, you can learn everything. I don't lose my time watching stupid Netflix. I prefer to invest my time to learn. I paid for courses to learn about all this, because I come from a normal family, and my dream was to have a beautiful life. I wanted to be a millionaire by myself. That's also why I divorced twice. When my two exes made me choose between them and my business, I said, “Habibi, bye bye.” Financial independence is very important to me. Nobody will control me. I believe in this. I'm a feminist. I believe in hard work. And then people, they respect you. What are your major monthly expenses? For myself and my family, I just spend what I want – because they deserve it. When it comes to business, of course, as a businesswoman, I need to know how much I expect. That's how we make money. But when it comes to myself – I spend around Dh100,000 a month. I love myself too much, because I was hurt in the beginning. I learnt to love myself. I learnt to take care of myself. I have very deep experiences. I only trust myself. What are your financial goals? A lot. I want Pink Madi to go global – not only here, but America, everywhere. I have projects to launch my own make-up. I also have a charity for animals. I love animals. I bring them all to my home. I have two dogs and three cats. Call me crazy, but I want my own island. I want it near the Bahamas. I want my own private jet. You ask me, I'm telling you. I want to go to the Moon. I want to have a place on Mars, inshallah. I'm an Aquarius – very eccentric. What you see is what you get with me. No filter. I'm very proud of myself. I don't listen to other people. I listen to my instincts. When they tell me to go right, I go left. And I always win – because I don't follow anyone.

events.title: The folly of just-in-time supply chains | Letters
events.summary: The folly of just-in-time supply chains Hannah Walker says systems designed to minimise expenditure in the name of efficiency can end up less capable of fulfilling their actual purpose The article by Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend on the dangers of excessive optimisation identifies a problem extending far beyond mathematics and artificial intelligence ( The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly, 8 November ). The widespread adoption of just-in-time supply chains illustrates it perfectly. By eliminating inventories and spare capacity, businesses reduced costs and improved efficiency, but frequently transferred those savings into risks that remained invisible until something went wrong. The disruption of global manufacturing during the pandemic exposed the consequences. The same thinking has shaped public services and national defence. Hospital beds, experienced staff, strategic stockpiles and redundant infrastructure can all appear wasteful when measured against immediate demand. Yet their value lies precisely in their availability when circumstances cease to be normal. Europe’s dependence on American military capabilities provides a particularly troubling example. What appeared financially efficient in peacetime has created strategic vulnerabilities as the reliability of US commitments comes into question. The fundamental error is not optimisation itself, but optimising the wrong objective. A system designed to minimise expenditure may succeed brilliantly at doing so while becoming progressively less capable of fulfilling its actual purpose. Resilience is not inefficiency. It is a form of insurance. Like all insurance, the value only becomes apparent when it is needed – usually in a crisis. Hannah Walker Wymondham, Leicestershire Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

events.title: Gen Z hasn’t made up its mind on AI, survey finds
events.summary: Gen Z is often cast as souring on AI, but they’re no more negative about the technology than their parents and grandparents. A new survey from Milltown Partners, shared first with Semafor, found that 73% of Gen Z adults haven’t made up their minds on AI, while half said they expect AI to harm society. That matches baby boomers (50%) and Gen Xers (48%), while millennials were the most upbeat, with 39% expecting harm. Companies and politicians are all eager to understand the generation’s stance on AI, given how much they drive tech trends and how AI and data centers played an outsize role in the US midterm election. The report also pointed to a paradox that seems to define young people’s relationship with AI: Many say it makes them worse at thinking for themselves and harder to find a job — but 46% said they use it every day, the second-highest rate behind millennials. Young people are also less worried than older generations about the existential risk that dominates much of the AI safety discourse. And they are more conflicted about their own use: 30% of Gen Zers said they sometimes feel guilty using AI, more than double the rate among respondents over 30.

events.title: My partner moved in with me — and my 30-year-old daughter. It hasn't always been easy, but it's worked for 9 years.
events.summary: Living together hasn't always been easy for the three of us, but we've built some great routines. Samantha Priestley In 2017, my partner moved in with my adult daughter and me. At first, we all had to make compromises and adjust to some growing pains. Viewing each other as adult roommates helped, and the three of us still live together now. I'd been dating my partner for a couple of years before we decided to move in together. He'd been staying over often, at first for just a night at a time, and then for few-day stretches. One time, he was setting off for work from my house, duffel bag in hand, and I said, "This is stupid. Why don't you just move in?" And so he did, but he didn't just move in with me. My adult daughter lives at home , so "moving in" meant joining both of us. There have been challenges, but nine years later — with my daughter now 30 — this is still our setup. We all had to make some compromises when my partner moved in My daughter moved back in with me after she finished school. Samantha Priestley I got divorced when my daughter was a teenager, and started dating again once she was an adult. Although she had left home for university, she came back to live with me after finishing her studies. When my partner moved in with the two of us, it was into the home I'd shared with my ex-husband. It didn't feel right, so we quickly decided to get a place of our own, and the three of us moved into our four-bedroom Edwardian terrace house a few months later. By this time, my daughter and I had both been pretty set in our routines … like sharing a bathroom. My daughter was used to taking as long as she liked to get ready, but with an extra person, she had to account for three people's schedules instead of two. Meanwhile, my partner was clearly used to leaving his things lying around when he lived alone, but now, he was with two women who liked things to be tidy. If he were moving in with just me, the two of us might have tried to compromise, but he definitely felt some pressure to fit into our world, rather than asking me and my daughter adjusting to suit him. For me, the biggest compromise I've had to make is with my time. My attention was only required by my daughter when I was at home, but now I had to split my time with the two of them, which could be tiring at times. I felt constantly conscious of not leaving either of them out. Take cooking, as one example. My daughter and I always enjoyed cooking together, so I made sure we kept doing it — to this day, we prepare dinner together almost every evening. But my partner likes cooking, too, so we made a new habit of making a big breakfast together every weekend. I've had to prioritize alone time with both my partner and my daughter My partner and I make sure to plan plenty of date nights. Samantha Priestley The biggest problem I've found is one that shows up in almost every family and housing dynamic: Cohabitation can be hard, and sometimes we bug each other. It's not uncommon for me to feel like I'm in the middle. It's not that my partner and my daughter argue or don't get along, but inevitably, there can be tension over who didn't take out the recycling or who used the last of the milk, and I feel the pull in both directions when there is. I've found that the best way to avoid this is to make sure we all get some space. My daughter and I go on vacation together three times a year, plus day trips , to give my partner time to himself. Meanwhile, my partner and I go out on date nights, leaving my daughter alone. Even just taking a walk by ourselves when we need air is a good way to get some alone time. We each have our own rooms in the house — my daughter has her own bedroom, and my partner and I both have home offices — which really helps. We don't have a traditional family setup, but we're still a unit I encouraged my partner to treat my daughter like an adult roommate. Samantha Priestley My daughter will always be my little girl in many ways, but she contributes financially to our home and has always split household chores , tasks, and responsibilities with me. So, when my partner moved in , I had to help him understand that yes, she's my daughter and I'll always look out for her — but she's also an adult, and neither of us expected him to take on a father-like role. "Talk to her like any other adult," I remember telling him. "Think of this like a house-share with a friend." That attitude helped our dynamic click into place and went a long way in helping the two of them build a friendship. Given my daughter's age, they were never going to view each other as father and daughter, but they do see each other as family. When my daughter announced she wanted to watch a bunch of old movies, we immediately decided that every Saturday would be movie night, and it's become our own little tradition. The three of us go out for dinner together, spend the holidays together, and even take trips together. Things are always changing in families, but for now, we're making this work. My daughter is currently saving up enough money to get her own place. In some ways, it will be great to have the space and time to live as a couple, because we never have. But I'll also miss living together as the three of us. It might not be the living setup any of us would have chosen, but sharing our home like this has created a bond between the three of us that's unique and beautiful.
