events.title: 10-year Treasury yield moves to 5.17% as traders weigh producer price report
events.summary: The 10-year Treasury yield stayed over 5% on Friday after October's producer price index , a measure of wholesale prices, came in slightly less than expected. The yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose 3 basis points to 5.133%. It reached a high of 5.174% earlier in the day. The 2-year Treasury note yield, typically more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was lower by less than 1 basis point at 4.855%. The longer-dated 30-year Treasury bond yield, sensitive to geopolitical risks, was 4 basis points higher at 5.47%. One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions. October's producer price index rose 0.3% versus September, less than the 0.4% expected by economists polled by Dow Jones. But on an annual basis, PPI rose 6.5% over the past 12 months, the biggest annual increase since November 2022. There was "no silver lining" in the inflation report, said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS, adding that core PPI — which excludes food, energy and trade services — increased 0.5% in October. "It is economics 101 that producer prices lead consumer prices and right now it looks like consumers will be on the hook for a fresh burst of factory inflation," he said. The moves come after 10-year Treasury yields jumped more than 13 basis points to more than 5% in Thursday's session , with the 2-year yield soaring more than 15 basis points. Investors now see a Federal Reserve rate hike next month as a certainty. Traders are pricing in 100% odds of a rise at the Dec. 9 meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds of a quarter percentage point hike now stand at 86%, with the chance of a half point increase at around 14%. Energy inflation remains a key part of the puzzle, with oil set for its second weekly decline as prospects of renewed strikes by the U.S. against Iran fade. Prices were choppy in early trading Friday. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December delivery were down 0.1% at $88.63 per barrel. Brent crude , the international oil benchmark, was higher by 0.3% at $96.11.

events.title: Microsoft reports progress in restoring service after global outage
events.summary: Microsoft reported progress, but not a full recovery, following an outage Thursday that affected Outlook, Teams, and Copilot across more than 70 countries. The consequences have been wide-reaching: Several police departments in the UK said Friday that the public shouldn’t report crimes via online submission forms, and should call them in instead. Schools and agencies in Australia and Japan had to go analog. At least one company delayed its earnings call. It’s the kind of issue that reminds the world how much of our digital infrastructure is reliant on just a few companies, each a potential single point of failure. Microsoft ruled out a cyberattack, a relief given the recent wave of AI-powered hacks. The other silver lining for the company: Jensen Huang has been taking up all the oxygen in the tech world. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Jensen Huang’s biggest mistake was getting too involved in DC
events.summary: Reed’s view Jensen Huang made a lot of mistakes, but the one that really brought him down was getting too involved in DC. The skillset of a great technologist is the opposite of someone who’s great at politics. Technologists have to think years, sometimes decades in advance. When they figure out a winning formula, they bet everything on it. That’s a really bad way to operate in Washington, where things move on two-year election cycles and commitment to any one idea, faction, or ideology is a liability if and when the political winds change. When Donald Trump was elected president for a second term, it seemed like the world was suddenly a fundamentally different place. The White House was open for business in a way never seen in history. It was irresistible for a lot of tech people (Elon Musk and Marc Andreessen also fell into this trap). For a while, it seemed like Huang was one of the few technologists to find success in DC. His friendship with the president helped advance his worldview — that America should export its technology around the world, even to China. But it was all a mirage. Political people understood this would never last, and it would end in hearings, investigations, and prosecutions. This has all come as a shocking surprise to many in the tech industry. Nvidia was aggressive in its policy positions in part because it had the backing of the president. It should have used that influence sparingly, and not just to get what it wanted but to make more allies on both sides of the political aisle. So far, the underlying allegations against Huang are unproven. The alleged spy who led to this mess may not even be a spy . And many in the tech industry are angry and want to fight back. That’s the wrong instinct. In the tech industry, the relentless will to win is perhaps the most redeeming quality of every operator. In DC, you can’t ever really win. You can only lose. The Nvidia scandal and the post-midterm tech industry peril are exactly the reason we came up with the idea for our convening, Silicon Valley & The World, which takes place next week in the heart of the industry. We’re bringing leaders in from around the globe to burst Silicon Valley’s bubble and make it a more worldly place. We have what I think is the best lineup of speakers ever assembled at a media industry convening and I hope Jensen Huang, who was supposed to speak, will reconsider. If you’d like to tune in, register for a virtual broadcast pass , or watch live on YouTube and at Semafor.com . Notable Palantir CEO Alex Karp, another CEO that developed close ties to Trump and Washington , told Politico Playbook that he is a “ progressive ” and a lifelong Democrat.

events.title: At 40, I moved my family of 4 to Spain. We spent that first year abroad learning from our mistakes.
events.summary: Moving from the US to Spain has meant embracing culture shocks and making a few mistakes. Courtesy of Brian Hodge About a year and a half ago, my family of four left the US and moved to Spain . We've adapted in many ways but still sometimes struggle with late mealtimes and limited store hours. Locals take their time at cafés and restaurants, and it's pushed us to embrace a laid-back attitude. I should've known that we were too early when we had to duck under the partially closed metal awning. We'd arrived after the restaurant's posted opening hours, but my suspicions were confirmed when we were greeted by a hostess who was still taking off her motorcycle helmet. Definitely too early. She suggested we come back later, with a reservation. Welcome to the struggle of finding dinner in Spain before 8 p.m. About a year and a half ago, my family and I made the bold decision to leave the US, sell most of our belongings — including our home — and move our lives to Spain . Although it's absolutely been a dream come true, there are still some cold-water-on-the-face moments that snap us awake and remind us how far we've come. We've gradually adjusted to new business hours and norms Restaurants are a little different in Spain than they are in the US. Courtesy of Brian Hodge Even simple things like dining out and shopping at local stores have required some readjusting. Restaurants typically open later and stay open later than they did back in the US, especially during Spain's languid, sunny summers. This all sounds very romantic until you have hungry children looking for dinner at 7:30 p.m. and most local restaurants don't open for another hour. Then dinner becomes a mish-mash of ham, cheese, and olives back home. It's possible to find inexpensive wines at the local market ... just check their hours first. Courtesy of Brian Hodge And don't count on stopping by the local supermarket on Sundays — ours is closed. Fish at the Mercado Central on Mondays? Forget it. Picture instead dozens of fish stalls, row after row of shops usually spilling over with squid, shellfish, swordfish, tuna, and more, all shuttered. I've also stopped counting how many times I've tried to pick up a few items at a local store in the middle of the day, only to be greeted by closed doors because the whole street has shut down for "siesta" (also known as a post-lunch rest). These breaks are common throughout Spain, and often last for two or three hours in the middle of the day, but can vary depending on the region. We like to look at fresh produce at the Mercado Central when it's open. Courtesy of Brian Hodge Although these shops often stay open later in the evening to help balance things out, we do miss the simple reliability of many local businesses being open all day. On the bright side, in Spain, restaurant and business hours seem to intentionally force us to slow down and plan ahead. Dining and café culture have also pushed us to slow down and enjoy meals more Café culture is alive and well in Spain. Courtesy of Brian Hodge In Spain, café culture is alive and well. The sidewalks frequently fill with workers, families, and neighbors of all ages, making the chairs and tables a lively extension of the neighborhood. They take their time sipping, chatting, and sharing food. Diners rarely seem to be in a rush — and it's considered poor form to eat while walking or commuting. We've found ways to adapt to our new country. Courtesy of Brian Hodge We've learned to budget more time for quick meals and the art of flagging down the waiter for the check — otherwise it simply won't arrive. It took a bit of getting used to, especially coming from a country where rushed meals are more normal, and the check can sometimes arrive at the same time as the food. However, there's no rushing you out of restaurants here. In fact, the Spanish even have a word, sobremesa , for the idle chatter and company that follows a meal. Allow extra time accordingly. Sometimes, ordering mishaps have actually worked in our favor One time, I thought I asked for the menu. Instead, I got three courses of food. Courtesy of Brian Hodge One of our first meals in Spain was at a local restaurant in our neighborhood. Buoyed by a healthy mix of overestimating our level of fluency and underestimating just how quickly waiters can talk, we were excited to experience a more authentic, truly Spanish experience. So when I thought I was simply asking for the menu, we could only laugh when we received a "menú del día" ("menu of the day"), heaping plates and platters as part of a three-course meal. In retrospect, the fact that the waiter talked for so long and in such detail about each dish should have been a sign, but it turned out to be an error in our favor. The multicourse meal was delicious, priced at only about 14 euros per person, and one of the best we've had. We now actively seek out menús del día whenever we're out. All in all, living here has meant planning more but also embracing a laid-back attitude In Spain, we've learned to embrace life at a slower pace. Courtesy of Brian Hodge Ultimately, we've learned to take things more slowly and make plans in advance when it comes to meals and errands — things we probably should've been doing anyway. And we've especially learned to appreciate our little adventure and the fact we were actually able to pull it off, despite all the bumps and bruises along the way. I'm not sure how long my family will stay in Spain , but we set out on this path to push ourselves outside our comfort zones and learn new things. On that count, even the mistakes have been a success. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The best pumpkin pie I've ever made uses a surprisingly easy recipe from Bobby Flay
events.summary: I'm a pretty big fan of Bobby Flay's recipe for pumpkin pie. Paige Bennett I previously tested three celebrity chefs' pumpkin-pie recipes, and Bobby Flay's was my favorite. Overall, Flay's recipe for pumpkin pie was easy to follow, and the dessert turned out delicious. The graham-cracker crust was sturdy, and the flavorful whipped cream really made this dish. I've baked more than 100 recipes from celebrity chefs , often putting them head-to-head to find the best dishes out there. When testing out star-studded takes on pumpkin pie , Bobby Flay's version of the seasonal dessert blew me away. The chef's " Throwdown Pumpkin Pie " recipe, found on the Food Network website, features a sturdy graham-cracker crust, creamy spiced filling, and decadent bourbon-maple whipped cream. Even better, it's pretty easy to make. Here's how I put it together and why I plan to keep this pie recipe in my rotation year after year. Most of the ingredients are pretty basic I already had a lot of the ingredients for Bobby Flay's pumpkin pie in my pantry and fridge. Paige Bennett Flay's recipe is a no-fuss option for people who love a homemade dessert but don't want to spend a full day making a flaky pie crust , as it uses a graham-cracker base instead. The recipe also doesn't require carving and roasting fresh pumpkin. Instead, canned pumpkin purée gets mixed with butter, eggs, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, granulated sugar, dark-brown sugar, heavy cream, salt, and fresh vanilla-bean seeds. Of course, this dish wouldn't be complete without the flavorful whipped cream made with heavy whipping cream, maple syrup, vanilla-bean seeds, and bourbon. The steps are easy to follow, too I crushed the graham crackers with a mallet. Paige Bennett Before baking this pie, I measured out all of the ingredients and organized them in groups for the crust, filling, and whipped cream. This made following this recipe a quicker, simpler process. Although the recipe calls for a food processor, I didn't have one when I first made this dish. Instead, I used a mallet to crush the graham crackers, which I'd sealed in a plastic bag to avoid making a mess. I then combined the crumbs with butter, sugar, and cinnamon in a small blender. The graham-cracker crust had to bake. Paige Bennett From there, I firmly pressed the graham-cracker mixture into a pie tin and baked the crust for 10 minutes at 350 degrees Fahrenheit to set it. Once the pie crust had been prebaked, I set the oven to 275 degrees Fahrenheit as instructed and got to work on the filling. Making the filling was also simple. Paige Bennett I started by whisking the eggs and sugar together before adding in the pumpkin, heavy cream, salt, vanilla, spices, and sugars.  Once I had the creamy filling ready to go, I strained it and poured it into my cooled pie crust. I ended up with far more filling than I needed for one pie. According to the recipe, this is intentional, and extras can be used toward more pies or frozen for later use. The crust wasn't perfect, but it held the filling just fine. Paige Bennett Luckily, Flay's whipped cream can be thrown together while the pie finishes baking. To do so, I combined heavy whipping cream, bourbon, vanilla-bean seeds, and maple syrup in a stand mixer. The recipe calls for Grade B maple syrup, but that's no longer a classification, so I use a dark Grade A syrup instead. It added a nice rich flavor to the whipped cream. My pie ended up baking for about an hour and a half. The pie and whipped cream paired together perfectly There's hardly a greater combination than pumpkin pie and whipped cream. Paige Bennett Flay's whipped cream beautifully balanced the pumpkin pie's pumpkin flavor and spices and was tasty on its own, thanks to the maple syrup, bourbon, and vanilla. The pumpkin pie itself had a great texture. Although the bottom of the crust was slightly too soggy, it still held together well. Plus, the dish maintained a good height and sported crispy edges. I wish the crust was just as tasty as the filling and whipped cream, though. In the future, I plan to add more sugar and cinnamon to the graham-cracker mix to boost its flavor. Even so, this pie was surprisingly easy to put together and utterly delicious. I'll definitely be making it again. This story was originally published on November 21, 2022, and most recently updated on November 13, 2026. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The fight over Canadian steelworker jobs
events.summary: Stelco’s US owner blames Trump’s tariffs for layoffs, but its support for those same tariffs has raised questions. Hamilton, Ontario, Canada – Chelsey Masteij had heard layoffs might be coming at Stelco, so she decided to use up some of her vacation days. She was making the most of the time off with her new dog when she got a call telling her not to come back to work. The 34-year-old had spent years trying to break into the male-dominated steel industry before finally landing a job at the company’s Hamilton plant about three years ago. list 1 of 4 Bank of Canada raises interest rates for the first time in three years list 2 of 4 European Union backtracks on Canada becoming ‘associate member’ list 3 of 4 Canada-EU summit: What do both sides want, and what’s at stake? list 4 of 4 US accuses Canada of election interference ahead of midterms She started as a general labourer in the cold-rolling department, later training to operate cranes and taking on shifts in the coke ovens. The work was gruelling and physically demanding, but Masteij grew to love the routine and the close-knit community of coworkers she came to consider family. When she shared photos of herself with Al Jazeera, all in protective gear at the plant, she joked that she hardly had any pictures outside of work. Masteij thought she might stay at Stelco until retirement. Instead, she was laid off on October 9. The news hit hard, and she spent much of the next two weeks sleeping. “I was in a complete mess,” she told Al Jazeera, her voice cracking as she recalled the experience. “I was kind of depressed.” Now, instead of working 12-hour shifts, Masteij spends much of her time at home, cutting back on expenses while she collects employment insurance. Masteij is among hundreds of Canadian steelworkers facing layoffs after Stelco’s American owner, Cleveland-Cliffs, announced in late September that it would temporarily shut down parts of its operations in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ontario. Stelco blames the move on United States President Donald Trump’s tariffs, which it says have made it harder to sell Canadian steel to US customers, and on competition from cheaper foreign steel entering Canada. But government officials and plant workers, including Masteij, are not convinced that is the whole story. “Right now, there are a lot of lies going on with what’s happened,” Masteij said. While US tariffs have hurt the Canadian steel industry, the union representing Stelco workers questions whether Cleveland-Cliffs is using difficult market conditions to serve its own business interests, with Canadian workers paying the price. “Everyone knows we’re being used as pawns, that these layoffs weren’t necessary,” said Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, speaking to Al Jazeera at his Hamilton office. In June 2025, Trump doubled tariffs on steel and aluminium imports, including from Canada, to 50 percent, making them more expensive for US buyers. According to Stelco, Canada’s exports of cold-rolled and coated steel to the US – used to make everything from cars to building materials – fell by 58 percent in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the quarterly average before the trade war. But demand has also fallen in Canada, where the auto industry, a major buyer of the cold-rolled steel produced at the Hamilton plant, has also been hit hard by Trump’s tariffs, said Colin Mang, an assistant professor of economics at McMaster University in Hamilton. “When they say that there is less demand for the product coming out of the Hamilton mill, that is correct,” Mang told Al Jazeera. But it is not just Trump’s tariffs that Cleveland-Cliffs blames for Stelco’s problems. During a July earnings call, CEO Lourenco Goncalves warned that the company might scale back production in Canada unless Ottawa did more to protect its steel industry from imports. “And that will have consequences for employment in Canada, but will have a positive financial impact on Stelco and on Cleveland-Cliffs,” he said. That was the first time Wells had heard jobs might be at risk. The union later offered to help Cleveland-Cliffs lobby Ottawa for stronger protections against foreign steel imports, believing Canadian workers might have more sway with the government. “They never took us up on our offer,” Wells said. Instead, the next call brought news of the layoffs. As of Saturday, 175 workers at Stelco’s Hamilton plant had received layoff notices, with the announced cuts expected to affect up to 500 workers there and in Nanticoke. Late last month, about 30 attended an information session the union organised in Hamilton, where they could learn about employment insurance and retraining opportunities. Many were frustrated by the lack of clarity about how long the shutdown would last. Some asked how their benefits would compare to their wages, while others wondered whether they would qualify for the full amount.

events.title: Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its stand-alone robotics team as its general models start running robots
events.summary: OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team, moving its researchers onto other teams. The company confirmed the reorganization when asked about it by Fortune. A company spokesperson said that robotics remains a core part of OpenAI’s long-term vision and portrayed the reorganization as a sign of the company’s commitment to robotics, rather than a retreat from it. OpenAI said it has reassigned its robotics research team to the company’s main research team, reporting to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams have been reassigned to the company’s larger Applied organization, which reports to OpenAI President Greg Brockman. The change came recently enough that OpenAI had already registered a booth at CoRL, a top academic robotics conference in Austin, this week. Though the conference app and floor plan marked OpenAI’s spot, when Fortune visited booth #208, it sat empty with OpenAI’s logo nowhere to be seen.  OpenAI had a robotics team in its early days but wound it down in 2020, with cofounder Wojciech Zaremba later citing limited robot data and a more efficient path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI)—the human-like AI that has been OpenAI’s goal since its founding—through other methods. In particular, OpenAI became increasingly devoted to training ultra-large language models on vast datasets of human-written text. This is the approach that eventually yielded the company’s breakthrough product ChatGPT in late 2022. OpenAI rebuilt a stand alone robotics team in 2024, announcing a partnership with the startup Figure to develop AI models for humanoid robots. That partnership ended in February 2025, when Figure said it would develop its own robot AI. OpenAI has said it is currently developing its own humanoid robot, with CEO Sam Altman targeting a first public demonstration in 2027. The company spokesperson said that despite the reorganization, OpenAI remains committed to bringing general-purpose robots into the world. The reorganization reflects a bet that is gaining traction across the AI industry: that general-purpose models built for language, code, and vision can also be used for “embodied AI”—where AI models control devices that can act in the physical world, such as robots, driverless cars, or drones. This would obviate the need to have separate robotics teams building specialized AI models just to be the digital “brains” for robots. Researchers have seen surprising performance when connecting GPT-6 Astra to robots, directly using the general-purpose AI model to perform some robotic tasks. Guanya Shi, an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute who had previously heard about OpenAI’s reorganization, told Fortune that he would interpret the move as a signal that OpenAI sees robotics as “no longer a special problem.” Instead, he said, they likely see robotics as a challenge that can be addressed as a downstream application of general intelligence—similar to the way the same underlying frontier AI models now power specialized coding tools, or tools for legal or financial work. OpenAI seemed to confirm this view in its response to Fortune. It said that at the start of the year, the company’s researchers assumed the best way to make progress on robotics was to build on its work on AI models such as Sora, a video generation model that, in order to create realistic videos, had to have some implicit understanding of how the physical world works. But since then, the company spokesperson said, the company’s general-purpose frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have shown that can be directly applied to robotics. This discovery is what motivated OpenAI to disband the stand alone robotics team and move the affiliated researchers onto teams working on more general AI models. The reorganization also comes at a time when OpenAI is under pressure to rein in its costs and show that it is more focused on a few, core products. Last year, Altman told the company that it needed to abandon “side quests,” and the company has jettisoned some efforts—including Sora—in order to reallocate computing resources to more core and potentially-profitable endeavors. The company is under pressure to stanch its heavy operating losses—which reportedly totaled $10.9 billion in the most recent quarter—as it seeks to close a new funding round and prepares for a possible IPO in early 2027. This line of thinking—that general AI models can be applied directly to controlling robots without the need to create specialized models with “spatial intelligence”—would seem to challenge the assumptions underpinning many of today’s robotics startups, which have raised billions on the premise that robots need brains of their own.  But Russ Tedrake, an MIT professor and cofounder and CEO of Walden Robotics, said robotics companies still have an advantage the AI labs don’t: Their robots are already gaining work experience in real places, such as on factory floors. Such “deployment” experience—and the data these robots gather—helps robots adapt to specific workplaces and tasks. Better foundational models make that site-specific data more valuable because robots can learn from it faster, Tedrake said. Recent experiments have tested how much work a general-purpose model can do without specialized training on robotic data. Researchers gave Astra camera images, robot information and a control interface that allowed the model to command the robot to take certain actions. In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8% success rate on a simulated manipulation benchmark—where the model commands a simulated robot in a digital simulation, as opposed to a real robot—compared with 51.0% reported by the best specialized robotic models on this leaderboard. Shi said advances in general models’ spatial and reasoning capabilities already let them handle tasks that previously required dedicated training. They can cope when a bottle is in a different position or the lighting changes, and reason about the sequence of a task or which step went wrong, he said. Meanwhile, large language models are powerful but slow and need to be hosted in the cloud, meaning the robot or device needs a constant network connection. Shi still sees a need for smaller, specialized models that can run on a robot’s onboard computer without needing a constant internet connection. “There may be different starting points for how to grow intelligence,” Pete Florence, cofounder of Generalist, a startup training general-purpose AI models for robots, told Fortune. He said it was unclear that any existing model would be the one that dominates robotics in the long-run. For its part, OpenAI said it was reassigning its robotics researchers to other teams because it now believes this is the best way to accelerate progress towards building general-purpose robots

events.title: Scott Bessent blames the Commerce Department for not cracking down on Megaspeed
events.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said it wasn't his department's job to crack down on Megaspeed and that reporters should ask Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why his department hasn't done so. Allison Robbert/AFP via Getty Images Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he supported cracking down on Megaspeed. Bessent said it was the Commerce Department that has refused to place the company on a trade blacklist. Megaspeed is the Singapore company at the center of the Nvidia scandal. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said it wasn't his fault that the Trump administration hasn't cracked down on the company at the center of the Nvidia scandal. "Commerce has the pen," Bessent said during an interview on CNBC on Friday morning, adding, "You all will have to ask them about their internal processes." Bessent's striking comments essentially threw Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and his department under the bus. It also follows an Axios report that Bessent confronted Lutnick during a meeting in the Situation Room about why the Commerce Department had not added Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company, to the "entity list," a trade blacklist that Lutnick's department controls. Bessent said he would not comment on what happens in the Situation Room but also did not deny the report. A spokesperson for the Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Alice Huang was a top executive at Megaspeed. The New York Times has reported that US officials suspected she was a Chinese intelligence asset. The Times also reported that Alice Huang had an affair with then- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . Jensen Huang apologized in a note to employees for having an affair on Sunday, but did not mention Alice Huang or the espionage allegations. Nvidia's board announced on Thursday that Jensen Huang had resigned. China has repeatedly denied that Huang was a spy. Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner, is facing scrutiny over whether its data centers helped Chinese customers access advanced Nvidia chips despite US export restrictions. Bessent said that his department and his deputy had been "pushing for months" for the action against Megaspeed. Bessent said that "there is a lot of leakage in the system" and that Chinese companies are getting access to chips superior to Nvidia's H-100. "President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100S, and so any leakage is very frustrating, because it hurts our great companies in the AI race and gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. As for the Nvidia founder, Bessent said the focus should be less on Huang's reported affairs and more on how Nvidia's advanced chips are entering China. "The story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles," Bessent said. "The real story here should be, did Nvidia know their client?" Bessent's comments underscore that Huang's ouster is far from the end of the controversy for Nvidia. "Was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure there was no leakage, and they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?" Bessent said. "And I think it's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The global economy's Achilles' heels
events.summary: A defining story of this decade has been a series of global economic shocks: pandemic, war and geopolitical shifts. New research quantifies a rising set of vulnerabilities for the global trade system . The big picture: Many crucial global goods are built on supply chains that have one or more Achilles' heels, a report from the consulting firm McKinsey finds — a critical input, concentrated suppliers and geopolitical strain. That manifests partly in physical chokepoints. The Strait of Hormuz is the one most in the news, but the McKinsey researchers identify a couple dozen others globally, through which 80% of maritime trade passes (although with varying levels of difficulty for shippers to route around). In effect, as the global economy has become more integrated over the last few decades, these vulnerabilities have become more pronounced — which in turn helps explain why the 2020s have brought an ongoing series of disruptive supply shocks. By the numbers: They find that the share of global imports that face at least two of three major vulnerabilities has risen to 23% in 2024 from 15% in 2000. The list of items with overlapping vulnerabilities includes basic materials like iron ore and more advanced items like lithium-ion batteries, smartphones and memory chips. What they're saying: "It's not necessarily that trade has gotten less reliable," Tiago Devesa, a co-author of the report, tells Axios. "I think it's more that we have the realization that we actually want to understand what are the potential points of failure, so we can anticipate them." "I think you could make a case that throughout all of these shocks, trade has continued to increase, and trade was actually a very important balancing mechanism," he adds. "It's been increasing precisely in part because we've integrated the fabric of the global economy much more, and in particular, we've led a specialization effort that led to more concentration around the world," says Devesa, a senior fellow at the McKinsey Global Institute. Reality check: Reducing vulnerabilities and building economic resilience isn't necessarily as simple as relocating a factory. "Some companies just change their suppliers or factory from a geopolitically distant country to a geopolitically closer country, and they think that they achieved resilience," said Jeongmin Seong, a co-author and McKinsey partner. "Even though you change the location of the final assembly, unless you eliminate the risk at this upstream level, you are still exposed." Between the lines: The steady march of globalization paid major dividends in recent decades in making goods more affordable and powering global growth. Now companies — and governments — are seeking to mitigate the vulnerabilities that system has created and that the last several years made plain to see.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters If you have one of these AI-generated homepages, you'd better download and save it quick Mozilla Thunderbird email service edges closer to launch with early access 2 days ago Firefox 156 arrives with a forest of forks in its wake September 19, 2026 Firefox and Thunderbird hit the fortnightly release treadmill September 2, 2026 Thunderbird to flap twice as fast from September August 20, 2026 Mozilla adds ad blocking to Firefox for iOS August 17, 2026 Solo, Mozilla's LLM-powered website builder and hosting service, is shutting down. All sites and data will be deleted on November 30. Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. S ome 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them – complete with custom domain names. Well, not any more. Now the Soloist.ai homepage says: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026." Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ , users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images. The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com , with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. So much for having the fiddly bits taken care of. It also points at a couple of other bot-based site-generating services – in case all this feels like a bit too much. We suspect that for the sort of technophobes that this was aimed at, it very probably will. Mozilla told The Register : "Experimentation is an important part of Mozilla's mission to make the internet better and give people more choice and control online. Sometimes, that means making the decision to bring a product to an end. Solo will officially shut down on November 30, 2026. We initially notified customers on October 1, providing a 60-day transition period, and have been offering support to help them download their website data and migrate their domains purchased via Solo Domains to another hosting provider." It seems that some 54,000 users were not enough to keep it going, and we can see that this would cost money to keep running. An HTML export is a start, though the FAQ doesn't explain how much work it will take to get a complete, functioning site running elsewhere. Buried in the dark recesses of the web is this vulture's own nearly 30-year-old homepage, created using a mixture of Claris Home Page (which was excellent) and Microsoft FrontPage (ever so slightly less so). We saw what a mess machine-generated web content was back then, and thanks to LLMs, we suspect it is almost infinitely worse now. Mozilla might have made a few bucks by finding a commercial partner to take on its users, and perhaps through them offer a paid site-and-domain transfer service. As we noted last year, it seems not to have negotiated anything with KaiOSTech, which maintains and sells what used to be the formerly FOSS FirefoxOS for use on low-end smartphones. events.title: SEC Proposes Executive and Director Compensation Disclosure Reforms
events.summary: Search Filings Search Filings Full Text Search Latest Filings Mutual Fund Search Variable Insurance Products Search SIC Codes CIK Lookup Public Dissemination Service (PDS) Search Assistance Submit Filings Submit Filings EDGAR Filer Management Portal EDGAR Filing Portal Online Forms Management Portal EDGAR Next Forms Index Filer Support & Resources Data & Research Data & Research Data Library Statistics & Data Visualizations Structured Data Investment Management Data Open Data at the SEC Rules, Enforcement, & Compliance Rules & Regulations Rulemaking Activity Submit Public Comments Staff Guidance No-Action, Interpretive, and Exemptive Letters Self-Regulatory Organization Rulemaking Public Petitions for Rulemaking Enforcement & Litigation Litigation Releases Administrative Proceedings Administrative Law Judge Orders and Initial Decisions Trading Suspensions Distributions to Harmed Investors Receiverships Compliance Examination Priorities Risk Alerts Compliance Outreach Program Proposed Rules What's New Whistleblower Program Featured Topics Featured Topics Crypto Task Force Cybersecurity Market Structure Analytics Saving and Investing for Military Personnel Saving and Investing for Teachers SEC-CFTC Harmonization Initiative Treasury Clearing Implementation About About Mission Commissioners Divisions & Offices Division & Office Directors Advisory Committees Budget & Performance Reports & Publications Commission Votes Contact the SEC Careers The Securities and Exchange Commission today proposed rule amendments to make its executive and director compensation disclosure requirements more principles-based and materiality-driven, providing investors with clearer, more concise, and less complex disclosures. The proposal follows the Commission’s review of its executive and director compensation disclosure requirements, including a request for public comment and a roundtable discussion with representatives from public companies, investors, and other experts in this field. This proposal builds on Chairman Atkins’ efforts to reduce friction for companies looking to join and remain in our public markets. The proposal would refocus these disclosures—last comprehensively reformed in 2006—on material information and improve investors’ ability to track equity awards through their lifecycle. The proposed amendments aim to reduce compliance burdens for registrants where there is not commensurate benefit for investors and would provide registrants with more flexibility to present their disclosures in a way that is consistent with how compensation programs are constructed today and better represents the intention of their boards of directors and compensation committees. “Today, the Commission proposed amendments to its executive compensation disclosure requirements contained in Item 402 of Regulation S-K. These amendments reflect a comprehensive reform of Item 402 that, together with other previously proposed actions, are central tenets of my agenda and focus on transforming the SEC’s public company disclosure regime to one rooted in materiality,” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins in a statement . “With the benefit of input from more than 80 comment letters received from investors, companies, and advisors in connection with the SEC’s roundtable on executive compensation in July 2025, today’s proposal aims to elicit more informative disclosure rooted in materiality.” The proposed amendments to Item 402 of Regulation S-K would permit registrants to tailor disclosure in a way that provides greater transparency regarding the registrant’s compensation practices and is more efficient for investors to read and understand. In support of these goals, the proposed changes would, among other things: Revise the named executive officers to encompass the principal executive officer and principal financial officer—the positions whose compensation are generally most material for investors due to their roles in managing a registrant’s most consequential matters—thereby reducing the number of named executive officers from typically five or more individuals under the current rule to two in most circumstances. Modify the primary executive compensation tabular disclosure requirements into three new tables (Earned Compensation Table, Granted Compensation Table, and Status of Equity Awards Table) with accompanying narratives that would replace the primary four tables required under the current rule. The proposed changes would retain material information required under the current tabular disclosure framework but would seek to streamline and clarify the presentation. Raise the minimum aggregate reporting threshold for perquisites from $10,000 to $150,000 and introduce a new de minimis tracking exclusion. The proposed amendments would retain disclosure of material perquisites for investors while reducing compliance burdens for registrants. Revise the Commission’s interpretive guidance regarding perquisites to give registrants more flexibility to make the determination of whether a benefit is a perquisite, so long as the determination is reasonable and made in good faith. Make the Compensation Discussion and Analysis (CD&A) requirement more principles-based, require registrants to address only three topics in the CD&A, and eliminate the list of 15 example topics contained in the current rule. The proposed changes would streamline the presentation of information, reduce complexity and repetition, and focus more clearly on material information. Simplify the pay-versus-performance disclosure requirement by reducing required performance measures and replacing the complex “Compensation Actually Paid” calculation with the total compensation earned amount from the proposed Earned Compensation Table. The proposed changes would continue to satisfy the statutory mandate of the Dodd-Frank Act while simplifying disclosure requirements. Limit the population used in the determination of “median employee” under the pay ratio rule to U.S. full-time employees and reduce the required frequency of the determination to every five years. Eliminate required check boxes from the cover pages of annual reports and certain potentially redundant disclosure requirements regarding the application of a registrant’s clawback policy that overly burden registrants without eliciting material information for investors. The underlying mechanics of a registrant’s clawback process would remain unchanged. The public comment period will remain open for 60 days following publication of the proposing release in the Federal Register. events.title: Why the data center slowdown concern is overblown. Two stocks to buy amid the fear
events.summary: No, the data center boom isn’t over. Not one utility CEO we spoke with at the EEI conference is anticipating a slowdown in electricity growth expectations. Power Insider exclusive: Two utility stocks that stand to benefit if data center business leaves Texas. Our exclusive with Texas billionaire and U.S. Ambassador to Italy Tilman Fertitta. GET THIS IN YOUR INBOX FIRST: Subscribe to CNBC's "Power Insider" newsletter. The demise of data centers has been greatly exaggerated. So says every utility CEO and energy-focused investor we spoke with at the Edison Electric Institute's annual conference in Arizona. Here's why... There is a lot of misleading, misdirected, or straight-up incorrect information floating around about data centers and the AI buildout. I'm not going to dive into the old water-use story — you can do your own research on that — but rather focus this week on what the insiders know: Some newly elected politicians either don't have the power to stop the buildouts or, if they do, the buildout will likely just continue somewhere else. Ohio and Georgia are important states to watch with their new incoming political class, but for the sheer importance in size and scope, I'll focus on the energy and data center capital: Texas. Incoming Governor Gina Hinojosa and incoming Senator James Talarico both campaigned on promises to go after what they believe to be affordability issues around data centers. I say "what they believe to be" because it's unclear how much data centers may raise your electricity bill, if at all. First and foremost, data centers are largely a state issue, meaning officials elected to federal office have little control over outcomes, at least for now. In Texas, any cancellations or moratoriums on new builds will come from the statehouse in Austin. That's where current Governor Greg Abbott has already, and rather quietly, put his own " pause " on data center permitting. That delay has been underway for a few weeks. Also, in Texas, the Governor has less direct power than in some other states. The power the governor does have largely derives from the authority to appoint those in charge of the all-important permitting process. In the Lone Star State, that power lies with two agencies: the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and the even lesser-known Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) . The PUCT regulates Texas' electricity, telecom, and water industries. It helps oversee growth of anything electricity-grid-related. So if a data center wants to connect to the public utility grid, it needs the commission's approval. Its chair — a pro-growth chap named Thomas Gleeson —is also on the board of Texas' electric grid powerhouse ERCOT and will serve his term with the utility commission through September 2029. Yes, three years from now. That agency gets involved when a data center or power provider wants to connect to the electricity grid. But what about facilities that are off the grid and have their own dedicated power sources? Texas has less control over what happens then. That said, it does have to authorize certain environmental permits, and that responsibility largely lies with the TCEQ. The TCEQ was " BBI " ( my own little term for "boring, but important" ) until data centers came along. It's not exactly the Alamo, but this obscure group — run by a regulator named Brooke Paup — is largely the "last stand" for permitting on those new builds. Paup was also appointed by Gov. Abbott and serves through next year. In other words, unless she and Gleeson step down or there is some way to oust them, the regulatory environment in Texas may not change much. The bottom line in this brief foray into the Texas regulatory swamp is to highlight that there are things for investors to consider around the data center/energy world that may not be at the top of the headlines. Important Note → Be mindful that I am an East Coast-based financial broadcaster and journalist, not an expert on Texas regulation or how the state operates. There may very well be things I don't know, things my sources aren't aware of, or other ways in which the new Governor and state House can assert power. For one, she recently said she may try to freeze electricity rates. Hint: that would be a terrible idea unless you want to damage the growth of badly needed new power sources like wind and solar. Disclaimer is done. Let's assume I am wrong on Texas and there is a larger push to slow or stop data center growth in the state. Conversations with some pretty smart people lead me to believe that if those facilities aren't built in that state, they will be built in another: Louisiana, Oklahoma, or another state. Sources tell me that Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry and his team are already working the phones, telling companies that his state would love to welcome new business. Same for Oklahoma. Both are gas-rich, have plenty of power, and are only too happy to grab any data center dollars.

events.title: I paid more for a house in a top school district. Then I sent my daughter somewhere else.
events.summary: The author said her family paid more for a smaller house to live in a good school district. Once they moved in, they weren't impressed with the learning environment. Unaihuiziphotography/Getty Images I paid more for a home in a top-rated school district, only to find the schools cold and rigid. I moved my daughter to a lower-rated Title I charter school that valued community and real support. My daughter is thriving in an International Baccalaureate program, and I have no regrets. When my husband and I were searching for a home, buying in an area with highly regarded schools for our four children was non-negotiable. We ended up spending more than we planned on a smaller house than we wanted to ensure our kids had access to a good education. Regardless of where my children's lives ultimately took them, I was confident a good school, defined by traditional measures, was vital to their future success and happiness. Moving into the school district with the city's highest-rated schools seemed like a no-brainer, and worth the financial sacrifice and reduced space. While my family ended up loving our neighborhood, with tree-lined streets and children riding bikes everywhere, we were ultimately disappointed in the schools . We decided to change course, a decision our friends and family still struggle to understand. We were disappointed with the neighborhood schools On paper, our neighborhood elementary school looked ideal. Yet I soon learned that its reputation as a great school depended heavily on its laser-like focus on improving standardized test scores. To me, it was obvious that this success came at a cost. Located in an affluent area, the school focused on academic achievement and maximizing "learning minutes" above all else. I felt that it lacked economic diversity, and kids and parents seemed to be in constant competition to outdo one another. Things got worse when the school instituted policies like "silent lunch," where kids were prohibited from talking during the time set aside for them to eat. A little rain was often enough to cancel recess, and the school ended most classroom parties. This created a culture in which my kids were ultimately not excited about learning and did not look forward to going to school each day. The author said she decided to move her daughter to a different school when she realized she wasn't looking forward to going to school each day. Courtesy of Jamie Davis Smith. We stuck it out, only to discover that when my older child started 6th grade, I discovered that I liked our neighborhood middle school even less. It's huge, with more than 1,400 students spread across just three grades. I was appalled by the continuation of a culture that seemed more interested in managing students than nurturing them, more focused on checking administrative boxes than ensuring real learning was taking place. When I met with my older son's teachers, for example, I discovered that some didn't know who he was; they were giving me information about another student with a similar name, a mix-up that was hard for me to accept. When it was time for my daughter to start middle school, she wanted to follow in her brother's footsteps and attend our neighborhood school. It would have been the easy choice: close to home, familiar, and, despite the challenges, still considered the best and most desirable school in the city, one other families fought to get into. Yet, I knew she needed a change. We decided to apply to other schools, even though they seemed less desirable on paper Friends in other school districts across the city thought I had lost my mind when I started applying to charter schools that, on paper, seemed less desirable than our neighborhood school. Some schools on my list had much lower test scores or higher poverty rates. When we applied, our top-choice school, where my daughter ultimately wound up, was a Title I school , with around half the student population qualifying for free or reduced lunch. Do you have a parenting regret? Email Jennifer Beck Goldblatt at jgoldblatt@insider.com to share your experience with Business Insider. The striking differences on paper between the charter school we sought out and our neighborhood school kept many parents from applying. Yet, what I see in action almost every day has convinced me I made the right choice. We're happy with our choice Teachers and administrators seem to genuinely care about the students at my daughter's school. They promptly answer my emails in a way that makes it clear they not only know who my child is but understand her. The community constantly rallies to help those in need, including running grab-and-go markets for families who need help putting food on the table and creating "walking trains" for kids whose parents can't take their children to school for a variety of reasons. The school principal is readily available to help students unlock the pouches they must use to store their phones every day and to meet with parents. My daughter and her classmates seem genuinely happy and challenged. Most importantly, my daughter is thriving. She has risen to the challenge of a difficult International Baccalaureate academic program . She has fantastic friends who live all over the city, from all walks of life and from around the world. That's its own kind of education, and just as important to our family. My thoughts have evolved I wish I had been open-minded from the beginning about what makes a good school and looked beyond the statistics presented on paper. Schools are more than the statistics presented in a few sentences on websites, and I've learned not to make assumptions about a school based on how many students qualify for free lunch. Even schools that show high academic achievement might not teach in ways that work for every child, depending on their learning style and personality. I now know test scores don't tell the whole story and that a school that is great for one kid might not be the best for another. I would make the same decision again without hesitation for my daughter. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Car bombings in Russia kill military officer, injure ex-Ukraine PM adviser
events.summary: Moscow blames Kyiv for a series of car bombings that have targeted people linked to the war with Ukraine. A car bombing in Moscow has critically injured an adviser to Ukraine’s former prime minister a day after a similar attack killed a military officer in St Petersburg. The explosion on Friday was the latest in a series of bombings and shootings that have targeted people involved in the fighting in Ukraine. Moscow has blamed Kyiv for the attacks. list 1 of 3 Ukraine claims record 3,000 Russian casualties in one day as war drags on list 2 of 3 Why is Ukraine attacking Russian warships in the Baltic Sea amid talks? list 3 of 3 Russia and Ukraine report overnight attacks amid US diplomatic push The Moscow explosion struck a car driven by Sergei Zavorotnyi, who previously worked as an adviser to former Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov, according to Russia’s Investigative Committee. Zavorotnyi was hospitalised with injuries, the committee added. It did not identify possible suspects pending a criminal inquiry. Azarov served as prime minister under Ukraine’s Moscow-friendly President Viktor Yanukovych, who was forced from office by protesters and fled to Russia in February 2014. Azarov, who also lives in Russia, told state-run TV that he was “shocked” by the attack that left his former adviser critically injured. He said he believes Zavorotnyi was targeted because of his criticism of the Ukrainian government. Zavorotnyi. 72, had worked as a journalist for Russia’s daily Komsomolskaya Pravda before becoming Azarov’s adviser. He wrote a book about Yanukovych’s ouster and ran an online outlet critical of Ukrainian authorities. Russia’s REN TV channel said he lost his left arm, suffered multiple other injuries and was in a coma after the explosion. Explosive devices triggered remotely Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said an explosive device was reportedly planted under the man’s car and detonated remotely as he was driving on Friday. “The investigative committee has already launched a criminal case into this explosion,” she said. A day earlier, in St Petersburg, a military serviceman was killed by a bomb in his vehicle, according to Russia’s Investigative Committee. It did not identify the victim or say who could be behind the bombing. The Fontanka news outlet said Thursday’s victim was a colonel, while other Russian online media said the victim was a senior air force officer. Shapovalova said preliminary reports indicated that the victim was a military serviceman, rather than a colonel of the Russian Air Force. Like the attack on Friday, he was also driving the car when the bomb went off, she added. “In both cases an explosive device was triggered remotely, and it was planted under their car,” Shapovalova said. “Here in Russia, all the attacks are considered to be orchestrated by the Ukrainian side.” Ukrainian authorities have not commented on either bombing.

events.title: Republicans redrew North Carolina to win nearly two-thirds of its House seats — the blue wave left them poised to hold less than a third
events.summary: During the 2026 election cycle, Republicans enacted a series of gerrymanders – a form of partisan redistricting – in a handful of states to give them a disproportionate edge over Democrats in their congressional delegations. Democrats responded with a successful redistricting effort in California and an unsuccessful one in Virginia . Gerrymandering has obvious implications for fairness and democracy, characterized by some as politicians picking their voters, not voters picking their politicians. There’s also a practical consideration for those doing the gerrymandering: The efforts can fail when they overplay their hand. By spreading their supportive voters across many districts, parties can create more seats that may lean in their direction. But if spread too thin, these efforts can backfire and net seats for the other party, particularly in a “wave” election year that favors the other party. This unintended consequence is often referred to as a “dummymander .” So, with such massive Democratic majorities poised to enter the 120th Congress, did Republican attempts to gerrymander actually end up costing them some seats in the U.S. House? The answer isn’t as clear-cut as you might think. Dummymanders in North Carolina and Ohio? Republican state legislatures in Ohio and North Carolina redrew their congressional maps in 2025 , crafting a set of districts they believed would maximize the number of seats they could win in the House. Despite both states being traditionally competitive in statewide elections, their state legislatures drew a collection of seats Republicans believed they would win: 12 of these 15 new seats in Ohio and 11 out of 14 in North Carolina included a majority of voters who voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election. But in 2026, Democrats across the country won dozens of seats that had previously seemed out of reach, including districts Trump won by double digits in 2024. Many of these seats were in heavily gerrymandered Republican seats. In Ohio and North Carolina, the size and scope of the midterm backlash against Trump and his party put many of the seats Republicans targeted in these states, including ones Trump won by as many as 20 points, in serious jeopardy. In the end, the Democratic wave overcame so many Trump-won seats in these states that their new delegations to Congress may be more Democratic than they would have been without the gerrymanders. Democrats held the line in the deep South Texas and Florida also targeted a series of Democrat-held seats to flip their way in 2026. Nine such seats across these two states, as well as a vulnerable seat held by Democratic U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures in Alabama, were the targets of gerrymanders that created new districts that Trump won in 2024, all by 9 percentage points or more. But once the 2026 Democratic wave swept through the deep South, these gerrymanders were essentially canceled out. Despite the gains the party projected, Republicans in these three states appear likely to enter the 120th Congress with delegations the same size as they had in the 119th. Other Republican gerrymandering attempts were successful, but only barely. In Tennessee’s 9th District, the last remaining Democratic seat in the state was gerrymandered into a district Donald Trump won by 21 points in 2024. Republicans did hold that seat as expected, but only by 2,500 votes, or just over 1 percentage point. Gerrymanders that worked – and didn’t Many of these gerrymanders were not maximally successful. But were they true dummymanders? In North Carolina and Ohio it does appear that Republicans overplayed their hand by counting on past Trump voters in a national environment that proved so favorable to the Democrats. In Ohio, a gerrymander that aimed for a two-thirds Republican majority in their House delegation will net them less than half of that in the 120th Congress . That outcome ended up producing a more representative result, one that was roughly in line with the two parties’ 2026 popular vote shares in the state. North Carolina was a more drastic dummymander: The Republicans aimed to design districts where they would win seats accounting for almost two-thirds of their congressional delegation. But the party is currently poised to hold , at best, less than one-third of their state’s seats. And California, which Democrats gerrymandered in reaction to Republican efforts in other states, is a partisan success story . The state is projected to send only 8% of their delegation to the House as Republicans, despite voting 30% for Republicans statewide. In Texas and Florida the story is more complicated. Democrats in those states retained most of the seats they held that their Republican legislatures targeted in their gerrymanders, thanks to historic shifts by Hispanic voters who had voted for Trump in the 2024 election. But gerrymanders can be effective beyond marginal, targeted districts. Taken as a whole, Texas’ and Florida’s district boundaries were drawn so favorably for Republicans that even a Democratic tsunami managed only to keep these states’ delegations identical in the next Congress, since many other districts remained safe for Republicans. In these states, Republicans still enjoy a greater proportion of House seats than their popular vote margins would reflect. And in a less Democrat-leaning election cycle, many of these gerrymandered seats could very well shift back toward Republicans. Failed GOP gerrymanders would have produced an even bigger blue wave As poor as the outcome of the 2026 midterms was for Republicans, it could have been even worse. In fact, some Republican states might count themselves lucky that their attempts to gerrymander failed in the lead-up to the midterms. In traditionally Republican states such as Missouri and Utah , courts struck down gerrymanders that would have created a series of districts that Trump won by around 20 percentage points . If the gerrymanders had not been struck down, Democrats’ shocking success in similar districts across the country could have netted them as many as five additional seats in these states. A similar situation played out in Indiana and South Carolina . New maps pushed by Trump that failed in their state legislatures were intended to produce even more lopsided Republican gains. But analysis from the Cook Political Report found that these maps might have netted Democrats as many as six out of South Carolina’s seven House seats, and eight out of Indiana’s nine. Instead, Democrats seem likely to end up with only a pair of seats in each state. What’s next in gerrymandering wars? The 2026 election cycle demonstrates that gerrymandering is a far more complex and dynamic proposition than it is often treated by pundits and parties. Wave elections of this size can often overcome the intended effects of gerrymandered maps, but subsequent elections might find them much more effective. events.title: The Jensen Huang Nvidia affair recalls China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ that dates back 2,000 years
events.summary: Extramarital activities have led to the resignation of one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.” Huang stepped down following media reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies . She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company under U.S. scrutiny for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips. Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair . And amid reports of a second with a company executive who reports to him , he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026. The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as central to national security – has turned a company matter into an international issue. China’s Foreign Ministry has denied the espionage allegations and accused the U.S. of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets have been leaked. Yet part of what makes the accusations so believable is history is dotted with examples of men being distracted, compromised or spied on by attractive men and women deployed for that purpose. Indeed, in China it recalls an ancient political tactic known as “meiren ji” or the “ beauty stratagem .” As a scholar specializing in U.S.-China relations , I believe that regardless of the particulars of the Huang case, the political logic behind the beauty stratagem – using personal relationships to obtain information, influence decisions and weaken opponents – remains relevant today. As such, it would be no surprise if the tactic was being used amid the growing U.S.-China competition over AI and advanced semiconductors. The beauty stratagem of Ancient China “Meiren ji” is one of “ Thirty-Six Stratagems ,” a Chinese military text of uncertain origin but generally believed to have derived from oral and written histories from the Warring States period — 475–221 BCE. Its 31st stratagem states that personal relationships can be used to influence political opponents and recommends exploiting an adversary’s personal desires and emotional vulnerabilities to weaken their judgment and undermine their leadership. The “Thirty-Six Stratagems” is both a playbook for warfare and a reflection on past experience. Indeed, one of China’s most famous beauty stratagem stories dates back more than 2,000 years to the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history. In the fifth century BCE, King Goujian of Yue, in modern-day southern China, was defeated by King Fuchai of Wu, its northern neighbor, and forced to submit. But Goujian secretly rebuilt his strength and prepared for revenge. According to the ancient historical text “ Wu Yue Chun Qiu ,” Yue sent two beautiful women – Xi Shi and Zheng Dan – to Fuchai, hoping he would become distracted by pleasure and neglect state affairs. The plan reportedly worked. Fuchai, seemingly enchanted by the beautiful women, gradually ignored Yue’s threat. Meanwhile, Goujian prepared for war and in 473 BCE Yue conquered Wu. Xi Shi’s actual role in Wu’s downfall remains unclear. Wu’s defeat involved poor political decisions and Yue’s military recovery. Still, the story illustrated an important idea in Chinese political strategy: exploiting an opponent’s personal weaknesses can sometimes be more effective than confronting him directly. A similar tactic appears in the 14th-century novel “ Romance of the Three Kingdoms ,” considered one of the classics of Chinese literature. It tells the story of Dong Zhuo, a powerful warlord who controlled the imperial court during the late Eastern Han Dynasty. To remove him, Wang Yun, a senior court official loyal to the Han Dynasty promised a beautiful young woman, named Diaochan, in marriage to Dong Zhuo’s military commander. He then offered the same woman to Dong Zhuo. The scheme fueled jealousy and distrust between the two men, eventually enabling Wang Yun to persuade Dong Zhuo’s underling to kill him. Wang Yun then briefly took charge of the imperial court on behalf of the Han emperor. The ‘honey trap’ of modern spyware In modern intelligence operations, using romantic or sexual relationships to approach targets, obtain sensitive information or exert influence is commonly called a “ honey trap .” It is, moreover, certainly not unique to China. Western and Soviet intelligence agencies used intimate relationships for espionage frequently during the Cold War . Modern China also has documented cases. One example involves French diplomat Bernard Boursicot and the Chinese opera performer Shi Pei Pu . The pair met in Beijing in 1964 and maintained a long-term intimate relationship. Throughout, Boursicot was providing French diplomatic documents to China. The spying was eventually exposed and both involved were prosecuted for espionage in France in the 1980s. A more recent example involves former U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang , a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Swalwell acknowledged in 2015 that he had been physically intimate with Fang on several occasions. At the time, Fang helped raise funds for Swalwell’s campaign and helped place an intern in his congressional office. Why Jensen Huang is strategically important Jensen Huang’s position would make him a prime target for such a “honey trap” operation. His company has become central to the technological competition between the U.S and China. As AI becomes increasingly important to economic development, military capabilities and national security, moreover, Washington has repeatedly tightened restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China, hoping to slow its access to computing power. Beijing is investing heavily in domestic semiconductor development . Yet Chinese companies still need advanced chips to train AI models and build data centers. From Beijing’s perspective , advanced AI chips matter not only for Chinese technology companies but for future military and technological competition. This puts Nvidia in a particularly important position and helps explain the national security concerns surrounding Huang. However, strategic motives do not prove an intelligence operation occurred. Jensen Huang’s importance does not, in itself, establish that he was targeted by a honey trap or that Alice Huang acted for Chinese intelligence. Those are allegations that still require full investigation. Espionage in the age of AI Yet it is surely true that in modern politics – just as in ancient China’s rivalries – rivals seek information about opponents, try to influence important decisions and exploit weaknesses to gain strategic advantages. What has changed is who controls important strategic resources. In ancient China, influencing a ruler through personal relationships could affect a country’s political and military decisions. events.title: Email addresses used in European school bomb hoaxes spotted in old infostealer logs
events.summary: Two email addresses used to send bomb threats that disrupted thousands of Italian schools this week were found exposed in infostealer logs for over a year, experts say. Researchers at Hudson Rock looked into the two university email addresses used to send the bomb threats. One, from Egypt’s Kafrelsheikh University, was scooped up by Vidar – a cybercrime tool that steals saved account credentials and passwords from an infected computer and leaks them to attackers – as far back as October 2021. The other, from Taiwan's Dayeh University, was found among the 284 million addresses included in the massive AlienTXTBASE infostealer dump , dated February 2025. The experts said that the two addresses in infostealer logs do not strictly mean that those behind the bomb threats gained access to the accounts using the previous infostealer compromise. However, it suggests that there was ample time for the universities and Microsoft, which both universities used for authentication, to take action against the accounts that they should have been aware were appearing in infostealer logs. Modern threat intelligence has made infostealer logs highly visible. "Both findings place credential exposure well before the disruption, creating a substantial window in which exposed access could have been investigated and secured," Hudson Rock said . The researchers said that they would need access to details such as the email headers, and data from email providers, including sign-in events and audit records, that could show them more about who sent the email and from what session. Understanding whether the sender authenticated into the account could rule out spoofing, but would not in itself provide proof that the sender used a corresponding password taken from an infostealer log, Hudson Rock noted. There are many ways to get around password-based authentication . The researchers said that in any case where a credential is detected among infostealer logs, the organizations responsible for those accounts must contain them, revoke their access, rotate secrets, and go looking for suspicious activity. "The disruption illustrates why credential exposure deserves attention beyond fraud and data theft," the researchers said. "An account associated with an ordinary university user can become a means of reaching schools, frightening families, and consuming emergency resources." The threats Around 6,300 of Italy's 7,476 state schools received fake bomb threat emails between November 11-12, although only around 390 of them evacuated their respective buildings. The emails contained messaging such as "we will annihilate you," and "we will carry out genocide against Italians," and mention of a "powerful explosive device… with a remote trigger." Early reports suggested that the emails came from a Taiwanese email address and were signed by a "Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan" – a fictitious state or region roughly mapping to "the land of Misogyny," with "vilayat" meaning an administrative region of the Ottoman Empire. Various theories have been reported about the identity of the sender, ranging from a teacher based in the Philippines whose email was compromised to a Russia-backed disruption operation. Neither are confirmed. Russia denied any involvement. Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Thursday evening that there was no credence to the emails, and that whoever was behind the coordinated hoax sought to invoke chaos across the country. "To date, there is no evidence of a concrete danger," she said, ANSA reported. "These messages aren't intended to shock, they're intended to scare. "Those who write them are primarily seeking our fear, wasted days, suspicion, and chaos. Investigators and the judiciary, along with their European colleagues, are working to determine who is behind them." Schools in France, Ireland, Northern Ireland, and Scotland also received similar emails this week. None of the respective police forces believed the threats were legitimate. Hundreds of schools across the Republic of Ireland received the emails, as did news organizations such as RTÉ, which evacuated its Donnybrook campus, disrupting scheduled programming. Around 300 schools in Northern Ireland received bomb threats, although the PSNI said these were being treated as a hoax, and that the risk to the public was deemed low. Likewise, Police Scotland confirmed around 1,000 schools were affected by the email campaign and that the threats weren’t believed to be credible. In France, three school districts confirmed they received similar threats. Separately, domestic and international rail travel, including Eurostar services to London, were interrupted on Thursday following bomb threats made to Calais-Fréthun station. The latest wave of threats follows similar happenings at other types of organizations in recent weeks, including airline operators, air traffic controllers, and blood banks. At least 34 flights across various operators in Europe were affected earlier this month. Some were forced into unplanned landings, such as an Aer Lingus flight which pulled up to a French air base instead of its intended target of Rome. Military fighter jets were also scrambled to escort others in Italian and Austrian airspace. ®
