events.title: I tried 5 fast-food chicken sandwiches. The best one surprised me.
events.summary: I compared chicken sandwiches from McDonald's, Wendy's, Burger King, Popeyes, and Bojangles. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I tried chicken sandwiches from five fast-food chains. Among the sandwiches from McDonald's, Burger King, Wendy's, Popeyes, and Bojangles, one stood out. Bojangles, which just opened a new location in New York City, impressed me with its crispy filet. Chicken sandwiches have become a major fast-food battleground , with chains putting their own spin on the classic menu item with different buns, sauces, and toppings. I tried chicken sandwiches from McDonald's, Burger King, Wendy's , Popeyes, and Bojangles, weighing flavor, texture, toppings, and price to see which one was worth ordering. Each sandwich varied from classic, simply dressed options to bolder takes with Southern-inspired seasonings. Here's how five fast-food chicken sandwiches compared. McDonald's delivered a classic chicken sandwich without much fanfare. Erin McDowell/Business Insider McDonald's crispy chicken sandwich, aptly named the McCrispy, was released amid the 2021 chicken sandwich wars and is available in classic, spicy, and — as of January 27 — a new, limited-edition hot-honey flavor. It cost $7.69, excluding tax, at my local chain in Brooklyn, New York. The sandwich comes with a large chicken filet, two pickles, and mayonnaise. Erin McDowell/Business Insider When I opened it, I noticed the sandwich had a very light smattering of mayonnaise. As someone who loves condiments, I found this a little disappointing. I was eager to see how it would affect the taste. The chicken sandwich was juicy enough without the excess mayonnaise, but it lacked the distinct crunch I was looking for. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The sandwich was moist but almost soggy. The bun tasted pretty artificial but held the sandwich's contents together perfectly, and in terms of size, I thought McDonald's nailed the bun-to-chicken ratio. I'd order it again, but it didn't blow me away. Wendy's served up a pretty traditional chicken sandwich. Erin McDowell/Business Insider It came wrapped in paper and cost $9.11, excluding tax, at my local Wendy's in Brooklyn, New York. It came topped with lettuce, tomato, pickles, and mayonnaise. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The lettuce looked a little limp on first inspection, and there wasn't much of it either. However, the chicken filet was large — it was practically spilling out of the bun. Unfortunately, this chicken sandwich was underwhelming. Erin McDowell/Business Insider While this sandwich impressed me in terms of size, the texture of the chicken filet let it down. It wasn't nearly as crispy as I would have liked, and it bordered on soggy. The toppings also lacked flavor, though the bun was soft and buttery, which I enjoyed. Even though it was the most expensive sandwich, I didn't think it lived up to expectations. Burger King's classic chicken sandwich was up next. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Burger King offers a few different chicken sandwiches — this classic Royal Crispy chicken sandwich, a spicy version, one with bacon and Swiss cheese, and its older original chicken sandwich, which is served in a longer bun with just lettuce and mayonnaise. The classic Royal Crispy chicken sandwich costs $7.49, excluding tax, at my local Burger King in Brooklyn, New York. Burger King's chicken sandwich comes topped with lettuce, tomato, and mayonnaise. Erin McDowell/Business Insider This was different than the more Southern flavor profiles served at chains like Popeyes, McDonald's, and Chick-fil-A. The amount of toppings was generous, I thought. Thick slices of tomato and lettuce leaves covered the entire chicken filet, and plenty of mayonnaise was smeared on top of its fluffy potato bun. The chicken filet was thick and juicy, but I wasn't crazy about the toppings. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The tomato tasted a little limp, and the lettuce lacked a distinct crunch. However, the chicken itself really impressed me — it was thick and tender, with a rich, briny flavor that I enjoyed. I also liked the bun, which was fluffy but sturdy enough to hold the sandwich together. I was left wishing the sandwich came with just mayonnaise and pickles, so the chicken could really shine through. Popeyes had a great chicken sandwich, even though it wasn't my favorite. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Popeyes practically invented the chicken sandwich wars after it introduced its signature sandwich in 2019, sparking fistfights, lengthy lines, and a ton of online discourse. The sandwich may not be as talked about as it once was, but it's still a fan favorite. It cost $7.99, excluding tax. The sandwich came with a more generous serving of mayonnaise and two thick pickle slices. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Popeyes puts mayonnaise on both buns and layers pickles under the chicken filet, setting it apart from other chains. The sandwich was delicious, but it didn't have quite the same impactful flavor as the winner. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The chicken filet crunched and flaked with every bite, and the thick pickle slices were actually tart — they certainly weren't just for show. The sandwich was also moist and tender, without being a soggy mess. Overall, I was impressed. However, another chain clinched the win. Bojangles' chicken sandwich delivered the most on taste and value. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The sandwich, which the chain updated in the aftermath of the chicken sandwich wars, features a large fried chicken filet on a buttery brioche bun. Its flavor profile is classically Southern, built around fried chicken, pickles, and mayonnaise. The chicken sandwich cost $8.74, excluding tax. The chicken filet is marinated in Bojangles' signature blend of spices and buttermilk. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Like the other chicken sandwiches, Bojangles' chicken sandwich was topped with mayonnaise, but it was thicker than the mayonnaise from other chains. It also came with two crunchy pickle slices. Bojangles' process of marinating its chicken helped to infuse flavor deep into the meat rather than just coating the surface. What really stood out to me, though, was the texture. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The filet was hand-breaded and fried in-store, creating an extra-crispy, craggy coating that delivered a satisfying crunch with every bite. The pickles added even more crunch, with a bright, briny flavor that cut through the richness of the fried chicken. The sandwich also had a subtle kick from the marinade — it wasn't overwhelmingly spicy, but it was enough to add flavor and keep each bite interesting. Together, the crispy breading and flavorful filet created a layered texture and flavor profile that set the sandwich apart from its competitors. The chicken sandwich wars are over — for me at least. I declare this sandwich the winner. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Sixth victim confirmed in DC condo-related shooting in US, police say
events.summary: Police confirm sixth victim in DC condo shooting; suspect dead after barricading himself and starting a fire. Police have said a sixth person was shot on Thursday morning in Washington, DC , bringing the toll to one person killed and five wounded in an attack they believe was linked to a dispute over maintenance issues in a condo building. In an updated statement, the Metropolitan Police Department said investigators had found a sixth victim, a woman, after officers initially located five other victims. list 1 of 4 Suspect turns gun on himself after deadly shooting in Washington DC list 2 of 4 What to know about the Logan Circle shooting in Washington, DC list 3 of 4 Deadly shooting in Washington DC list 4 of 4 Washington residents hold vigil after deadly shooting She was conscious and breathing with a “non-life-threatening gunshot graze wound”. “The victim self-treated the wound,” police said. Two women and two men were taken to hospital, all conscious and breathing. James Stuart, the 46-year-old manager of the building in which the suspect lived, died at the scene. Police believe the suspect, a 55-year-old doctor named Matt Wade Lambert, targeted Stuart while Stuart was doing his morning workout at the gym. The shooting started just before 8am local time (13:00 GMT) at a VIDA Fitness gym in the city’s Logan Circle neighbourhood, about a mile north of the White House. Police said Lambert shot Stuart inside the gym on the ground floor of the building before going back to his apartment on the seventh floor and firing on people below from his patio. Five others, some of whom had been working at a construction site across the street. Police have not detailed the circumstances in which the sixth victim was shot. The shootings unfolded in less than five minutes, according to interim police chief Jeffery Carroll. Lambert then barricaded himself inside his apartment, where he talked to police negotiators over the phone. Police say he fired at least twice through the door while officers were outside, but no officers were injured. He also broke the gas line connected to his fireplace and started a fire, which the building’s sprinkler system contained. Police said Lambert spent most of the conversation with negotiators talking about the dispute with building management. “Most of the conversation was about the homeowners associations and challenges with that,” said Carroll. “While our negotiators were communicating with the suspect, they did hear a single gunshot,” he said, adding that Lambert then stopped talking. When tactical officers forced their way into the apartment, they found him dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound. Police said inside the apartment, they found a shotgun, a rifle, and a handgun, all of which had been used in the shooting. According to court records cited by The Associated Press, Lambert had filed a lawsuit alleging that he had not been able to enjoy his penthouse since 2024 because of mould, moisture and water problems that began after work had been done on the building’s exterior. The lawsuit was ongoing, and Lambert appeared to have shared details of the dispute, including photos and an engineering report on an X account called ofMiceandMold. His lawyer, Joel Braithwaite, told reporters on Thursday that the condo where Lambert had lived since 2017 looked like “a warzone” and that Lambert had spent more than $300,000 on the lawsuit.

events.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
events.summary: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates. events.title: Ford throws open the doors to its new Vault, unveiling 125 rare historic vehicles
events.summary: Ford is throwing open the doors of its historic vehicle collection at the new Vault in Romulus, Michigan ROMULUS, Mich. -- Ford will open the doors to its new Vault this weekend to some lucky gearheads and fans of history. The 123-year-old carmaker on Saturday will allow select members of the public and employees into the Ford Vault to take a gander at everything from rare concept cars and Hollywood Mustangs to historic police cruisers and even a 1938 ambulance. Tickets were snapped up quickly, but Ford Motor Co. said there will be future showings. “You don’t create an experience like this and a space like this and then hide it away,” said Ted Ryan, Ford’s Archives and Heritage Brand Manager. “We’re going to find a way to make it available to the car community in Michigan as soon as we can.” Ford’s collection of historic vehicles once was housed at its Dearborn, Michigan, headquarters and other locations. Its vast new home, the Vault, is situated inside a former Amazon fulfillment center in Romulus, another Detroit suburb, and measures 79,000 square feet (7,339 square meters). “I can tell you, after working here for a couple weeks, I'm averaging about 20,000 steps a day,” said Ryan. The Vault brings together 125 of the Heritage Fleet's historically significant vehicles, including race cars, design concepts and vehicles tied to pop culture. “Here, we can actually have a purpose-built space for the cars,” Ford Archives Manager Ciera Casteel said. “That's our legacy. That's what we do here. That is what this company is.” Microsoft apologizes for email disruption, says AI agents not responsible Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE — A 2005 Mustang GT proof-of-concept that paved the way for the Shelby GT350. Engineers nicknamed it “Johnny Cash” (inspired by his song “One Piece at a Time,” about an autoworker who cobbles together a car out of mismatched parts). “It's like Frankenstein. Things have been bolted onto Johnny over the years. This is the first time he's ever been displayed,” Ryan said. — The first three cars to cross the finish line at Le Mans in 1966, a race immortalized in the 2019 Matt Damon/Christian Bale film, “Ford v Ferrari.” — A 1910 right-hand-drive Model T that was built in the U.K. and remained there until 2025, when it was added to the Heritage Fleet. — A 1973 Mustang convertible used in "The Mary Tyler Moore Show.” The vehicle was sold in 1974, and remained in private ownership until Ford bought it last year. The body underwent a restoration in 1999, while the interior remains original. The carmaker built the Vault to be a working archive, giving today’s designers and engineers access to the ideas and experiments that shaped the company as they work on what comes next. “There's ‘surprise and delight’ moments throughout the building,” Ryan said. 8 dead, including 2 children, after building collapses in Brooklyn 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

events.title: US Treasury warns against rate hikes during US-Iran war energy ‘shock’
events.summary: Despite Treasury’s Scott Bessent’s remarks, financial tracker CME Fed Watch forecasts rate hike in December likely. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called on the Federal Reserve not to hike interest rates because of an “energy supply shock” tied to the US-led conflict with Iran. “I think the Fed should understand that this is an energy supply shock,” while the underlying US economy is very strong, Bessent said in an interview on CNBC on Friday. list 1 of 4 US sanctions Indian and Turkish firms accused of helping Iran list 2 of 4 US Treasury sanctions eight Canadian money exchange firms over Iran ties list 3 of 4 US Treasury chief Bessent moved to military base after ‘Iranian threats’ list 4 of 4 Bessent’s relocation: From US to EU, is Iran bringing war to Western soil? “So I think that to hike too much into an energy supply shock when it’s coming down, these are very noisy numbers,” he said. “The Fed’s supposed to look into the future, not look in the rearview mirror.” The central bank opted to maintain interest rates during its last policy meeting, leaving them at 3.75 to 4 percent. CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, forecasts an 89.4 percent chance that rates will be raised to 4.00–4.25 percent at the next meeting, scheduled for December 9. Despite pressure from the White House to cut interest rates, the Federal Reserve has held them steady amid inflationary pressures stemming from the US-Israeli war on Iran . Since the conflict began, the Fed has maintained rates five times and raised them once. Much of that pressure has come from rising energy prices. By September, energy prices had climbed 20.4 percent year over year. Although October’s energy price data has since been released, the Labour Department was unable to collect data in October 2025 because of last year’s government shutdown. As a result, it cannot provide a year-over-year comparison for October 2026. Bessent’s remarks come amid a stronger-than-expected US jobs report, which bolsters the case for rate hikes. The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, according to the Labour Department’s release last Friday. “I’m not going to tell the Fed what to do. I am going to say they should have an open mind,” Bessent said. The Fed made three rate cuts over the same period last year, he noted. “And now to reverse just based on an energy supply shock, a reversal in a dramatic way isn’t something that I would do if I were on the Fed. But I’m not on the Fed.” Bessent’s remarks come as some top Fed officials are pushing for the opposite. On Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he planned to support a quarter-point increase at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting unless the core consumer price index — one of the central bank’s key measures for assessing the rate of inflation — came in at 0.3 percent or more. “In that case, I believe a 50-basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting,” he said at a conference in London hosted by King’s Business School and the Money Macro and Finance Society. The CPI report subsequently came out, showing a 0.4 percent monthly increase. Consumers are feeling the rising costs at the petrol pump, as prices are declining but remain high. The average price for a gallon of petrol is $3.87 ($1.02 per litre), down from $4.34 ($1.14 per litre)this time a month ago, but still well above the $2.98 ($0.79 per litre) price recorded on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran.

events.title: Jaguar Land Rover reports £451m quarterly loss after cutting 4,000 jobs
events.summary: JLR chief executive calls for EU and Britain to join forces amid competition from Chinese electric carmakers Jaguar Land Rover has reported a £451m quarterly loss as it counts the cost of cutting 4,000 jobs, while its chief executive has called for the EU and Britain to work together in the face of competition from China. Britain’s largest automotive employer reported revenues rising to £5.9bn between July and September, but it recorded £530m in costs from the job cuts announced near the end of that period amid tough trading conditions. JLR said it expected the vast majority of the job cuts to be achieved via voluntary redundancies, with 3,000 already confirmed. Most of those people will leave at the end of November. JLR said it had scraped into profit from its operations if it ignored the restructuring costs, but it was hurt by falling sales in China and the Middle East. Many European carmakers are struggling as they face competition from Chinese rivals at the same time as they invest in electric car production. PB Balaji, JLR’s chief executive, said on Friday the “onslaught of competition” from China meant the UK and EU should stop plans for new post-Brexit trade barriers on each other. The automotive industry is lobbying the UK and EU intensely to delay the implementation of “rules of origin” on 1 January, which threaten to impose 10% tariffs on UK-EU electric cars that use batteries from Asia. The EU is also considering “made in Europe” rules that would lock UK-made cars out of subsidies. “Now is the time for actually fostering this entire electrical ecosystem,” Balaji said. “It’s so important for us that we all hold hands, stick together and ensure that we get the system to evolve into the world of electrics.” He added: “We just need time to ensure all these plans start coming into fruition.” The company, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata, previously sought to target China for growth, only to write off billions in investments in 2019 as a new wave of Chinese carmakers led to massive overcapacity in the country. The hardware giant already supplies its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems E2000 in all-flash, all-disk, tiered and hybrid configurations, but - we're told - the latest combination offers up to 41 percent more data throughput per storage rack. The E2000 line embeds the Lustre open-source parallel file system, and is generally intended to fit NVMe Gen 5 solid-state drive (SSD) building blocks. For the refreshed hybrid configurations, HPE is combining SSDs with new 32 TB SAS-4 (24 Gb/s SAS) HDDs and new enclosures supporting 74 or 100 drives. HPE says it'll deliver up to 116 GB/s of read throughput and 92 GB/s of write throughput per rack, with up to 32 percent more usable storage capacity per rack for expansion to support the growing size of datasets in HPC, especially where sites are mixing AI and traditional simulation-style workloads. One of the reasons behind these new hybrid configurations could be the ballooning cost of storage, caused by the relentless demand for AI infrastructure skewing the price of components such as memory and many other things. But prices for silicon-based NAND flash SSDs are growing faster than those of good old hard drives , as our colleagues at Blocks & Files reported. HPE says that as demand for data-intensive workloads grows, prices for large SSDs have soared. The company claims the new hybrid configurations let research institutions and national laboratories spend less on storage and put that money toward compute node purchases, without giving up on the performance they need. “When making long-term investments in environments where advanced workloads are rapidly evolving, our customers want scalable, dense, and flexible systems to help them address dynamic shifts in requirements," said Trish Damkroger, HPE senior veep for HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions. The latest hybrid configurations are expected to go on sale in early 2027. HPE's other introduction is a Rack Management Controller, providing what HPE calls "intelligent liquid cooling” via real-time monitoring, leak detection and automated control features. It integrates with HPE Supercomputing Management Software to gather telemetry and provide control. Several platform-specific versions will be offered, each tailored to different rack-scale systems. Support will launch with HPE's own Cray Supercomputing GX5000 infrastructure, naturally, with versions for Nvidia’s NVL72 and AMD’s Helion and Helios kit to follow. events.title: Inside the aftermath of the Logan Circle shooting
events.summary: It took just minutes for a gunman to shoot six people and upend one of D.C.'s busiest neighborhoods. The big picture: Thursday morning's violence left one person dead in a Logan Circle gym and five others injured nearby. The gunman later shot himself, police said. The massive police response shut down streets, sent nearly a dozen schools into lockdown and forced residents to shelter in place. By evening, the streets around VIDA Fitness, where the shooting began, were quiet. Several nearby businesses remained closed, with police tape blocking off storefronts and officers standing watch. Councilmember Brooke Pinto held a vigil . People left flowers and notes outside of the VIDA . "Logan Circle is still a place for love," read one. "VIDA, you are and will continue to be a safe haven for many," read another. But life also carried on: A delivery van unloaded Christmas trees at Whole Foods, and 14th Street bars put out signs advertising happy hour. Flowers and handwritten notes line the outside of VIDA Fitness. Photo: Mimi Montgomery/Axios One note reads: "VIDA, you are and will continue to be a safe haven for many." Photo: Mimi Montgomery/Axios What we know: At an afternoon press conference, interim MPD chief Jeffery W. Carroll identified the suspect as 55-year-old Matt Wade Lambert, who lived in the apartment building connected to VIDA Fitness. The man killed was 46-year-old James Stuart, the building's manager and a Northwest D.C. resident, Carroll said. Police believe the shooting was linked to an ongoing dispute between Lambert and his condominium association over maintenance issues, including mold. The timeline: Police responded to a shooting inside VIDA Fitness, at 15th and P streets NW, just before 8am. Additional reports of shootings nearby followed. Carroll said the shootings themselves likely unfolded in less than five minutes, though investigators are still reconstructing the timeline. Police announced a sixth shooting victim — a woman with nonfatal injuries — on Friday morning, per the Washington Post . The victims: Stuart was pronounced dead inside VIDA. Police say the gunman then returned to his apartment, where he fired at people below from an upper-level private balcony. Two men and two women were hospitalized, one of whom suffered serious injuries. The standoff: Lambert barricaded himself in his apartment, where he broke a gas line connected to his fireplace and started a fire inside the apartment, per police. Flames were visible outside the building, but sprinklers helped contain the blaze. Police recovered gasoline and other flammable materials. Police negotiators heard a gunshot while speaking with Lambert by phone, after which he stopped responding. Officers forced entry and found him suffering from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The weapons: Investigators recovered a handgun, shotgun and rifle from Lambert's apartment. Carroll said the suspect used all three firearms, none of which were registered in D.C. People stand behind police tape in Logan Circle early Thursday. Photo: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images A U.S. Park Police helicopter flies above the scene. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images U.S. Marshal officers move position at the scene of the Logan Circle shooting. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Residents cross a street as law enforcement responds to the shooting. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Behind the scenes: Lambert had been fighting his condo association over alleged leaks and mold, per court records. He filed a lawsuit against the group in March 2025. Months later, he told now- Washington Sun reporter Michael Brice-Saddler that he'd spent nearly $200,000 on legal and engineering fees. In those interviews, Lambert said he knew Stuart's daily gym routine. What we don't know: Police have not determined whether Lambert knew the five surviving victims or deliberately targeted them. The precise timeline and extent of the suspected planning also remain under investigation. Context: The shooting prompted a massive response from local and federal authorities, including MPD, D.C. Fire and EMS, U.S. Park Police, Metro Transit Police and other federal law enforcement agencies. Asked whether the show of force was due to the shooting's proximity to the White House, roughly a mile away, Carroll said it was because police were responding to an active shooter. "The expectation is folks will go there to try to stop the loss of life," he said. Mayor Bowser confirmed the White House had been briefed. President Trump has surged federal law enforcement in D.C. through his Safe and Beautiful Task Force . In a speech before the midterms last week, Trump declared D.C. "one of the safest cities in the country." Asked about Trump's role in reducing crime during Thursday's morning briefing, Bowser pushed back: "I praise MPD for bringing down crime in the city, and I praise our prosecutors." Editors note: This story has been updated to add details about a sixth shooting victim.

events.title: Truck and bus crash in India’s Assam state kills at least 24 people

events.title: UK-EU deal will ‘dissolve’ £60m a year of costs for plant trade, says Angela Eagle
events.summary: Signing of agreement to smooth movement of food, plants and animals next week will not recoup huge sums firms were forced to spend The removal of border checks and paperwork on plant imports will “dissolve” £60m of annual costs for the horticulture industry when the UK and EU’s new post-Brexit deal comes in, the environment secretary has said. Before the UK-EU summit on 20 November , Angela Eagle said she hoped paperwork headaches for importers would “disappear” after the changes, although the move would not help businesses recoup the large sums they spent to deal with border controls. “If we get the ink dry on 20 November, which I very much hope we will … all of that uncertainty, the extra cost, the paperwork and the potential problems if things get stuck at borders would all disappear,” Eagle told the Guardian during a visit to a plant nursery in Kent. “The cost, that £60m, can just dissolve and people’s potential to both export back into the EU and get their imports in … gets easier and more predictable.” The UK’s departure from the bloc triggered the introduction of border checks on imports and exports of plants, food and animal products, from sausages and cheese to trees and leather goods. Exports of British food and drink to the EU have collapsed by more than a third since Brexit, according to analysis by the National Farmers’ Union, with egg, chicken and potato producers badly affected. The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal, largely agreed between the two sides in May , is due to be signed at next week’s summit. It will permit the removal of the vast majority of physical checks and most of the accompanying certificates and paperwork. This will save businesses in the horticulture sector the current cost of trading with Europe , including plant health inspection fees, phytosanitary certificates, document and ID checks, port fees, agents’ fees, additional labour costs and extra haulage costs. These costs total £60m a year, according to calculations by the industry body the Horticultural Trades Association (HTA), but do not include late delivery penalties or sales lost because of port delays or damage to goods. These savings should put “downward pressure on food prices”, Eagle said, although she would not confirm the deal would lower the cost of food in the UK. The promise of the deal was welcomed by Provender Nurseries, one of the UK’s largest wholesale nurseries, which sells thousands of plants, trees and shrubs to local authorities, parks and landscapers from its base at Swanley in Kent. However, the company has already spent at least £500,000 on building a post-Brexit control post on its eight-hectare (20-acre) site, which will become obsolete once the deal is implemented. Richard McKenna, the managing director of Provender, said the business constructed the “sealed building and bought four electric forklifts to operate in it” to allow inspections of lorry loads of valuable trees and shrubs imported from the continent. The company decided to build the site to reduce the “delays and damage” it had experienced when smaller loads were inspected at government-run border control posts such as Sevington . “It cost a lot for a barn, but it gave us security as a business,” said McKenna. Despite this, McKenna hopes the SPS deal will convince some of Provender’s European suppliers, previously deterred by the paperwork and potential pitfalls of post-Brexit trade with the UK, to restart exports. “We need to see the small print on the agreement,” he said. “It could have been sooner, but we are pleased that it is happening.” The deal is not expected to be implemented until the first quarter of 2028, meaning businesses such as Provender will still be subject to the current border arrangements for more than a year. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning In the meantime, Fran Barnes, the chief executive of the HTA, called for “some easements as a transition arrangement that are pragmatic” to help horticulture businesses, such as fewer or no checks on imports of lower-risk products. Eagle conceded the implementation date was later than the mid-2027 targeted when the former prime minister Keir Starmer announced his EU “reset” deal in May 2025. Starmer’s replacement by Andy Burnham led to a “pause” in negotiations with Brussels, said Eagle, with the upcoming November summit pushed back from July. The original target was “always a very, very ambitious timescale,” she said. “That extra time has meant we could deal in a more coherent way with some of the knottier, thornier issues on things like pesticides.” The UK has continued to use some pesticides and fungicides that are banned in the EU . This has prompted industry concerns that British potatoes grown in 2027, treated with pesticides banned in the EU, could need to be thrown away if the resulting frozen chips went on sale after the deal’s implementation.

events.title: ChatGPT’s new Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out for you
events.summary: ChatGPT can now shop for you. On Friday, OpenAI launched a new wallet feature that lets its agents, called dots , help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf. The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express. OpenAI says that users are fully in control of the purchases, as they’re able to review the items, the total, and the payment card that will be used to complete the transaction before the checkout occurs. In addition, users will approve the purchases directly with a security check like Face ID or a fingerprint, which creates a record of their transaction. The addition comes as consumer-facing AI tools are working to find the right product-market fit, in terms of how they can help people be more efficient as they complete various tasks. While companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity on its app. Other personal AI agents, like Instinct, also support making purchases on users’ behalf. It’s no surprise, then, that OpenAI would want to enter this space more with an agentic shopping feature of its own. To get started, ChatGPT subscribers add their eligible payment cards to the new ChatGPT Wallet, then ask their dot to help with a purchase. (This setup is a one-time thing; users don’t have to re-enter their payment information every time they buy.) When it’s time to transact, ChatGPT’s Wallet charges the selected card using a payment token, which is a substitute for the user’s actual card details, so that information isn’t shared with either the dot or the merchant. The merchant will automatically receive what it needs to fulfill the order from the dot, like the shipping address and contact information, OpenAI says. The company notes that customers who shop via their dots will still be able to earn their credit card rewards and be able to take advantage of protections that typically come with cards, like being able to dispute transactions. The limited availability at launch will allow OpenAI to test and improve the feature and its capabilities before rolling it out more broadly. In the future, the company plans to offer users more control over the feature by allowing them to set spending limits or configure other parameters around purchase categories or time periods, so they can pre-approve purchases that their agent can then handle more autonomously. It also aims to make the agentic shopping feature an option at a broader number of supported retailers. This could be a challenge in some areas, where retailers are blocking AI agents from using their site ; on the shopping front, the largest retailer to ban AI agents is Amazon, as it aims to steer users to its own AI agent, Alexa, instead. To help retailers adapt to agentic commerce, OpenAI also published a Commerce Partner Playbook that offers tools and guidance to sites that want to support customers using agents. events.title: Women are taking pay cuts and 'white-knuckling it' to manage menopause and work: 'I feel like I'm sitting on the sidelines'
events.summary: Save and Invest Why everyday Americans may choose to work until they die Work Why this startup gave workers a month to work from anywhere in the world Work These women were laid off on mat leave. It's legal—and a persistent issue Health and Wellness How staying close to your grandparents may benefit their health Work Shonda Rhimes says she was a micromanager, 'pain in the butt' early in career Around 2020, Amy Terry noticed she didn't feel like her usual self. The 50-year-old Michigander was working as a director of programming at a health association when she says she began experiencing symptoms like memory loss, low energy, mental processing difficulties — or, as she describes it, "waking up every day feeling like you were slogging through mud." "I went from being this highly competent professional person to barely being able to get through phone calls," Terry says. As the healthcare system strained under the weight of the Covid-19 pandemic, Terry, like many other people, struggled to get care. When she finally did, she found out it wasn't Covid-19. It was perimenopause. Terry got through a few more years juggling her symptoms with her job, but by 2023, she couldn't hold out any longer. She quit to start independent consulting. Women, and some trans and non-binary people, often experience career setbacks stemming from menopause that can hurt them financially and professionally. Four in 10 women who have experienced menopause or perimenopause say it has negatively affected their life or work, according to a recent survey of over 3,800 U.S. women from Gallup and Melinda French Gates' Pivotal, a group of organizations focused on social progress for women and young people. Of them, roughly 28% felt limited in the effort they could give at work, 15% decided against pursuing a promotion or leadership role, 12% reduced their hours, and 10% took an extended leave from work or didn't return. "This isn't just a health issue," says Jasmine Escalera, career expert at resume builder site LiveCareer. "It's a workplace issue." A 2023 Mayo Clinic study estimated menopause symptoms drove $1.8 billion in lost work time per year in the U.S. alone. Perimenopause, the transitional period before menopause, typically begins in one's 40s and can last several years, often bringing symptoms like hot flashes, sleep issues, irritability and lower energy, according to the Office on Women's Health . Menopause typically occurs in one's 50s and marks 12 months since a person's last period, but is often used colloquially to include the preceding perimenopause as well. The timing of menopause can create a perfect storm. It frequently comes at a time in many women's careers when they're breaking into leadership or approaching their peak earning years , which is often between the ages of 35 and 44 for women, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It also typically happens when many are caregiving for aging parents or raising children. This can make for an impossible choice for many women. "Women have fought so hard for their place in the workforce," says Mimi Wied, who began perimenopause around a decade ago. "They don't want to lose it by looking like they can't handle it." The career consequences for women "may increase the gaps we're trying to decrease," Escalera says, referring to disparities such as those in women's pay and senior-level representation relative to men. "That is a definite talent breakdown." For Terry, becoming an independent consultant cost her employer-sponsored healthcare at the time she most needed it. It also drastically changed her income: She says she took around an 85% pay cut in the transition. "These are supposed to be my highest-earning years," Terry says, "and I feel like I'm sitting on the sidelines." Many women are unprepared for menopause because of social stigma around discussing it, poor health education and dismissal of women's health issues. "I've been in the healthcare environment for 30 years; if I can't figure this out, I don't know how anyone can," says Terry. Wied also says she didn't know what to expect. The answer quickly became apparent: The 48-year-old from Brenham, Texas, says she experienced everything from night sweats and sleeplessness to anxiety and rage. "Sometimes I didn't feel in control of my own mouth and my body and my actions," she says. Wied left her job as a museum docent for a secretarial role paying roughly $20,000 less when she worried her irritability would affect her capacity to help visitors, she says: "If I could have quit working, I would have." When women do scale back at work because of menopause, they may struggle to regain that professional ground later. Terry's job switch wasn't just downshifting to a part-time role: "It's an entire change in the trajectory of your career," she says.

events.title: Jensen Huang and the End of the Founder Fairy Tale
events.summary: It was July of 2024, and Jensen Huang was punchy. I had agreed to travel to Denver, Colorado, to interview the Nvidia CEO at SIGGRAPH, the annual confab of computer graphics PhDs and practitioners. Early that year I’d conducted a lengthy sit-down interview with Huang for a WIRED magazine feature, which apparently went well enough—both for WIRED and for Nvidia’s executive communications team—that I had been asked to interview Huang again at this conference. Another opportunity to grill the CEO of the modern world’s most consequential company? Yes, of course. I began preparing. What ensued was, in a word, bizarre. During the first prep call for the conference, the type of call-in which PR handlers typically try to coax specific questions out of journalists to prevent an ambush, a youngish, vaguely familiar woman took the lead. This was Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter. She was clearly intelligent, commanding respect. She told me about the slides Jensen would be presenting on stage at SIGGRAPH and offered suggestions for key moments when I might tee him up to talk about the slides. Slides? Tee up Jensen? What kind of “interview” was this? I raised my concerns with both my editors and Nvidia. We agreed that I would ask the questions I intended to ask him, which included questions about the environmental impact of data centers, and that Huang would also be referring to slides. Let’s just say the interview didn’t go smoothly. (It’s on YouTube .) To this day, former and current Nvidia workers sometimes tell me that I “handled” the whole thing well. Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and, immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me. Then I was guided offstage, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg hopped on, where he and Huang had a lovey-dovey fireside chat. As a longtime journalist I’m used to occasional adversarial interactions; I really don’t lose sleep over them. This was just a CEO being a CEO. Huang later agreed to meet with me again, in December 2024. But that interview in Denver had underscored for me how much Jensen Huang wanted to control the narrative. Not just wanted to; he assumed he would . And to a large extent he did. Until this week. Narrative has always been a critical part of Huang’s success. He was not just your average electrical engineering nerd who toiled away on something that would eventually find a product-market fit. By Huang’s own telling, he was an immigrant founder, an underdog, a wife guy who chased (and eventually married) his college sweetheart, a scrappy startup guy who dined at Denny’s in the early days. A visionary who worked Sundays and who didn’t sleep well because he always heard the hoof steps of competitors. A parent who brought his kids into the corporate fold. A man who loved Nvidia so much he tattooed an abstract version of the company logo on his arm. Huang built the highest-valued publicly traded company in history. That part’s not just fairy tale. It’s true. Now, it’s starting to read more like a Greek tragedy. Back in January 2024, when I sat down with him for our first-ever in-person meeting, Huang right off the bat talked about the importance of storytelling. Here’s an excerpt: Jensen Huang: Somebody who I really admire, as a leader and a person, is Shantanu Narayen, the CEO of Adobe. He said he always wanted to be a journalist because he loved telling stories. WIRED: It seems like an important part of building a business, being able to tell its story effectively. Yes. Strategy setting is storytelling. Culture building is storytelling. You’ve said many times you didn’t sell the idea of Nvidia based on a pitch deck. That’s right. It was really about telling the story. Of course, even then, Huang was caught up in the crosshairs of the US–China AI war and at the mercy of regulators, as I wrote at the time. After Donald Trump’s reelection that year, Huang once again deployed his storytelling skills and lobbied the Trump administration to loosen export controls, so he could sell some of his company’s chips to China. Another crucial part of the Huang lore is that he ran a “flat” organization, with a few dozen top executives reporting to him. (This is sometimes reported as being “60” people; insiders have told me at times it’s closer to 35.) Huang once said the structure allowed Nvidia “to adapt a lot more quickly, which we need because our technology is moving so quickly.” Huang was also known to be controlling of all aspects of the business—participating in every significant meeting, seemingly aware of every moving part, and staying in the loop on sourcing, supply chains, and the company’s allocation of chips. This is where Huang’s cult of leadership, and his Nvidia storytelling, may have come to a stupidly disappointing final chapter.

Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen's blunder will rock the world 2 hours ago Microsoft 365 services are slowly recovering from a prolonged outage that has handed critics of single-vendor dependence a particularly unwelcome case study. Ever wondered what it would be like if your IT supplier abruptly pulled the plug? Perhaps the result of a mood swing by an unpredictable political leader? For affected Microsoft customers, the disruption has offered an unwelcome preview. Email? Gone. Messaging with Teams? Iffy. Collaboration? Nope. The list of problems in what Microsoft delicately called a "Service Degradation" is breathtaking. The company put the incident's start at 1826 GMT on November 12. Exchange Online fell over. Viewing recently used files in the Microsoft 365 application was problematic. Copilot threw a wobbly. Microsoft 365 Education was affected (unfortunate, considering the changes the company has made ), and so on. At 1401 GMT on November 13, Microsoft reported: "We're continuing to see improvements in service availability," but the damage has surely been done. If the outage halted work at your organization, then questions will have to be asked. Even Microsoft's rivals had some sympathy for the engineers and administrators dealing with the problems. Jos Poortvliet, co-founder of Nextcloud, told The Register : "Mistakes happen in the IT industry. This holds true for companies of all sizes, including us. Our heart goes out to all the admins today. "This incident shows how dependent organizations are on a single ecosystem. Especially in critical infrastructure, monopolies are increasing the risk of stalling businesses globally if an incident occurs. "When everything is hanging on a single vendor, companies can't switch providers quickly to get back up and running, or have a second setup as backup, or pull the plug when under attack and keep working air-gapped." Similarly, Civo CEO Mark Boost noted that IT whoopsies were a way of life. "Every technology provider will experience failures," he said. "The real concern isn't that Microsoft has suffered an outage. It's that we've allowed so much of our critical infrastructure to become concentrated in the hands of so few companies, creating enormous single points of failure." Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, also commented: "The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK's digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services." This week, Microsoft warned users to treat its unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 as " permanently vulnerable ." Moving to Exchange Online brings its own dependencies, however. Beyond any compensation claims, Microsoft may face awkward conversations about those dependencies when contracts come up for renewal. And there are alternatives. Although perhaps not so extreme as the measures overheard by one vulture in a German shared workspace: "Germany's love of the fax machine – we are finally getting our chance to shine! Our British colleagues cannot email; we have reverted to the natural way of the fax.

events.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
events.summary: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. November 13, 2026: Huang was not confident in his successor, Colette Kress; reports describe Huang as ‘broken’ More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. November 12, 2026: Democrats launch investigation into Nvidia; Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick summoned to testify before Senate Banking Committee In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy. “Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states. That same evening, Senator Tim Scott (R-SC) requested that Huang and Lutnick both testify before the Senate Banking Committee. “The American people deserve answers,” Scott wrote on X. November 12, 2026: Huang was having a third affair with another Nvidia employee, according to Reuters After Huang was already ousted from Nvidia, we continued to learn more incriminating claims about the former CEO. According to Reuters, Huang had a third affair with an additional, unnamed employee of Nvidia. November 12, 2026: Jensen Huang resigns, CFO Colette Kress named as interim CEO; Huang agrees to testify before Congress Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors.

events.title: Turkiye and Qatar sign mutual defence agreement
events.summary: The pact was signed after ​the President met Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim ‌bin Hamad ​Al Thani in Istanbul on ⁠Friday. Turkiye and ⁠⁠Qatar have signed a mutual defence agreement after a meeting between Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan and Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim ‌‌bin Hamad Al Thani in Istanbul on Friday. “President Erdogan stated that we would continue working together to prevent ⁠⁠the resurgence of ⁠⁠war in the Gulf region and establish a basis ⁠⁠for dialogue and ⁠⁠achieve peace,” ⁠⁠the Turkish presidency said in a statement on X. list 1 of 4 Qatar Grand Prix was ‘right decision’ despite regional tensions: MotoGP list 2 of 4 From the UK to the Gulf, are US overseas bases becoming liabilities? list 3 of 4 Australia’s friendly against Jordan moved to Qatar over security concerns list 4 of 4 US denies Iran’s claim it hit two radar sites in Bahrain Erdogan’s office said the agreement would “add a new dimension to relations between Turkiye and Qatar”, while the Qatari Emir praised the deal as a “strategic partnership”. In a post on X, Sheikh Tamim wrote that he “discussed ways to build on what has been achieved and identify priorities for joint action in the coming period” during talks with President Erdogan. A statement by the Amiri Diwan said multiple agreements were signed by the two governments, including a memorandum of understanding “on cooperation in the field of peace, reconciliation and conflict resolution”. Speaking to Al Jazeera, security analyst Yusuf Alabarda said that since the start of the Iran war, countries in the region “are feeling the effects of the war and no one is feeling secure”. “All the Gulf countries, but especially Qatar, understood that their security guarantees from the United States are not working properly. The Turkish troops in Qatar are very important but I can say that in the near term Turkish weapons and air defences might be deployed to Qatar to guarantee its safety, which is very important to Turkiye, so this agreement will help move forward these military deals,” Alabarda said. In August, Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed a regional defence pact under which the three countries would come to each other’s aid if one of them was attacked. Ratified by the Turkish parliament last week, the pact links NATO member Turkiye, which has the alliance’s second-largest military, with Pakistan, the Muslim world’s only nuclear-armed state. Turkiye has said the agreement is not aimed at any other country and remains open to other states, including Egypt. In October, Qatar, Indonesia, Pakistan and Turkiye signed a multilateral memorandum of understanding on defence cooperation in Doha. The agreement, known as “Badr”, aims to bolster cooperation between the participating countries.

events.title: Nvidia scandal draws in Commerce Secretary Lutnick, who reportedly agrees to testify about China chip sales
events.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to appear voluntarily before the Senate Banking Committee after Chairman Tim Scott asked him to testify on Dec. 10, according to NBC. Lawmakers are scrutinizing the Commerce Department’s oversight of Nvidia chip exports to China and its enforcement of export controls. Scott also asked former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to appear on Dec. 3 as lawmakers examine national security concerns tied to recent reporting about Huang and Nvidia. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, as the fallout from ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy intensifies. Lutnick was summoned by Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott amid scrutiny over whether Nvidia could have supplied advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies and thereby potentially threatened U.S. national security. Huang and Lutnick both received letters on Thursday evening requesting them to testify in separate hearings on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. The letter to Lutnick asked the commerce secretary to testify regarding "recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns." "Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News on Thursday. CNBC contacted the Commerce Department for comment. The letter to Huang said that reports about his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy "raise significant national security concerns." Huang has acknowledged an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought over $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia AI chips over the past two years. The scandal, in addition to reports of a separate affair with a senior executive at Nvidia, led to his resignation on Thursday. There is growing bipartisan scrutiny of the Commerce Department Secretary's approach to chip policy and whether his department was doing enough to restrict the supply of AI chips to China. Lawmakers are also questioning whether the department was overseeing Nvidia's exports thoroughly enough Senator Jim Banks has been particularly scathing, saying Lutnick "appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur," in an appearance on Fox News on Thursday. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, said on Thursday "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military." In a joint letter with incoming Senate Foreign Relations Chair Chris Coons published Wednesday, they said all documents relating to the export of Nvidia chips to China must be preserved. Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. and Rep. Richard E. Neal, D-Mass. told Lutnick they were investigating the approval of sales of Nvidia chips to companies with links to the Chinese government, military and sanctioned entities. Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. said on Thursday that Congress needed to investigate the role of the Commerce Department in approving the export to China of AI chips, but added that he had confidence in Lutnick. Criticism is mounting on President Donald Trump 's administration for declining to include over 100 companies highlighted as national security risks on a trade blacklist, including China's AI startup DeepSeek and memory chipmaker CXMT, Reuters reported in June. Lutnick is a long-standing friend of Trump, with their relationship spanning over three decades, and is widely regarded as a close confidant of the President.

events.title: Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, putting annual rate at 6.5%, the highest in nearly four years
events.summary: The producer price index, a measure of wholesale prices, rose 0.3% in October, slightly less than the 0.4% forecast. On an annual basis, PPI surged 6.5%, the biggest increase since November 2022. Markets continued to fully price in an interest rate hike of at least a quarter percentage point when the Fed meets in December. Wholesale prices increased less than expected in October, but inflation pressures persisted and the Federal Reserve is likely still on target for an interest rate increase soon. The producer price index , which measures the prices domestic producers get for their products before they reach the consumer, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.3% for the month, against the Dow Jones consensus for a 0.4% increase, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. Stripping out food and energy, core PPI posted a 0.3% gain, meeting expectations. On an annual basis, headline PPI accelerated 6.5%, up 0.2 percentage point for the highest annual rate since November 2022. The report comes just a few weeks ahead of the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting, Dec. 8-9. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase in the central bank's key overnight borrowing rate, with slight odds that the Federal Open Market Committee might opt for a half-point hike. Stock market futures added to gains following the release while Treasury yields were mixed. Earlier this week, the BLS reported that inflation at the cash register was hotter than expected. The headline consumer price index saw a 0.4% increase in October while core was up 0.3%, both 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. Because of the government shutdown in October 2025, the BLS couldn't collect some data and refrained from putting out a 12-month inflation figure for CPI. However, the figures showed that the Fed remains a good distance from its 2% inflation goal. "Today's PPI data – which shows some signs of improving, albeit still too-high – is unlikely to change the Fed's approach in December because the CPI data was already outside their comfort zone," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management. Moreover, policymakers are beginning to worry that inflation generated by the Iran war and higher fuel prices, along with President Donald Trump's tariffs, are beginning to spread through the economy. The Fed generally would look through such price pressures as temporary, but the breadth of inflation could indicate that inflation is becoming more entrenched. "We've had some signs of trouble now for several months in a row," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said in a CNBC interview Friday. "If you look at how broad-based the inflation is, it's not just that we're above the target and have been for some time. It's that in categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you're still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way." Stripping out food, energy and trade services, PPI saw an increase of 0.5% in October. Goods prices increased 0.5% in October, with more than 60% of that move driven by goods excluding food and energy, which actually saw a 0.1% decrease. On an annual basis, the goods index jumped 10.2%, the biggest 12-month surge since October 2022. Final demand services prices increased 0.2%, most of which was linked to transportation and warehousing services, and within that category a 3.9% gain in truck transportation of freight. "We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," Goolsbee said. "Inflation is rising; it's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks." Other items in the PPI report also showed multiyear gains. Prices for intermediate processed goods soared 14.6% from October 2025, the biggest annual gain since July 2022. Intermediate prices for services posted a 6.9% increase, the most since November 2022.

events.title: EU agrees on five countries to represent Europe in Ukraine peace talks
events.summary: European leaders believe a US-backed process will allow Moscow and Washington to decide the fate of the conflict. Europe will send a team of diplomats from the European Union and five individual countries to the next round of Ukraine talks, a top EU official said after a summit focused on how to avoid being shut out of negotiations on ending the nearly five-year war. European Council President Antonio Costa said on Friday that the continent will be represented by officials from the 27-nation EU bloc and five members of the “Coalition of the Willing” that backs Ukraine: the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy and Poland. list 1 of 3 Russia and Ukraine report overnight attacks amid US diplomatic push list 2 of 3 Why is Ukraine attacking Russian warships in the Baltic Sea amid talks? list 3 of 3 France slams Israel’s ‘demagogic’ ban on opposition leader Melenchon “Europe must speak with one clear voice and united voice in all discussions that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent. And this is ultimately a team effort,” Costa told a news conference at the end of an EU leaders’ meeting in Dublin, Ireland. Europe has been concerned that US-backed trilateral negotiations could leave them sidelined and Kyiv vulnerable as Moscow and Washington decide the fate of a conflict that has roiled the continent. After talks in Moscow with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, US envoys said that Europe would join future negotiations – but the Kremlin appeared to slam the brakes on that plan, saying no decision had been made. Kyiv is eager for support from European allies, but Moscow does not want European countries involved in direct negotiations, arguing they are financing and supplying Ukraine’s military effort. German ⁠Chancellor Friedrich Merz pleaded earlier on Friday for ⁠US President Donald Trump to create no ⁠surprises during expected talks with Putin in China next week. “Some here in Dublin fear this could turn into a ‘second Anchorage moment’,” ⁠said Merz on ⁠the sidelines of the EU meeting, a reference to the Alaska summit where they were stunned by Trump’s overtures to the Russian leader in the absence of Ukrainian or European envoys. “I therefore ⁠want to state ⁠our message to ⁠the United States very clearly: please, no surprises. Continue ‌to play as part of ‘Team Europe’ ‌and ‘Team ‌Ukraine’.” European leaders had previously discussed whether Europe should be represented by one person or a team. Supporters of a single envoy, like Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, argued that the absence of a united European voice has allowed individual countries or small groups to engage in freelance diplomacy. “There are too many different groupings discussing the issue,” she said. The EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas, a former prime minister of Estonia, laid claim to the envoy role earlier on Friday, saying, “I’m the one who is representing Europe in the foreign and security policy.” She added, “I know that the Russians don’t want me, but, you know, do we have a say, ‘Who is representing Russia?’ We can’t send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending.” Al Jazeera’s Milena Veselinovic, reporting from the summit in Dublin, said that although Kallas put herself forward for the role, “there isn’t unanimous support behind her”, as she is seen by many as “uncompromising” on Russia. US and Russia seek clarity on European voice US and Russian diplomats have criticised Europe for not being united. After the US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia in the United Arab Emirates this week, US envoy Jared Kushner said that “if Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation.” Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said the Kremlin has not confirmed that Putin agreed to expand the trilateral talks to include Europe. Even though Russian officials say they are ready to talk to European leaders, they have also criticised Europe, our correspondent said, noting that Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has even compared European leaders to “spiders in a jar”. “During the Thursday meeting here at the Kremlin, the Russian side spoke about a revision of security architecture in Europe,” Shapovalova said. But “at the same time, Moscow refuses to keep EU leaders at the negotiating table during the peace talks,” she noted.

events.title: Inside energy’s next chapter at Adipec 2026, powered by $67bn in deals
events.summary: Following a year of supply disruptions and heightened geopolitical uncertainty, the $67 billion (Dh246 billion) in agreements signed at Adipec 2026 underscore the energy sector’s proactive approach to tackling questions of security and resilience in the face of growing demand. Taken together, the agreements spanned gas supply, infrastructure, logistics, industrial capacity and digitalisation, reflecting an industry focused on strengthening resilience across the entire energy value chain. The world’s biggest energy show closed out the week with more than 50,000 deals over four days, a 26.4 per cent increase on 2025. In total, Adipec 2026 brought more than 240,000 attendees and 2,260 exhibiting companies representing 170 countries to Abu Dhabi to showcase solutions, discuss opportunities and forge partnerships. Collectively, the agreements announced in Abu Dhabi pointed to a new phase for the energy industry, one defined by investment in resilience, infrastructure, intelligence and cross-border partnerships rather than supply growth alone. Record energy sector participation More than 40 government ministers and policymakers attended, including representatives from Germany, Canada, Egypt, Austria, Japan, Kazakhstan and Nigeria, underscoring the show’s role as a global platform for energy dialogue and investment. They were among the 1,800 speakers spanning governance, energy, technology, finance and more. “The breadth of international participation, from energy, advanced technology and investment sectors, the record exhibition scale and billions of dollars in agreements advanced this week are particularly significant against the backdrop of this year’s extraordinary challenges,” said Abdulmunim Saif Al Kindy, chairman of Adipec 2026. “They demonstrate what Adipec is here to do: connect energy, technology and capital to turn ambition into action. They also reinforce Abu Dhabi’s position as a trusted global centre for the energy industry and the UAE’s commitment to working with partners around the world to strengthen energy security and unlock long-term economic growth,” he added. Over more than 40 years, Adipec has become the annual gathering of the energy industry. Deals are made here, capital is mobilised, new technologies are introduced, and projects are accelerated. As Karim Badawi, Egypt’s Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources, said, "The world needs more energy, and to be able to unlock and deliver this energy, it can only be done through collaboration and partnership.” He was speaking alongside ministers from Romania, Azerbaijan and Venezuela at a session titled Beyond borders: can national energy strategies deliver a connected global system? Tackling complex challenges for future security The energy sector must overcome a complex array of challenges. On the one hand, demand is rising as populations grow and new pressures come from artificial intelligence and industrial development. On the other hand, energy-transition imperatives require that production expands to renewables and alternative fuels while leveraging traditional energy sources to avoid supply deficits. Most industry leaders (93 per cent) expect demand growth to require several energy sources, according to the Adipec Global Energy Report 2026 , which surveyed more than 1,800 executives in ten markets. Investment needs span the entire value chain, from oil and gas to renewables and nuclear power at the upstream end, to logistics solutions that get energy to consumers in the form of terminals, grids, pipelines and storage. The International Energy Agency estimates that 3,000GW - the equivalent of a year’s worth of energy for more than 2 billion homes - of advanced-stage renewable and storage projects are waiting for grid connections. Digital infrastructure, such as AI and data centres, is adding to demand as technologies move from experimentation to wide-scale deployment. The range of partnerships announced at Adipec this year demonstrates how complex the energy business has become. But they also reveal how the sector is responding and the broad directions ahead. Preparedness is now the biggest priority, as UAE Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and Adnoc Group chief executive Dr Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber said in an address on the event’s first day. He said ensuring energy security was now the top question for “every family, every farmer, every industry and every business owner”, and reiterated that the solution would come from teamwork among the sector’s leaders, many of whom were present at the event. “The choices we make today will determine the energy landscape a decade from now,” he said. "Let’s apply the lessons we have learnt. Let’s build capacity and everything that supports it. Let’s forge partnerships that hold when it matters. And if you want a partner you can count on, you are in the right room, in the right city, in the right country. Because when it counts the most, you can count on the UAE.” Turning ambition into action Agreements announced in Abu Dhabi show how the industry is translating resilience from ambition into action. Among the major deals last week, the investment company XRG agreed to acquire Anglo-Dutch energy group Shell’s stake in Australia’s North West Shelf LNG project for $1.5 billion as it seeks to expand its international gas portfolio while strengthening energy links with Asia-Pacific markets. Separately, the Abu Dhabi-based industrial zone Ta’ziz reached financial close on $1.39 billion (Dh5.1 billion) for two projects in Ruwais: a logistics gateway terminal and an ammonia facility capable of producing one million tonnes of the alternative fuel a year. Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) took a final investment decision on the Ruwais Diyab unconventional gas project, aimed at producing and supplying the UAE with 345 million standard cubic feet of raw gas a day from 2029. Project announcements at the show also reflected cooperation across national borders and industrial sectors. Indonesia’s Special Task Force for Upstream Oil and Gas (SKK Migas) also announced several agreements, including partnerships with PT Pertamina, Halliburton Worldwide, and Tara Industries. They covered drilling services, offshore vessel support and establishing a new surveying and mapping company in Abu Dhabi to serve the subsea energy cable sector. US-based Baker Hughes signed four agreements with Adnoc, covering production efficiency, well productivity, gas turbine upgrades and UAE national development. Adnoc also announced LNG supply agreements with India’s Gujarat Energy, for four million tonnes of LNG from 2028, and with TotalEnergies for up to 1.6 million tonnes of LNG. Among the more future-focused deals is an agreement between the Abu Dhabi Department of Energy (DoE) and Evolve Fuels to study the feasibility of synthesising sustainable aviation fuel in the emirate using renewable sources.
