events.title: I moved to Seattle from India for my husband's job. The loneliness, cost of living, and toll on my body shocked me.
events.summary: Neha Shah. Diaspora Nutrition After moving from India to Seattle, Neha Shah was most shocked by the immediate toll on her body. Instead of looking for another engineering job, she pivoted and founded a nutrition business. She said one of the most unexpected parts of moving was the urban loneliness she experienced. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Neha Shah, the 38-year-old founder of Ayurvedic Intelligence , who is based in the Seattle metropolitan area. It's been edited for length and clarity. I expected my transition of moving from India to the US to revolve around adjusting to the weather, learning a new corporate culture, and building a routine. Instead, I ended up rebuilding my entire identity, starting with my health. When my family and I were living in India , I saw the move to Seattle for my husband's job as an exciting next step. My plan was straightforward: settle into our new home, navigate the job market, and pick back up with my software engineering career in one of America's biggest tech hubs. The biggest shock after arriving in the US wasn't cultural; it was physical. Within months of moving, my body began reacting intensely to my environment. I developed chronic bloating, persistent fatigue, systemic inflammation, and stubborn weight gain. What made it so baffling was that my diet hadn't changed: I was still cooking the same traditional meals from scratch that I'd eaten every day in India. This derailed my return to software engineering and sparked the foundation for Ayurvedic Intelligence, my business as an integrative nutrition and health coach. As an engineer, I couldn't accept vague answers to my health issues I started digging into the biological reality of migration and discovered dietary acculturation: how shifting to a new food environment alters the microbiome, and how differences in agricultural processing, soil quality, water, and food infrastructure in the West affect the human body. That's when I saw a massive, unaddressed gap in the wellness industry. Realizing that many South Asian immigrants might've been silently suffering from the exact same "environmental bug" without a culturally intelligent framework to fix it, I knew I had to build the solution myself. I worked as an engineer in India from 2010 to 2012 and then took a five-year break to immerse myself in motherhood and family life. After I moved to the US and experienced health challenges, I became a Certified Holistic Health Coach through the Institute for Integrative Nutrition (IIN) and a Certified Ayurvedic Nutrition Practitioner. Jharkhand and the Seattle area are starkly different While Seattle offered great professional opportunities, my daily rhythm changed entirely. In Jharkhand, walking and community interaction were built into the day, with fresh produce coming from short, local supply chains. In the greater Seattle area, my life instantly became car-dependent. Seattle has been investing in its transit system. The Link light rail has expanded significantly, ridership has been climbing, and the park-and-ride model works well for office commuters, but it's just different culturally from India, where people are used to long train rides or making do with what's walkable. For daily life outside the office commute, like a spontaneous errand, a fresh produce run, or school pickup, a car is still practical for most families in the Seattle area . The cost-of-living shock was its own separate adjustment In India, domestic help, fresh produce markets, and extended family support made daily life manageable, even on a modest income. In Seattle, my family spends between $5,000 and $7,000 a month on housing. Groceries cost us more in a month than my mother spent in a month cooking for eight people. In India, I walked into a clinic, saw a doctor the same day, paid what felt like nothing, and walked out with a prescription. In Seattle, I learned what a deductible was, what a copay was, and what it meant to wait three weeks for an appointment for something that felt urgent. The salary advantage in America is real, but it narrows once you account for what life actually costs here . In India, my income covered rent, food, household help, and healthcare, while still leaving room. In Seattle, the same proportion of income covers rent and health insurance , and not much else, without careful management. In India, I'd never once thought about loneliness My mother lived 12 hours away from me by train, but that distance felt like nothing because connectivity was so woven into daily life that a phone call and an overnight journey could close it entirely — and making that journey was normal. My neighbors in India were family-adjacent. They showed up with food without being asked. If I were sick, someone next door would know before I had decided whether to mention it. The social infrastructure of Indian life is so total that I did not recognize it as infrastructure until it disappeared completely. Here, my next-door neighbors smile politely when we cross paths and then close their doors. They're not unkind, just self-contained in a way I had no reference point for. I remember standing in my apartment on a Sunday afternoon, completely alone, with rain on every window, thinking: this is what people mean when they say quiet. I had never experienced quiet like that before. Becoming a mother in America was nothing as I expected — and that felt good In India, motherhood is a community project. My mother would've been there for the delivery and moved in for the first 40 days. New mothers are fed specific warming foods, given daily oil massages, and surrounded by women who have done this before. The knowledge passes through presence and through someone who watches and gently corrects them. What I didn't expect was how good I felt doing it differently. My parents flew in. We recreated as much of the traditional care as we could: the warm foods, the rest, the rhythm, but without the extended network came no competing opinions, no anxiety passed down through well-meaning relatives, and no one projecting their fears onto my newborn or my body. Just my parents, my husband, and enough quiet to actually hear my own instincts for the first time. The loneliness of American motherhood is real, but the mental clarity that came with it genuinely surprised me. Finding a community in Seattle was more straightforward than I expected Many tech-focused cities in America have large, educated, deeply rooted Indian diaspora communities . It started with my husband's colleagues at Amazon. Then social gatherings, flea markets, and cultural events. One introduction leads to another, and before long we had a circle that understands both worlds without needing explanation. The homesickness never fully disappears, but it becomes manageable when you stop treating connection as optional and start treating it as a commitment. We also make visiting every year, or every other year, a non-negotiable. My advice for tho

events.title: What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs
events.summary: Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO raises questions about the company's role in AI financing. Investors are watching whether a leadership change alters Nvidia’s role in backing AI companies. Smaller AI infrastructure companies may be more sensitive to any pullback in Nvidia’s support. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny. Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive. Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change. "Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday. The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure. Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier. On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.77%, nearly 6% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Tech stocks slumped Thursday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 0.3% as markets digested the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Thursday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers. It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July. Neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday. CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.75% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped 18% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress. It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li. "We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said. "However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added. CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday , before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person." "There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us." Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted. The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions. "Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies." — CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters You can probably guess what he blames for the excessive workload Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia chief executive 1 day ago Quantum leap: IBM plans to scale beyond 1,000 qubits in 2027 with Nighthawk r3 processor 1 day ago The latest FreeBSD report is here, and the AI debate is ongoing 1 day ago Orbit Global Menu: A working global menu addon for GNOME 1 day ago US bit barn boom sees energy needs grow 10x as fast as grid capacity 2 days ago Arm's Lorenzo Stoakes isn't quitting Linux kernel development, though he's stepping back from some of the patch-review work he used to handle. Stoakes is a principal software engineer at Arm and he's a busy chap. Aside from writing the forthcoming book The Linux Memory Manager , in his CV [PDF], he says: "I hold four maintainerships: memory mapping, memory mapping (locking), memory mapping (madvise) – essentially the entirety of the userland API to memory management – and the reverse mapping which connects physical to virtual memory." Even so, he plans to soon be doing a little less. Earlier this week he posted an email to the Linux kernel mailing list to say that he was planning to drop some of his workload. "Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generated series, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offer review except in those areas I maintain. […] Apologies for doing this, but given the current trends I'd like to do something to make my inbox a little more manageable." As it happens, this came just the day after the Paramount Penguin himself said that he saw signs that the AI patch tide was "starting to turn." "I am retaining my maintainerships and have no plans on giving those up, I just want my inbox to be less horrendous. "And yeah, AI is part of the reason; in general, it's gone from 'once a week' to 'daily' to 'half of what I see in review'. "But the AI wave is hitting [memory management] across the board, really." I am retaining my maintainerships and have no plans on giving those up, I just want my inbox to be less horrendous "I have a habit of burning myself out over weekends and evenings – you can see my involvement on a thread talking about that here - which gives you a sense of my views if you read back through that thread." At the Open Source Summit last month, the Reg FOSS desk joined the "Ask the Expert" session with Greg Kroah-Hartman , and he too expressed worrying sentiments: "The onslaught of the LLM-generated patches… we don't have enough people to review them all… We need more reviewers. We don't have enough. All of the maintainers are burnt out, and we have been for ten years." "I want to go down to two Long Term Support releases – four, maximum. Six is too many. We're too busy. We don't have the manpower. It’s crazy." On Red Hat's model of offering 10 years of support for products with a given version of the kernel: "Debian does it right. Debian and Yocto run the world. I've argued for years that the RHEL and SLES model is broken. events.title: NHL’s next TV deal will test the league’s strength while media companies prepare for NFL rights increase
events.summary: The NHL can begin formally negotiating a new media rights deal with its incumbent partners — Disney/ESPN and Skydance, the new owner of TNT Sports — on Jan. 1. How much the NHL can extract from its media partners will likely set the bar for other media rights set to come to market, including MLB. The NHL is asking for an increase of between 50% and 100% for rights, based on early talks with media partners, sources told CNBC. One of the biggest developing stories in entertainment and sports is how the world's biggest media companies judge the value of non-NFL rights. The NHL will be the first public test into this new era of media valuation. The NHL can begin formally negotiating a new media rights deal with its incumbent partners — Disney/ESPN and Skydance, the new owner of TNT Sports — on Jan. 1. The league wants an increase in overall rights fees between 50% and 100% over its current deal, according to sources familiar with the matter. The NHL inked a 7-year, $4.5 billion deal with ESPN and TNT Sports in 2021. Whether the league actually gets that type of increase is still unclear — and that will be one of the most watched data points in the world of sports business next year. National media rights for the NHL currently make up about 13% of its annual revenue, which is around $8 billion, according to CNBC estimates. Disney/ESPN and Skydance want to renew a deal with the league, according to people familiar with the matter that asked not to be named because the discussions are private. Both companies have engaged in preliminary conversations with the league in the past few weeks, and while there's still work to do in terms of price, there's mutual interest in getting something done. In its current deal, ESPN has access to 100 exclusive games for the 2026-27 season. Fifty-three of them air on ESPN or ABC, and the other 47 exclusive stream on ESPN. Under current terms, the league's playoffs are split between Disney and TNT Sports. Disney is particularly interested in acquiring the rights to more playoff games, one of the people said. The NHL had its most-watched playoffs on record last season, averaging 1.8 million viewers per game. The Stanley Cup averaged 5.2 million viewers — the largest audience since 2019. It was played between the Carolina Hurricanes and the Vegas Golden Knights — not exactly marquee NHL franchises. Last year's regular season averaged 546,000 viewers across ESPN/ABC and TNT Sports, up 25% from a year ago — the highest average in more than a decade. The sport is also having a moment culturally. Earlier this year, HBO Max said its hockey-romance series "Heated Rivalry" averaged a whopping 10.6 million viewers per episode. International hockey competitions, such as the league's annual "4 Nations Face-Off" midseason tournament and the 2026 Winter Olympics, have drawn huge ratings. The last "4 Nations Face-Off" game — 2025's U.S. vs. Canada final — drew 9.3 million viewers. This year's Gold Medal men's hockey game between the U.S. and Canada averaged a stunning 26 million viewers on NBC and Peacock in the U.S., according to Nielsen data. That made it the most-watched sporting event in U.S. history with a start time before 9 a.m. ET. "We think we've got the best content," NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman said on CNBC last month . "Our ratings have continued to increase. We were up dramatically into the double digits last year. So we view ourselves coming into the marketplace in a very strong position. Having said that, the marketplace is extremely competitive and extremely fragmented. But, I believe that with fierce competition that's going on between traditional television and the newer media platforms that there'll be a great opportunity for us to both expand our reach and get paid what we think is an appropriate reflection of our value." Recent history suggests the NHL will get the rights increase it wants. The NBA nearly tripled its national media rights revenue, signing an 11-year, $77 billion contract with Disney, Amazon and NBCUniversal in a deal that started last season. The NHL also renewed its TV rights deal in Canada just last year with Rogers Communications, scoring an increase of more than 100% annually when adjusting for currency fluctuations. But recent history may not match up to present reality. While Skydance is interested in getting a deal done, the company's top priorities are paying down debt and saving money to pay for what's going to be a huge NFL rights increase — potentially $1 billion per season or more, two of the people said. Skydance is dead set on renewing the NFL, said one of the people. Those talks will likely occur in 2028, as the league has an opt-out clause at the end of the 2029-30 season. The NHL was a meaningful sports property to Warner Bros. Discovery. The company could use its loyal fanbase and sizable playoff ratings to help justify distribution fees to pay TV providers while marginally adding some subscribers to HBO Max.

events.title: Apple, Alphabet and Uber survived major founder transitions. Nvidia will be a harder test
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s sudden resignation leaves Nvidia facing an unusually difficult transition after losing its founder CEO. Companies like Apple, Alphabet and Uber have prospered after losing high-profile leaders, but those transitions were generally less abrupt. Nvidia’s next permanent CEO will need to manage the fallout from Huang’s departure while maintaining its competitive position as rivals develop their own chips. Jensen Huang is not the first CEO to leave a company he helped build. But experts told CNBC that his sudden resignation f rom Nvidia at a critical juncture is unique and leaves his eventual successor with challenges in leading the company that's powering the artificial intelligence boom. In 33 years, Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman U.S. intelligence believes is a spy for China , made the company he co-founded the world's most valuable. Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein wrote on X that he was "indispensable" but "the graveyards are filled with indispensable men," referencing a quote attributed to French leader Charles de Gaulle. While the board looks for a new CEO and CFO Colette Kress does the job temporarily; analysts say Huang's charisma and bullish drive will be hard to replicate. "I'm not sure we've seen a situation quite like this, where the founder and CEO of one of the world's largest companies faces such a sudden departure amid scandal," Michael Withers, professor of management at the University of Notre Dame's Mendoza College of Business, told CNBC. Whoever follows will "face challenges that go well beyond those of a typical CEO replacing a founder," he added. Apple 's image was inseparable from Steve Jobs when he resigned in 2011. But unlike Nvidia, the company had had other CEOs — and an internal successor. Tim Cook invested in Apple's chip strategy and services business and became a key corporate diplomat in dealings with the U.S. and Chinese governments. He was known as an operator who controlled Apple's supply chain. Cook had "considerable preparation" for becoming CEO, Withers said. Apple's market cap went from about $350 billion to $4 trillion in his 15-year tenure. Larry Page and Sergey Brin left their executive roles at Alphabet in 2019, 21 years after founding Google. Page and Brin's departures were expected. Page said at the time that it was the "natural time" to simplify the company's management structure. Alphabet shares are up more than 300% since then under Sunder Pichai. Travis Kalanick left Uber in 2017 after mounting pressure over a series of scandals and governance concerns. But his departure "unfolded over several months, and while it certainly attracted attention, it pales in comparison to what Nvidia is currently facing," Withers added. Former Expedia CEO Dara Khosrowshahi repaired the organization and found a path to profitability . What's different about Huang's departure Withers said successor CEOs often struggle "under normal circumstances" to juggle maintaining what made a company successful while establishing their own leadership. "It becomes considerably more difficult when the transition follows such a high-profile scandal involving the company's founder," he added. Huang had an extraordinary 60 direct reports, as part of a flat structure that favored fast communication over layered hierarchies. Withers told CNBC Nvidia did not appear to have a succession plan for Huang, who is also often described as inextricably linked to the company. "We're talking about a company that was, until recently, the largest in the world by market capitalization. That's a pretty remarkable situation," he added. As well as having to "step out of his shadow," the new CEO will have to deal with the "scandal" arising from Huang's conduct and "the extent to which it sticks with Nvidia," Withers said. Huang's successor will also have to tackle the longer-term business strategy, while picking up the relationships he managed. Huang cultivated a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump and accompanied him to China in May . Huang consistently pushed for the U.S. to relax export restrictions that prevent Nvidia from selling its chips to the world's second-largest economy. He also managed close relationships with the bosses of the company's key suppliers, from SK Hynix to Samsung. Storm Uru, co-head of the Global Innovation team at Nvidia investor Liontrust Asset Management, said two key priorities were changing company culture and managing the supply chain. The supply chain was "where Jensen was able to provide a vision for the future and able to bring people to the table and to expand capacity to enable the build-out of this technology," Uru told CNBC, adding it mattered especially "when supply chains are already so tight." Nvidia continues to face rising competition from rivals such as AMD and hyperscalers, which are ramping up efforts to develop their own chips.

events.title: Will Democrats try to strip US-Israel initiative from Pentagon funding?
events.summary: Midterm gains give party room to overhaul NDAA funding, including provision to integrate US-Israeli military industries. Washington, DC – After a commanding performance in the United States midterm elections, advocates say Democrats are uniquely positioned to strip a controversial measure from a Pentagon funding bill that would codify integration of the US and Israeli military industries. Earlier this year, Democratic leadership had already opposed the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), a sprawling $1.15 trillion package that, along with supplemental bills, includes funding for much of President Donald Trump’s military wishlist, including the “Golden Dome” missile shield and his so-called “Trump-class” battleship plan. list 1 of 3 What’s next for US Republicans and Trumpism? list 2 of 3 Trump says Israel, Gulf allies must repay Iran war cost: What does it mean? list 3 of 3 Father, child among eight Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza Top party officials, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, had attached their opposition to the Trump administration’s war with Iran and wider affordability issues facing US citizens. Advocates say the leadership must also send the message that the US-Israeli defence production integration is a non-starter. The current Senate version of the bill, under Section 219, calls for the creation of a so-called “United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative” that would “expand and accelerate bilateral defense technology research, development, testing, evaluation, coordination, and industrial cooperation”. Cavan Kharrazian, senior policy adviser at Demand Progress, told Al Jazeera that “Democrats need to make it clear right now that their votes for the NDAA depend on substantial changes, including US-Israeli military integration and Iran war prohibition”. Opposition to Pentagon funding has historically been politically fraught, with lawmakers wary of appearing to not support the US military. But while a version of the funding package passed the Republican-controlled House of Representatives in May, Democrats delayed the Senate version via a procedural vote in July. They now face a December 11 deadline when current stopgap funding ends, meaning they would need to pass another stopgap measure or the full NDAA to maintain Pentagon funding. Because the NDAA requires 60 votes to pass, Democrats can exercise outsized leverage in the remaining days of this congressional session, Kharrazian explained. Republicans, meanwhile, face a ticking clock before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress in January. “[Democrats] have the leverage to filibuster the NDAA until these provisions are stripped out and they need to commit to blocking NDAA consideration until those changes are secured,” Kharrazian said. “An amendment vote alone is insufficient if Democrats then let the bill advance with the provisions intact.” To be sure, Democrats, eager to show they are delivering on voter affordability concerns, have signalled they will seek some overhaul to the current NDAA and related supplemental bills. Defence industry analysts have predicted a major constriction in Pentagon funding, which also includes a stalled $360bn supplemental package. However, it has been unclear if that would extend to the US-Israeli military development initiative. “We must push for the development of a more realistic and sustainable approach to our national security – one that does not require a defense budget in excess of $1 trillion or one paid for with draconian cuts to critical domestic programs,” Representative Adam Smith, currently the ranking Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, said in a statement shortly after the November 3 election results rolled in. He echoed Schumer, who wrote in a July “dear colleague” letter that Republicans were seeking a Pentagon funding bill “that would dump billions more into the defense industry while long overdue investments in American communities wait”. Smith had initially supported, but later opposed, the provision to integrate US-Israeli military development. But Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who are both seeking to retain their leadership positions in their respective chambers, have not publicly stated their positions. Critics have long warned that the initiative would establish an opaque new avenue for the Pentagon to provide US tax-funded support to Israel via joint development ventures, while dodging congressional oversight. It would also make future policy pivots more difficult, entrenching Israeli-developed technology into US military programmes. Some have characterised the initiative as the next phase of Washington’s decades-long military support for Israel, with both US and Israeli officials acknowledging direct military aid has become increasingly politically fraught .

events.title: Uber confirms hackers stole thousands of drivers’ license information in data breach
events.summary: Uber is notifying thousands of drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers. In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California , the ride-hail giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber’s data. The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider. TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers’ information, including billing data and some private AI datasets. Online productivity startup Notion confirmed its data was also stolen in the Fireworks hack. “The notices to drivers are in relation to a security incident impacting one of our third-party vendors, Fireworks.ai, which had access to some Uber data,” an Uber spokesperson told TechCrunch, deferring our questions to Fireworks. Uber did not say how many customers are affected by the breach, nor how many drivers it was notifying about the incident. When reached by email, a spokesperson for Fireworks confirmed that the company identified a security issue involving unauthorized access to some of its systems, which affected customer data, but the spokesperson did not address our questions about the incident. According to data breach notices seen by TechCrunch, the stolen data includes driver’s licenses of 2,567 individuals in Massachusetts, 3,430 people across South Carolina, and 1,873 residents of Rhode Island. A filing with Illinois showed that some state residents had their driver’s license information stolen, but that the number of affected people was pending. Uber also notified drivers who live in California, but did not say how many had their information stolen. The number is expected to rise as more data breach notifications roll in. Fireworks attributed its breach to a financially motivated cybercriminal group whose goals are to sell stolen tokens for accessing large language models, or LLMs. No known cybercriminal group has taken credit for the data theft. This is Uber’s second known data breach this year. The company reported a security incident at its Uber Freight truck shipping unit, for which an extortion gang took credit for stealing data. events.title: Most affairs don't matter except to the people involved. Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen's blunder will rock the world
events.summary: It's a story as old as time. Billionaire nerd boy meets girl. Girl is later suspected of being a spy. News at 11. Oh, and it's also been reported that he was having an affair with one of his direct-report employees. When Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes a "romantic" blunder, he doesn't do it halfway. The boss of the world's most valuable company – well, it was until recently, anyway – publicly resigned yesterday, November 12, as CEO, president, and board member, effective immediately. We don't know if he jumped or if he was pushed. He left after admitting to having an affair. Although he never named an affair partner, one of the affairs was reported to be with Alice Huang, AKA Huang Le. She's head of the Chinese company Megaspeed, which was an Nvidia partner. Megaspeed is accused of being a front for China's government that was used to transfer Nvidia chips to China, although this hasn't been proven. Some US officials also suspect [PDF] she's working for Chinese intelligence, although the DoJ said it hasn't yet reached a conclusion about this. The final nail in Jensen's coffin came when The New York Times reported he had also allegedly had an affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell. Jeeze, guy! In the aftermath, Nvidia's CFO, Colette Kress, was appointed interim CEO. She won't, I suspect, be in the job for long. CFOs are not CEOs. The jobs aren't remotely the same. In most companies, Huang would be replaced by the COO. That can't happen here. Nvidia doesn't have a COO. Both inside and outside of Nvidia, Huang is seen as Nvidia, and Nvidia as Huang. These days, billionaire CEOs are perceived as God-kings who know all and rule all. Much more often than not, that's BS. That isn't the case with Nvidia. Huang co-founded Nvidia on April 5, 1993. He was appointed CEO on day one, and he never left the job. At first, the company staggered forward. When it released the GeForce 256 in 1999 , which it marketed as the first GPU, it started on its path to becoming the chip manufacturer of choice for PC gamers. It still is today. That's a great niche, but it doesn't make a company a trillion-dollar business. No, the path to that dizzying height came when, in 2006, Nvidia unveiled CUDA . This programming architecture opened its GPUs' parallel-processing capabilities to scientific and other non-graphics workloads. From there, CUDA would become the foundation for most high-performance and AI computing. Huang was at the center of it all. He still was until now. At KubeCon North America , the trade show for Kubernetes, used in well over half of all AI projects, I spoke to many Nvidia employees. There were two things they all mentioned. First, they were in a state of shock. Maybe the top brass and government officials both in China and the US knew Huang was fooling with fire; the developer rank-and-file folks I spoke to hadn't had a clue. The second was that every month, Huang held an all-hands meeting where, instead of a per-forma corporate pep rally, he answered questions from everyone and gave them real answers. He knew his technology well and actually led his company instead of just impressing gullible stock buyers. Nvidia can't replace him. It really can't. I'm reminded of when John Sculley forced Steve Jobs out at Apple in 1985. If you're not old enough to remember, Apple did fine for a while, but then by the mid-90s, it lost its way. Apple got its mojo back, and started its rise to being one of the world's top companies only after Jobs came back in 1996 . The big difference, of course, is that Huang's not coming back. I heard many people say that Huang was "too big to fail." True, morality no longer matters much in the US – see Trump's kleptocracy – but this is different. Huang betrayed not just his wife, but his board, employees, and stockholders. If, as some suspect, the board knew full well what was going on, they should be tossed out too, but that's a story for another day. Oh, and as for Trump's suggestions that Apple's former CEO Tim Cook should become Nvidia's CEO? Give me a break. Now the question of the day is: how can Nvidia recover from this blow? I don't think it can. I used to say that I didn't know where the AI companies were going, but I was sure that so long as capital kept flowing into Big AI, Nvidia was the one company you could count on that would make money . I think I was wrong. What does that mean? In the short term, Nvidia stock, after dropping 14 percent in early trading on Thursday, is down "only" five percent. Despite all the Sturm und Drang over Huang's departure, the NASDAQ is actually, when I wrote this, up. Even Nvidia's bonds are holding steady . Amazon and Google, which have their own horses in the AI TPU races, are hoping, of course, that Nvidia's misfortune will help them lever open the AI hardware market. In these early hours, I don't see that happening. Frankly, I'm amazed at how stockowners are shaking off Huang's resignation. The AI fever dream, for now, is continuing unabated. That said, can this go on? This irrational exuberance rests on the belief that, no matter what happens, AI will continue to rule the stock market. Eventually, though, the bubble may pop, and that could put some strain on the global economy. For now, people are ignoring how bad this blow is, or perhaps they're not aware of it. In a few years, I expect Huang's affair will be seen as the first needle in the AI bubble. ®

events.title: ElevenLabs’ new app combines meeting note-taking and dictation for teams
events.summary: In the last few months, Fireflies , Wispr Flow , and Granola have all released competing capabilities in the dictation and meeting note-taking space. The newest entrant in that category is voice AI giant ElevenLabs , which this week released an experimental app called ElevenAI that combines meeting note-taking, dictation, and agent integration. Launched during its 11/11 Summit in New York, ElevenAI is still in preview, and you have to sign up for early access instead of just downloading an app. ElevenLabs, valued at $22 billion , is very much positioning this as a product that lives within a team as compared to a productivity tool for an individual. ElevenAI packs all the features typically found in other apps in the category. It can take meeting notes across your meetings and notify other participants that the conversation is being recorded. Users can query data across meetings and get live assistance during a chat, helping them recall a key detail from older conversations. ElevenLabs also allows companies to integrate ElevenAgent and take follow-up actions such as writing a draft email based on meeting notes. Plus, there’s a dictation feature, which lets users convert speech to cleaned-up text in any app with support for over 90 languages. The company said that the app is capable of understanding industry-specific terms across dictation and meeting transcription. ElevenAI allows the company to use its own model as a showcase and also utilize its agent platforms for better context funneling. The startup’s positioning might not be to directly compete in the productivity market, but rather to give enterprise teams an option to not buy licenses to a notetaker and use its solution instead. All meeting-related tools are rushing to become central knowledge hubs for companies while aiming to automate knowledge extraction and follow-up actions In the last week, the company also launched its v3 series of Scribe speech-to-text models with live transcription capabilities and the ability for companies to fine-tune models using their own data, a tool to pick the right language model based on use case , and a routine creator that automates tasks based on the transcript. events.title: Scoop: Israeli spy chief in D.C. as Netanyahu presses Trump to resume war
events.summary: The director of the Israeli spy agency Mossad is in Washington Friday for talks with senior Trump administration officials about the war in Iran , according to three sources with knowledge of the matter. Why it matters : The visit by Roman Gofman, one of Benjamin Netanyahu's closest confidants, comes as the Israeli prime minister is pressing President Trump to resume the war against Iran. Driving the news: Gofman is meeting with CIA Director John Ratcliffe, the sources said. He is also expected to travel to Miami to meet White House envoy Steve Witkoff, one of the sources said. Mossad, the CIA and the White House declined to comment. State of play: Trump has so far rejected pressure from Netanyahu to return to combat. The two discussed the Iran war during a Nov. 5 call, per a U.S. official. Instead, the president has sided with Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE to continue the naval blockade and economic pressure campaign against Iran, while seeing if a deal is possible. "I could end it immediately. At the request of the nations that I'm looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a little bit more civilly," Trump said on Thursday. "Saudi Arabia has asked me to please just let it be the way it is now for a while, because [Iran is] disintegrating. Qatar, Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain, all of them would much prefer the waiting period." The intrigue: Netanyahu has lost his majority in parliament after the Oct. 27 election in Israel. His opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, has received a mandate to form a new government. It is unclear whether he'll be able to do so. In the meantime, leaders of the Israeli opposition are concerned Netanyahu will try to launch an attack on Iran — or provoke Iran to attack Israel — in order to undermine Eisenkot's efforts, sources say. Netanyahu would be removed from power if Eisenkot succeeds. On Thursday, Netanyahu met with Eisenkot for two hours and briefed him on the situation with Iran. A source close to Eisenkot said he doesn't think the current situation demands immediate military action against Iran.

events.title: Content creator's ascent from Lagos streets to catwalk
events.summary: Nigerian Rachel Ojuromi’s recent Chanel fashion show appearance was the culmination of six months of social media work that took the content creator from experimental shoots on Lagos’ bustling market streets to the Paris catwalk. Her designs, made from what she could forage in local shops and second-hand clothes stalls, were created with her childhood friend-turned-stylist Debby Fasingha. Their videos on Ojuromi’s Instagram — Give Rachel a Shot — attracted 720,000 followers and helped her grab the attention of Chanel’s creative director, Matthieu Blazy. Although Ojuromi first aspired to a career in medicine, the 22-year-old now works as a filmmaker. In 2023, she founded the Process Africa platform that promotes young African creatives, but she wants their art to be appreciated for what it is rather than tied to its continental origin. — Leah Quinn

events.title: DR Congo tin exports to revive US sector
events.summary: Tin mined in DR Congo will be exported to the US as part of a broader partnership with Washington giving American companies preferential access to Kinshasa’s minerals. A Pentagon-backed smelter will produce the metal essential to the manufacture of radar and other military electronics. Emirati-controlled mining company Alphamin Resources said it had signed a two-year agreement to supply up to 3,600 metric tons of tin annually from its Bisie mine in conflict-hit eastern DR Congo to US metals firm Nathan Trotter . The shipments would account for nearly a fifth of the mine’s annual production and feed a $65 million smelter in Virginia that is expected to begin operating in 2027. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: DR Congo president enacts referendum law
events.summary: DR Congo’s president has signed a law allowing the constitution to be changed or replaced through a referendum, a move opponents warn could pave the way for him to seek a third term in the mineral-rich country. Félix Tshisekedi, in power since 2019, is due to complete his second and final term under the current constitution in just over two years. He said in May he was not seeking constitutional changes to stay in power, but would accept a third term if the Congolese people wanted it. The country was ruled by dictator Mobutu Sese Seko for three decades until his overthrow in 1997. After years of war, its 2006 constitution introduced safeguards against a return to dictatorship, including presidential term limits. But Tshisekedi’s predecessor, Joseph Kabila, still stayed in office for two years after his final term expired. Opposition leaders have joined forces to resist any attempt to extend Tshisekedi’s rule, organizing protests at home and seeking support from European governments. They argue that a referendum cannot override the constitution’s ban on changing presidential term limits. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: Bessent puts Megaspeed heat on Lutnick: "Commerce has the pen"
events.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a Friday interview that while his department and others agreed on placing Megaspeed on a special list of companies that pose national security concerns, the Commerce Department "has the pen." Why it matters: Bessent didn't deny reports of tension between him and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who has come under scrutiny for his inaction over Megaspeed. The Singapore tech company has been accused of illegally diverting U.S. chips to China, and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted he had an affair with an executive from the company. The U.S. has identified the woman, Alice Huang , as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Driving the news: " Treasury, War, USTR, and State — they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent said on CNBC Friday morning. "You ... have to ask them about their internal processes," he added. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. events.title: Portugal vs Denmark: UEFA Nations League – predictions, how to watch, teams
events.summary: Playing their first game since Cristiano Ronaldo announced his retirement, two-time champions Portugal face Denmark at home. Who : Portugal vs Denmark What : UEFA Nations League, Group A4 Where : Braga Municipal Stadium, Braga, Portugal When : Saturday, November 14, at 7:45pm (19:45 GMT). How to follow : Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:45 GMT before our live text commentary stream A new chapter in Portuguese football starts on Saturday, as the national team moves on from the departure of their record scorer and longstanding captain, Cristiano Ronaldo. list 1 of 3 Inside the circle: Senegal’s wrestlers turn tradition to Youth Olympic gold list 2 of 3 ‘We are here’: Kurdish club Amedspor shakes up Turkish football list 3 of 3 Harry Kane: How the ‘runt of the litter’ conquered a historic Ballon d’Or Ronaldo ended his 23-year association with the Selecao last week, announcing his retirement in a lengthy video on social media, weeks after a public rift with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus. The 41-year-old, a polarising football icon who wore the much-adored No 7 shirt for his country, said it was now time to “pass it on to the future”. Playing their first game without their biggest star, Portugal face Denmark in Saturday’s home fixture, having already confirmed their spot in the quarterfinals. With three goals each, forwards Goncalo Ramos and Joao Felix have orchestrated Portugal’s attacking play in Ronaldo’s absence, while Denmark’s charge has been led by Rasmus Hojlund, who has netted three of his team’s seven goals so far. Two-time holders Portugal will be confirmed as group winners if they avoid defeat against Denmark, who are second in the standings. The Danes have a bit more complicated path to secure their spot in the last eight on Saturday – they need to win against Portugal and hope that neighbours Norway do not beat third-placed Wales in a clash of the bottom two. How have Portugal played in the Nations League? Portugal have a perfect record in the competition, with four wins out of four. They began their title defence with a 1-0 home win over Wales before beating Norway 2-1 , a game in which Ronaldo was an unused substitute. Shortly afterwards, Ronaldo stormed out of the national camp , but his absence did not trouble the team as they thrashed Denmark 4-2 in another away game before winning 2-1 at home against Norway to reach the quarterfinals. How have Denmark played in the Nations League? Denmark have won two games and lost two. Their campaign started with a 3-2 loss in Norway, but they bounced back with a 2-0 home victory against Wales. The third match saw them fall 4-2 at home to Portugal before they beat Wales 1-0 away. What happened when Portugal and Denmark last met? Goals from Joao Cancelo, Goncalo Ramos, Vitinha and Felix gave Portugal a 4-2 win over Denmark on October 1. Mikkel Damsgaard and Rasmus Hojlund scored for the hosts in that game at Copenhagen. Opta’s supercomputer has given Portugal a 59.4 percent probability of victory, while Denmark’s odds stand at 19.4 percent. There is a 21.2 percent chance the game ends in a draw. (Last five matches, latest game first) Cancelo and Francisco Conceicao are suspended, while Rafael Leao, Nuno Mendes and Nuno Tavares are out with injuries. Probable Portugal XI : Diogo Costa; Diogo Dalot, Ruben Dias, Renato Veiga, Flavio Nazinho; Ruben Neves, Vitinha, Bruno Fernandes; Joao Felix, Goncalo Ramos Denmark will be without Patrick Dorgu, and they will have to be cautious with six players one booking away from suspension. Probable Denmark XI : Mads Hermansen; Rasmus Kristensen, Joachim Andersen, Oliver Provstgaard, Joakim Maehle; Morten Hjulmand, Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg; Gustav Isaksen, Mikkel Damsgaard, Mohamed Daramy; Rasmus Hojlund Portugal vs Denmark: TV channel, livestreaming Middle East and North Africa: beIN SPORTS United States: FOX Sports, FuboTV, ViX You can find your regional broadcaster on UEFA’s official broadcaster listing .

events.title: Ghana sets out $10B investment plan
events.summary: Ghana aims to invest $10 billion over four years to expand domestic production and reduce its dependence on raw commodity exports, as the West African country seeks to turn its recovery from a debt crisis into employment growth and higher incomes. Presenting the budget, the finance minister told lawmakers “too little value” was added domestically. As part of the push to shift the economy, Africa’s largest gold producer wants to phase out exports of unprocessed minerals by 2030. Much of the skilled employment linked to its mineral wealth currently takes place abroad, the finance ministry says. The government is targeting economic growth of 8% by 2030 and the budget has allocated $2.6 billion to support agriculture, energy, and manufacturing over the next year. Ghana completed an IMF bailout program this year and now plans to repay about $3 billion in domestic and international debt ahead of schedule. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: Can Netanyahu launch a strike on Iran before he leaves?
events.summary: PM’s caretaker government can legally go to war, though it would likely inflame domestic divisions. Despite losing its majority in last month’s parliamentary elections, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is still in power in a caretaker capacity. That will continue until a new governing majority is formed – a process that could take months as Israel’s opposition struggles to form a coalition. list 1 of 3 Why is Trump saying ‘no deal necessary’ with Iran as he sidelines JD Vance? list 2 of 3 US denies Iran’s claim it hit two radar sites in Bahrain list 3 of 3 Iran threatens unlimited response over Strait of Hormuz after US attack And while he may be politically weakened, Netanyahu is reported to be weighing new military action against Iran , despite a lack of enthusiasm from the United States, his own military establishment, and the politicians vying to replace him. But does Netanyahu’s caretaker government actually have the authority to send Israel back to war, and how would such a move be received at home? What military options does Israel’s caretaker government have? Officially, Israel’s caretaker government has the same authority as a regular government. Article 30 of the country’s Basic Law states that an interim government continues to carry out the same duties until a new one takes its place. However, Israel’s Supreme Court has previously ruled that an outgoing government must avoid irreversible policy moves unless they are urgent – a principle known as the “duty of restraint”. In practice, Netanyahu can still initiate military action with the approval of his caretaker government, which he could present as “urgent and in the national interest”, Neve Gordon, a professor of international law at Queen Mary University, London, and the author of “Israel’s Occupation”, told Al Jazeera. Or Asher, a researcher at the Tel Aviv-based Tachlith Institute, told the Reuters news agency that security issues generally are “the clearest exception” to a caretaker government’s duty of restraint. “The Supreme Court has historically avoided intervening in decisions to go to war, and parliamentary oversight is at its thinnest in the weeks after the new Knesset [parliament] ⁠⁠convenes and before its committees are formed,” said Asher. “A caretaker prime minister can legally take Israel to war, including against Iran,” he added. Ehab Jabareen, an analyst and Palestinian citizen of Israel, told Al Jazeera the government’s caretaker status raises the “political burden of proof”. “Netanyahu would be asking the country to accept the consequences of a decision that could outlast his government,” he said. Is Netanyahu pushing for a return to war with Iran? On Wednesday, Israeli media reported that the security cabinet chaired by Netanyahu had ordered the military to step up preparations for an attack on Iran. “The directives issued by the security cabinet to the Israeli military could lead it to carry out activities that could trigger a war,” public broadcaster KAN reported. That followed reports that Netanyahu has been repeatedly calling US President Donald Trump to press for a new military campaign against Iran, conversations that on at least one occasion became heated, according to Israel’s Ynet News site. On Thursday, a US military official was quoted by KAN as saying that Washington had told Israel to get ready for a potential new round of confrontation. But the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) later dismissed the reports, telling Al Jazeera they were “mere speculation”. According to Israel’s Channel 13, the Israeli military establishment sees no urgent need to attack Iran. It said that assessment had been presented to Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the next government, during a briefing on Wednesday. The opposition has demanded that Netanyahu avoid any military action unless it is critical. Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman, a member of the opposition bloc, said the prime minister’s caretaker government must not “make decisions that could drag Israel into war without parliamentary oversight and without the full agreement of all security officials”. Eisenkot echoed this sentiment in a letter to Netanyahu on Wednesday, saying that deploying Israeli forces “without a direct and immediate threat that cannot wait could have devastating consequences for Israeli democracy and public trust in the institutions of government”. The Israeli premier responded by insisting the government makes all decisions based only on “security considerations”. How would Israeli parties and the public react to renewed war? “Obviously, those who voted for Netanyahu and parties from his coalition would be in favour, while most of those who supported the so-called change bloc would be upset at Netanyahu’s use of the war to try to remain in power and block their electoral success,” said Gordon.

events.title: My husband started working from home after years of commuting. I didn't expect it to change our marriage so much.
events.summary: Courtesy of the author I'd worked from home for years while my husband spent several nights a week traveling. When he began working remotely, I became his only daily companion outside video calls. We had to create boundaries between our professional lives and our marriage. In the tenuous months after COVID, my husband, Mark, got laid off when a larger corporation bought out his company. He found another job quickly — hours away, in Northern New Jersey — and rather than move, he commuted, spending two or three nights a week in hotels and working from home on Fridays. As an artist and writer, I was already working from home full-time, and I liked the new rhythm of his workweek. While Mark was away, I took over every surface of the house: the dining room table for painting, a second craft table when I had multiple pieces going. The author took over the dining table with her art. Courtesy of the author On Thursdays I'd clear my projects off the table and cook something better than the salads I had been eating in his absence — chili or a tray of baked penne — while the dogs waited at the door for the sound of his car in the driveway. On his Fridays, when Mark worked from home, I'd take my laptop to the coffee shop to write proposals and plan my social media posts, giving him the run of our small house. Then, at the end of last year, his latest company was bought out, too. Bracing for the worst, we waited to see what this sale would mean for us. Would the new company keep the guy who'd racked up all those hotel bills? Mark updated his résumé and waited. A couple of months in, word came back: no more commuting . He could work from home full-time. We celebrated with a bottle of Barolo. We were empty nesters The timing felt advantageous: our son had just moved out. Mark moved his desk out of our bedroom and into the now spare room of our little two-bedroom Cape Cod. It afforded him a door he could close behind him. Then reality set in. Plenty of couples have had to figure out working from home together, but most get some warning, or at least a slow slide into it. We got neither. One week Mark was commuting and living out of hotels ; the next he was working out of our small house full-time. And I was no longer just his wife. I was his coworker, his only lunch companion, and his only witness to a bad day, often in real time. The author's husband started working from home and she needed to keep the dogs quiet. Courtesy of the author What had seemed like a windfall turned into a logistical puzzle. Keeping the dogs quiet during his Zoom calls. Clearing my art supplies off every surface each evening instead of leaving a piece mid-process. I was used to loudly grunting my way through a Peloton ride on my own schedule and pushing lunch back an hour if a piece of writing was going well. Mark's days ran on a schedule — a set lunch, a hard stop in the evening. His office had a door. Mine didn't. He'd walk through my workspace and ask if he could eat the leftover pasta or whether I'd fed the dogs, right as I was trying to land a pivotal sentence. Showering and shaving became optional for him some days, which was not exactly a recipe for romance. We both got irritable There was a social gap, too. I left the house constantly — book club, shopping, pedicures, the coffee shop. Mark didn't, except to walk our dogs in the woods behind our house. He could go a week seeing only me and the talking heads on his screen. We both got irritable. Constant close quarters, it turns out, doesn't make you yearn for your partner. We knew something had to give. So we made rules. I couldn't get an office door, but I started wearing a red bandana when I didn't want to be interrupted. I negotiated to leave art out overnight, within limits. We started eating off TV trays on those nights, and we moved a small figurine between a.m. and p.m. on the dog food bin so neither of us fed them twice. I put in the Peloton headphones and refrained from making my pained noises. We signed up for a meal kit delivery service, and whoever finished work first started dinner. We built in solo nights — guys' night at the brewpub for Mark, movie nights with our daughter for me — and a standing weekly date night, so we could encounter each other "outside of work." We looked forward to those date nights, showering (non-negotiable) and dressing for the occasion — and leaving the job behind. Our work life, like our marriage, is ever evolving. We have learned to lean into the changes. One part diplomacy, one part trial and error. In that spirit, I took advantage of the relaxed atmosphere on our most recent date night to hint that a stand-alone art studio in our backyard might be the next step in our evolution. Mark just nodded and smiled but, wisely, didn't commit. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Ukraine claims record 3,000 Russian casualties in one day as war drags on
events.summary: Meanwhile, Russia appears to suggest it has control of half of unoccupied Donbas. As Ukraine, Russia and the United States engaged in their first peace talks since February this week, the front lines continued to deteriorate for Moscow as its casualties rose to a possible new record without any significant territorial gains. Ukraine’s military said it had caused more than 26,000 Russian casualties – meaning those killed and seriously wounded – in the first 10 days of November, suggesting this month’s figure could mark a new record topping October’s 54,400. list 1 of 4 Regional security dominates European talks in Dublin amid hybrid attacks list 2 of 4 Russian court jails rights lawyer for 12 years on treason charge list 3 of 4 Russia and Ukraine report overnight attacks amid US diplomatic push list 4 of 4 Why is Ukraine attacking Russian warships in the Baltic Sea amid talks? On November 9, Ukraine also claimed a new daily record of 2,980 Russian soldiers killed or wounded. That marked the fourth reported daily record this year. Al Jazeera cannot independently verify casualty claims by either side. This cluster of new casualty records in the autumn, accompanied by a lack of any significant territorial gains by Russia, suggested that Moscow was not coming any closer to its goal of seizing the last remaining quarter of Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region this year. A group of pro-Ukrainian hackers from Belarus said they had accessed records of the Russian state statistical service, Rosstat, and discovered an official tally of 450,000 Russian fatalities for the entire full-scale invasion, since 2022. Independent assessments indicate that Russia has seized a net 117sq km (45sq miles) this year, a poor showing for its pains. Yet, Russia was as defiant as ever at peace talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11. Presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation, told Vesti television after the talks concluded that he would be satisfied “only when we win and sign a peace agreement on our terms”. Russia has demanded territory Ukraine is not willing to surrender, and said NATO needs to pull out of all the former Soviet bloc countries which joined it since 1997. Medinsky called for “a new, comprehensive, and just security system in Europe,” because the one put in place after World War II “is functioning very poorly, and, in fact, the entire system is sick. In Ukraine, a festering wound has simply burst.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saw it differently. “When the Russians now talk about a security architecture for themselves … What they really want is to freely interfere in the affairs of other countries, and to use force whenever they want, and to make sure that no one can support liberty inside Russia,” he told the Danish parliament, the Folketing, on the day the talks concluded. Although US negotiators agreed to table the subject of a European security architecture at Abu Dhabi, the three European powers present – Germany, France and the United Kingdom – did not, and they were excluded from the proceedings. “We did not communicate with them. We don’t really understand what their status is here,” Medinsky said. Europe agrees with Ukraine that such a discussion puts the cart before the horse. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is a complex and potentially dangerous one,” Zelenskyy said on the eve of the talks. “First, we must discuss how to end Russia’s war against Ukraine. Second, what the security infrastructure will be for Ukraine.” Ukraine has asked for an ironclad guarantee of military intervention if it is attacked again, as offered in NATO’s Article 5. Instead, Zelenskyy said, the Trump administration offered “something similar to NATO”. Russian President Vladimir Putin received the US negotiating team in Saint Petersburg after talks in Abu Dhabi, and repeated the Russian position that the presence of European peacekeepers in a post-war Ukraine would also be “absolutely unacceptable”. Zelenskyy attributed Russia’s absolutism to its inaccurate understanding of realities on the ground. “Putin lives in a different reality,” he told journalists in Copenhagen on November 11. “When I received the second report from our negotiating group after the meetings in Abu Dhabi, they told me that the Russians believe and claim that they have already occupied half of the [part of the] Donbas region which is actually under our control. These were military officers, Russian intelligence.” Russia’s defence ministry has claimed to have seized 3,600sq km (1,400sq miles) of Ukraine this year, and Putin has repeated the claim. Still, Abu Dhabi did produce some results. Russia and Ukraine said there would be a new POW exchange of at least 1,000 or possibly 1,500 prisoners on each side. And Zelenskyy said de-escalation steps were discussed. In the run-up to Abu Dhabi, Russia pounded Ukraine’s cities. “For 10 days and nights, Ukraine faced constant alarms,” said its General Staff.

events.title: Russia plans to launch hundreds more satellites for its Starlink alternative in 2027, Ukraine says
events.summary: Russia plans to launch hundreds of satellites into orbit for its Rassvet system. Roscosmos/via REUTERS Ukrainian intel says Russia plans to launch hundreds of satellites for its Starlink alternative this year and next. Kyiv said on Friday that Russia is pressing ahead with its Rassvet constellation despite setbacks. Meanwhile, Ukraine continues to face disruption to its Starlink services. Russia plans to launch nearly 20 additional satellites this year and hundreds more next year as it accelerates the deployment of its Starlink alternative, Rassvet, Ukraine's military intelligence agency said Friday. The new assessment comes as Ukraine continues to face restrictions on its Starlink services , which it says are disrupting its drone operations. Russia has already launched 30 satellites this year for Rassvet, a low-Earth-orbit satellite internet constellation that it has billed as comparable to SpaceX's Starlink, which is widely used by Ukrainian forces. Rassvet's deployment has faced setbacks , including difficulties with launch and dependencies on foreign components, Ukraine's GUR military intelligence agency said in a statement. Two of the 30 Russian satellites launched this year have already "deorbited," and while 26 have reached a stable position at an altitude of roughly 320 miles, none have reached the planned 500-mile altitude — though they are maneuvering toward it, the GUR said. Russia plans to expand the constellation to up to 48 satellites by the end of the year and launch another 240 next year to cover 94% of Russian territory with speeds of up to 150 Mbps, the GUR said. Moscow plans to bring the constellation up to 408 satellites by 2031 and 924 by 2035. The Rassvet satellites, each weighing little more than 600 pounds, rely on laser communication instead of ground stations to transfer data. Russia uses the Soyuz-2.1b three-stage rocket to launch its satellites into orbit. Ukraine has attacked production facilities that manufacture this family of rockets in an attempt to disrupt Moscow's space industry. Ukrainian forces are facing another round of Starlink service disruptions this week. Stringer/REUTERS Rassvet's main control center is in Moscow, but the GUR said Russia plans to build a network of ground stations across the country. Neither Russia's defense ministry nor its US embassy responded to a request for comment on the GUR's assessment. Rassvet is considered to be Russia's alternative to Starlink, SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service that has been crucial for Ukrainian battlefield operations . Kyiv's forces also use Starshield, the military-grade variant. Russia was able to use Starlink in Ukraine until earlier this year, when Kyiv pressed SpaceX to disable its terminals . Starlink became a particularly significant asset for Ukraine in the months that followed, supporting a mix of combat operations by providing reliable communications for its drones. Last month, however, Ukraine was hit with  sudden restrictions on its Starshield services . Its forces endured speed limits for more than a week that severely affected its front-line operations. The shocking disruption came amid high tensions between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy infrastructure . Starlink services are available in Ukraine and Russian-occupied territory, but not inside Russia. Ukraine appears to be in the middle of another Starlink outage. On Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv had once again detected speed limits of 100 miles per hour. On Friday, Ukrainian defense ministry sources told Business Insider that these speed limits were being recorded across all Russian-occupied territory, but not on Ukrainian-controlled land. Zelenskyy said the disruption is affecting Kyiv's ability to intercept Russian attack drones. Ukraine's defense ministry is in talks with SpaceX to resolve the issue and is seeking more information from the US Defense Department, the sources said. Ukraine's attack in August on Russia's Progress Rocket Space Center, the Rassvet satellite deployments, and the impacts of repeated Starlink outages underscore how space has emerged as a key focus of the war. events.title: Nvidia’s next CEO will have to keep an entire industry alive
events.summary: Reed’s view Nvidia got caught without a succession plan for CEO Jensen Huang, but it wasn’t for lack of trying, according to people briefed on the effort to hire a replacement. Before the 63-year-old founder was ousted, the company did try to hire an external number two, according to a person familiar with the search. It was difficult to find candidates, though, because none wanted to work in Huang’s shadow. The Huang hangover might still be a problem even after he’s gone. There’s a Slack group at the company, for instance, titled “Stand with Jensen,” and people familiar with the search process estimate there are fewer than 10 people in the world truly capable of running the company. The next Nvidia CEO doesn’t just have to keep its own products shipping on time. The person who takes the top job also has to keep the entire industry alive. There’s really no replacing him . Notable Several names have been floated for who could replace Huang, including Apple’s hardware chief Johny Srouji, Arm CEO Rene Haas, or even, on President Donald Trump’s suggestion , former Apple CEO Tim Cook.

events.title: Hydropower generation in the Southwest fell to record lows this summer
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-923, Power Plant Operating Data Prolonged drought conditions affecting the Colorado River Basin led to record low hydropower generation this summer in the Southwestern electricity supply region, which includes Arizona, New Mexico, and small parts of Nevada and California. Hydropower generation from April through August 2026 was 19% lower than during the same period last year and 28% lower than the 10-year average, according to the latest data from our Form EIA-923 survey. Water elevations at Lake Powell and Lake Mead, which are formed by the Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam , respectively, hit record lows. To be able to generate hydropower at the Glen Canyon Dam, Lake Powell should have an elevation of at least 3,490 feet, also known as the minimum power pool. At the end of September, this elevation reached 3,518 feet, less than 1% above minimum power pool. The Hoover Dam requires an elevation of at least 950 feet at Lake Mead, which by the end of September reached 1,038 feet, 9% higher than minimum power pool. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation manages most dams across the Colorado River Basin. Seven states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) depend on the river for hydropower generation and for other water supply needs. To mitigate the risk of Lake Powell’s water elevation falling below the minimum power pool, water was released from Flaming Gorge , a reservoir located in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Additionally, water releases from Lake Powell were reduced to maintain an elevation of at least 3,510 feet given the most probable water inflows. However, lower water releases from Lake Powell could also impact water elevation downstream at Lake Mead, in turn affecting hydropower generation at the Hoover Dam. To address this possibility, the Department of the Interior decided to reduce the collective water consumption of California, Arizona, and Nevada by 1.25 million acre-feet each year over the next two years. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Short-Term Energy Outlook , November 2026 We expect hydropower generation in the Southwest will total 6.13 billion kilowatthours (BkWh) in 2026 in our November Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), 9% lower than last year and 24% lower than the 10-year average. In 2027, we expect hydropower generation in the Southwest to total 6.1 BkWh, 0.5% lower than this year. This year’s El Niño could bring more precipitation than normal, providing some drought relief and improving the hydropower generation forecast in the region. However, one good water year likely won't eliminate the effects of multiple years of water scarcity. According to the STEO, hydropower generation in the Southwest is expected to account for about 4% of the region's generation mix in 2026. That share has declined from a peak of 8% in 2011.
