events.title: Nvidia lost its founding CEO. Can it keep its momentum?
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s hasty exit, analysts say, will have little near-term effect on the company’s business. Nvidia’s founder Jensen Huang resigned after a scandal, but analysts say the chipmaker’s AI business should stay strong in the near term. The article says tech companies often do best when founders are replaced by leaders with deep technical and product skills, not mainly finance or sales experience. Apple, Microsoft and Intel show that successor choice can shape long-term success, while Nvidia now needs a leader to plan for rivals and the next AI shift. Advice to Nvidia’s board: choose a techie. As the chip giant’s directors seek a replacement to Jensen Huang , the history of successions at Silicon Valley companies suggests that the odds of long-term success are better with a person steeped in technology and product development rather than finance, sales or marketing. Replacing a founder is a defining moment for any company, whether it has been planned for years or is a sudden departure; whether the company is thriving or faltering. For Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder and former chief executive officer, the fall came remarkably quickly. He resigned on N ov 12 after the disclosure of affairs with a woman identified by US intelligence as a Chinese spy and with an executive who reported to him. Nvidia’s business as the leading chip supplier to artificial intelligence data centres is flourishing. Huang’s hasty exit, analysts say, will have little near-term effect on the company’s business, despite a big stock-market reaction – the company’s shares have fallen 14% in the past five days. But the best tech leaders steer their companies towards opportunity. At Nvidia, founded in 1993, Huang recognised more than a decade ago that chips used mainly for image-processing in computer games could be repurposed as the hardware engines for AI software. It was a huge bet for the small company – and paid off. “You can coast on the founder’s work for years with good execution,” said Steve Blank, a Silicon Valley entrepreneur and investor, who is an adjunct professor at Stanford University. “But you can lack the founder’s vision to see over the horizon and identify what’s next. That’s why the best successors have a lot of technical acumen as well as business acumen.” Over the years, the results for tech companies replacing founding executives have been decidedly mixed. In 1985, Apple co-founder Steve Jobs was forced out after clashing with his CEO, John Sculley, who had come from Pepsico. Under Sculley, Apple enjoyed years of rising profits. But the company eventually struggled to compete against lower-cost personal computers based on Microsoft’s Windows software and Intel’s microprocessors. Scully left Apple in 1993. Three years later, with Apple’s survival uncertain, Jobs returned and became CEO. A renowned product team leader, he led a corporate renaissance, introducing new digital devices including the iPod and the iPhone that transformed the product categories of music players and cellphones. In 2011, shortly before he died, Jobs named Tim Cook as his successor. Cook has a degree in industrial engineering as well as a master’s in business administration (MBA). While some analysts said Apple lost some of its innovative spark, today the company is valued at US$5.16 trillion (S$6.64 trillion), the most valuable in the world. In September, Cook became executive chair and John Ternus, a mechanical engineer and product development executive, became the company’s CEO. Intel did not fare so well. While Andrew Grove did not found the chipmaker, he was among its first employees and led the company for nearly two decades. Grove emigrated from Hungary, learnt English and earned an undergraduate degree and a doctorate in chemical engineering. Grove led Intel’s drive to dominate the market for microprocessor chips, the electronic brains of personal computers. He became the face of Intel and one of the architects of the personal computer industry, named Time magazine’s Man Of The Year in 1997. Grove’s immediate successor in 1998, Craig Barrett, was also a technologist. But later successors were less so – and Intel’s fortunes declined precipitously. As part of efforts to help revive American chip manufacturing, the US government said in 2025 that it would invest nearly US$9 billion in Intel for a stake of just under 10%. Some of the biggest tech companies have learnt that technical expertise at the top is indispensable. Bill Gates, co-founder of Microsoft, stepped aside as CEO in 2000 and handed the job to his long-time business partner, Steve Ballmer. Ballmer was known as a brilliant sales and business development executive, and a tireless, hands-on manager. During his years as CEO, from 2000 to 2014, Microsoft’s sales and profits rose steadily. But Ballmer’s lack of tech expertise contributed to an erosion of Microsoft’s reputation as an industry leader.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Admins with archives of ancient files brace for the wave of tickets from confused users Mozilla leaves Solo website owners to go it alone as hosting shuts down 3 hours ago Email addresses used in European school bomb hoaxes spotted in old infostealer logs 3 hours ago HPE debuts hybrid storage configs: Rising SSD costs hit supercomputing 3 hours ago Microsoft outage gives customers a crash course in dependence on Redmond 4 hours ago Another Linux kernel developer steps back from some duties due to overload 4 hours ago Microsoft is retiring some legacy layout settings in Word, potentially rearranging documents created or last saved in Word 2010 or earlier. "Affected documents may show layout differences, such as text reflow, changes in spacing or page count, or images and shapes moving to another page," the Windows biz said . The advice, if silly little things like page layout in a document matter, is to "consider exporting it to PDF before the change." Compatibility Mode lets a newer version of Word open a document created in an older version, such as Word 2010, without changing its layout. Newer features are switched off while the document is open this way. Users can convert the document to unlock newer features, although people using older versions of Word may then have difficulty editing parts of it. Microsoft has not identified the individual settings being retired, saying only: "We are retiring a set of compatibility options in Microsoft Word (desktop app) for documents in Compatibility Mode." The reason? "To simplify how Word handles document layout and provide a more consistent experience across platforms." Administrators may therefore want to check older templates, forms, and other documents whose pagination needs to stay put. The change is due to begin rolling out in the Windows version of Word from December 2026 and be completed by January 2027. The Mac version will follow in early 2027. Microsoft Word is more than 40 years old, and its first Windows version was released as the 1980s drew to a close. The word processor has evolved over the decades and is a mainstay of Microsoft's productivity suite. Compatibility Mode helps keep older documents from having their layouts abruptly borked the way Word does so well . Siri AI also has onscreen awareness, so it can answer questions or take actions based on the content on the user’s screen. When paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, Siri AI can draw on a user’s personal context, such as their Calendar, Messages, and relevant information across their apps, to provide more personalized responses. And it can take action across apps to help get things done. With powerful new features and unrivaled privacy protections, Siri remains the world’s most private digital assistant. Even when the whole household shares HomeView, personal content stays private to each person, appearing only when a user is recognized by face and their paired iPhone or iPad is present and recently unlocked. 4 Designed to fit in any space, HomeView can be placed on a tabletop as the center of the home or wall-mounted to fit in spaces like the entryway or hallway. Both models work seamlessly with the Home app to manage settings, automations, and smart home accessories. The tabletop model is available in four beautiful colors: silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray. The wall-mounted model is available in two: silver and space gray. events.title: Outlook outage: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' as service returns for many
events.summary: Microsoft on Friday issued an apology for the global Outlook outage that disrupted email access for millions of people around the world. As services were resuming , the US technology giant briefly explained what had happened, ruling out hackers or other nefarious possibilities. “The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” Microsoft said in a statement. “We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions,” it added. The company promised to give a more detailed explanation about what had happened once its review was finished. We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services. This was a technical issue… — Microsoft (@Microsoft) November 13, 2026 Microsoft also offered an explanation for why the problem took so long to resolve. “Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration … We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners,” the statement read. Users began receiving emails again in their Outlook accounts starting at about 5.20pm local time, on desktop and mobile versions of the app. The restoration came after Microsoft said on Friday that its email services were being restored in parts of the Asia Pacific region, after “broader improvements” were observed in North America and “sustained improvements” across much of Europe. The company acknowledged that some users might continue to experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery “as mitigation progresses across the remaining affected infrastructure”. The disruption affected Outlook, Teams and the Copilot AI service for millions of people, companies and governments around the world on Thursday, and the issue continued into Friday. “Traffic is being gradually restored and we're seeing improvements in key customer scenarios, including mailbox access and delayed email processing. However, some users may continue to experience intermittent issues ,” Microsoft said in an update. Analysts told The National that a continuing outage of Microsoft’s collaboration tools would have a “cascading” effect on businesses, with the financial impact increasing with its duration. Microsoft emphasised that it would carry out a robust investigation for customers. “We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” the company said.

events.title: Debate in New York City over city-run groceries is not just about food, but something bigger
events.summary: Five city-run groceries in a city of 8 million won't substantially lower food prices, but the experiment might cause shoppers to think differently about the role of government. Spencer Platt/Getty Images New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow. Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants . But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices. Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers , supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses . What explains this pushback? As a food policy scholar , I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs. The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government . In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food. It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see. That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly. If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide. Some immigrant owners of New York grocery stores have warned that city-run alternatives will undercut them. Scott Gries/Getty Images How the plan will work New York City has committed US$70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all. While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices. In this respect, the stores offer a “ public option ” – a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives , like public schools and city hospitals. Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable. At his May announcement , Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.” A fresh form of intervention Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses. In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business. A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program , known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods. These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them. FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers. Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets. This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare. This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “ the submerged state .” Bringing the state into the open Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways. First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food. If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate. Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable. To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. events.title: UK’s biggest insurer hit by rise in subsidence claims after record hot summer
events.summary: Increase reported by Aviva after Hastings Direct said claims were up 140% in August and Axa said it had been a ‘surge year’ The UK’s largest insurer has been hit by a rise in subsidence claims after an extremely hot summer left households across the country grappling with the fallout from the growing climate crisis. Aviva said on Friday it had experienced the jump amid an industry-wide surge in households filing subsidence claims with their insurers to cover repairs, which typically are needed to address cracks, sloping floors, and off-kilter doors and windows. It follows two record hot summers in the UK; August this year was the joint hottest month ever recorded around the world. Drier summers cause the ground under houses to shrink, which undermines a property’s foundations. It then expands in wetter winters, which can further damage homes. Aviva experienced a “peak subsidence period” between July and September, with claims continuing into October, its chief executive, Amanda Blanc, told Bloomberg in an interview on Friday. Aviva would not provide any further detail on the scale of the increase in claims. Blanc said homeowners could reduce the risk of subsidence by keeping a close eye on drains, pipes and gutters, and fixing any leaks that could affect the ground under homes. “It’s about managing trees and plumbing,” she said. A number of fellow insurers have also experienced a rise in claims in recent months. Hastings Direct said it received record subsidence claims in August , up 140% compared with a year earlier. Axa, one of the UK’s biggest home insurers, has said it has been a “surge year” for subsidence. The value of claims have also hit a record high. The average subsidence claim in the UK hit a high of £20,000 between April and June, more than £2,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Association of British Insurers. Insurers paid out £72m for domestic subsidence claims, compared with £60m in the same period last year. Millions of homes are at risk of subsidence because of the worsening climate crisis, according to the British Geological Survey, which estimates that up to 11% of UK homes – more than 4.2m houses – could be at risk by 2070. Older properties with shallow foundations and those built on clay-rich soil are facing the biggest threat, with areas including London, Essex, Kent and areas around Oxford among the most vulnerable. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning But despite the rise in subsidence claims, Blanc said Aviva was in rude health, having reported a 19% rise in general insurance premiums to £11.8bn in the third quarter. “Aviva is in great shape,” she said in a statement released alongside the company’s financial results. “Our performance has been excellent in the first nine months of 2026, demonstrating once again the benefits of scale across our diversified business. We continue to deliver strong, profitable growth, particularly in the capital-light areas of general insurance and wealth.”

events.title: Global oil supply returns to surplus for first time since start of Iran war, says IEA
events.summary: Supplies outstripped demand by almost 2m barrels a day in October as market shows ‘tentative signs of rebalancing’ The world’s oil supply is swinging back to a surplus for the first time since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, the International Energy Agency (IEA) has said. Oil supplies outstripped demand by almost 2m barrels a day in October, the Paris-based agency said, as “Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand”. The market was “showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran”, the IEA reported. It comes after months of disruption to the global oil market as the Middle East conflict blocked shipments via the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply normally passes. The conflict has triggered a rise in energy prices this year. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, traded at about $72 a barrel in February, before the conflict began, and hit $126 a barrel by the end of April. However, this week prices fell to their lowest level since late August, at $89.66, after the US president, Donald Trump, told reporters that the war with Iran was “ effectively over ”. Brent crude was trading at about $95 a barrel on Friday. There are still concerns around continued attacks on oil tankers in the Middle East, and this week reports emerged that senior Iranian officials believe the US could be planning further military strikes . However, the IEA said it expected global oil supply to average 105m barrels a day in the final three months of the year, 1.7m higher than forecast demand. The agency had previously expected a deficit in the fourth quarter. The recovery in global oil supplies has also eased pressure on emergency stockpiles, which have been diminished by the Iran conflict. The IEA said its members would speed up the release of remaining emergency oil stockpiles pledged earlier this year, adding a further 71m barrels to the market by the end of February. The stocks are held in refineries, oil terminals, power stations and at offshore fields in the North Sea. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The Opec+ oil cartel said this week that it had pumped 41m barrels a day of crude in October, up from about 2m in September and at 97% of its prewar volumes. Global oil demand is also expected to fall by 2.68m barrels a day this year to 103.2m a day, the IEA reported. Consumption is forecast to rebound next year but is still expected to remain below 2025 levels, with growth mostly in petrochemical feed stocks as the market for vehicle fuel is hit by “high prices, electrification and fuel efficiency”.

events.title: Oil supplies bounce back, but prices are still high
events.summary: Oil markets are heading into an unusual period as the Iran conflict remains in dangerous limbo: The supply crunch is easing, but prices could stay stubbornly high. Why it matters: While gasoline prices have dropped lately, don't expect pre-war levels anytime soon even as Middle East exports fitfully recover. Getting oil out of the region is expensive, which filters down to consumers. The threat of new attacks can keep oil costs higher, too, thanks to the risk premium embedded in prices. The big picture: Traders are watching the state of potential diplomacy — and the possibility of a prolonged stalemate. Oil prices jumped yesterday after President Trump said on his Truth Social that "we don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed." Driving the news: Crude oil export levels bounce around, but have recently returned to pre-war levels at times, barrel-tracking firms and analysts say. Yet shipping threats will "persist in 2027," and attacks spiked last month ( see the chart above ), per political risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft. A new agreement on navigating the Strait of Hormuz would just be a piece of the puzzle — if it ever happens. "The threat of a renewed wave of shipping attacks will remain high as long as the underlying confrontation over Iran's nuclear and missile programmes remains unresolved," the firm's analysis states. Catch up quick: Tracking how much supply is returning is a moving target, and higher production from countries outside the Middle East — including the U.S. — matters too. The oil market is "showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the International Energy Agency said this morning . Crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf region rose to 82% of pre-war levels last month, though recovery of refined product shipments is weaker, its monthly analysis states. With supply rising and oil demand lowered by the conflict, IEA predicts the global market will return to a surplus this quarter. Yes, but: Insurance and shipping costs are elevated, and that puts upward pressure on prices. "Both Iran and the Houthis have demonstrated that they can severely restrict oil flows from the region using a range of attacks and tactics. This is something that will have to be priced in," Torbjorn Soltvedt, a senior Verisk analyst, tells me via email. And there's no guarantee that higher tanker transit and increased shipments through pipelines that avoid the Strait of Hormuz won't be curtailed by fresh attacks. Zoom in: Goldman Sachs estimates that the tanker market's "adaptation to Mideast shipping risks" accounts for most of the $20-per-barrel year-over-year increase in average costs for shipping oil. These freight rates reflect vessel availability, insurance, fuel cost, logistics, travel distances and more. What we're watching: It's unclear how much more oil can keep leaving the region in the near term, as intermittent attacks keep happening. "The current recovery may be close to the limit of what the existing logistics system can sustain," HSBC's Kim Fustier said in a recent note. The bottom line: "We would not equate [oil] exports with normality," Fustier writes. She cited substantial volumes of well production that remain curtailed, lower refined product shipments, and "and the cost of sustaining exports." events.title: Oil market to return to surplus for first time since start of Iran war, IEA says
events.summary: The global oil market is to return to a surplus for the first time since the start of the Iran war, despite supplies remaining tight, the International Energy Agency has said. Global oil supplies have outpaced demand for the first time since the conflict broke out in late February. Crude inventories rose by 1.7 million barrels per day in October as exports from the Gulf recovered faster than worldwide demand, the Paris-based IEA said in its monthly market report on Friday. Inventories climbed by 2.3 million bpd to 105.4 million bpd last month, raising output by an "extraordinary" 5.3 million bpd since August, the IEA said. Gulf oil exports, excluding Oman, hit 18.4 million bpd in October, which was 26 per cent below prewar levels as attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz continued. That narrowed the year-on-year output decline to 2.9 million bpd, compared with an average loss of eight million bpd loss from March to September, the agency added. The higher export rates also prompted the IEA to "significantly" raise its expectations for global oil supply for the remainder of 2026, with fourth-quarter estimates now 3.3 million bpd higher. The oil market is "straightening out" and "showing tentative signs of rebalancing", the IEA said. But the agency acknowledged that global oil demand continues to be weighed down by high prices and disruptions to exports of refined products and liquefied petroleum gas from the Gulf, which largely remain at about half of prewar levels. The agency forecasts that global oil demand in 2026 will fall by 2.7 million bpd to 102.3 million bpd, a slight decrease from its October projections . Demand is to recover by two million bpd in 2027, it added. While LPG, ethane and naphtha will account for about 80 per cent of the expected increase next year as supply chains normalise, transport fuels will see a modest gain, "as high prices accelerate electrification and fuel efficiencies across the global car fleet", the IEA said. The "severe tightness" in supply is still particularly pronounced for diesel, which has soared to record levels, especially in the US. Persistent attacks on Russian energy infrastructure continue to choke off the country’s diesel supplies to international markets, adding to losses from the Middle East, the IEA said. "At the same time, Atlantic Basin refineries, particularly in the United States, are running hard to capture high margins, while improved crude availability in Asia and fresh Chinese product export quotas could support higher refinery throughput rates in the region," it said. "Notably, the accelerated release of IEA emergency diesel stocks over the coming months will provide a critical bridge across the supply gap until the global refinery system and product output recover." The oil market is gradually recovering from the effects of the Iran war, which is now in its ninth month. While the US has signalled that it does not plan to carry out further military action against Tehran, a resolution to the conflict remains unclear. Oil prices have been volatile throughout the war, but have markedly declined over the past weeks. At 5.02pm UAE time on Friday, Brent was up 0.35 per cent at $96.16 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate shed 0.18 per cent to $88.58 a barrel. The IEA's supply and demand balances suggest that the global oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of 2026, with a more substantial build in 2027. "As always, downside risks to the forecast persist, as attacks on shipping undermine maritime security, which is pivotal to a sustained recovery," the agency said.

events.title: Microsoft’s latest email outage turned into a full-blown global cloud crisis
events.summary: Microsoft is slowly recovering from its daylong outage after much of the company’s systems were hit by a cascading software issue. The problems, which started Thursday, were initially flagged as affecting the company’s services in the U.S. and the Americas, but quickly spread around the world, as engineers struggled to recover downed servers. What began as an Outlook email and Teams video conferencing outage soon developed into a full-blown meltdown affecting the company’s cloud services for both consumer and business email, files, and documents. The outage also knocked out the company’s Copilot AI tools and Defender security screening software, and prevented system administrators from accessing their internal Intune dashboards and features. Some users reportedly experienced issues with accessing their cloud-based Windows computers. Microsoft hasn’t yet said what caused the issues, only saying the outage involved “a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable.” The company said it continues to investigate the cause. The outage affected a broad range of industries, including TechCrunch’s own email. We’ve reached out to Microsoft for comment about the incident. As of Friday morning on the U.S. East Coast, Microsoft’s Outlook email service had begun to recover and some emails have been trickling in. The recovery comes after engineers initially could not find the cause of the issue that was causing servers in Microsoft’s data centers to fail. Doug Madory, the director of internet analysis at Kentik, a company that monitors internet traffic worldwide, said in a post on Bluesky that traffic was returning to Microsoft’s services after about 18 hours of downtime. Microsoft said in its latest status update on Friday that there was “no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident,” and later noted that there was “not related to cyber or AI / agents.” That may be some solace for the millions who went without their email and online services yesterday, but the company is likely to face questions about its inability to swiftly recover from an outage of its own making. A Microsoft spokesperson did not respond to our questions asking if the company has the technical means to detect malicious activity, such as logs, or if Microsoft has a way to check what happened. “We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure,” said Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president for Copilot, agents, and platform, in a statement on Friday. “Our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward.” The last major incident affecting Microsoft services was in September , when a dayslong outage hit Microsoft’s cloud services. During that outage, Microsoft blamed a “core authentication configuration” issue that prevented users from accessing the service. events.title: I binged 100 TikToks in an hour at a movie theater — and had some surprisingly deep feelings about it
events.summary: Content creator Max Zavidow screened over 300 of his TikToks on the big screen at Cherry Lane Theatre. Michelle Paradis I spent my Wednesday afternoon bingeing one creator's TikToks in a movie theater. Max Zavidow, a New York-based comedian and content creator, screened over 300 of his TikToks. Zavidow wanted people "to feel the agony" of re-watching all his videos — and see his career arc. One hour, 100 TikToks, one big screen. That's how I spent my lunch break on Wednesday. Max Zavidow , a New York-based content creator with 1.4 million TikTok followers, booked the historic Cherry Lane Theatre to screen more than 300 of his TikToks. Perched in the front row with a camera livestreaming his reactions, Zavidow watched (almost) every single video he's made in the past five years flash before his eyes. He cringed, laughed, and reflected on his career. Zavidow's live reactions to his own TikToks: cringing and laughing. Max Zavidow "It is hard to watch your old work," he told me. The screening was, in part, a parody of Shia LaBeouf's "#ALLMYMOVIES," in which the actor livestreamed himself for 72 hours watching his films in 2015. Zavidow, who started posting TikToks at the end of 2021, wanted the screening to "paint a complete picture" of what it means to have a career as a content creator and "evolve on the internet." "I wanted people to feel the agony of me having to look back," he said. The whole ordeal took four hours. I stayed for one. Meanwhile, TikTokers and creator-economy peers popped in and out of the dark theater. The event was free and invitation-only, done in partnership with the theater, which is owned by A24, and produced by Love Letter. "I had six days to pull it together," Zavidow said. Zavidow sat front row at the screening of his TikToks. Michelle Paradis My viewing experience may not have been as groundbreaking as sitting through Nathan Fielder's " You Can See Everything ." Still, I walked out of the theater with more thoughts about TikTok, entertainment, and the creator's career arc. Here are three lingering takeaways. 1. TikTok and Instagram on the TV may not be a bad idea after all I'll be honest, I've been skeptical about social media coming to TV. That's partly because I don't use a TV to watch TV. I usually watch HBO and Netflix on my iPhone . Watching Zavidow's TikToks on the screen, however, was great. Who would have thought watching TikToks while sitting at a 90-degree angle would be pleasant? Zavidow's "#ALLMYTIKTOKS" is a parody of Shia LaBeouf's "#ALLMYMOVIES" stunt from 2015. Michelle Paradis "Getting it on a big screen was a way to say, 'I take this really seriously, and you guys are saying that the big screen is serious. Great. Let's put our TikToks on the big screen,'" Zavidow told me. There was an added cinematic effect to watching videos one would usually watch alone with headphones, on a big screen in the company of dozens of other people. 2. Doing the same thing again and again — sometimes — pays off Zavidow's 316 TikToks were split up into chapters, starting with "See What Sticks." Then, there was the era of "Walk and Talk," "Still Talking, Less Walking," a brief moment of shanties and comedic rhymes, and eventually, "Really Short Films," where Zavidow zeroed in on more narrative fiction. Zavidow split up his TikToks into chapters. Michelle Paradis At certain points, we watched pretty much the same video slightly tweaked. A new angle, a different setup for the joke. "It was so hard to watch all my old videos and be like, 'Oh my God, dude, another one?'" he told me. Making it as a creator requires testing out formula after formula. "At a certain point I found something that worked," Zavidow said. "So I did that for a while." 3. I love screen time — it's the ads and distractions that give me dread When I walked out of the theater to a sunny corner in the West Village, I felt … at ease. Sitting through an hour of uninterrupted short clips designed to make me laugh felt almost as satisfying as a nasal rinse. There were no ads. No buttons to press. No comments to read. No need to move my thumbs. My mind was still — empty. Peak brain rot . Maybe that's OK. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The Download: Silicon Valley’s blind spot and Nvidia’s chip-tracking plan
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong? —Aaron Zamost, a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley have built careers claiming to see the future. Yet five weeks before the midterms, many gathered at the White House to pose with Trump and endorse his “Super Intelligence” agenda, despite growing opposition to AI and data centers. Their decision to lash themselves to President Trump was a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.  Here’s why Silicon Valley’s tech leaders may be less visionary than they think . Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility Nvidia representatives told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it was possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review on Thursday, despite an industry group claiming they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips and prevent their smuggling to China. The act is drawing renewed attention following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair. Find out what the proposed tracking measures would involve . —James O’Donnell More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can control robotic limbs and computers, and even “speak.” The people who volunteer for trials of these devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for ethical trials to respect participants’ autonomy—and access their own brain data whenever they want. events.title: How AI Is Helping Care Teams Get Patients the Right Care, Sooner
events.summary: From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients. Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI outputs and guiding decisions, while NVIDIA technologies provide the compute behind the applications. Read on to learn how healthcare teams are using AI to improve and speed patient care. Dyania Health Uses AI to Turn Decades of Patient Records Into Better Care Hospitals hold decades of patient history, most of it written in free text, as physicians’ notes, operative reports, imaging and pathology reads and discharge summaries. To understand one patient’s full story, a clinician would need to read through years of charts . Dyania Health , a New Jersey-based clinical AI company, built Synapsis AI to do just that. Synapsis AI is a clinical reasoning engine: It works across every note, report and lab result in a patient’s record, connecting findings that may be years apart to answer clinical questions the way a specialist reviewing the chart would. The output is a set of clinical signals, each traceable to its source in the record, that tells care teams which patients need attention and why. Clinicians review the evidence and make every decision. Keeping Patient Data Inside the Hospital Walls Synapsis AI runs on NVIDIA-accelerated computing inside a health system’s own firewall. The entire health system’s patient records can be processed onsite, so patient data is never shared and never leaves the hospital. Processing records this way takes chart review off the desks of clinical teams and lets them spend that time with patients. But Synapsis AI still requires clinician input — it’s an assistive tool that surfaces evidence from medical records that a clinician must still confirm and act on. Dyania builds and trains its clinical models with NVIDIA NeMo open libraries, then uses NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM to optimize them to run faster and more efficiently on the hospital’s own GPU servers. Cleveland Clinic used Synapsis AI to support a study of more than 7,800 aortic valve replacement patients between 2005 and 2021. Synapsis AI reasoned across each patient’s record, including every echocardiogram added in the years after surgery, and used this information to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and reintervention risk at the three-, five- and ten-year mark after a patient undergoes an aortic valve replacement procedure. The AI platform completed chart review across the full cohort that would have taken clinicians years to complete by hand. “Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients,” said Dr. Lars Svensson , chief of the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic. The same approach can be applied to any healthcare challenge where the answer sits inside the medical record, such as identifying patients eligible for clinical trials, closing care gaps in cardiology and oncology, and populating clinical registries. events.title: The datacenter industry is using propaganda to fight opposition | Samuel Woolley, Dean Jackson and Maia Woluchem
events.summary: The datacenter industry is using propaganda to fight opposition Big tech has used misdirection, disinformation and jargon to obscure the harm the facilities can cause to communities “Antifa”. “Commies”. “Chinese bots”. Everyone from tech leaders to the president has called datacenter resistance a “ documented psyop ” and a “ Chinese PR thing ”. But why do they make these claims? Our new research finds that the datacenter industry uses propaganda, disinformation, and information control to mold public opinion and undermine community opposition. Big tech’s opening pitch about datacenters was typical: they told Americans that these facilities brought jobs and tax revenue . They spread this message through mailers , text messages , TV spots and targeted digital ads . But much of the spending behind these multimedia campaigns flowed through opaque non-profits and dark money groups with tech industry ties, hiding the source of these efforts. Groups like “ Elevate New Mexico ” have passed themselves off as local initiatives while obscuring their connections to corporate entities in the datacenter space. As environmental concerns mounted, the industry turned to misdirection and jargon to obscure datacenters’ impact. Developers continue to use terms such as “ closed-loop cooling ” and “ behind-the-meter power ” to deflect concerns about water and power consumption. But while these approaches can mitigate consumption, the effect is smaller than often implied: closed-loop systems may simply shift demand for water up the supply chain to power plants, while behind-the-meter generators still rely on the grid for backup and stability while competing with it for components. And those industry figures about job creation? They are often presented without any context. To give an example, an ad by Build American AI – an industry advocacy group connected to Lead the Future, an industry Pac funded by OpenAI and Andreessen Horowitz – boasts that datacenters have created 57,785 jobs in Texas. But industry figures can also be misleading: of the promised jobs, how many are permanent jobs remaining after construction? How many are cafeteria workers, landscapers, and custodial staff – who often work for subcontractors without benefits? And are those subcontractors included when industry reports the average salaries for the jobs they do create? A similar story applies to other tax benefits. When companies mention the tax revenue they bring to communities, they rarely include the exemptions and abatements they received. Those incentives are often unnecessary to attract projects and eat directly into budgets for schools and social services. Some jurisdictions even track the precise number of dollars they forgo through such abatements. But even when agreements allow communities to claw back money from underperforming projects, local leaders are often hesitant to do so because they don’t want to admit a project has failed. In other words, accountability is rare. The industry fights to keep critical details about projects under wraps, sometimes working with local authorities to do so. In The Dalles, Oregon, for example, Google paid the city’s legal fees after it withheld records about a datacenter’s water use. (The city agreed to release the information in a settlement with the Oregonian newspaper.) Most datacenters do not report their water consumption at all, hampering policymaking. As for the public, their visibility into the process is limited by non-disclosure agreements. Local and state officials, operating in a low-information environment and starved of resources by anti-tax policies, welcomed these facilities at first. The public has been more skeptical. With time, some government officials have joined them. Yet, local organizers and activists told us that they now see decisions about their economic future as pre-determined by big business and opaque governments. They criticized the lack of transparency, the late stage at which the public was consulted, and community benefits agreements they felt were inadequate compared to the burdens they were being asked to bear: higher electric costs, air pollution, noise, water depletion, and a change in the character of their communities. Industrial tycoons have historically manipulated leaders, laws, and regulations to their advantage. This time, though, resistance has been fierce. Perhaps that is why the industry has stooped to smearing its opponents as useful stooges of foreign propaganda. In May, Kevin O’Leary – the millionaire Shark Tank star who is developing one of the world’s largest datacenters – called two activists “proxies for the Chinese government”. He later admitted he had “ no evidence ”. Even so, similar theories have gained traction among tech executives and Washington policymakers. And it has percolated to the local level, where activists and organizers tell us they face this invective – and much more – online.

events.title: FTC to block $3.5B veterinary merger
events.summary: The Scoop The FTC is flexing its regulatory muscle again. The antitrust regulator is planning to file suit to block a $3.5 billion veterinary deal later today, according to people familiar with the matter, seeking to prevent a private equity-owned company from acquiring a smaller rival. The regulator plans to cite increased costs for pet owners and veterinary clinics as part of the suit to block CD&R and TPG-owned Covetrus from acquiring MWI Veterinary Supply, the people said. Covetrus and MWI are both national suppliers of medical supplies and products. The Commission believes that the combination would result in a highly concentrated market, the people said. Neither Covetrus nor MWI returned a request for comment. Rohan’s view Under Andrew Ferguson, the FTC, unlike the Justice Department, has managed to focus on its regulatory mission — even if it has allowed many mergers to pass uncontested. It has used its enforcement tools to execute President Donald Trump’s agenda, which has recently centered on affordability. It is that focus, Washington insiders say, that has now given Ferguson a degree of latitude to pursue cases and merger enforcement that he desires. The FTC is also planning to block a $5 billion merger of two uniform and office equipment suppliers, Semafor reported . The FTC plans to set a last-rites meeting — a precursor to that formal suit — in the coming days, other people familiar with the matter said. Notable Merger investigations neared a record low in 2025 , according to the DAMITT database maintained by law firm Dechert.

events.title: A private equity giant just snapped up a creator company, and it points to the next phase of investment in the sector
events.summary: Eric Tencer, managing director at H.I.G. Growth, and Jake Rosen, founder of Jake Rosen Entertainment, are hunting for creator-economy deals. H.I.G. Growth H.I.G. Capital is betting on the creator economy, starting with the acquisition of Jake Rosen Entertainment. The PE giant envisions building a Whalar Group-style company serving brands and talent. PE is playing a small but growing role in the creator economy, a sign of the sector's maturation. The creator economy is catching private equity's eye. H.I.G. Capital, an investment giant with $76 billion in capital under management, has formed a platform called Waveborn to acquire creator-economy companies, starting with the management firm Jake Rosen Entertainment. The effort comes via H.I.G. Small-Cap & Growth, an arm of H.I.G. Capital. Terms for JRE weren't disclosed. The plan is to build on JRE by acquiring other companies that span the core parts of the creator-economy ecosystem: brand relationships , content production, and creator monetization . The companies didn't give details on the war chest, but cited Whalar Group as the type and scale of company they sought to build. Whalar spanned an agency, talent management, and influencer-tech companies and was valued at $400 million in 2025 before selling its agency to Accenture Song earlier this year. The creator economy has seen explosive growth. Ad spending in the category has grown four times as fast as media overall and is set to hit $44 billion this year in the US, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau . H.I.G. Capital's entrance into the sector reflects financial giants' increasing recognition of the creator economy's potential. It also shows how financial buyers are taking a roll-up approach to fuel the industry's expansion, rather than waiting for it to reach scale. Eric Tencer, managing director of H.I.G. Growth, said factors like the IAB stats, along with his personal experience, forged his conviction in the space. "I've got a 10th grader and a 7th grader at home, and I've been fighting a losing battle around, 'Why don't you just watch normal TV or movies,' and they go straight to TikTok and Instagram," he said. H.I.G. Capital's view is that the ecosystem of businesses serving brands and creators is fragmented, while creators are building increasingly complex companies that require more expertise. Tencer said H.I.G. Capital chose a talent management agency for its first acquisition because it believed that putting creators at the core would help it determine its growth road map. Its plan is to acquire more companies to complement or bolt on to JRE, helping it offer more services to its roster of 400 mid-tier to macro lifestyle creators . "I never want one of our creators to leave us for a different agency because they say, 'I want to go to them because you're not able to offer X services,'" said Jake Rosen, JRE's founder. Rosen said he's bullish on the middle-income creators his agency serves. "A lot of brands on the high side do not want to risk their entire budget on one mega creator," he said. "On the other end, yes, a lot of people are seeing success with micro, smaller creators, but it's a lot on the brand and agency to have 100 creators on a campaign." Private equity is getting more active in the creator economy Private equity firms are playing a small but growing role in funding creator economy companies. That's happening mainly by backing or setting up firms like Fixated (funded by Eldridge Industries) and Wonderloom Media (backed by Content Partners) that become acquirers, said James Creech, founder of the advisory firm Quartermast , which wasn't involved in the JRE deal. That's similar to H.I.G.'s strategy. Creator economy companies haven't traditionally fit private equity's criteria for mature companies large enough to meet its investment requirements. Strategic buyers — such as ad holding companies or talent agencies — are often willing to pay more for creator economy companies than PE firms are. Rosen, who founded 25-employee JRE in 2019, said that when he started a sales process earlier this year, he decided that going the PE route would allow him to be actively involved in future M&A and JRE's growth. He felt that the corporate buyers he spoke with wanted him to adapt to their processes. "Having a seat at the table, and to be able to have that voice for the future, was something that was really important to me," he said. Creech predicted private equity's role in the creator economy would follow H.I.G. Capital's lead. "Other private equities have the same thesis," he said. "There are growth equity players who want to buy a core business, put in more capital to fuel expansion. It reflects the continued maturation of the space." 2026 continues to be the busiest period on record for the sector, with 118 deals involving creator-economy players so far, compared to 93 in all of 2025, according to Quartermast Advisors. events.title: South Africa’s Ramaphosa takes AI pitch to Musk's turf
events.summary: The News South African President Cyril Ramaphosa is due to land in California this weekend for a week-long push to court billions in American AI infrastructure investment. The roadshow will throw him into the backyard of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, whose regulatory clash with Pretoria is at the center of a widening diplomatic rift with Washington. Ramaphosa is likely to face questions about domestic ownership rules which Musk, who was raised in South Africa, has slammed as “openly racist” and cited as the reason his Starlink satellite-internet venture does not operate in Africa’s biggest economy. The working visit , which kicks off on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World summit , unfolds against a deepening diplomatic row as Washington steps up pressure against Pretoria over everything from race policies to its foreign policy choices. South Africa was recently also removed from the African Growth and Opportunity Act preferential trade program. US Ambassador L. Brent Bozell III warned in recent weeks that South Africa’s mandatory local equity ownership transfers under Black Economic Empowerment laws, a policy designed to address dispossessions caused by South Africa’s racist past, are holding back “billions with a B” in American capital. Ramaphosa, whose itinerary includes meetings with Google, Cisco, Palo Alto Networks, and Microsoft, is bringing eight cabinet ministers, including his finance, trade, energy, and communications chiefs — in a bid to capture a slice of America’s $650 billion AI capital expenditure this year. Speaking to the press ahead of the trip, Ramaphosa’s spokesman Vincent Magwenya said South Africa aims to court American capital while firmly “safeguarding digital sovereignty, policy autonomy, data protection, and responsible AI governance.” The BEE controversy Under South Africa’s BEE rules, companies in regulated sectors like telecoms and mining must hand at least 30% of their local ownership to Black people to secure operating licenses — a redress policy that prompted Bozell to say that “time for dialogue has ended” after South Africa failed to meet US demands for regulatory reforms, and executive condemnation of inflammatory political rhetoric. The stand-off has triggered US visa restrictions on unspecified South African officials deemed responsible for “government sponsored discrimination,” led Washington to pull PEPFAR funding to the country, which poured $8 billion into treating the world’s largest HIV/AIDS caseload over two decades, as well as the AGOA ejection. Tiisetso’s view Ramaphosa’s flight to California deliberately skips a potentially frosty reception in Washington. The itinerary, which starts off at Semafor’s inaugural Silicon Valley & The World summit, tells you everything you need to know about Pretroia’s game plan. It is a bold geopolitical arbitrage, an attempt by Pretoria to wall off diplomatic tensions to chase a slice of billions of dollars in AI spending. Pretoria has reasons to believe US boardrooms can look past Washington’s hostility. To start with, boardrooms seem to have a high tolerance for political noise when the economics make sense, if what has been happening in the background is anything to go by. The value of trade between these two countries rose in 2025, industrial giants such aluminum producer Alcoa and transportation behemoth Wabtec keep writing checks despite tariffs, visa curbs, and Bozell’s warning that billions in investment are frozen over South African domestic policies. Next week, we will find out if commerce can keep outrunning politics. Room for Disagreement Sakeliga, a pro-business lobby group, took South Africa’s telecoms regulator to court, arguing that forcing companies to hand over 30% of their local equity to obtain a license acts as a hard barrier to entry that shuts out global players like Starlink . Notable SpaceX has floated a $110 million local infrastructure commitment alongside hundreds of millions rand in free satellite broadband for rural schools as an alternative to handing over its local equity to Black South Africans.

events.title: Israel’s VCs see opportunity for challengers in Nvidia’s turmoil
events.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation has been received with worry in Israel, the company’s “second home,” as Huang described it in 2023. The company’s importance flows both ways, as the semiconductor giant has provided a major boost to Israel’s economic forecasts in recent years. Intel, Microsoft, and many homegrown startups also conduct a sizable share of their R&D in Israel. But owing to Nvidia’s stronghold on AI given the centrality of its GPUs for training LLMs and using them, many in the country are wondering how much of a reshuffle will result from the company’s leadership crisis. As with everything at Nvidia, Huang drove the company to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox for $6.9 billion in 2019 and use the company as the base for its largest R&D facility outside of the U.S. Nvidia also made plans to build a multibillion-dollar campus in northern Israel. “Jensen brought Nvidia to Israel with the acquisition of Mellanox, so there is a strong positive sentiment towards Nvidia and Jensen in Israel’s tech community,” Israeli repeat cybersecurity entrepreneur Pavel Gurvich told TechCrunch. Beyond the 6,000 locals Nvidia employs, the bigger question is whether the company will remain as committed to Israel with someone else at the helm. As a result, his line of succession is being observed just as closely by those who hope the company continues to do so as by those who don’t want it to happen. The latter have already gathered that they may be in for disappointment. In a 2023 interview that is now doing the rounds on X, interim CEO Colette Kress had declared that as Nvidia’s CFO, she typically started her day “with Israel meetings, and only then continue[d] to California.” Kress may not remain in charge in the long run, but the many names floated for the role include two Israelis , Apple’s Johny Srouji and Nvidia’s Michael Kagan — although they’re not at the top of the still quite tentative list . Regardless of who gets chosen, Huang’s successor will likely have less of a grip on Nvidia and the tech industry as a whole. But investors don’t think that would cause demand for Nvidia’s product to fade away. According to Yanai Oron, a general partner at Vertex Ventures Israel, “slower decisions at Nvidia could give competitors an opening, but if that uncertainty also slows AI spending, they could end up with a bigger share of a smaller opportunity.” Nvidia has been responsible for a vast share of the spending in the global AI industry. Under Huang’s leadership, the company used its cash reserves to massively invest across the spectrum, both in companies and in its own next-generation chips . Such an empire may not be doomed to fall with its architect’s ouster, but it does seem less likely to become a full-on monopoly. According to Adi Levanon, a founder and managing partner at Selah Ventures, “[Huang’s] departure doesn’t dismantle Nvidia’s technology or ecosystem, but it could give competitors more room to shape what comes next.” And now that companies globally are deploying increasingly demanding AI agents into their workflows, there’s been a lot of interest — and some venture capital — flowing into developers of AI-specific chips and inference software that could compete with Nvidia’s. “These challengers now have a window to prove a different approach delivers better economics; a leadership change alone won’t win them the business,” Levanon said. events.title: Why a Western defense giant is helping Ukraine build its own version of a battle-tested British artillery gun
events.summary: Ukrainian soldiers are using the L119 Light Gun, and now BAE Systems is helping Ukraine to develop its own variant. Scott Peterson/Getty Images BAE Systems is helping Ukraine develop its own version of a British artillery gun. The agreement paves the way for Ukraine to manufacture a version of the L119 Light Gun domestically. BAE says the goal is to help Ukraine build and sustain its own weapons. A major Western defense firm is helping Ukraine build its own version of a battle-tested British artillery gun, part of a broader push to help the country produce and sustain its own weaponry. BAE Systems signed an agreement this past summer with a Ukrainian partner to develop and test a locally tailored version of the 105mm Light Gun, paving the way for domestic production of the towed howitzer. BAE Systems' Light Gun family includes the L118 used by British forces in the Falklands War and the L119, adopted by the US Army as the M119 and used in Iraq and Afghanistan. BAE Systems describes the Light Gun as "one of the world's most battle-tested artillery capabilities," while the US Army characterizes it as "one of the most versatile weapon systems in the US Army inventory." Giles Ambrose, the engineering, technology, and strategy director at BAE Systems, told Business Insider that Ukraine needs the ability to produce its own weapons rather than depend on foreign suppliers. "The need of the Ukrainians is sovereign capability as opposed to equipment supply ," he said. Ukraine has increasingly embraced producing its own weaponry rather than buying or receiving it from allies, as it seeks greater control over its defense, shorter production and repair times, and reduced vulnerability to allies' changing political priorities. A Ukrainian Light Gun variant would be made to Ukrainian standard. Scott Peterson/Getty Images Ukraine is already using the L119. The UK began supplying them in 2022 to help fight Russia's invasion. Ambrose said that "it's been proven that it really works for the operational needs of the end users in Ukraine," citing its reliability, lightweight design for easy movement, and smaller size. Although drones have transformed the battlefield, artillery systems remain essential to Ukraine's fight, with a recent major operation showing that artillery still matters. Guns like the L119 can deliver sustained fire against Russian positions, complementing drones used for surveillance, targeting, and precision strikes. The new agreement between BAE Systems and a local strategic partner is intended to build on that experience by giving Ukraine the ability to manufacture its own version of the weapon. The agreement grants a license to a Ukrainian partner, which BAE will not name publicly, and provides the engineering expertise, product specifications, and technical information needed to produce the artillery gun. Ambrose said the variant will "be performing to the same specification, albeit built to Ukrainian standard." The goal is to achieve "the same product specification, the same performance," he said. The difference is that "there will be manufacturing processes, specifications pertinent to Ukraine, unique to a Ukrainian industrial base, which will make it easier and maybe more preferable to use in building this gun." Ukraine's battlefield is dominated by drones, but artillery can still play a big role. Chris McGrath/Getty Images This variant "gives Ukraine the ability to optimize for their industrial base" and "will then maximize the battlefield availability," Ambrose said. "But our role in it will mean it will still perform the same as what is out there performing today." The new license agreement allows BAE's partner to produce a test article, which must be successfully manufactured and qualified before production can move forward. BAE will continue providing engineering expertise and support. The agreement also advances efforts to help Ukraine maintain and repair its weapons domestically, reducing the need to send equipment overseas. BAE Systems works with another British company, AMS Integrated Solutions Ltd, in Ukraine to maintain, repair, and overhaul the light guns already in service there. Keeping that work in Ukraine speeds up repairs and gets weapons back into action faster. Ambrose said it "means we're able to upskill in-country engineers and build industrial capability around those systems." "We, BAE Systems, provide the engineering expertise and with that, decades of through - life artillery support capability," Ambrose said. "AMS bring their in-country facilities, their maintenance expertise and Ukrainian engineering skills, to deliver repair and overhaul capability." BAE Systems also has a contract to repair Archer artillery systems donated by Sweden inside Ukraine, and that includes working with Ukrainian soldiers who receive technical training on maintaining the equipment. BAE Systems is a major player in artillery systems. It has a new 94,000-square-foot artillery development and production site in the English city of Sheffield that is now operational. "It is the home of UK Howitzer production and is at full operating capability now," Ambrose said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: New York is running out of room for its waste even with Statue of Liberty-sized landfill
events.summary: One company is proposing elongating the life of the dump, pungent smell and all, several more decades A s a visual representation of how New York is running out of places to put its waste, the largest active landfill in the state is a striking one. The hulking Seneca Meadows landfill is already the height of the Statue of Liberty and its operators are seeking to raise it even further, to the consternation of nearby residents. The landfill, situated in the scenic Finger Lakes region in the northern reaches of New York state, has grown since the 1980s to now sprawl across 350 acres of deposited trash, mounded up to the height of around 300ft – roughly the same height of the Statue of Liberty. “All around the lakes is pretty flat until you see this monster of a hill,” said Mark Pitifer, a marketing administrator at Waterloo Containers, a glass packaging company that sits next to the landfill and is dwarfed by its neighbor. “I mean it’s incredible, it’s like being in downtown New York City only instead of a building, it’s trash.” Locals in the nearby towns of Waterloo and Seneca Falls, the latter famed as the birthplace of the women’s rights movement in the US, had hoped the bulging landfill would be closed when its permit expired last year. But the operator, Texas-based Waste Connections, has proposed elongating the life of the landfill for several more decades via 47 acres of newly lined disposal cells and adding another 70ft to the trash heap’s height. As New York state authorities mull whether to grant this expansion, the landfill has become a central point of grievance over the pungent smell, water pollution and planet-heating pollution given off by the places we dump our rubbish. Seneca Meadows is now the largest source of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, in the state, according to a study last year based on researchers using aircraft measurements. The operator, Waste Connections, did not respond to questions from the Guardian; it defends its environmental protections measures and record in statements on its website. The increasing size of landfills also raises uncomfortable questions about how much waste we produce and what to do with it. Seneca Meadows receives around 6,000 tons of trash each day from across New York, with 1,500 of those tons originating from New York City, which sends its rubbish to landfills hundreds of miles away that are rapidly filling up and are set to be completely full within the next 16 to 25 years . If burning rubbish or casually dumping it into rivers and the ocean is too environmentally harmful, what is to be done with our waste beyond continually supersizing landfills to the point they become a major climate , as well as local, hazard? “We are at the precipice of a crisis,” said Emily Gallagher, a Democratic member of the New York state assembly who recently took a tour of the Seneca Meadows site and has convened a hearing on the state’s waste storage policies. “There is this huge mountain of trash that is off gassing almost 24 hours a day … contaminating the Finger Lakes, contaminating the groundwater,” she said of the site. “People we met in town are in really bad shape, we need to shut this expansion attempt down now.” Gallagher said intense lobbying and donations from interests aligned with the plastics and fossil fuels industries has stymied strict measures to reduce waste and enforce more recycling – she estimated 80% of the Seneca Meadows contents could be recycled. But she added there needed to be a broader societal reckoning with the tsunami of trash, much of it from cheap and disposal items, we create. “We say throwing away but there is no away,” said Gallagher, whose district includes a part of New York City’s borough of Brooklyn. “The problem is that it will take a culture change that people won’t want to do until it is forced in their faces. We used to have a much more circular economy, where people reused and rewashed everything, but we have been indoctrinated into a convenience culture, even if it then causes us more inconvenience.” Dealing with trash is “gross problem”, Gallagher acknowledged. “But we need a much deeper conversation about it rather than continuously pushing it to the side because it’s uncomfortable and it confronts our human desire for comfort and our laziness,” she added. The municipal government of New York City has pointed to recent efforts to reduce its waste, such as the pickup and composting of organic matter, which makes up around a third of what is left as trash in the city. Yet New York City residents still create around 12,000 tons of trash a day and it will need to go somewhere. The city does not send residential trash to Seneca Meadows – although some private contractors do – but will be sending it further and further from the city, which has not hosted its own waste for several decades.
