events.title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
events.summary: Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.” The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart , who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.” Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control. He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it . The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough . Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.” In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition —an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy. The guidelines, published on Tuesday , lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.” As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.   The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants. Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data . Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data. Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement. But people who have brain implants designed for turning thoughts into words might feel differently.  The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors. “It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.” The guidelines also address what comes after a trial. Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some issues with funding. When we last spoke a few years ago , he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about brain surgery here.) Ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp. But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again. Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has said she felt she “became one” with her implant. When the company that made it went bust two years later, the device was removed against her will —an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights. Researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines. Participants should be given plenty of time to prepare for the surgery to remove it. And researchers should set aside extra funds to support trial participants who have to do that. Some of the guidelines are vague and may overlap with existing ethics standards. They don’t all spell out explicit solutions. They were also developed with feedback from a small group of individuals—the number of people living with BCIs is still very low . The team hopes to grow and expand on the guidelines over time. Burkhart also plans to discuss them with researchers at an upcoming neuroscience conference . “This is a living document, and this is version one,” says Chandler. “It’s just the starting point.” This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. events.title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
events.summary: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda. Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers , the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs . For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.  What were they thinking? The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us. Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election. Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC. But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else. In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment. Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die. Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind. In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of. Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “ violence and death to our enemies ” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”? I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all. Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology. The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand. There’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “ masculine energy ,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10. Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration. Instead, Big Tech tied itself to Trump and made its most important goals and investments—many related to grid access and data center permits—immediate targets for Democrats. In tech, you can always sunset a feature or update some code. But in politics, there is no undo button for failures that change public perception. The tech elites’ decision to visibly align their businesses with a temporary movement has left them no credible way to pivot now that the climate has changed. As one Meta employee who has worked closely with Zuckerberg put it, “Mark is a long-term thinker, but he never charts a plan of how to get there. It’s spray and pray and see what happens.” As for whether employees expect the company to do a strategic postmortem? “Facebook has never really done that.” “Move fast and break things” might work in a startup, but it’s a terrible strategy for building reputational goodwill. Previous technological leaps, like the rollout of fiber-optic technology and wireless infrastructure, avoided partisan politics. But by kowtowing to the Trump administration, Silicon Valley made artificial intelligence a culture-war issue. Now, when citizens vote on data center proposals from California to Florida , they are no longer considering only technical or economic concerns, but political ones. Tech leaders didn’t see this coming because they were too focused on the urgency of the AI race to understand how reputational damage could undermine the intangible goodwill—and ultimately the very tangible infrastructure—necessary to win it. The industry’s misreading of the moment has already punctured one myth Silicon Valley holds dear: that its leaders can always see what’s next. Aaron Zamost is a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square.

events.title: How Trump’s War on Offshore Wind Upended a “Limitless” Future for Thousands of New England Workers
events.summary: The Vineyard Wind farm off the coast of Massachusetts in May Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light On a hot July day in 2022, then-President Joe Biden gave a speech from the ruins of a coal-fired power plant on the southern coast of Massachusetts.  Standing where ships once delivered coal for combustion, he said the same dock would soon launch components for wind power out to sea. He praised an Italian company’s plans to build a new factory there, set to create 250 jobs and supply American-made undersea power cables to what was then a line of offshore wind projects waiting to be built along the coast. Four years later, weeds and tall grass have reclaimed the dirt lot on which Biden spoke.  The company never came. Ben Berke/Ocean State Media Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light Then-President Joe Biden gave a speech at Brayton Point in Somerset, Massachusetts, in 2022. Four years later, the promised factory has been canceled. Prysmian Caleb Kenna for ProPublica An architectural rendering of plans for an offshore wind cable factory on Brayton Point, compared with a 2026 photograph of the same area. A 20-minute drive east, in New Bedford, hundreds of workers who helped assemble wind turbine parts from Canada and Europe over the last three years have given way to seagulls and geese. The birds shuffle along the now-empty pier the state of Massachusetts spent $140 million to build for offshore wind development.  In nearby Providence, Rhode Island, a newly built factory that manufactured offshore wind turbine foundation platforms has emptied out. Ben Berke/Ocean State Media Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light Union members worked for three years assembling turbines on New Bedford’s waterfront. The wind developer that planned to use the port facility next has instead delayed its project indefinitely. Amid the Trump administration’s multifront war against offshore wind, the cost on the ground in New England, the launchpad of the country’s offshore wind industry, can be seen in empty warehouses, silent marine terminals and ledgers recording hundreds of millions of dollars of state investment that may not be recouped.  ProPublica partnered with Ocean State Media, The Connecticut Mirror and the New Bedford Light to document the consequences of the administration’s efforts. James Estrin/The New York Times/Redux Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light A factory that made turbine components on Providence’s waterfront is now sitting empty. Many offshore wind projects faced a precarious future before President Donald Trump retook office. Rising construction costs driven by inflation and supply chain shortages forced some developers to back out of contracts to build wind farms and supply electricity to states. Various groups have also fought construction of projects saying they disrupt marine ecosystems and mar coastal views. But last year, the administration temporarily forced five projects to stop construction , further clouding the horizon. Courts allowed the developers to proceed, but that has not eliminated the threat. Last month, the U.S. Department of the Interior asked a court for permission to reconsider a key permit for one of those five projects, Revolution Wind, which is already up and running and can power more than 350,000 New England homes at maximum capacity.  The administration also has frozen future development on all offshore wind farms, including a cluster of projects that haven’t been built but proposed to power up to 1.7 million New England homes. It has blocked or is seeking review of the permits that would allow these to be built. Meanwhile, the administration is paying other wind developers billions of dollars to sell back their leases and walk away.  At a press conference Monday, Trump said he supports a bipartisan bill that would accelerate U.S. energy development. When a reporter pointed out that the bill includes wind energy, Trump said he would not approve “wind turbines ’cause wind turbines are a major loser.”  The upheaval has had ripple effects. The cable company Biden touted decided not to build its factory, citing “long-term trends in the U.S. market.”  Port cities like New Bedford, Massachusetts, and New London, Connecticut, are left trying to hold onto the economic gains they have made building wind farms. Read More About On-the-Ground Impacts From Our Partners The Connecticut Mirror: Offshore wind offered a ‘limitless’ future for Connecticut. Trump scuttled the plan. The New Bedford Light: Fishermen’s offshore wind work drying up Ocean State Media: Offshore wind saved a struggling New Bedford union. Now its future is uncertain. As recently as last winter, New Bedford, a historic whaling and textile manufacturing center, had hotels, offices and piers buzzing with offshore wind workers. Local businesses from caterers to cleaners to fuel suppliers landed new contracts servicing the wind industry.  In New London — another port once central to the whaling industry — officials worked with one of the world’s largest wind developers to pump more than $300 million of public and private funds into a state-owned pier. Despite significant cost overruns and some early construction challenges, the effort transformed the pier into a staging area for the wind industry. Wind turbine components are stored at the State Pier in New London, waiting to be loaded onto installation vessels en route to Danish wind developer Ørsted’s offshore wind farms. The last of three consecutive projects is expected to be completed next year, but no others are fully permitted. Sarah Gordon/The Connecticut Mirror Over the last four years, the pier has been a hive of activity. Hundreds of workers were employed loading and offloading turbine parts — with blades the length of a football field — from specially designed ships, some with names drawn from Greek mythology. Local companies also found work supporting the industry, including one that offered water rescue training for people working on construction sites offshore. “I think the future just looked limitless, ” said New London Mayor Michael Passero. Before wind, Passero said that officials tried for years to attract different industries to the pier, which is overshadowed by larger port facilities in New York and Boston. It was often used to import and store large piles of road salt. New London Mayor Michael Passero in front of the New London State Pier. Danish wind developer Ørsted is currently using the pier as a staging area for its offshore wind projects, but no tenants are lined up once that work is completed. Sarah Gordon/The Connecticut Mirror The most recent wind project based at the pier is scheduled to finish work next year. Port officials have yet to find a tenant to occupy the space.   “They’ll be back to the old days of trying to lure cargo here,” Passero said.  Amid Trump’s war on wind, a frontline of union and nonunion workers watches opportunit

events.title: World shares log modest losses as investors assess impact on AI sector from the Nvidia scandal
events.summary: HONG KONG -- Shares were mostly lower Friday in Europe and Asia, but losses remained modest as investors assessed how Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO might affect the global artificial intelligence industry. A global outage for Microsoft web services disrupted email accounts and some other applications worldwide but appeared to have scant direct impact on markets. Microsoft said in an update Friday that the outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down. In early European trading, Germany's DAX edged 0.1% lower, to 26,748.60 and the CAC 40 in Paris also shed 0.1%, to 8,353.98. Britain's FTSE 100 fell 0.1% to 10,856.66. Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.5% to 61,142.35. Shares of chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron were up 1.7%, while memory chip maker Kioxia Holdings dropped 2.3%. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group lost 5.1%. South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index declined 1% to 5,290.53. Samsung Electronics, one of South Korea’s most valuable companies, was down 1%. Memory chipmaker SK Hynix fell 3%. Taiwan’s Taiex gained 1.4%, with its leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., adding 0.4%. The departure of Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and has been a key architect of its role at the center of the AI boom, has raised questions about the company's future. Its shares fell 4% after his resignation was announced. Huang had been the face of Nvidia and was deemed by some in the industry as bigger than Nvidia itself. Huang stepped down after his affair with a Chinese tech executive raised U.S. national security concerns . Nvidia's longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will be its interim CEO. A lynchpin of the AI boom, Nvidia trades off with Apple as Wall Street’s most valuable company and has invested heavily in other AI firms. Market watchers will be keeping a keen eye out for what Nvidia's woes might mean for pending public debuts of AI companies, such as Anthropic’s pending IPO, valued at $1.3 trillion . Microsoft apologizes for email disruption, says AI agents not responsible Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index gave up 1.6% to 23,637.60. The Shanghai Composite index slid 0.6% to 3,634.35. Australia’s S & P/ASX 200 slipped 0.7% to 9,082.20. On Thursday, Wall Street’s benchmark S & P 500 slipped 0.4%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.4%, while the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite also declined 0.4%. Stocks were also under broad pressure as oil prices climbed after U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday the U.S. didn't “need a deal with Iran” even as the conflict in the Middle East drags on. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” he posted on social media. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” Early Friday, Brent crude, the international standard, was up 0.3% at $96.07 a barrel. It was trading near $72 per barrel in late February before the Iran war began. Benchmark U.S. crude edged 0.1% higher, to $88.08 a barrel. The U.S. dollar rose to 159.92 Japanese yen from 159.84 yen. events.title: The AI boom will survive without Jensen Huang, but there's a $500 billion funding hole to fill
events.summary: The AI boom without Jensen Huang will test a hard truth: Even if the tech world has grown somewhat less reliant on Nvidia's chips, it remains highly dependent on its checkbook. Why it matters : With rival chips maturing and recent software breakthroughs, the tech ecosystem has achieved what would've seemed impossible a year ago: a viable path around Nvidia. But replacing a CEO willing to bankroll startups, backstop billions in cloud debt and aggressively fund rivals to the AI giants will be much harder. The big picture : The next chapter without Huang will be more cautious, but the industry is capable of absorbing the change, for two key reasons: 1. New chips - Semiconductor competition has become harder to contain. At OpenAI and other startups, a longstanding joke was that the best way to get a discount on Nvidia chips was to openly talk to Google or others about alternatives. Huang would often swoop in enthusiastically, eager to lock in a customer. The progress of custom chips from Google, Amazon, Microsoft and OpenAI , as well as new deals with Broadcom and Nvidia rival AMD, gives those conversations more substance. Customers have options, and far more leverage than ever. AI itself has also made those offerings easier to use. Anthropic says its Mythos model helped run certain workloads on AMD chips in about three days , compared with six to 12 months in the past. 2. Washington - In DC, China hawks are ascendant. Huang's departure strengthens calls from administration forces, some lawmakers, and companies such as Anthropic that have pushed for tighter controls on chip sales. Legislation is rapidly advancing to cut off loopholes and strengthen export restrictions for advanced chip sales to China, and the Commerce Department is reportedly preparing additional ways to limit such access. Cutting off those routes could help protect America's lead and offer a major pre-IPO boost to Anthropic and OpenAI. Reality check : Alternative chips and leaps forward in software won't solve the near-term computing crunch that all the big players in AI are facing. Nvidia's chips remain the most sought-after because they are the most widely supported, making them critical for the industry's smaller players and important for the big companies who need maximum efficiency out of each data center they build. There are two reasons a strong Nvidia still remains essential: 1. Finance - The company's checkbook will be far more difficult to replicate than its computing power. Nvidia has made $530 billion of off-balance-sheet commitments and guarantees , including to buy memory and backstops for data centers and certain companies building them, according to data firm SemiAnalysis. Smaller cloud providers, often called neoclouds, as well as a vast array of startups all over the world, have lost perhaps their most enthusiastic champion . Nvidia will remain a formidable competitor, but it will almost certainly become less aggressive about startup funding, acquisitions and backstops, tempering its efforts to spread exposure among institutional investors in ways that some critics said resembled the mortgage bubble. 2. Open models - Nvidia has been the most enthusiastic funder and champion of the Western open-model ecosystem—giving developers cheaper alternatives to the expensive offerings from frontier AI companies. Its pending acquisition of Hugging Face , licensing agreement with model-developer Poolside, backing of Reflection and development of the Nemotron family of open models extend well beyond chip sales. Without Nvidia, it's not clear whether the U.S. will be able to develop open-weight alternatives to China, since many don't have a clear or easy path to financial returns given that such systems are often free to download. What we're watching : Whether the industry's growing freedom to choose its chips can compensate for an Nvidia that is suddenly much less willing to finance its ambitions. Bottom line: Huang's departure won't derail America's AI ambitions. But it leaves a hole in the ecosystem that will be harder to fill than any shortage of Nvidia chips.

events.title: ‘I’m in the trenches’: The payroll processor on her own front line
events.summary: The Signal Insight Jennifer Morgan, who became the first female leader of a DAX-listed company when Germany’s SAP named her co-CEO in 2019, now leads a US business processing $1 trillion of payroll data each year. UKG, formed in 2020 from the merger of Ultimate Software and Kronos, provides HR services and workforce management technology to organizations employing 65 million hourly and frontline workers in industries including retail, healthcare, and manufacturing. Since arriving in 2024 from Blackstone, one of UKG’s private equity owners, Morgan says she has not seen those jobs become much more vulnerable to AI disruption. But she has struck partnerships with the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI, seeing opportunities to “give the worker agency” with AI-powered tools that let them plan schedules around their childcare, or volunteer for overtime when they need to earn extra money. Morgan’s pitch to employers is that pairing these tools with data-driven insights into wages, absenteeism, and inefficiencies in schedules can cut billions of dollars from corporate America’s $1 trillion-a-year attrition bill. Replacing just one hourly worker costs the average employer about $5,000, she notes. Morgan’s strategy is to reposition UKG from a provider of administrative support tools to a “workforce intelligence hub” that uses shift data to inform operational decisions in real time. She has overhauled the company’s leadership, replacing about 80% of her direct reports and 40% of the tier below them, to bring in more people with experience of operating at the scale and speed this moment demands. But she has also tried to stay on her own front line, spending a quarter of her time with customers, which include Marriott, the Mayo Clinic, PepsiCo, and the Transportation Security Administration. And she says that sharing their positive and critical feedback with her staff has been equally important. Here’s how she sees AI bridging the gap between companies and the workers who are often furthest from their headquarters, yet closest to their customers. Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson: What will AI mean for frontline workers? Jennifer Morgan: Think about a world where that frontline worker on their app can say, “I need to make $500 extra between now and the end of the month. What are the shifts that are available for me to do this? Oh, and by the way, here’s my school schedule; schedule around this.” Or workers who need access to their pay before [their] paycheck arrives; one of our customers [who offered early “earned wage access” saw] the retention for people who took advantage of that was 14% higher. AI gives the worker agency because AI can be a better advocate for what they need. That’s what’s been missing. If you think about the person who’s trying to put the schedule together, they don’t have all that texture, and they definitely don’t have it in real time. So that’s where the expectation gap gets bigger and bigger, because what the worker needs and what the operation needs are different. Do you think you have better insight into what’s happening in companies’ workforces than they do? Yes. Whether we’re talking to Pepsi or T-Mobile, we can show them what we see happening. We can talk to them about their overtime, their wages, absenteeism, and the attrition that’s happening because people don’t get the hours that they want. If they get too many [hours], or they don’t get enough, they leave. That information is ready in real time, [but] companies look at that after the fact. What does private capital bring to this very expensive and uncertain AI transition? I remember when I read my first investment memo at Blackstone for a company we were looking at, my first reaction was, “I wish somebody had given this to me when I was the co-CEO of SAP.” Having somebody who can unemotionally look at your business and tell you all the opportunities, all the great things, and all the things that you can address to make it even better, as a leader, that’s what you’re looking for: Just take out the filter and give it to me. I love having a board with both investors and operators, because operators understand all the nuance and all of the intended and unintended consequences of what could happen if I do X or if I do Y. Investors tend to look at things very unemotionally, factually. And it helps bring a level of focus. Do you ever see tension between that left-brain and right-brain way of looking at the business? Absolutely. I remember, again, my first investment committee meeting at Blackstone. We were talking about [investing in] this one company and all of a sudden there was this strong intellectual debate. I’m thinking to myself, “Oh my goodness, they don’t like this company.” But it was really about just getting to the right answer. There were no corporate politics. It was just that intellectual honesty about what this was, what we could do, what you needed to believe in order to get to where everybody wanted to go. So that is really positive when you’re able to have those discussions, and make change at a pace that I don’t have to constantly worry about the [next quarterly earnings]. Because the amount of change that we’re making to the organization is a lot, and the longer you wait to react, the more you have to catch up, and the change is twice as much and twice as hard. UKG was put together from two different companies. To what extent has your job been about defining a single culture? [I was asked] as a new CEO, “Jen, are we going to be a product-led culture? Are we going to be a sales-led culture? How are we going to define it?” I said we’ve got to be customer-led. To be a winning culture, you’ve got to understand what’s going on outside the four walls. And so I spend a lot of my time sharing what I’m hearing. I’m used to being in bigger companies, and when you’re talking to tens of thousands of employees, you don’t tend to just go out there unscripted, off-the-cuff. But because things are changing so fast, people don’t want [a script], they want perfect imperfection. Like, “Give it to me straight. I don’t want to feel like you’re giving me the glossy. Tell me the challenges. Tell me what’s happening.” The more that I bring the outside in, the more that becomes a common language [across] product, engineering, marketing, and sales. And one of our challenges as you continue to grow, is you have to connect all those dots. Leaders today have to be on their own front line. As a CEO, I’m trying to find the most unfiltered, real-time feedback and people who are going to give it to me straight. CEOs get concise, need-to-know briefings. But the nuance really matters. How do you spend your time, between customers, employees, and your top team? I try to spend at least a quarter of my time with customers, because that contextualizes everything. So if I look at something that’s not going well in a company, you can usually find the answers by going out and hearing from your customers. My biggest fear is to have one

events.title: Palantir's NHS cancer app gets plenty of praise, precious few users
events.summary: Only a handful of NHS trusts are using the cancer app on the controversial £330 million Federated Data Platform (FDP) run by Palantir, while newly released figures raise questions about which trusts are benefiting. Cancer 360 was designed to bring cancer patients' data from disparate spreadsheets and electronic health records into a central system, helping health professionals prioritize treatment. Pilots began four years ago, and trusts are not charged directly for the FDP. Yet official figures put Cancer 360's uptake at just five or six trusts. Freedom of Information responses gathered by grassroots campaign group No Palantir in the NHS also reveal discrepancies between reported benefits and recorded use. In June 2025, NHS England said that Cancer 360 "drastically cut down diagnosis times" and referred to a pilot at Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust, which saw the proportion of patients diagnosed within 28 days climb from 72 percent to 85 percent. The trust began trials in 2022, while working with Palantir under a £23 million contract awarded without competition, before the US firm was awarded the FDP contract in late 2023. Critics argued the FDP procurement was flawed as Palantir had developed use cases under £60 million in non-competitive contracts which were then carried over to the FDP. Last year, NHS England said Cancer 360 served 46 registered teams and 239 active users, and processed 52,000 patients. In June 2026, NHS England said there were five trusts using Cancer 360 as of March 2026. Of those, only two were listed as benefiting. In July, health minister Preet Kaur Gill repeated the five-trust usage figure in a Parliamentary answer . Official data released in October said that as of June, six trusts were using Cancer 360 and five were benefiting, but did not identify the trusts or explain the increase. The stats have since been removed from the NHS England website but are archived here . In June, NHS England responded to a Freedom of Information request . It said six trusts reported unique users logging into the Cancer 360 app over the last 12 months. However, two trusts cited as having run successful pilots – Chelsea and Westminster Hospital and Royal United Hospitals Bath – were listed as having zero unique users logging into the system during that period, according to NHS England's reply. Both trusts were said to have received benefits from the system, according to a FoI response sent to campaign group Foxglove in June this year. The Register asked both trusts and NHS England to explain the discrepancy. One of the six trusts said to be logging into the cancer app, East Lancashire Hospitals, reported just one unique user. It later confirmed in an FoI response in August that it was not live with the FDP. It had planned to adopt the platform, leading with Cancer 360, but did not have a date for going live with the app. No Palantir in the NHS also identified trusts that considered Cancer 360 but decided against adopting it. East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust considered using the app but rejected it because there was "no immediate requirement for it," according to its FoI response . In its FoI response , Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust said it did not adopt the app because of issues around the metadata requirements. Meanwhile, official figures on cancer diagnosis waiting times show wider improvements across England. Given Cancer 360's limited uptake, those national gains cannot simply be credited to the app. In July this year, the UK's statistical regulator told NHS England to ensure ministers are briefed accurately following a row over data used to promote the purported benefits of the Palantir-run FDP. Campaign group Foxglove had found that nearly a third of NHS trusts using Palantir's health data platform were performing fewer patient procedures than before it went live and that Chelsea and Westminster Hospital accounted for 84 percent of the reported fall in outpatient waiting lists, while only 16 trusts were using the FDP tool. The Office for Statistics Regulation began assessing NHS England's claims about the FDP's performance and the quango included more caveats on its website. Scrutiny of the FDP's reported benefits comes as the government decides whether to continue the Palantir-led contract beyond February 2027. The initial contract was provided for a term of up to seven years, with a maximum value of £330 million. Reports this week suggest the government is set to renew the contract , but run a parallel procurement to find an alternative to Palantir as pressure mounts to reduce lock-in to a single vendor and boost sovereign technology. Palantir was founded with startup money from a CIA-linked VC firm and has relied on close ties with the US intelligence, military, and immigration services since its inception, although its recent growth in the wider business market is notable. ®

events.title: Heat pumps: How much heat does your home really need?
events.summary: Installing a heat pump is a big decision Published 13 November 2026, 09:29 GMT Floorplans. Air duct diagrams. Heat pump specifications. Most people in the market for a new heating system probably don't want to think about this level of detail. But, perhaps surprisingly, some do want to think about those things. In extreme depth. Every day, roughly 150 new users sign up to an app called Cool Calc, which works out the heat requirements of properties in the US. Just over one third of those new users are not tradespeople but private homeowners, says founder and chief executive Bill Fiore. When choosing a heating system, people can find themselves bombarded with information – how powerful a heat pump do they need, for example? It isn't always easy to take a tradesperson at their word. "As an overall trend, we are seeing homeowners be more informed," explains Fiore. "They want to do a calculation on their own." Cool Calc is used by tradespeople and homeowners to work out heat loss A heat loss calculation is a figure, usually measured in watts, that defines how much heat a home loses during cold weather. It's worked out room by room and is a key part of designing an efficient heating system. This estimate is especially important to get right when installing a heat pump, which is sized fairly precisely, according to the projected heat loss. Should that calculation be off, the heat pump will likely perform poorly. You could be left with an underpowered device that struggles to warm your property, for example. Given the costs involved, homeowners are often anxious to ensure installers avoid such mistakes. Certain new technologies are not, for the moment, helping, adds Fiore. "People are going to AI and they're getting a lot of misinformation because it's not backed by anything credible," he says. Cool Calc is planning to integrate with AI chatbots to try and improve the quality of the advice they spew out. It is probably a good idea to be cautious about your new heating system's design, says Kevin Kircher at Purdue University. He and colleagues recently conducted a study, yet to be published, examining the heat loss calculations provided by tradespeople to roughly 75 US homeowners. "We were surprised," says Kircher. "The heat loss calculations often led to overestimating the design heat loads by a factor of two or more." That would result in oversized systems that use much more power than necessary. Not only that, some people reported charges of more than $1,000 (£745) – and in one case as much as $2,500 – just for a heat loss survey, adds Kircher. Besides using excessive amounts of energy, an oversized heating system can also feel uncomfortable, says Dan Dempsey, a former senior engineering fellow for a major heating and cooling provider in the US. Dempsey, who took part in Kircher and his colleagues' study, lives in Indiana. He says it is his retirement hobby to monitor the performance of heating and cooling systems in the homes of friends and family members, by analysing data from their smart thermostats. "I spent five years manually downloading everything, every week," he says. He points out that oversized systems tend to cycle a lot, meaning they switch on and off again in quick succession. This leads to discernible swings in temperature: rooms that fail to remain at their target temperature of, say, 20C, but rather fluctuate, which feels uncomfortable, says Dempsey. For people seeking a better understanding of their home's heat loss, various free or partially free apps, including Cool Calc and AutoHVAC, are available. There are options for UK homeowners, too, such as web app Heatpunk. Heat loss apps help drive business to renewable energy firms says Andy Rankin Many things can influence the heat loss figure, including the amount of insulation in your home, whether the building has double or triple glazing, and also the size of your radiators. Heatpunk allows people to draw a floor plan of their home and input data about the property in order to estimate its performance. Thousands of people use it every month, mostly professional installers, says Andy Rankin, founder and managing director of Midsummer Energy. The web app also suggests specific heat pump models for each property, based on the results of the calculation. Naturally, these are models available through Midsummer Energy. "It's been a very effective marketing tool," says Rankin. Dwellow, another company that offers heat pump installations in the UK, is keen to follow suit. The firm recently launched its own heat loss estimator. While professional heat loss calculations remain essential, getting people to do their own "self surveys" first could ultimately reduce how much time professional heating engineers must spend analysing properties says Ian Mclaren, Dwellow's co-founder and director.

events.title: Microsoft outage to have 'cascading impact' on businesses
events.summary: The continuing outage of Microsoft’s collaboration tools will have a “cascading” effect on businesses, with the financial impact increasing the longer it stretches, experts say. Microsoft 365 tools Exchange Online and Outlook were affected, with Teams, SharePoint Online, Copilot also likely to face an impact from the interruption that began on Thursday. The company is still working on fixing it. “The continuing outage of Microsoft’s collaboration tools, especially emails and scheduling, will not only impact communications, but also have a cascading impact on decision-making, revenue and service delivery,” said Saurabh Verma, vice president, ICT growth advisory at consultancy Frost & Sullivan. “The actual dollar impact or revenue loss would go up with every passing minute, as millions of organisations across critical and non-critical sectors are deeply embedded with MS 365 suite.” Microsoft's outage reports on November 12 reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour on Downdetector, which monitors internet disruption. Microsoft's outage reports on November 12 reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour on Downdetector. Microsoft says its Exchange Online incident began at 16:17 UTC. Reports to Downdetector about Outlook began climbing at about 17:25 UTC, 12:25 in New York. By 18:25,… pic.twitter.com/7FQ4dDsfbm — Downdetector (@downdetector) November 12, 2026 The financial consequences from such an outage are significant, said Morey Haber, chief security adviser at BeyondTrust. “Lost productivity, interrupted transactions, missed revenue and recovery expenses can quickly accumulate into millions of dollars across affected organisations,” he said. “While Microsoft may offer contractual service credits under applicable Service Level Agreements (SLAs), these typically represent a fraction of actual business losses. Credits generally offset future service charges rather than compensate customers for lost revenue, operational disruption, or reputational damage.” The outage may also affect software as a service (SaaS) tools using MS’s 365 application programming interface (APIs), which refers to rules that allow software apps to communicate, Mr Verma said. “With MS having a significant market share in collab tools, there is no escaping and second solution to it. No product in today’s age and time is immune to such outage,” he added. The outage “exposes the severe operational fragility of single-vendor cloud concentration” across global businesses and financial markets, said Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial. It has caused a considerable amount of disruption to financial workflows, although on the capital markets side, the core stock exchange matching engines are largely unaffected, he added. The Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange said on Friday that some of its electronic services may be temporarily unavailable, while email notifications may take longer than usual to reach users. The exchange said it is closely monitoring developments and working to restore all services and operations to normal as soon as possible. “Institutional execution desks lost their primary email channels during a turbulent week of trading and were therefore forced to revert to phone calls and WhatsApp to confirm settlements,” Mr Valecha said. Richemont, the Swiss luxury group that owns Cartier, was forced to delay its results. On the banking side, payment clearing was not affected at all, although payment networks and banking portals that required a secondary login were all having problems, he added. Technology disruptions have been common in recent years, as digital usage continues to soar. In October last year, Microsoft's Azure portal went down, affecting hundreds of thousands of people trying to access apps, games, websites and other services. That came in the same month that an outage of Amazon Web Services, which lasted for about 15 hours, disrupted several AWS-hosted services and platforms. In June this year, several web platforms, apps and internet services including X , Zoom, Reddit, Canva, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Teams , Fortnite and Discord also experienced significant disruption. Managing outages The lesson from the outage isn't that Microsoft is unreliable, but that every cloud platform will have a bad day, said Samir Elabed, cybersecurity engineer and founder of SECyber. For companies to reduce the impact, they must have an out-of-band communication channel agreed in advance, such as a phone tree, SMS or a secondary messaging app, so staff aren't left guessing, he said. “Keep your business continuity and incident-response plans somewhere you can actually reach during an outage. If your continuity plan lives in SharePoint, you don't really have one,” he said. It is also important to identify the most critical processes, such as payroll, customer service and sales, and decide on a manual or alternative workaround for each, he said. “Run tabletop exercises that treat a major cloud outage as a realistic scenario, not a remote one,” he added. For finance companies to mitigate risk, they must use out-of-band communication channels such as independent messaging platforms, dedicated voice lines and secondary SMS modes so trading desks and crisis teams can co-ordinate immediately when primary email services go dark, Mr Valecha said. “This is exactly what desks in Singapore have used,” he added. “Decoupled identity and access management can also be explored. If a single vendor handles both email and single sign-on, an outage locks staff out of third-party applications that are otherwise running normally.” Also, although the Microsoft outage is not a cybersecurity issue, hostile actors could be looking to take advantage of those affected, offering a resolution or assurances, said Aiden Sinnott, principal threat researcher at Sophos Counter Threat Unit. “People should exercise caution when receiving emails, texts or calls purporting to be from Microsoft or other affected businesses, particularly banks or shops,” he said. “Be aware of requests for urgent action, sharing of personal information and avoid clicking on links sent via message or email.” Mr Elabed agreed, calling an outage “a gift to attackers”, with phishing emails typically sent within hours. “Businesses should send a short message to staff early on, through a channel that isn't affected, explaining that the issue sits with the provider, that IT will never ask them to re-enter passwords to fix it and how to report anything suspicious.” He called for phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication and conditional access, and urged IT teams to review sign-in logs for unusual activity even after services are restored. “The attack often comes after the outage, not during it,” he added. The Bank of England, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, and the Bank of Thailand today published the findings from their collaboration on foreign exchange (FX) settlement under Project Meridian FX APAC. footnote [1] The project showed that synchronisation – a service that coordinates movements of central bank money – could be one approach to supporting interoperability across wholesale settlement environments built on different technologies and operating models. This marks significant progress in making cross-border FX transactions safer and more efficient, and supporting interoperability as different forms of money evolve in different ways. In light of the Bank of England’s plans to launch a live synchronisation interface in 2028, footnote [2] the findings provide valuable insight into how the approach could be developed into a live service. Building on the earlier work, footnote [3] Project Meridian FX APAC tested payment-versus-payment FX settlement footnote [4] and multilateral net FX across the three central banks’ test environments, spanning both Real-Time Gross Settlement and Distributed Ledger Technology-based settlement systems. The project encompassed a wider range of currencies, technologies, infrastructures and time zones. Partior, the project’s delivery partner, developed, integrated and tested the Synchronisation Operator footnote [5] prototype for the trial. The trial demonstrated that synchronised settlement can be achieved across central bank systems with different technologies and capabilities, while identifying the requirements and trade-offs involved. They also demonstrated how multilateral net FX settlement can support banks in using their liquidity more efficiently by netting payments against each other. The project also examined the legal, regulatory and oversight considerations for applying synchronised FX settlement across diverse wholesale settlement systems. The analysis was informed by perspectives from the Reserve Bank of Australia and Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, who participated as observer central banks. The project’s findings and insights are published across three complementary reports: Introduction and Executive Summary , Technical Report , and Policy Report . Together, they set out the experimental results, key technical findings and policy considerations. These results provide insights for further exploration of synchronisation as a means of enabling safer and more efficient FX settlement across diverse wholesale settlement systems. Future work could involve extending the existing approach to additional jurisdictions and industry participants, a wider range of currencies and transaction scenarios, and further consider the legal arrangements needed in practice. Tom Mutton, Executive Director of Payments, Innovation and Fintech at the Bank of England, said, ‘Innovation has the greatest impact when it addresses real world challenges. Project Meridian FX APAC provides practical evidence of how synchronised settlement could help reduce risk and improve efficiency in cross-border FX transactions. The results provide a strong foundation for further collaboration as we explore how this approach could be developed towards real-world use’. Kenneth Gay, Chief FinTech Officer at the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said, ‘Cross-border settlement increasingly takes place across systems built on different technologies and operating models.

events.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
events.summary: Innovations A wave of announcements this week, including several from SEMICON Europa and electronica 2026 in Munich, highlighted advances in semiconductor manufacturing, advanced packaging, automotive chips, and AI hardware. Manufacturing Infineon reported an industry-first milestone in 300mm silicon carbide manufacturing , fabricating functional power devices at its Villach, Austria fab using existing silicon processing equipment. The larger wafers can accommodate 2.3 times as many chips as 200mm wafers, potentially lowering manufacturing costs for automotive, industrial, and AI data center power devices. imec completed baseline process flows for its NanoIC silicon-interposer platform , including TSVs and multiple routing layers for chiplet and 3D integration. A silicon-interposer PDK is planned for early 2027. Chips and systems AMD introduced its 6th-gen EPYC server and embedded processors, including models for semiconductor ATE; an AI GPU with 288GB of HBM4; and tamper-resistant FPGAs for security-critical systems. Arm introduced the Cortex-M42 processor to bring ML and DSP capabilities to cost- and area-constrained intelligent endpoints in a compact, AHB-based design. Google added two new 8th-gen TPU systems : TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and higher rack compute density, and TPU 8tx for secure and confidential inference. TPU 8tx pairs Google accelerators with AMD EPYC CPU hosts. Fallout continues after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation : Congressional investigations: Senators are seeking the preservation of records related to chip exports and Megaspeed, calling for tighter AI-chip export controls . House committee leaders also requested a closed-door Nov. 18 briefing from Huang. Inaction questioned: President Trump authorized tougher action on suspected Nvidia chip diversion three times this year, but Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick resisted over concerns that tighter restrictions could escalate trade tensions with China , Axios reported. Separately, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter contacted a senior Commerce Dept. official in late summer 2025 seeking information about the Megaspeed chip-smuggling investigation, indicating Nvidia’s legal leadership was aware of the investigation before the current scandal. The company subsequently characterized its Megaspeed dealings as “ normal .” Circular financing: Nvidia’s web of financial ties across the AI industry is facing fresh scrutiny after Huang’s resignation. The Financial Times says Nvidia made more than 120 investments this year and held or committed about $124B in equity investments by July, raising questions about whether its aggressive dealmaking and financing of companies that buy its chips will continue without him. Policy fallout: The episode has renewed debate over export-control enforcement and Chinese intelligence targeting of U.S. technology companies, with CFR highlighting enforcement gaps and CSET urging scrutiny without overreaction . Deals and funding Siemens plans to acquire Lauterbach , a provider of hardware-assisted debugging and real-time trace tools for embedded software and complex SoCs. The deal is expected to close in H1 2027. Mitsui Chemicals confirmed it will acquire JSR in a transaction valued at approximately ¥1.84T ($11.9B), combining two major Japanese materials suppliers, including JSR’s photoresist and advanced materials businesses. TSMC approved investments of up to $1B in OpenAI and Anthropic , allocating up to $500M for each, plus a separate $500M investment company focused on the semiconductor ecosystem. Fractile raised $720M to develop frontier AI chips that stack DRAM directly on top of logic to speed up output token generation. Memory Samsung Electronics broke ground on a previously announced HBM advanced-packaging facility in Asan, South Korea , accelerating the planned start of production by a year to June 2028. TSMC is reportedly considering 3D DRAM production at Nvidia ’s request, potentially through new capacity or an acquired fab. Still, TSMC said that it remains focused on its core logic foundry business. Vertical Compute and imec expanded their collaboration to integrate magnetic memory directly above 16nm logic . Winbond approved NT$73.1B (US$2.2B) in spending to expand its 300mm memory fab in Kaohsiung, Taiwan . China, meanwhile, leads in critical-mineral production and downloads of open AI models. CSIS says Chinese rare-earth shipments to the U.S. remain about 75% below pre-restriction levels , despite agreements intended to restore supply. U.S. chipmakers have also faced scandium shortages and delays in obtaining Chinese export licenses. Counterpoint Research says soaring memory prices are driving up smartphone costs , with memory now accounting for 54% of a low-end phone’s bill of materials, up from 20% in Q3 2025. Prices are expected to keep rising through Q1 2027. events.title: How Novig became the third biggest prediction market site despite launching only months ago
events.summary: Since bursting on the scene two years ago, prediction markets have become one of the buzziest new sectors in finance, pulling in billions of dollars in revenue, and driving daily news headlines. The young industry is dominated by two giants, Kalshi and Polymarket, but numerous other companies are trying to muscle into the field. That includes the sports-focused prediction market Novig, which only launched as a federally regulated prediction market in August, but has already claimed the number three spot by one widely used industry metric. Over the past 30 days, Novig handled $1.8 billion in trading volume on U.S.-regulated exchanges, according to the PM Pulse, a newsletter that tracks prediction market volume using data from research firm Aldrin. That figure is small next to Kalshi’s $33.3 billion and Polymarket U.S.’s $6.3 billion. But it’s about $300 million ahead of Crypto.com, the fourth-place contender, and its volume is up 80% from the previous 30 days. The volume figures don’t account for combos, or multi-game parlays, which Sam Schwartz, who runs the newsletter, says can inflate volume without producing proportionally more revenue for the exchange.  Novig’s ascent is notable given how little money it has raised compared to other prediction markets. Founded in 2021, the company enjoyed modest growth and raised $30 million as it pursued a sweepstakes-based business model that allowed it to operate in certain states. But a shift in the legal landscape led Novig this year to become a federally regulated prediction market, helping it raise a new $75 million Series B round in February at a $500 million valuation. The company is also reportedly raising a new round of capital at a $2 billion valuation, though Novig declined to comment on future fundraises.  While Novig has raised $105 million in total, that figure is dwarfed by Kalshi’s fundraising, which amounts to roughly $3.8 billion across 13 funding rounds, according to Tracxn data, including two $1 billion rounds since May. Polymarket, meanwhile, has raised roughly $3.3 billion across eight rounds, including $1 billion from New York Stock Exchange owner Intercontinental Exchange , and another $1 billion in a round led by Donald Trump Jr.-backed venture capital firm 1789 Capital. “There are very few companies I think outside of AI that have achieved our level of growth in the span of two months,” Novig cofounder and CEO Jacob Fortinsky told Fortune . Novig’s explosive growth, which has seen it swell from 20 to 100 employees this year, is due in no small part to Sydney Sweeney. The actress, who is a part owner of the company, starred in a viral ad campaign called “Just Sports” that made Novig a household name for millions. In the 30 days after the campaign launched in September, Novig says first-time deposits rose 362% and mobile app downloads jumped 261%, compared with the 30 days before, according to internal data the company provided. Its annualized gross revenue also reached about $200 million in October, up from about $29 million in August. During the rollout, the app briefly hit No. 1 on the App Store’s top free sports apps chart. Novig’s early success comes at a time when conventional sports betting platforms like DraftKings and FanDuel are diving into the prediction markets industry too, while a host of smaller startups are also fighting to carve out a niche. It has been a difficult race, given how much weight the behemoths pull. Kalshi, which has held the top slot for months, accounts for roughly 64% of trading volume excluding combos over the past 30 days, and Polymarket’s U.S. and DeFi arms together hold about 23%. That leaves just 13% of the market split among the rest of the field, with Novig capturing 3.5% of that—edging out established competitors like Crypto.com and DraftKings’ DKeX platform to claim third place. Why sports only Like other prediction markets, Novig makes the case that it offers sports traders a better deal than conventional betting platforms. The company notes that it runs a peer-to-peer exchange where users trade against each other, not against the house, which gives traders tighter prices and lower costs than traditional sportsbooks and most prediction markets. “That’s the main reason Novig saw growth early as a company—it’s just such a natural draw to the professional and sophisticated users out there… they want to get the best odds possible,” Schwartz explained. Unlike many of its competitors, the company has zeroed in on the most popular event contract category out there: sports. Much like it marketed in its Just Sports campaign, Novig repeatedly emphasizes that it does not offer trades on politics or pop culture, and that its users must be 21 or older—a distinction from Kalshi and Polymarket, which allow 18-year-olds to bet on their platforms.  At first glance, focusing only on sports contracts might seem like a missed opportunity for Novig to capture huge, headline-grabbing volume spikes. When the midterm elections arrived, for instance, trading in politics and election contracts on Kalshi reached $729 million on Election Day alone. Over the full week, elections accounted for more than 70% of Kalshi’s volume growth excluding combos, according to data published by the PM Pulse. All of this, of course, resulted in a wave of free marketing since political news reports frequently cited odds on the platform. But once election week is over, political trading drops off sharply. Schwartz noted that on most other days this year, elections made up less than half of 1% of Kalshi’s daily volume. Sports, on the other hand, are on the calendar nearly every day, and they drive more than 80% of prediction market trading. That steady pace is what Novig is built around. Limits to growth While Novig’s low-fee model has succeeded in drawing sophisticated, high-volume traders, it doesn’t appear to be a major factor when it comes to the average retail bettor. “The majority of users out there are not price sensitive,” Schwartz said. Sportsbooks like DraftKings and FanDuel, along with Kalshi, keep winning customers despite charging more. There is also an ongoing legal battle over the legality of sports-related prediction markets, which is widely expected to land at the Supreme Court next year, and has already led several states to move aggressively against the platforms. So far, state-level restrictions haven’t badly dented growth, but Schwartz said a drawn-out battle could slowly shrink access. Kalshi has already had to shrink its footprint from 50 states to 47 after bans in three states, including Nevada and Michigan, and Schwartz predicts a handful of others may do the same. The timing of a Supreme Court ruling matters, too. Schwartz called it about a coin flip whether the justices rule in June 2027 or June 2028, and said the court would likely need to take the case by mid-January for a 2027 decision. events.title: Microsoft outage hits MAS, banks’ e-mails; banks offer customers alternative contact channels
events.summary: The Association of Banks in Singapore said banks affected by the disruption had also put up notices on various channels to alert customers to the outage. SINGAPORE – Banks in Singapore whose e-mails and communications have been affected by the global Microsoft outage have reached out to customers with alternative ways to access help, including customer service hotlines and relationship managers. Meanwhile, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said it was closely monitoring the situation. The financial regulator has also experienced disruption to its e-mail services, but said its operations remained unaffected. The Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS) said banks affected by the disruption, particularly those providing retail banking services, have put up notices on various channels, including their websites, to alert customers to the outage. Checks by The Straits Times show that DBS, UOB, OCBC, HSBC and Maybank Singapore are among those affected. ABS director Ong-Ang Ai Boon said banks were making alternative contact arrangements available to customers while the disruption persisted. Customers are advised not to click on unknown or unsolicited links or respond to messages relating to the disruption as these could lead to phishing attempts, scams, credential theft and malware infections. The advisory comes amid concerns that cybercriminals could take advantage of the disruption to impersonate banks or send fraudulent messages to customers seeking information or help. DBS, Singapore’s largest lender, said responses to e-mails would be delayed because of the Microsoft outage. DBS customers can, however, continue to perform transactions via the bank’s ATMs, debit/credit cards, DBS/POSB digibank and PayLah!, all of which remain unaffected. They can use DBS/POSB digibank to receive push notifications. DBS wealth and corporate clients can also contact their relationship managers. The bank also warned customers to beware of scammers claiming to be from DBS or technology companies offering to resolve system issues. Maybank Singapore said in a Facebook post that all its digital and physical banking services remain safe and operational, though e-mails may be delayed. It directed customers to its digital channels, ATMs and self-service terminals. OCBC said responses to customer inquiries may be delayed. Those requiring urgent help should reach out to their relationship managers or the bank’s customer service hotlines. It too reminded customers to be vigilant against scammers taking advantage of the disruption. Microsoft suffered a major global outage, bringing many of its widely used tools, including e-mail and cloud storage, to a standstill. In Singapore, Downdetector began recording reports at about 2am overnight, with numbers continuing to climb on the morning of Nov 13. MAS, in a banner displayed on its website, said it was monitoring its systems and the broader situation closely. Members of the public can continue to contact the central bank through its online feedback form. Financial institutions seeking to reach MAS can also use alternative channels, including phone calls or the online feedback form, it added. ABS/Association of Banks in Singapore

events.title: C++26 stumbles at finish line over Contracts dispute
events.summary: The next version of the C++ programming language may be delayed at the last minute due to a dispute over a security-enhancing Contracts feature. Contracts have deeply split C++ technical maintainers. One group backs the C++ creator Bjarne Stroustrup , who is against the technology in its present form in grounds it was hastily implemented. But others are eager to see Contracts implemented, even arguing the tech's detractors are poisoning the C++ development process itself. The disagreement boiled over just before a vote to ratify the new version of the language. In October, the Draft International Standard (DIS) of C++26 failed its ISO ballot — the next-to-last stage in the International Organization for Standardization’s approval process during which a standard's technical details are formally ratified by a set of national standards bodies. The ballot saw 13 votes cast in favor, 9 against, and 12 abstentions, failing to meet the ISO requirement of having no more than 25 percent negative votes. Contracts was the major sticking point for those voting nay. Contracts dispute Contracts allow developers to add preconditions and postconditions to code, as well as assertions that check whether specified conditions hold. Such checks can help catch programming errors that might otherwise lead to undefined behavior. Design by Contract has long been a feature of languages like Ada and Eiffel . Developers have proposed adding Contracts to C++ for at least a decade, after when they were abruptly yanked from C++20 owing to concerns over dangerous defaults. But Stroustrup roasted the revised proposal ( P2900 ) that made it into C++26. “The P2900 contracts and extensions aim to change the nature of C++ and are an existential threat to C++, adding complexity and bloat,” Stroustrup and his colleagues wrote in a paper last August. They noted that the implementation is messy, outdated, not sufficiently tested , and could be more effectively implemented as a library. Not everyone agrees. Andreas Fertig , a member of the C++ standardization committee, feels that the criticisms have already been vetted and that vetoing the proposal this late in the C++ release process is damaging to C++ itself. “The topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting ‘no,’ an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken,” Fertig wrote in a blog post . The elephant in the room is, of course, the ongoing criticism of how easy it is for developers to accidentally create security holes in C++, leading more than a few projects to adopt Rust . Adding controls might, as Stroustrup notes, hamper C++’s chief attribute of being a blazing-fast language . Sore losers Fertig accused Stroustrup and Co. of being sore losers. “Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes,” he wrote. But in this case, “the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust." Unlike Fertig, Harry Bott, CEO of the C++ Alliance – which maintains the open source EDG C++ compiler front end – does not see the Contracts discussion as disruptive to C++ itself. “The draft being sent back isn’t a failure of the process—it’s the process working as intended,” he wrote to The Register by email. “That doesn’t mean the process can’t improve. The goal should be to learn from this and strengthen the process so C++ can continue to evolve in a way developers can rely on.” Where to now? With the ballot failing at this late point of the standardization process – a rarity in C++ history – the language risks missing its expected shipping date of this year. That outcome may force everyone to refer to the new version as “C++27” rather than C++26. (That’s only the informal name; the official name of this eighth version of the language, should it be released next year, would be “ISO/IEC 14882:2027.”) ISO C++ working group WG21 is meeting next week in Búzios, Brazil, for the confronto final. According to a blog post from Thibault Ricord-Marchal, a software engineering consultant at the Paris-based Margo consultancy , the group faces a number of choices. They can carve Contracts out of the spec so the rest of C++26 can ship. That will be messy work, though. The undo button has to be smashed on a lot of library hardening already done using Contracts. Another option is moving Contracts into a separate technical specification, where work can continue to refine the technology. Or they could do a minor revision, vote again and hope the balmy Brazilian weather chills everyone out.®

events.title: Oil on track to post second weekly decline as Trump eases fears of renewed war with Iran
events.summary: Oil prices were on course to post a second weekly decline as supply concerns eased, after US President Donald Trump signalled that he is not keen to restart the Iran war. But further attacks on ships in the region mean prices remain volatile. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, was down 0.24 per cent at $95.59 a barrel at 8.53am UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, was trading 0.54 per cent lower at $88.26 a barrel. Both Brent and WTI are set for decline of more than 2.5 per cent decline for the week, after plunging about 13 per cent last week. Mr Trump this week indicated that he is not planning to resume the war with Iran after his Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the midterm elections. He also said on Thursday that the US was no longer looking to reach an agreement with Tehran. “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, hundreds of billions of dollars, and we’ve got their strait,” Mr Trump said in a post on Truth Social. But attacks continue on ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz, the global chokepoint for two thirds of global crude supply and liquefied natural gas, putting upward pressure on oil prices amid supply risks. This week, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed there were explosions on two supertankers carrying more than four million barrels of oil in the strait. A tanker was also struck by a projectile while travelling east in the Arabian Gulf, with casualties reported, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said yesterday. Attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure by Yemen's Houthis also pushing prices higher. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said that a pumping station on the kingdom's East-West oil pipeline and the Yanbu oil installation on the Red Sea coast were hit on Thursday. Saudi Arabia has been exporting much of its crude through the pipeline since the beginning of the war, owing to disruption in the strait. Meanwhile, gold rose on ⁠Friday after prices ​reached a more than one-year low in the previous session. Spot gold climbed 1 per cent to $3,917.70 per ounce at 9.55am UAE time. Gold prices dropped below the $4,000 level as markets expect a December increase by the US Federal Reserve.
