As The Register reported yesterday , the outage started on Thursday at around 18:00 UTC and saw Microsoft 365 users unable to access email, attend Teams meetings, use cloud PCs, consult Copilot, or enjoy full access to another 15 hosted services. The software giant says the outage impacts Microsoft 365 services “that interact with Exchange Online and email services.” Services that don’t need Exchange Online remain functional. The software giant initially blamed the outage on a mysterious “problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.” Microsoft thought it found a fix but quickly admitted “Actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief.” In the hours since, the situation has not improved markedly, and Microsoft is still struggling to restore service. It has also changed the language it uses when discussing the possibility that a cyberattack is the reason for the outage. As of 04:11 UTC, the company said it could find “no indication this is the result of malicious activity.” An update time-stamped 05:46 UTC stated “As of now, we are not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident.” Microsoft’s status page includes only the company’s most recent update, but its RSS feed preserves each missive. That feed tells a tale of woe that we have distilled into lowlights and present in chronological order: We’re applying infrastructure capacity improvements where possible in an effort to help support traffic in regions coming online; We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed that change is not taking as expected; We’re reviewing traffic flows and affected infrastructure to identify opportunities to optimize routing. This includes verifying the reasons for service failures so we can develop specific actions to improve stability; We’re identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied to increase capacity in the face of sustained traffic management imbalances; We're observing partial recovery across regions in which we've applied these adjustments; however, these actions aren't resulting in sustained recovery; Current actions we are taking include scaling up virtual machines to increase capacity and reduce load. However, we are encountering issues with the machines being stuck in a bad state, preventing our changes from syncing as expected. Microsoft’s latest status update doesn’t suggest this will be over any time soon. “We’re continuing to pursue multiple workstreams to pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx and advance the recoverability of the backend servers,” Microsoft wrote. “We’re taking a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure to improve the ability to confirm the developed changes were applied. We’re tracking the results of this approach to verify the servers are showing the anticipated recovery and performance intended.”

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters It wasn't the not-very-legal source code raid that caused it, but a colleague who punted a pager Ye olde server consolidation has made Cisco push top-of-rack switching to 100G 2 days ago Smart meters to cost the UK billions: 2G switch-off means replacing 12-13 million 3 days ago Cisco to link all future products to its SaaS-y Cloud Control management tool 3 days ago Doom delivers five minutes of terminal violence on an IBM mainframe 5 days ago Internet governance about to get its quadrennial stress test at ITU meeting 5 days ago Working in tech support can be thankless when gormless colleagues leave you sleepless. Which is why, each Friday, The Register runs a new instalment of On Call – the reader contributed column which ensures your work to keep tech alive doesn't remain unnoticed. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Tim" who told us that while working for a phone company he once rewrote 2,650 lines of C as a six line shell script. He performed that feat after being asked to fix a data transfer program that, strangely, included a bespoke implementation of the venerable File Transfer Protocol (FTP). "Writing the script took eight hours, most of it tracking down the source code of FTP so I could see if it would do what I wanted," Tim wrote. This story took place before the World Wide Web became the way to find information online. To find the code he needed, Tim therefore used a Wide Area Information Server (WAIS) to search remote databases. "In those days, there was no Linux and AT&T had licensed the Unix source code to universities with the strict proviso that it never be made publicly available," Tim explained. "It took me quite some time using WAIS to track it down – the security could have been better – and read the code." Having found what he needed, Tim wrote his script, which ran overnight to collect data from the telco's switches, tidied up the raw info, and uploaded it to a mainframe. "It would automatically page me if it couldn't connect to a switch or mainframe after three attempts," he explained. The script worked fine, but the telco's networks didn't. Tim's pager was soon going off two or three times a night, every night. After two weeks of interrupted sleep, Tim's manager kindly told him to give the pager to a colleague. But that colleague habitually left the pager at work, forgot to turn it on, or conveniently placed it out of earshot. So Tim reluctantly took back the pager and endured another few weeks of nightly interruptions. How many consecutive sleepless nights have you endured while On Call? events.title: Politicians back focus on cost of living
events.summary: Targeted action on the cost of living is among the Government of Jersey's priorities for the next political term Published 13 November 2026, 06:23 GMT Politicians have backed the Government of Jersey's key priorities for the next political term which includes action on the cost of living. States members adopted the Common Strategic Policy , external which lays out the Council of Ministers' priorities for the political term until 2030. The priorities are centered around four pillars including targeted action on the cost of living, restoring Jersey's competitiveness, investing in homes and infrastructure and maintaining financial stability. Chief Minister Lyndon Farnham said the government was determined "to make Jersey a more affordable place to live" but Reform Jersey co-leader Lyndsay Feltham said the policy lacked "real action". The policy was backed with 31 votes in favour, 10 against and two abstentions. Ministers first published the proposed policy in September and this week politicians debated a number of amendments proposed by backbenchers. This included adding a priority about government transparency and promoting democracy , bringing the total number of priorities up from 11 to 12. Reform Jersey co-leader deputy Lyndsay Feltham does not support the government's Common Strategic Policy Listen to the latest news for Jersey Deputy Feltham's amendments to add actions to the policy about household affordability and employment rights were rejected and members also voted not to include reference to rental stress. The Reform Jersey co-leader said she was worried about the gaps this left behind. "What I really wanted to see from government was something more sustained and a sustained commitment to reduce everyday cost of living," said Feltham. "They've committed to a review of household affordability. A review doesn't put food on the table or a roof over somebody's head. "I am really concerned that ministers aren't going to actually take any action." Chief Minister Senator Lyndon Farnham believes the Common Strategic Policy reflects islanders' interests However, the chief minister said the policy recognised islanders' concerns such as affordability, housing, economic growth, investing in infrastructure and protecting the environment. In his closing speech, Farnham said their contributions "reflected a shared commitment to securing the best possible future for our island". He said the policy "will send an important message to islanders that we are putting their interests before our political disagreements". events.title: Cider makers fear future for orchards as costs grow
events.summary: Cider maker Matilda Temperley said the budget had been "disappointing" Published 13 November 2026, 06:21 GMT Rising costs could force the cider industry to reduce their reliance on British-grown apples, according to several well-established businesses. Higher alcohol duty, energy bills and packaging costs are making it harder to stay profitable, according to a producer in Somerset. The government said it was supporting the sector by increasing the value of Small Producer Relief, which provides lower alcohol duty rates for some smaller and medium-sized producers. Matilda Temperley, director of Burrow Hill farm near Martock, said it would be a "tragedy" to stop using its own apples due to climbing costs. Temperley, whose farm has been growing apples for 300 years, said recent increases had added to pressures already facing the industry, adding at 6% alcohol, their traditional cider is taxed at a higher rate than mass produced cider. Christmas market fears as roadworks cause long delays Published 13 hours ago Gritters out for the first time this autumn Published 1 day ago No radical change after nationalisation, GWR says Published 23 hours ago "By next February, we will have seen a 61% increase in tax on our standard 50cl bottles," Temperley claimed. She welcomed the rise in Small Producers Relief but said other mounting costs outweighed it. "We've got huge, energy costs, then almost a 90% increase in tax costs since 2020." "The thing that will happen is that if you're a big cider maker, you're going to look to cut your costs and the only way to cut costs is to stop using British apples," she said. "That's a real tragedy because cider should be made from these beautiful orchards". Isaac Stell says ultimately it will be the consumer who pays Isaac Stell, a financial analyst at Wealth Club in Bristol, said that having pledged not to raise the main rates of income tax, national insurance or VAT for working people, the recent budget focused on other areas to "help plug the fiscal hole." He said producers were also dealing with higher employer National Insurance contributions and increases in the minimum wage. "Inevitably, some of those additional costs will find their way through to the pubs, clubs and restaurants that producers supply, and ultimately to an already squeezed consumer. " Matthew Showering said like his apples - his business is growing The Showerings family, known for producing Babycham, has been making drinks in Shepton Mallet for more than 14 generations. "Our business has grown a lot in the last ten years - we've gone from having 80 employees to around 350 now," the firm's managing director Matthew Showering said. "We've had a good couple of years, we're making drinks that are popular and growing." While acknowledging rising costs, Showering said he would rather see less government intervention. "We don't want any help from the government, we'd rather they keep out of things as much as possible." Matt Gillett from Tricky's Cider with his apple picker Johnny Matt Gillett from Tricky's Cider in Low Ham said the size of his operation means he will be eligible for the Small Producer Relief but adds he will not see a huge benefit as the Alcohol Duty is a "fairly substantial" part of his monthly outgoings. Gillett remains optimistic, and said he would not consider importing pulp or concentrate to cut costs. "We are a craft producer here in Somerset and are proud of the fact we take from local orchards, traditional orchards, and use the fruit that is available here in this county." A spokesperson for the Treasury said: "The cider industry makes a vital contribution to our rural economy and communities, and cider continues to benefit from significantly lower duty rates than other alcoholic drinks. "But we know the industry is facing continued pressures, which is why the Budget provides additional support by cutting costs for pubs and bars that are vital customers for the industry and poured pints continue to benefit from draught relief." events.title: ‘They’ve cut all entry-level jobs’: unlikely seaside town on frontline of AI threat
events.summary: Bournemouth became a hub for thousands of finance jobs after the 1980s big bang, but new tech risks hurting Dorset’s economy A few minutes’ drive from Bournemouth’s sandy beachfront, on the site of a former farm, lies an unlikely nerve centre of international finance. Here, miles from the glass towers of London’s Canary Wharf, more than 5,300 staff including compliance officers, analysts and software engineers help process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day for the largest US bank, JP Morgan. The sprawling five-hectare (13-acre) campus, which hosted just 650 workers when it opened in 1986, has solidified Dorset’s status as one of Britain’s largest financial hubs outside London. Now, the financial services industry accounts for 10% of the county’s turnover – the total revenue generated by all businesses in the area – with 2,500 companies, including Nationwide Building Society, the insurer LV=, and the asset manager Rathbones, collectively employing 24,000 staff, according to the Dorset Chamber of Commerce. But along with other regional finance centres outside London, from Leeds to Birmingham, and Swindon to Cardiff, it faces an existential threat from AI. Bosses are considering how the technology can help automate costly human-led jobs, putting at risk a swathe of back-office roles, such as data processors, compliance checkers and entry-level analysts. The Barclays chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, last month announced 5,000 job cuts linked to advances in AI , while another London-headquartered bank, Standard Chartered, said in May it was planning to slash 7,000 roles as it doubled down on artificial intelligence. AI now poses the biggest threat to the UK’s financial workforce since the 2008 financial crisis, says Caren Evans, a national officer for the Unite union, referring to an era when banks needed multibillion-pound taxpayer bailouts and subsequently embarked on swingeing cost cuts. Unite members, who include staff at NatWest, Lloyds and Barclays , are “very very worried about AI”, Evans says. “They’re worried about losing their job, they’re worried about having future skills, they’re worried about having sustainable careers.” All that is hitting staff morale. One Barclays employee said they felt “very undervalued and insignificant”, adding: “It’s kind of hard to be enthusiastic about your work when you know, at any moment, senior executives are thinking about how to get rid of you. You’re not seen as an asset, you’re seen as a problem to be removed.” The JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, has warned of the fallout from AI, saying widespread job losses could spark “civil unrest” unless governments and business supported displaced workers. He said retraining programmes, and even state-sponsored wage support, relocation schemes and early retirement could be needed to ease the blow. In Dorset, the banking tech push has already left its mark, with bosses closing Barclays House in Poole in 2022 after 46 years of operation. “It was the original site that all the cheques in the country used to go through, to be checked,” Gareth Sherwood, the president of the Dorset Chamber of Commerce, says. “And of course, that went with digitisation.” That office block still stands empty today. Sherwood’s organisation has been coaching local business to embrace AI and increase productivity. “There’s winners and losers in all change,” he says. But “we would still encourage people to use human beings”, both to support local jobs, but also mitigate cybersecurity risks and unplanned outages. “You can’t switch a human off in the same way that you can switch an AI off,” he adds. But if cost-cutting bank bosses start to axe back office roles at pace, there would be ripple effects throughout regional economies such as Dorset. Demand for professional support from law firms and consultancies could start to dry up, and the wider ecosystem of services, such as gyms, hairdressers, restaurants and estate agents, could start to suffer. “The collateral would be to some of the more service aspects of [the economy],” Sherwood says. “And it’s hard enough to keep young people in this area.” The Conservative councillor Lawrence Williams has served Littledown and Iford, the ward hosting JP Morgan’s campus, since 2011. He originally moved to the area in the early 1980s, shortly before the bank – then known as Chase Manhattan – took up its lodgings on former farmland. The 76-year-old regularly meets JP Morgan bosses, but says he has heard nothing of AI-related job cuts. The bank itself says the Bournemouth campus is a “centre for financial innovation”, adding: “AI will enable us to do more, and we train our people to make the most of it.” But if companies start to follow in Barclays’ and Standard Chartered’s footsteps, that “could hit quite hard”, particularly for an economy otherwise reliant on seasonal tourism, Williams says.

events.title: An iconic puzzle comes home as production of the Rubik's Cube returns to Hungary
events.summary: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles BUDAPEST, Hungary -- More than half a century ago, a Hungarian architect, sculptor and professor invented what would become one of the world's most popular and beloved puzzles whose appeal has spanned generations: the colorful, mind-bending, six-sided Rubik's Cube. Now, after selling more than half a billion units and becoming a worldwide cultural touchstone, production of the cube is returning to Hungary, where its inventor, Ernő Rubik, first conceived of the iconic object that bears his name. Hungary “is the home of the cube. The cube was born here,” Rubik, 82, said on Tuesday at the opening of a new, fully automated Rubik's Cube production line in the Hungarian city of Jászberény. The journey of the Rubik's Cube began in 1974, when Rubik was teaching design at the Academy of Applied Arts and Design in Budapest. Seeking to create a three-dimensional object that was “infinite,” he said, he completed a prototype — then made of wood — of a cube that could rotate on multiple axes and was made up of 27 blocks. Recognizing its consumer value, Rubik soon began producing more of the puzzles. Beginning in 1977, an initial 5,000 units of what was then called the “Magic Cube” were sold at specialty shops in the Hungarian capital. The invention — or what Rubik prefers to describe as a “discovery” — gained popularity, and after having difficulties procuring materials for the cubes in then-socialist Hungary, he realized: “We were not prepared for that size of production ... We can’t fulfill the needs of the market worldwide.” The cube was licensed to a British and then a U.S. toy company, and its production was moved abroad. By the early 1980s, its popularity had exploded in what Rubik called “the first big wave,” in which he said 200 million units were sold between 1980 and 1983. While sales of the cube dipped after its initial success, it still attracts plenty of users eager to try their hand at solving the puzzle. Millions are sold every year. At the new production line in Hungary, a series of robotic arms assembles the cubes and tests them for functionality and durability — a level of automation Rubik said was “very different” than in the early days when the cubes were assembled by hand. The new line in Jászberény plans to produce 1 million cubes annually. Steve Radewych, a senior vice president with Canadian toy company Spin Master, which owns the Rubik's Cube trademark, said at Tuesday's opening that the theme of the day was: “Back to its roots: The cube comes home.” Microsoft apologizes for email disruption, says AI agents not responsible Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE “Ernő, your discovery is more than a toy,” Radewych told Rubik. “It's a global social phenomenon.” Radewych noted the “incredible staying power” of the Rubik's Cube, and the fact that the puzzle continues to hold the fascination of young people even today. “The cube represents an intellectual journey, a symbol of intelligence, problem-solving and cognitive discipline,” he added, which “has brought joy — and frustration — to many generations.” The cube has enjoyed another surge in popularity in recent years as global competitions have proliferated, measuring who can solve the puzzle the fastest. The current record, set only last month in China by nine-year-old Xuanyi Geng, is 2.51 seconds, according to the World Cube Association, which organizes and certifies competitions across the world. Rubik, who does not consider himself a speed competitor, said that for him, the cube represents a “transformable sculpture,” the place where art and engineering meet and users can manipulate and change the cube in nearly endless variations. “If you are doing something, creating something, you have the chance to do something that is meaningful — that’s one part — and beautiful,” he said. 8 dead, including 2 children, after building collapses in Brooklyn 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

events.title: Fallout from the Nvidia scandal may dampen the exuberance around the AI boom
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation has sent ripples throughout the global technology industry, with competitors itching to take advantage of the uncertainty surrounding the chip giant Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's stunning resignation has sent ripples through the global technology industry, with rival chipmakers itching to take advantage of the uncertainty and others wondering if the downfall of one of AI's biggest cheerleaders will dampen the mood around the civilization-altering technology. Huang, who stepped down Thursday following reports of extramarital affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy, was the very public face of a company that dominates the market for computer chips used to train and run AI models. In March, Huang predicted Nvidia will be grappling with a $1 trillion backlog in orders for its chips by the end of the year, doubling his estimate from a year earlier. A linchpin of the AI boom, Nvidia trades off with Apple as Wall Street's most valuable company and has invested heavily in other AI firms. Some of Nvidia's biggest rivals, such as Broadcom, Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, saw their shares advance Thursday following Huang's departure as investors predicted that its customers will look to diversify their suppliers. In the end, analysts say, this might not be a bad thing. “This could turn what has effectively been a monopoly into a horse race again, as competitors rush to meet growing demand,” said Bret Greenstein, chief AI officer at the global consultancy West Monroe. “Nvidia did not create that demand, and a shift in this part of the market could ultimately diversify the supply chain, create more choice for customers and strengthen the broader AI industry in the years ahead.” Nvidia carved out an early lead in tailoring its chipsets known as graphics processing units, or GPUs, from use in powering video games to helping to train powerful AI systems. Demand soared as tech companies scrambled for more chips to build and run AI systems. In annual filings, Nvidia has identified competitors including Advanced Micro Devices, or AMD, Intel, Broadcom and cloud services companies like Google, Amazon and Microsoft. While these other players are established and respected within the industry for their chips, they have been trying to catch up to Nvidia. Nvidia has had an advantage from the start and as soon as a competitor releases something just as good, Nvidia has put out the next better chip, said Jay Aldebert, chief growth officer of International Services Inc. “Nobody’s just sitting still,” he said. While some competitors saw bumps to their share prices Thursday, “their gains are going to be smaller than Nvidia’s losses,” said Chester Spatt, a finance professor at Carnegie Mellon University. But Spatt said he also anticipates chip purchasers could also become “much more reluctant to concentrate their purchases with a single source.” The incident is also sure to prompt elected officials to seek stronger export controls on American-made chips, but that could be a boon for Chinese chipmaker Huawei , another Nvidia competitor. Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, said she suspects Chinese AI firms could accelerate efforts to secure overseas computing capacity ahead of tighter controls. “Chinese chipmakers have already rallied on Nvidia’s troubles, but China’s AI developers depend heavily on Nvidia’s ecosystem,” she said. “This could be both an opportunity and a headache for China.” While Huang is not the only face of AI — OpenAI's Sam Altman , Google's Demis Hassabis and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton are among the others — he's been an influential one. A celebrity-level industry evangelist with President Donald Trump's ear and support, he has advocated for a light touch on AI regulation and has been bullish about AI’s potential to transform society, creating faster economic growth and more scientific breakthroughs. Microsoft apologizes for email disruption, says AI agents not responsible Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE “Jensen Huang’s resignation is a watershed moment for Nvidia, which now has to prove it can maintain its AI dominance without the leader largely responsible for building it,” said Asa Hiken, a senior analyst for research firm eMarketer. “And given the broader AI industry’s heavy dependence on Nvidia’s chips, Huang’s departure introduces uncertainty well beyond the company itself.” Lee, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, said the resignation fallout will ripple across the AI ecosystem. “Obviously Nvidia’s technological leadership won’t disappear, but Huang had played an outsized role as its chief strategist, dealmaker and — very importantly — political advocate, with close access to both Washington and Beijing,” she said.

events.title: Coal protest to go ahead on harbour after court rejects police objections
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Supreme Court rejects police objections to approve Rising Tide anti-coal protest on Newcastle Harbour The group Rising Tide has staged protests in the Port of Newcastle for more than a decade. ( ABC News: Romy Stephens ) The NSW Supreme Court has rejected a challenge from the state's police commissioner to a climate protest planned in Newcastle. The protest, organised by Rising Tide, is set to see hundreds of activists paddle out in the Port of Newcastle. The court heard the flotilla will stretch across the harbour, blocking the shipping channel for up to 40 minutes. A climate protest on Newcastle Harbour will go ahead as planned after the Supreme Court rejected an application by NSW Police to stop it. Rising Tide's Paddle for the Plant flotilla is set to see hundreds of people in kayaks take to the water tomorrow. Handing down his judgement this afternoon, Justice Edward Muston said he had to balance the interests of the public with the concerns of police. "The public interests in the facilitations of political expression through assembly outweighs the legitimate concerns which have been expressed by the commissioner," he said. Protest organisers in NSW must submit a notice of intention to hold a public assembly to the police commissioner, known as a Form 1. The NSW Police Commissioner opposed this application and asked the Supreme Court to prohibit the event due to safety concerns for those attending and other users of the harbour. Without a Form 1, protesters run the risk of being charged by police for offences including obstructing people, vehicles or vessels. Police have argued their resources have been stretched on the water and land during previous anti-coal events. ( ABC Newcastle: Carly Cook ) The court heard up to 785 people on kayaks and other watercraft would enter Newcastle Harbour tomorrow morning to unfurl a 20-metre-long series of connected floating letters that will read "Coal Exports Equals Climate Chaos". They also plan to form a continuous line spanning the harbour for about 30 to 40 minutes, blocking the shipping channel, before returning to shore. On Wednesday, barrister David Hume SC, who acted for NSW Police, told the court transport officials and police predicted dire consequences. "Everyone has looked at this [event] saying it poses an unacceptable risk," Mr Hume said. The Assistant Police Commissioner echoed those calls, citing an incident last year where protesters were washed hundreds of metres down the harbour. Police watch on as protesters previously demonstrated against fossil fuels at Newcastle's port. ( ABC News: Romy Stephens ) "I have not seen any Rising Tide event run safely yet," Assistant Commissioner David Waddell said. The number of watercraft will be capped at 785 — more than double previous anti-coal protests in the port. Rising Tide's barrister Michael Green told the court the event would have a kayak safety team, swimming in the channel would be banned, and life jackets mandatory. He said people attending would also be briefed on hand signals they could use to raise the alarm if they get into trouble. Rising Tide's Anne Hodgson told the court it would be a family-friendly event and ruled out the prospect of civil disobedience. Ms Hodgson told the court it was hoped global media would cover the event. The world's biggest coal port in Newcastle has been a focus for groups fighting climate change. ( ABC Newcastle: Carly Cook ) "Yes, as the COP31 meetings are on, we would like that," she said. COP31 is the United Nations Climate Conference — the largest international summit to negotiate and advance global cooperation on climate change. On the eve of the court action, Newcastle City councillors banned Rising Tide from protesting on community land "now and into the future", sparking fears among activists about their right to peacefully protest. Newcastle's Lord Mayor Gavin Morris used his casting vote on Tuesday to pass a motion opposing the use of community land for the purpose of Rising Tide's events and protests. Newcastle Lord Mayor Gavin Morris used his casting vote this week to ban Rising Tide from protesting on community land. ( ABC News: Keely Johnson ) "The constant request for them [Rising Tide activists] to remain within the boundaries has been broken, and it's been a constant breaking of promises," he said. "Sadly, they keep pushing the boundaries beyond the realms of safety and something just needed to be done.

events.title: Salmon farm antibiotic use impact 'completely unfair' cray fisher says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Impact of salmon companies' use of antibiotics 'completely unfair', cray fisher says Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Kodey Rolston says "fishermen are being impacted so deeply by what salmon farming has done". ( ABC News: Jano Gibson ) A Tasmanian cray fisher says the wild-caught fishing sector has been "impacted so deeply" by salmon companies' use of antibiotics. Following salmon company Tassal's use of an antibiotic, two commercial fishing areas are being closed from Sunday until February 14 to protect export markets. Premier Jeremy Rockliff says it is important "we get the balance right". A commercial fisher says the impact of salmon companies' antibiotic use in Tasmania is "completely unfair" on smaller, wild fishers. Kodey Rolston, who works as a deckhand on a cray fishing boat, said while he was a supporter of the salmon industry, "fishermen are being impacted so deeply by what salmon farming has done". The Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE) is closing two commercial fishing areas from Sunday until February 14. Commercial rock lobster fisheries closed due to antibiotic trade risk Commercial rock lobster and dive fisheries in parts of Tasmania's south-east will be closed for three months to "mitigate trade risks" linked to antibiotic use. The commercial taking of rock lobster and the setting of rock lobster pots will not be allowed within parts of the Southern Channel "therapeutic management area" (TMA). Commercial divers will not be allowed to take short-spined sea urchins, long-spined sea urchins and periwinkles in the Northern Channel TMA. Under the state government's Aquaculture Therapeutant — Wild Fisheries Market Access Management Plan, released last month, wild fisheries near salmon pens treated with antibiotics get temporarily closed. The closures are to protect export markets as some countries have zero tolerance for antibiotics in wild-caught fish. Man who burned shoebox of tax records fined for resulting bushfire Tasmanian premier apologises for 'outcome' of Christmas post AI data centres to self-administer funds in Tasmanian community deal The two new closures are linked to salmon company Tassal's recent use of the antibiotic oxytetracycline (OTC) at its salmon farms at Great Taylors Bay and Meads Creek in the lower D'Entrecasteaux Channel. The company said the closure accounted for 1.6 per cent of the state's historical rock lobster catch. A map showing the areas of the rock lobster fishery that will be closed from Sunday. ( ABC News: Hamed Akrami ) But Mr Rolston said the closure area was "vital to the crayfishing industry". "Down south is our safe haven for abalones, for crayfish. "It's a multi, multi-generational fishing ground and it's being locked off all together because the salmon farms want to just dump as much antibiotics in the water as they can to try and save their own arse and not cooperate with other businesses," he said. "I actually don't have anything against the salmon farms. "In all honesty, I'm very much for them — they provide a lot of jobs all around the state. Tassal says the rock lobster fishery closure accounts for 1.6 per cent of Tasmania's annual rock lobster catch. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) Tasmanian Greens leader Rosalie Woodruff said the government was expecting the wild-caught fishing industry to "do all the heavy lifting". "Wild fishers have been sidelined and the interests of big salmon companies have been put first by the government," Ms Woodruff said. "They've refused to put in place any regulations to constrain the operations of salmon farming in the Channel." 'Important that all industries work together': Premier Premier Jeremy Rockliff said it was important "we get the balance right". "The industry is in a transition and a very quick transition in terms of antibiotic use because of the investment that's going into breeding, for example, will mean that in future years there'll be less reliance on antibiotics if at all, and that's the space we need to get to. "We're in a transition time now and I know it's difficult … I feel for industry outside of the salmon industry very much. "It's important that all industries work together, we get the balance right." In a statement yesterday, Tassal said the closure was a "precaution to protect export market access". "Public Health has confirmed swimming and recreational fishing remain completely safe. "We recognise the consequences for any affected commercial rock lobster fishers and are working with the wild fisheries sector on appropriate support, with monitoring underway to support reopening as soon as possible.

events.title: Outlook outage expected to cost Australian businesses billions of dollars
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Microsoft Outlook outage cost to businesses 'billions' The Microsoft outage has been ongoing for more than 12 hours. ( Reuters: David Ryder ) Experts say the Microsoft outage is likely to cost businesses billions. RSM Australia Risk Advisory partner, Ashwin Pal, says small business will be hit the hardest. The financial impact is expected to last weeks. The Microsoft outage is calculated to cost Australian businesses billions of dollars, with experts warning small businesses will be the hardest hit by the technology failure. A widespread outage, which started about 3:15 am AEDT, on Friday, has hit platforms including Outlook, with many users having trouble accessing emails and encountering errors across the Microsoft suite of products. Workers across multiple types of businesses have reported being unable to access email or SharePoint, with some resorting to using fax machines to keep operating. Microsoft outage live: For the latest on the issues affecting the tech giant's apps, read our blog. RSM Australia Risk Advisory partner Ashwin Pal said the cost to professional service businesses, such as lawyers or accountants, would be hundreds of thousands of dollars per hour. "It's not just the initial downtime, it's more actually about then the catch up effort because that costs money," he said. "Because now when things do normalise, you're going to have to spend money to actually catch up because of all the backlog." Ashwin Pal says Monday's backlog of work will be costly. ( Supplied ) He said the impact of the outage was amplified by the 3.9 million businesses globally that used the Microsoft suite, with many not having backup systems, resulting in huge costs to the economy. "This is what happened with CrowdStrike. So when the outage happened, because of where we are in the world in terms of time zones, we felt the impact first. "As the US and Europe come online, and they can't operate, it's going to get worse. So you're going to have a multiplier effect." Outlook down as Microsoft outage hits Australians Microsoft says it has begun restoring access to its email and other online services after Australians experienced outages for several hours today. He said the repercussions would be most keenly felt by small businesses, due to operating on thin margins. "You take a CBA as an example, they'll be able to absorb an impact like this a lot easier than the five-person accounting shop down the road," he said. "They were already actually working on very thin margins. All of a sudden they're actually out for three, four, five days or whatever it takes for them to recover. That could be the final straw." Owner of small Queensland business Regal Shower Screens, Tracey Tucker, said the lost day of business would cost at least $30,000, but there were numerous flow-on effects. "I'm paying my girls sitting in here in the office to do nothing," she said. "The phone rings, they can't order anything. "Then it puts undue pressure because if it's back online on Monday, everything we missed Friday, we're going to try to catch up on." Experts say the outage will hurt small business the most. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic/Illustration ) She said the outage meant the business would struggle to meet its promoted deadlines because the glass manufacturers would also be inundated on Monday. "It's going to put pressure on everybody down the track because our girls are going to get yelled at, like, 'You just said my shower's going to be two weeks now, it's two and a half weeks', all because we can't send the order through today." Service delivery manager with telecommunication company Hubify, Chloe Mombeshora, said she had received numerous calls from less tech-savvy clients who were unsure what was happening. "They're thinking that their internet is down, they don't know what to do," she said. She added some clients had raised concerns the inability to communicate could impact their businesses' reputations. Some Outlook users were receiving notifications for emails they could not open. ( ABC News: Liana Walker ) IT support specialist James Coates said he had been inundated with requests for help but was unable to reply through his helpdesk because it used Outlook. "We actually have to call each client individually, every single personal phone number, every single Teams number, hope it gets through and update them that way because the email service is just not working on their end either," he said. He said he also could not do other work over concerns it would not be saved. Do you know more, or are you affected?

events.title: Outback cattle flown to Kazakhstan
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Hereford cattle from the middle of Australia flown to Kazakhstan Ben Hayes (second from right) alongside livestock agent Tim McKean, inspecting cattle with Kazakhstan buyers. ( Supplied: Undoolya Station ) A buyer from Kazakhstan has taken nearly 300 head of cattle from the Northern Territory after flying out to inspect them. Cattle producer Ben Hayes says Kazakhstan's government has an initiative to boost its national herd. Federal data shows Kazakhstan imported more than 1,000 head each of cattle and sheep in October. Nearly 300 head of cattle from a station near Alice Springs have been flown to Kazakhstan, in what local producers hope is the start of a new market. The distance from Alice Springs in the middle of Australia to Kazakhstan is roughly 10,000 kilometres. Ben Hayes from Undoolya Station said he got a call from his livestock agent one day with an interesting offer. "He asked if we had some heifers for this Kazakhstan job and we did," he said. "The buyer from Kazakhstan actually flew out here [with an interpreter], took a quick look and ended up taking them. "They got trucked down to Melbourne, where they stayed in quarantine for about a month and were then loaded into crates and onto the plane." Cattle from Undoolya Station ready for export to Kazakhstan. ( Supplied: Undoolya Station ) Mr Hayes said the animals were flown from Melbourne to Singapore and then onto Kazakhstan. "There was a weight limit on them of about 180 to 250 kilograms and they had to be preg-tested empty." He said the money paid for the animals was "on-par" with what he would normally receive in the Australian market. But he said the chance to be involved in the sale to Kazakhstan was "very special". "To know that our heifers are now becoming breeding stock for Kazakhstan is a feather in our cap, in Australia's cap," he said. ABC Landline has been told some cattle from Mt Riddock Station in the NT were also purchased for the consignment. According to data from the Federal Department of Agriculture, there were two flights of breeder cattle out of Victoria last month totalling 1,252 head. Another flight to Kazakhstan took 1,617 breeder sheep. It is understood Australia last exported cattle to Kazakhstan in 2019. It is a long way from Alice Springs to Kazakhstan. ( ABC Landline ) This is not the first time Undoolya Station has flown cattle to a distant market. In 1981, Undoolya steers were flown direct out of Alice Springs to Korea. "I was only a little fella at the time, but my father and grandfather flew steers out of Alice Springs on a Flying Tiger aircraft, straight to Korea" Mr Hayes said. "I don't know why they wanted steers, but that's what happened, Alice Springs is an international airport, it was a good opportunity." Undoolya Station is the Northern Territory's oldest pastoral lease. Established in 1872, the property has been owned by the Hayes family since 1906. events.title: ‘I spend less, that’s all that matters’: life in the world’s most electrified countries
events.summary: Owning an electric car, driving an electric motorbike taxi, riding scooters – we speak to people in Oslo, Kigali and Shanghai about their everyday routines T he race to electrification has emerged as a key theme of this year’s UN climate summit: increasing the use of electricity – particularly from clean sources – has the potential to improve daily life for people around the world. The summit’s co-hosts are now trying to get countries to promise to increase their electricity use to 35% of all energy used by 2035. The global figure currently stands at 23%, but some countries are already striding ahead. As 100,000 delegates, negotiators and world leaders thrash out the details in Antalya, Turkey , the Guardian spoke to three people in Norway, Rwanda and China to find out what life looks like in more highly electrified countries. Norway is a world leader in the race to 100% electrification. In September, a record 98.81% of new cars sold were electric, and hydropower produces 90% of all electricity . But with rapidly rising energy demands, including from new datacentres, authorities warn that the country could soon face a power deficit and higher energy prices. Unni Berge, 47, lives in Oslo with her husband and two teenage sons and works as the head of communications at the Norwegian EV Association. She describes how electricity features in a typical day: “I use electricity in my three-bedroom flat and I have district heating [where heat is transported around a local network from a centralised source rather than individual boilers to heat homes and buildings]. For electricity we are connected to the Norwegian central grid, which is mainly hydropower. “I live in a rather energy-efficient flat, so our electricity bills are comparatively low. In October, we spent 730 Norwegian kroner [£57] on electricity for our apartment, and in September it was 500 kroner. “I go to work by bus. Almost all the buses in Oslo are fully electric. I also have an electric car, but driving in the middle of Oslo for work is not an option because we have a lot of restrictions on cars in the city centre. In my street, the bus comes every fifth minute, so I don’t have to plan. I go outside and a bus comes. “I mostly use my electric car on weekends. A lot of the trips are driving to sports activities with my two children, who are 18 and 15. I also train a handball team, so I use it to go to a lot of handball matches and tournaments. “We charge our car with a charging box in our garage where, like most apartment garages in Oslo, we have built a collective charging system. If everyone put their charging on at the same time it would go slow, but in practice that doesn’t happen. “I have a large battery on my EV so I charge it once every two to three weeks. Of course we pay for the electricity and a system fee, but it’s much cheaper than petrol and diesel. “In my office, we have district heating, which is quite common in Oslo in larger buildings, then we use electricity for light and computers. Lunch is made in my office in the internal canteen with electricity. At work I use Microsoft Copilot, which is a really helpful tool, but of course there are big questions there – energy demands will get too high if everyone is using AI more. “I come home and use electricity to make dinner, watch television and go to the cinema. Growing up in a small village on the western coast of Norway , we also used wood for heating as well as electricity. But it is fair to say that electricity is common part of Norwegian life and has been for a long time. “What has changed is that our transport sector is also now run on a rising amount of electricity: passenger cars, buses and also ferries. That happened quite fast. Heavy goods vehicles are also increasingly electric, so of course that changes the system and society. “Perhaps because of the war in Ukraine and more extreme weather conditions, people are becoming aware that they are quite dependent on electricity, so in recent years there has been debate on how to prepare for a crisis. In previous power cuts, some people have used their electric cars as a battery to power electric equipment. “There is also a big debate about electricity prices. In Norway we have nearly 100% renewable electricity, but even so we are connected to the European grid. So the gas prices still influence our electricity prices. And when we have dry winters, electricity prices rise because if we have less snow, the hydropower gets less water. Rising numbers of datacentres is also something consumers are starting to wonder about – what this development is going to look like and how much energy it is using.” An e-motorbike taxi driver in Kigali, Rwanda Six years ago, the Rwandan government embarked on an enthusiastic promotion of e-mobility by removing a number of taxes on e-bikes and vehicles and offering incentives for businesses operating charging stations.

events.title: Haze-linked First Resources, Bumitama post higher profits for Q3
events.summary: First Resources posted a 40.1% rise in its underlying net profit to US$122.7 million for the third quarter. First Resources posted a 40.1% rise in Q3 underlying net profit to US$122.7 million, helped by higher palm oil sales and stronger output after buying Austindo Nusantara Jaya. Bumitama’s Q3 net profit rose 1.9% to 614.1 billion rupiah, as better plantation and mill productivity lifted production, though dry weather hurt shipments. Both firms said biodiesel demand and higher energy prices may support palm oil, but they also stressed zero-burning policies and cooperation with authorities over the haze. SINGAPORE – Two palm oil companies linked to the transboundary haze in October reported higher profits for the third quarter ended Sept 30, in separate business updates published on the morning of Nov 13. Palm oil producer First Resources posted a 40.1% rise in its underlying net profit to US$122.7 million (S$157.9 million) for the third quarter of 2026, from US$87.5 million in the year-ago period. The increase was boosted by higher sales of palm oil products and fruit bunches harvested from oil palms, it said. Sales were up 24.9% at US$578.6 million for the quarter, compared with US$463.3 million in the third quarter of 2025. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation rose 26.6% to US$207.4 million in the third quarter of 2026, up from US$163.8 million a year ago. For the nine months ended Sept 30, sales grew 36.5% year on year to US$1.6 billion, driven by higher sales volumes. A net inventory drawdown of 28,000 tonnes over the nine-month period, compared with a build-up of 80,000 tonnes in the corresponding period in 2025, also supported higher sales volumes. The group’s stronger production output in the first nine months of 2026 was also attributable in part to the full nine-month contribution from Austindo Nusantara Jaya, an Indonesian agribusiness company acquired in May 2025. However, profits were partially offset by foreign currency translation losses resulting from the depreciation of the Indonesian rupiah against the US dollar. The group said it expects demand for palm oil to remain supported by Indonesia’s biodiesel programme. In addition, elevated crude oil prices arising from geopolitical tensions in the Middle East are expected to support biodiesel economics and crude palm oil demand. Performance supported by productivity improvements Meanwhile, Bumitama reported a 1.9% increase in its net profit to 614.1 billion rupiah (S$43.4 million) for the quarter ended Sept 30, compared with 602.9 billion rupiah in the previous corresponding period. For the nine-month period, net profit rose 30.6% to 2.4 trillion rupiah, up from 1.9 trillion rupiah in the year-ago period. Revenue increased 9.7% to 4.2 trillion rupiah in the third quarter, up from 3.9 trillion rupiah a year ago. For the nine-month period, revenue was up 20% at 16.3 trillion rupiah. Bumitama said its performance was supported by productivity improvements in its plantations and mills, particularly during the earlier part of the quarter. In July, internal production of fresh fruit bunches reached 383,203 tonnes, accounting for almost 40% of the quarter’s production. Quarterly production of crude palm oil increased 14% year on year to 368,323 tonnes. However, exceptionally dry weather conditions in its Kalimantan estates during the third quarter put additional pressure on logistics infrastructure and disrupted shipments, said Bumitama. Consequently, third-quarter revenue declined compared with the second quarter. The prolonged dry season also heightened the risk of land and forest fires across parts of Kalimantan. Fires affected certain areas within or adjoining the group’s concessions, including community-managed, conservation and unplanted land, the group noted. Bumitama said that elevated energy prices and Indonesia’s biodiesel programme coupled with a relatively constrained palm oil supply growth could provide a “supportive backdrop” for palm oil fundamentals heading into 2027. However, market conditions remain subject to uncertainty. These include changes in global energy prices, supply-and-demand dynamics, and the potential effects of prolonged dry weather on future production, it added. Both First Resources and Bumitama reiterated their commitment to upholding a zero-burning policy, and cooperating with the Indonesian and Singapore authorities in relation to the haze.

events.title: Jane Street more than doubled its Nvidia stake last quarter, filings reveal
events.summary: Jane Street, one of Wall Street’s leading quantitative trading firms, more than doubled its Nvidia holdings in the third quarter, according to regulatory filings released Thursday and reviewed by Fortune. The securities filings show the firm’s positions as of Sept. 30—just over six weeks before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The scandal has led Nvidia shares to fall nearly 13% over the past five days, reaching a 17-month low intraday Thursday. The regulatory disclosure, known as a 13F, doesn’t reveal exactly when Jane Street purchased the shares, or how much the firm has gained or lost on its bets though. The market maker held 23.8 million shares worth about $5.44 billion at $228.38 at quarter end, according to the 13F. That’s over double the 11.8 million shares held, worth $2.4 billion, in the second quarter. Nvidia was its second-largest holding behind SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust. Jane Street declined Fortune ’s request for comment. The filings show what Jane Street held in late September, not what it owns now, and leave out short positions. Jane Street traders could, in theory, have shorted Nvidia after the reporting period ended and made money from the subsequent decline. The filings alone cannot tell us whether they did, though. Options add another layer of complexity to this. The 13F also discloses that Jane Street holds a large amount of puts and calls, which are reported using the value of the underlying shares, rather than the market value of the options themselves. Those notional figures can make positions look far larger than the sums actually invested, while revealing little about the firm’s overall exposure once offsetting trades are taken into account. A large reported position, in other words, is not necessarily a huge directional bet. Huang stepped down on Thursday after more than three decades at the helm of the company he cofounded in 1993. In his place, Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO. Huang’s departure comes days after bombshell media reports about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former exec at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence authorities suspect of working for Beijing.  In a message to employees on Sunday, Huang admitted that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and apologized. He also said he supported an independent investigation into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.  The bad news didn’t stop there for Huang, though. Just three days later, the New York Times reported that the 63-year-old also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Reuters reported Thursday, citing two people familiar with the matter, that he had an intimate relationship with another Nvidia employee, as well.  Reuters reported in August, citing a person familiar, that Jane Street had so far generated more than $40 billion in trading revenue in 2026. That surpassed its $39.6 billion total for all of 2025 and comfortably beat trading revenues for the nation’s largest banks. Still, there have been some signs of cracks. That same Reuters report over the summer said Jane Street took a $15 billion hit, partly from its exposure to AI-focused hedge fund Situational Awareness. Situational Awareness, started by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, sold the bulk of its equities portfolio to Ken Griffin’s Citadel after the market downturn triggered margin calls. Jane Street told employees that the drawdown had left its investment roughly flat for the year, though it remained profitable over the full period, per Reuters. Jane Street has not confirmed this report.  The story was updated with Jane Street’s decline to comment. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: ST Engineering Q3 revenue rises 9% to $3.4 billion, declares interim dividend of 5 cents per share
events.summary: Defence and public security was the group’s largest revenue contributor for the nine-month period, generating some $4.3 billion. SINGAPORE – ST Engineering’s revenue for the third quarter ended September rose 9% year on year to $3.4 billion, from $3.1 billion in the previous corresponding period, the group said on Nov 13. The technology and engineering company declared a third-quarter interim dividend of five cents per share, up from four cents a year earlier. Its first-quarter and second-quarter dividends were four cents and five cents per share, respectively, bringing the total for the first three quarters to 14 cents per share. For the first nine months of 2026, revenue increased 10% to $10 billion, from $9.1 billion in the same period a year earlier. Excluding LeeBoy, its US-based construction equipment business divested on Sept 4, 2025, revenue grew 13% on a rebased basis. Defence and public security was the group’s largest revenue contributor for the nine-month period, generating some $4.3 billion, up 7% year on year. Excluding LeeBoy, revenue from the segment grew 13%. Third-quarter revenue rose 8% to $1.4 billion, or 12% on a rebased basis. The increase was led by marine and digital systems and cybersecurity businesses. The segment secured $5.5 billion in new contracts in the first nine months, including $1.8 billion in the third quarter . These included a five-year contract to supply 40mm ammunition to the British Ministry of Defence, projects involving defence command-and-control systems in Singapore, and maintenance and support services for the US Navy’s fleet. Meanwhile, commercial aerospace revenue rose 12% to about $4.1 billion in the first nine months, supported by higher contributions from engine maintenance, repair and overhaul work and nacelles, a container for aircraft parts. Revenue for the third quarter increased 7% to $1.4 billion. The segment secured $4.2 billion in new contracts in the first nine months, of which $1.4 billion was won in the third quarter . The latest wins included its first Airbus A220 airframe heavy maintenance contract with an Asia-Pacific operator and airframe maintenance agreements with Asia-Pacific airline customers. Revenue from urban solutions and satellite communications increased 15% year on year to about $1.7 billion in the first nine months. Third-quarte r revenue also rose 15% to $600 million, with higher contributions from both businesses. The segment secured $3.5 billion in new contracts in the nine-month period, including $2.4 billion in the third quarter . Wins included turnkey rail services for the Taoyuan MRT Brown Line and Green Line Extension in Taiwan, integrated smart security management solutions contracts in Singapore and tolling infrastructure modernisation work for the Tampa-Hillsborough Expressway Authority in the US. Across the group, contract wins totalled $13.2 billion in the first nine months, including $5.6 billion in the third quarter. The nine-month figure excluded $1.7 billion in New Jersey Turnpike Authority order book recognition. The group’s order book stood at a record $37.7 billion as at September, up from $33.2 billion as at end-2025. About $3.1 billion is expected to be delivered in the remainder of 2026. ST Engineering also reported a record-low operating expenses-to-revenue ratio of 9% for the first nine months, compared with 10.2% for the whole of 2025. The 2025 figure excluded a one-off impairment loss of iDirect group. Separately, ST Engineering said it is exploring long-term opportunities in the nuclear energy sector, drawing on its capabilities in complex, safe and mission-critical environments and partnering organisations with complementary expertise. Its current collaborations include those with the Agency for Science, Technology and Research, Sembcorp Utilities and Commonwealth Fusion Systems. Areas of activity include factory-fabricated structural modules, such as protective steel structures, and advanced materials for fusion reactors , including tungsten coatings for reactor’s inner walls . The group also sees opportunities to apply its capabilities in digital twin technology and artificial intelligence, advanced materials and manufacturing, and large-scale systems integration.

events.title: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
events.summary: How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under scrutiny over exports of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December. Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines. Senator Tim Scott sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," the South Carolina Republican posted on X. "The American people deserve answers," he added. Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily on 3 December, but also warned the panel could issue a subpoena to compel his testimony. Three House of Representatives committees - on intelligence and foreign affairs and a panel on China - have also sent a letter to Huang summoning him for a closed-door interview on 1 December. How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House Published 7 hours ago How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions Published 1 day ago Lutnick is under scrutiny because unnamed officials in President Donald Trump's administration have been briefing US media that the commerce secretary stalled efforts to tighten export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China. A commerce department spokesperson told US media that Lutnick had "proactively" agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee. Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang. On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive. Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing. Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday. According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company. Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close. Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently? Published 1 day ago The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal Published 1 day ago Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort". One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company. It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said. Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public. Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared. Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information. The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures. Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming. But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data. Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.

events.title: Outlook email outage: Microsoft says service recovery completed in parts of Asia-Pacific
events.summary: Microsoft said on Friday its email services were being restored in parts of the Asia Pacific region, as it extended its email timeout to 48 hours to resolve an outage that affected systems globally on Thursday. The disruption affected Outlook, Teams and the Copilot AI service for millions of people, companies and governments around the world on Thursday, and the issue continued into Friday. "We've made additional progress towards service recovery, with recovery actions completed across portions of the affected infrastructure in the Asia Pacific region," the company said in its most recent update on Friday. "Traffic is being gradually restored and we're seeing improvements in key customer scenarios, including mailbox access and delayed email processing. However, some users may continue to experience intermittent issues." Reducing email queues and backlogs "remains a priority, and the extended 48-hour email timeout window remains in place to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up", it added. The focus is now on extending the recovery actions across affected infrastructure in other regions. "At this time, we have no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident," the company added. "We will continue to treat this with urgency until full mitigation, and we will share a full post-incident report with root cause and defence-in-depth actions after mitigation is complete." The company delayed its email timeout window to 48 hours to help protect and keep delayed messages, such as emails sent from other providers, from being bounced back. After hours of troubleshooting, the company said its investigation indicated that failed checks "may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health". "We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service", it said. “We're implementing these actions more broadly across affected regions as we seek to attain persistent recovery. ” The company said it was working to recover its front-end servers. To improve server stability and traffic, Microsoft previously said it was “adjusting traffic protocols, redistributing traffic and applying strategic traffic blocking measures”. Microsoft's outage reports on November 12 were recorded in 74 countries and territories in about an hour on Downdetector, an online service that monitors internet disruption. Microsoft said its Exchange Online incident began at 4.17pm in the US (8.17pm UAE time) on Thursday. In two hours, reports on five Microsoft services reached 19,650 a minute, compared with fewer than 15 a minute on an average Thursday, Downdetector said. Outlook reports peaked at more than 2,000 times their normal level. “Reports about Microsoft 365, Copilot, Teams and OneDrive each rose more than a hundred-fold, and Azure about 100-fold. Xbox, GitHub and LinkedIn, also Microsoft's, rose far less,” DownDetector said. Microsoft's outage reports on November 12 reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour on Downdetector. Microsoft says its Exchange Online incident began at 16:17 UTC. Reports to Downdetector about Outlook began climbing at about 17:25 UTC, 12:25 in New York. By 18:25,… pic.twitter.com/7FQ4dDsfbm — Downdetector (@downdetector) November 12, 2026 The outage "highlights the need for resilience in all our critical systems", said Jack Hidary, chief executive at tech company SandboxAQ. "The energy grid, the telco network and the applications layers are all now essential to business continuity. Often these outages occur not from cyber attacks, but from code updates within the system that has unforeseen consequences. "Code simulation [CodeSim] is emerging as a new field that can detect potential impact of code updates before they are committed to production. CodeSim will prevent many of these outages in the future," he added. Microsoft's status website first acknowledged the problem on Thursday. “Users may be unable to connect to their mailboxes in Exchange Online through multiple connection methods,” a message on the Microsoft page said. Over the course of the day, the company added to its tally of products that users might not be able to access. Services for technologists, including cyber security software, file-sharing services and administrator tools, were also disrupted. We're investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas. More details can be found in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1550543. — Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 12, 2026 For Outlook specifically, Microsoft classified the issue as being a “service degradation”. A social media post from Microsoft explained efforts to rectify the problem. “We've begun redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load,” it said. Later on Thursday, data from Downdetector indicated that services started to recover for some users. For many, however, problems continued for several hours. Microsoft later confirmed through its service health status update page that the technical issue broadly affected the company's Microsoft 365 productivity suite. The technology company also said it was able to gain more insights into the cause of the problem experienced by so many users around the world. “We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable,” the update said. Governments and various companies around the world were also affected by the problem. As a result, many sought to calm the frustrations felt by patrons and customers through social media posts. “Due to a wide-scale outage impacting Microsoft 365 across North America, the State of Michigan is currently experiencing technical issues with email and other Microsoft applications,” Michigan's Department of Technology, Management and Budget said in a post. “Responses to emails may be delayed during this time.” Later on Thursday evening, Microsoft said it was still looking at “all available pathways to restore service”, but that those efforts “have not provided the anticipated relief”. The company indicated that it was pursuing a different strategy of “re-isolating a portion of infrastructure” and also restarting certain components that it speculated were causing the problem. More than seven hours after the problem was first reported, Microsoft warned that certain servers that were returned to service might become unresponsive once traffic started moving through them.

The document reveals that Singapore’s Police Force (SPF) and Customs agency commenced an investigation into Ms. Huang’s company, Megaspeed, in February 2025. “The suspected domestic offences pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offences,” the Ministry wrote, adding that the exec “was not investigated for espionage.” Singaporean authorities wanted to know if servers bought by local companies, but exported to Malaysia without ever touching Singaporean soil, might have ended up in a third country. It is not unusual for Singapore-based companies to acquire goods that never reach the island, because it promotes itself as the ideal spot from which to run an operation that trades across Asia. Singapore does so because it is tiny – the whole nation is the same size as the five boroughs of New York City. That small size means Singapore restricts the number of datacenters that can operate on its soil. Those limits are a big reason why Malaysia’s Johor region, which is under 20kms from the border with Singapore and a joint special economic zone, has become a major datacenter province. Singapore needs deals like that to thrive but works hard to ensure its hospitality is not abused. Which is why it felt Megaspeed’s activities worthy of investigation. US authorities were interested too. On 24 June 2025, the Bureau of Industry and Security, which regulates sensitive goods subject to export controls, visited Megaspeed in Singapore to check the hardware it bought arrived at its intended destination. Ms. Huang attended that event and later met the SPF for an interview. That meeting ended with the SPF impounding her passport, so it could keep her in Singapore while the investigation continued. As the matter progressed, the SPF suspected perennially troubled server-maker Supermicro had a role in this situation. Readers may recall that the US Department of Justice indicted two Supermicro execs for conspiring to ship servers to China in contravention of US law. Supermicro investigated the matter and parted ways with three staff who acted improperly. The company has denied ever selling to Megaspeed. Singaporean authorities say they received only “limited cooperation” from Supermicro, so in July 2025 the office of the nation’s Attorney General asked US authorities for help. “Since September 2025, SPF has repeated this request on several occasions to the US Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation,” the statement reveals. “Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company.” In February 2026, the SPF “concluded that there was insufficient evidence to establish that Huang had committed any offences relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.” But the police did decide that Ms. Huang provided inaccurate information “to downplay her role in Megaspeed.
