events.title: Mount Isa's $145 million critical minerals pitch one step closer
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mount Isa critical minerals hub gets early government backing Federal and state governments have agreed to fund a feasibility study into a new research facility in Mount Isa. ( ABC News: Harriet Tatham ) A business case for a $145 million critical mineral research hub in Mount Isa has secured funding for a feasibility study. The centre will provide early analysis and testing for prospective mines trying to scale operations in the region. The federal and state governments have agreed to tip in $241,250 each to fund trials, with an additional $482,500 to come from Mount Isa City Council. Mount Isa's push to reinvent its regional economy with a new mineral research hub has secured state and federal backing for a feasibility study. Mount Isa City Council and the University of Queensland released a business case earlier this month for a $145 million critical minerals research centre. The facility would allow mining companies to analyse rock samples from local mineral deposits to see what minerals were present and if they would be viable to mine. The $145 million centre is expected to create up to 50 permanent jobs. ( Supplied: Mount Isa City Council ) In July 2025, Mount Isa's underground copper mine closure saw nearly 500 workers sacked in the 19,000-strong community, forcing the council to search for economic alternatives. While Mount Isa's economy has been affected, exploration and investment across the wider North West Minerals Province has boomed, with about 85 critical minerals projects underway. Sustainable Minerals Institute director at the University of Queensland Rick Valenta said the proposed hub would allow industry to scale operations quickly. Rick Valenta (right) says the facility will help mines understand what minerals are in deposits and how they could be mined. ( ABC Rural: Eric Barker ) "The reason you can't just find a deposit and put it into production in a year is because you've got to answer … 'What's the content of the metal that you're after? And … how do we get the metals out of that rock?'" Professor Valenta said. "[At the moment], those rocks would be going elsewhere in Queensland … Australia or the world … [and] that involves a cost and a delay. "This centre is aimed at providing a local solution to that sort of thing." The proposed research centre would be situated between the George Fisher Mine and Mount Isa Airport. ( Supplied: Mount Isa City Councill ) Mount Isa Mayor Peta MacRae said she hoped the research hub would help future-proof the city by giving mining companies a dedicated site to research problems locally. "[Currently] minerals are just going to be ripped up and shipped," she said. "What we want to do is add the value and do as much processing as we can … to help us secure the future for our communities." Peta MacRae hopes the project will centralise some of the regions' mining investment into the town's economy. ( ABC News: Abbey Halter ) The proposed hub is expected to create up to 50 permanent jobs and would be located near the Mount Isa Airport. On Friday morning, Federal Assistant Minister for Resources Anthony Chisholm confirmed funding would be released to consider the proposal. "We want to make the most of these opportunities … and ensure that Mount Isa remains a great place to live and work and attract people at the same time," he said. "We know that there is enormous potential, but it's about proving that and then also ensuring that we can attract the industry investment." Anthony Chisholm says the cenrre is about proving Mt Isa's potential and attracting industry investment. ( ABC News: Tim Little ) The federal and state governments have agreed to tip in $241,250 each to fund a feasibility study, with an additional $482,500 to come from Mount Isa City Council. If successful, the hub would operate in conjunction with similar facilities in Mackay and Townsville. Initial testing and analysis would start at Mount Isa's centre, before small-scale piloting took place in Mackay followed by large-scale trials in Townsville.

events.title: Chris Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate majority leader
events.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday that he'll challenge Chuck Schumer for majority leader. Why it matters: Van Hollen's bid gives grassroots activists nearly three weeks to pressure Senate Democrats before they cast secret ballots in the Dec. 1 leadership election. The attempt to oust Schumer (D-N.Y.) underscores that deep divisions are plaguing the Democratic Party despite its overwhelming midterm success . Van Hollen (D-Md.) has served in the Senate since 2017 and has been in Congress since 2003. Schumer has been the Senate Democratic leader since 2017 and has served in the Senate since 1999. Driving the news: "In this election, the American people called for change," Van Hollen said in a statement on Thursday. "They called for a change from Donald Trump's disastrous policies — but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn't working for working people." "It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people. That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader." In a statement of his own, Schumer said: "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader." Zoom in: Van Hollen acknowledged he's the "underdog" in the race but claimed Thursday on MS NOW he has "more than 10" senators on his side. "[T]he time is now for change," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said Tuesday. He appeared with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who demanded a plan for change from party leadership. Progressives have accused Schumer of not fighting hard enough against President Trump and the MAGA agenda. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) is a vocal backer of Van Hollen for majority leader. The other side: Schumer has far more public backers at this stage than Van Hollen. That includes Sen. Angus King (I-Maine), Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (Ohio) and Democratic Sens. John Fetterman (Pa.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Kirsten Gillibrand (N.Y.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii) and Sheldon Whitehouse (Rhode Island). events.title: Who is Colette Kress, interim Nvidia CEO after Jensen Huang exit?
events.summary: Chief financial officer, reportedly disparaged by Huang during summer meeting, to take over on short-term basis The hunt is on for a new Nvidia CEO. It comes after a whirlwind week, which saw the company head and co-founder, Jensen Huang, resign amid multiple allegations of extramarital affairs , including one that involved an alleged Chinese spy and two with company employees. Nvidia immediately named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as the interim CEO. It’s possible she could stay on permanently, but the company could also name another candidate for the full-time role. Names that have been floated include Ian Buck, who manages Nvidia’s AI hardware and software products, and Rene Haas, a former Nvidia employee and the current CEO of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker. Whoever takes over from Huang will have tremendous sway in the burgeoning world of artificial intelligence. The entire AI ecosphere relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Nvidia is also a central driver of the US economy and one of the world’s most valuable companies, with a market cap of around $4tn. Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, is known as an ambitious and visionary CEO who had a hand in most all aspects of the business. He led in an unusual management style, having about 60 direct reports, giving him more control over the company’s daily functions. His son and daughter also work at Nvidia, with his daughter seen as his possible proxy, but neither appear to have sufficient experience to take the helm. Kress, 59, joined Nvidia in 2013 as the CFO after working in finance roles at Texas Instruments, Microsoft and Cisco. She’s a regular contributor to the company’s quarterly earnings calls, and has overseen Nvidia go from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar AI juggernaut. People who know her describe Kress as a calming contrast to Huang’s often confrontational style, Reuters reported. “Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” Harvey C Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia’s board of directors, said in a statement on Thursday. “The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team.” But that sentiment may not be shared by Huang. During a meeting this past summer, the CEO said Kress was “a deer in the headlights” and interrupted her presentation, a person familiar with the comments told the Wall Street Journal . Huang insinuated during that August meeting that Kress was not someone who could help him make decisions. However, Kress praised Huang in a memo to employees on Thursday, saying she would continue “building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years”. Many investors, analysts and industry sources who spoke to Reuters questioned whether a finance executive could preserve the technological risk-taking that turned Nvidia into an AI chips powerhouse. “Putting [Kress] in the interim role makes sense to keep the markets calm, but I don’t think she is the long-term visionary that Nvidia needs to continue its current trajectory,” said Anshel Sag, principal analyst at Moor Insights and Strategy. Kress, who said in her memo that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” , will serve as both the CEO and interim CFO until the board names a permanent successor. The board said it was starting a search for Huang’s permanent replacement and is considering internal and external candidates. Along with Kress, Buck is seen as a possible successor. He has worked at Nvidia since 2004 and in charge of deploying generative AI in partnership with the world’s top AI companies, including Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, OpenAI and more. Haas, the CEO of Arm Holdings, is also well-known at Nvidia, having worked there for seven years as a vice president and general manager before joining Arm in 2013. Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, is also being named as a possible replacement for Huang. Her company is Nvidia’s most direct and fierce competitor; she’s also a distant cousin to Huang. Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Kress could face congressional questions about the company’s oversight of chip sales involving Chinese military-linked institutions and south-east Asian intermediaries. In a 2023 interview with an Israeli publication, Kress credited her two young sons with urging her to join Nvidia in 2013 because they knew its chips from their video games. She became a billionaire in 2025 based on the value of her Nvidia equity, according to media reports, and Forbes said her net worth of $1.2 billion in mid-2026 put her in 32nd place on its list of America’s richest self-made women.

events.title: US firm Advent seeks to sell Singapore tutor chain Learning Lab again, sources say
events.summary: Advent invested in The Learning Lab in 2014, but there has been no publicly available information on how much stake it holds. Advent International is trying to sell Singapore tutor chain The Learning Lab again, its second attempt since 2021, sources say, with a planned price of US$400 million to US$500 million. Some sale proceeds will repay a S$265 million private credit facility from KKR, HPS Investment Partners and Nomura, which matures in 2027. The deal comes as private education investment in Asia fell 87% to US$240 million in 2025, with AI worries and many firms still trying to exit investments. SINGAPORE – US buyout firm Advent International has put up Singapore’s tutor-chain The Learning Lab for sale, marking its second attempt since 2021 to unload the asset, in part to repay debt, according to people familiar with the matter. Advent has hired an adviser to kick-start the sale process and plans to offer the company for about US$400 million to US$500 million (S$514.6 million to S$643.3 million), said the people who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. Some of the proceeds will be used to settle a S$265 million private credit facility jointly provided by KKR & Co, HPS Investment Partners and Nomura Holdings in 2023 and which will mature in 2027 , they said. Representatives for Advent, KKR and Nomura declined to comment. HPS did not respond to a request for comment. Private money has been pouring into schools in Asia in recent years as investors seek to profit from growing demand for quality education. Financiers such as Apollo Global Management and KKR have bought stakes and lent to school chains, hoping that a growing number of rich people in the region would fuel expansion. But private equity and venture capital investment in education services in Asia slumped 87% to US$240 million in 2025 , according to S&P Global, citing more rigorous deal selection and the potential impact of artificial intelligence on the sector. Another key challenge is the backlog of private equity firms seeking to exit companies they have bought into. Advent invested in The Learning Lab in 2014, but there has been no publicly available information on how much stake it holds. People with knowledge of the matter said Advent fully owns the learning company. The Learning Lab provides education for pre-school, primary, secondary and junior college students in Singapore, according to its website. It also has online services for other Asian markets including Malaysia, Vietnam, Thailand and Indonesia. In Singapore, the company charges about S$702 a month for its junior college programmes. events.title: ATSB releases preliminary report into young pilot's NT crash
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ATSB releases preliminary report into Bob Bramley's NT plane crash Bob Bramley was flying to pick up passengers for a return trip when his plane crashed. ( Supplied ) The Australian Transport Safety Bureau has released its preliminary report on the August crash of pilot Bob Bramley. Bramley is believed to have died when his plane dived into the water off Groote Eylandt, in the Northern Territory. Fishermen witnessed young Tasmanian pilot Bob Bramley's plane crash in waters off the Northern Territory in August "at very high speed", a report has revealed. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) today released its preliminary report into the crash in the Gulf of Carpentaria on August 25 this year, which is believed to have killed 23-year-old Bramley. Northern Territory Police conducted extensive marine and air searches at the time, which recovered parts of the plane, but Bramley has never been found. At the time, 23-year-old Bob Bramley was working as a charter company pilot. ( Supplied. ) As a teenager, he became a passionate advocate for suicide prevention, and sought to raise awareness by becoming the youngest person to circumnavigate Australia solo by plane. Friends and family expressed their shock and sadness in the wake of the crash, remembering Bramley as a "beacon of hope", and for his love of flying. The ATSB report detailed the circumstances of the August crash, but noted the investigation is continuing and that a final report will be published at its conclusion. Fishers found plane parts in sea after crash The report, which refers to "the pilot" but does not identify Bramley, details his movements on the morning of August 25, as he prepared to fly between the small communities of Gove and Numbulwar in the Northern Territory. At the time, Bramley had been working as a pilot for aviation operator Air Frontier for more than a year, and had been the company's senior base pilot for the Arnhem region since April. The report noted that after fuelling the plane and lodging a flight plan, the Beechcraft 58 Baron plane departed from the Gove Airport at about 11am, with only the pilot on board. "The flight plan for the return to Gove indicated four passengers were to be on board," the report noted. The ATSB's map of Bob Bramley's final flight on August 25, 2026. ( ATSB/Google Earth ) About half an hour later, at 11:27am, fishermen in a boat south-west of Isle Woodah in the west of the Gulf of Carpentaria watched the plane pass overhead. "They expected the aircraft to pull up; however, it did not change trajectory, and it impacted the water at very high speed. "The witnesses motored to the impact point and found a fuel/oil slick on the water surface along with many small floating fragments of shattered airframe." NT Police image of wreckage underwater at the crash site. ( NT Police ) No audio recording of cockpit before crash The report noted that the Baron was not fitted with, and was not required to have, a flight data recorder or a cockpit voice recorder. The ATSB said the flight wasn't detected by radar, and data tracking the flight was recorded by Bramley's iPad, which it was transmitting to the online platform OzRunways. The final data point was transmitted at 11:24am, about 23 kilometres north of the crash site. Bramley made two radio broadcasts during taxi and take-off, and phone records indicated "maintained a messaging stream with their partner" throughout the flight. The report noted Bramley's qualifications to operate the Baron aircraft, that he held a valid medical certificate and that he had completed a multi-engine instrument proficiency check the previous month. Bramley had more than 1,138 hours total flight time, more than 300 of which were in the Baron. The Baron itself was initially built in 1978 and had been serviced most recently in June in Darwin. The report noted no significant weather activity was observed on the day, consistent with the witnesses and other pilots flying in the area. The report noted Bramley made two radio broadcasts during taxi and takeoff, and "maintained a messaging stream with their partner" throughout the flight. ( Supplied: Lachlan Bennett ) Large parts of plane, including engine, found in sea floor In August, NT Police Acting Assistant Commissioner Peter Malley said the search for Bramley and the crash site had been particularly difficult, adding that "tiger sharks and crocs" had complicated efforts. NT Police confirmed today that human remains had not been found. Police divers had to contend with sharks and crocodiles during search efforts.

events.title: Government back to the drawing board on backpacker crackdown
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Government reconsidering backpacker, UK working holiday visa overhaul The government is reconsidering its controversial overhaul of the working holiday visa scheme. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The government is reconsidering its controversial overhaul of the working holiday visa scheme. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke says he is also looking at ways to reduce the number of British backpackers coming to Australia. Business leaders are urging the government to provide certainty to industries that rely on backpackers to fill jobs. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has all but confirmed the government is going back to the drawing board on its proposed backpacker crackdown, as it grapples with the twin issues of a surge in UK working holiday-makers and pressure to rein in overall migration. On Friday, Mr Burke said Australia must "find a way" to reduce the number of UK backpackers arriving and staying in the country under a free trade deal introduced in 2023, which allows British citizens to live in Australia for up to three years without specific work requirements. "We can find a way to bring that back to something more sensible and in the national interest, without jeopardising the other parts of the free trade agreement," he said. In August, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese ruled out imposing regional work requirements on backpackers from the UK, which apply to other working holiday-makers seeking to extend their visas beyond 12 months. The favourable treatment has led to a steep increase in the number of British backpackers coming to Australia, up from 47,238 in 2023/24 to 79,412 in 2024/25 according to Home Affairs data. "The conversations with the United Kingdom continue," Mr Burke said. The government had also proposed introducing a ballot system for non-British backpackers seeking to extend their stay into a second or third year, to dramatically reduce visa numbers. The Australian newspaper reported the government was now considering delaying the rollout of the ballot system until early next year, after farming, tourism and hospitality groups warned the changes could cripple their industries. The report suggests the government is considering lifting the cap on third-year visas from the proposed 5,000 to 20,000 (down from the current 31,000) and imposing longer regional work requirements on visa-holders. Mr Burke said the government was continuing to engage with industry stakeholders, but the "parameters" around reducing the overall number of working holiday-makers were unchanged. "The total number of working holiday or backpacker numbers that I've announced at the National Press Club, I cannot shift from," he said. He described potential changes to the implementation as "tweaks" that would allow businesses to "get the best possible use out of people, while they are here". "I am completely open to that," he said. Industry urges government to make quick decision Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) chief executive Andrew McKellar said there had been "extensive discussions" between the government and affected industries about the backpacker issue. He warned the original proposal risked disrupting businesses outside major cities, particularly in regional areas that relied on working holiday-makers to fill jobs. "And those regional areas really need those people to be coming out there and to be undertaking that work, supporting work in those areas," he said. Andrew McKellar says the government must move quickly to grant businesses certainty. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) Mr McKellar said business groups wanted the government to "make a decision", warning the "clock is ticking" for businesses seeking certainty ahead of summer. "Let's ensure that those people who are already here can continue with their plans … and that there's a fresh set of rules for anyone else who's coming in," he said. Backpackers are not migrants, advocate says Agricultural advocacy group WA Farmers president Steve McGuire welcomes a "walking back" of the visa changes. Steve Mcguire says backpackers should not be treated the same as migrants. ( ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding ) "What we're seeing with these changes is they're [the government] indicating they're listening," Mr McGuire said. "It's relief for the moment but there's still more work to be done. "It means those staying their second year have a lot more incentive to do six months regional." WAFarmers wants the Commonwealth to separate working holiday visa numbers from overseas migration quotas. "Our argument is they shouldn't even be in that number, they should be taken out," Mr McGuire said.

events.title: Stocks recover from Nvidia whiplash, dollar climbs with US yields
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down on Nov 12 after reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy. Stocks in Asia steadied after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned over affair claims, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, shaking the AI sector and chip supply chain. Investors lifted US Treasury yields and the dollar as they priced in a bigger Fed rate hike in December, while the yen stayed near 160 per dollar and risked intervention. Markets also tracked wider fallout from the AI slump, with Nvidia shares and related stocks falling, while rivals may gain and senators sought testimony on the company’s recent troubles. SINGAPORE – Stocks in Asia were on steadier footing on Nov 13 after a turbulent week dominated by revelations of extramarital affairs involving Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang that culminated in his resignation, in a blow to the global AI boom he helped advance. US Treasury yields climbed, with the two-year yield hitting a one-month high, lifting the dollar as investors weighed the prospect of an outsized 50 basis point rate hike by the US Federal Reserve in December. Huang stepped down on Nov 12 after reports of the affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, which plunged the chipmaker into crisis and sent shockwaves through the AI industry. His exit could have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy and the broader artificial intelligence industry and supply chain, given Huang’s push to preserve access to the Chinese market as well as his close ties with US President Donald Trump. “His departure leaves a vacuum that will be difficult to fill... We do not assume existing commitments change, but new deals could take longer or require more compensation as investors look for reassurance about Nvidia’s role,” analysts at JPMorgan said in a note. “The bigger implications are for the rest of the AI trade, particularly GPU (graphics processing unit) financing and infrastructure deals in which Nvidia would presumably be involved as a supplier, investor or provider of contractual support.” Nvidia shares fell 3% in extended trading, while those of its customers, including South Korea’s Naver, extended declines on Nov 13 , with Naver down 2.75%. Jon Zauderer, Citi’s head of specialist sales, said competitors such as AMD, Arista and Broadcom could benefit from the Nvidia fallout. “If you think about the uncertainty that’s created about a potential management change, investors are going to look for alternatives,” he said. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was up 0.26%, reversing some of its 1.3% fall from the previous session. South Korea’s Kospi rose 2.35%, while Japan’s Nikkei added 1.4%. The recovery in global equities also follows last week’s market meltdown sparked by US Republicans’ electoral drubbing, which stoked fears that tighter regulation could slow the AI infrastructure build-out that has helped send stocks to record highs in 2026 . Nasdaq futures and S&P 500 futures rose more than 0.2% each, while EURO STOXX 50 futures fell 0.37%. US Senate Banking Committee chairman Tim Scott sent letters on Nov 12 to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Huang, asking them to testify over the recent developments at Nvidia. Concerns over the AI outlook also spilt into metals, with London copper prices hitting a four-month low in the previous session on fears of weaker demand, while shares of Australian-listed miner Capstone Copper Corp fell more than 5% on Nov 13 . The two-year US Treasury yield peaked at 4.8920% in the early Asian session, while the benchmark 10-year yield rose to a three-week high of 5.1433%. Investors now see a 14.5% chance of a jumbo 50-basis-point Fed hike in December, up from zero a week ago, according to the CME FedWatch tool. “Right now, the US Fed has three hikes priced in for effectively the next 12 months... The (most recent) CPI (consumer price index) print obviously was a bit hotter than expected. If those kinds of prints continue to happen, we can definitely see the Fed hiking three more times. It’s very within the realms of possibility,” said Manusha Samaraweera, fixed income investment director at Capital Group. The increasingly hawkish Fed expectations in turn boosted the dollar, which was on track for a weekly gain of 0.9%, its biggest in more than a month. The strength in the greenback, meanwhile, weighed on the yen, which languished close to the key 160 per dollar level on Nov 13 , leaving traders on alert for any intervention from Tokyo. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York said on Nov 12 it bought 79.4 billion yen (S$638.9 million) in the spot market on July 31, selling euros from the Exchange Stabilization Fund as part of a joint US-Japan intervention this summer to shore up the yen.

events.title: The US has been holding secretive talks with a regime it accused of genocide
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Donald Trump's quest for rare earths reopens US talks with once-isolated Myanmar regime Min Aung Hlaing, pictured in Malaysia, has been trying to rehabilitate Myanmar's image. ( Reuters: Azneal Ishak/Pool ) The United States has reopened direct talks with Myanmar, raising alarm among advocates and analysts. It marks a reversal of efforts to isolate the military junta after it took power in a 2021 coup. Analysts believe the US's desire to access Myanmar's rare earths could influence diplomacy. As US President Donald Trump prepares to meet Asian leaders in the Philippines next week for the 49th ASEAN Summit, his administration is holding secretive talks with Myanmar's military-backed government, the same regime the US has accused of genocide. Five years ago, Washington imposed sanctions on Myanmar's military leadership and downgraded diplomatic ties following a 2021 coup that ousted an elected government . This year, however, senior Trump administration officials have travelled to Tokyo and Myanmar's capital, Naypyidaw, for talks with coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing. The goals of the diplomacy include countering China's influence in the region and potentially gaining access to Myanmar's "bountiful rare earth resources", according to a US State Department document . But the outreach has raised concerns among human rights advocates that Washington's pursuit of strategic interests could help rehabilitate a military leadership accused of widespread atrocities. Debbie Stothard believes pressure on Myanmar's government should not be weakened, with attacks on civilians ongoing. ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) "It's pretty shocking and almost illogical that the US would engage in secret talks with a sham president elected by a sham election," said Debbie Stothard, chair of the International Network for Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. "The military junta views engagement at this level as something that's encouraging and positive for them. "They see this process as legitimising them, and that is very bad news indeed for civilians on the ground and for regional security." The diplomatic opening followed the detention of an American businessman at Yangon airport on June 11 by Myanmar authorities. Adam Castillo, 40, a former head of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar, was detained for three months after being accused of financial impropriety, allegations he denied. Adam Castillo was detained in Myanmar earlier this year. ( Supplied ) A former US Marine, Mr Castillo was reportedly lobbying Washington to lift sanctions against Myanmar in exchange for negotiating American access to the country's vast rare earth deposits. He also ran one of Myanmar's largest security companies. Mr Castillo's detention provided an opening for Washington to establish direct contact with the military leadership, said Hunter Marston, director of the Lowy Institute's Southeast Asia Program. "A delegation of US representatives travelled to Naypyidaw to secure the release … that was the supposed setting or context for the US delegation to visit Myanmar," Dr Marston said. "But it also paved the way for more substantive discussions about changing US policy and engaging with the Myanmar military regime. "It seems like his detention was essentially hostage diplomacy, and the release was used tactically to secure talks with Washington. "I think that played right into the hands of the Myanmar regime, but I think it also served as a useful pretext for Washington to engage in discreet talks with the military." Analysts believe the discussions surrounding Mr Castillo's release may have opened the door to broader negotiations over access to Myanmar's rare earth minerals, potentially in return for a normalisation of relations. Since his release in September, meetings between senior US officials, led by Michael Vance, the Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research, and Myanmar's military-backed government have continued. The latest took place in Tokyo in October. Rare earths are essential to manufacturing a wide range of modern technologies, from computer screens and electric vehicles to solar panels and advanced weapons systems. Clusters of rare earth mines along the Lwe River network in Myanmar. ( Reuters: 2025 Planet Labs PBC/Handout ) They are also crucial for producing the semiconductors or chips that power artificial intelligence, Dr Marston said, making them "really important to a number of US business interests". "Whoever supplies today has the upper hand in the race for artificial intelligence," he said.

events.title: Genting Singapore shares fall as high rollers play less, resort revamp continues
events.summary: Genting Singapore expects the renovation works at Resorts World Sentosa to improve its hotel offerings and broaden the property’s appeal over the longer term. Genting Singapore’s profit fell 42% to S$54.7 million and revenue dropped 13% to S$566.1 million, as high rollers played less at Resorts World Sentosa. Casino revenue fell 22% to S$315 million, hit by weaker premium gambling and a lower share of wagers kept in September, though Genting said this matched regional trends. RWS is still being upgraded through 2027, with marketing, events and new Weave openings aimed at drawing premium visitors and boosting long-term appeal. SINGAPORE – Shares of Genting Singapore were down by more than 6% at 57 cents at noon on Nov 13, after the company reported another quarter of shrinking profits, as high rollers played less at Resorts World Sentosa (RWS) and ongoing renovations at the resort crimped visitor footfall and spending. Net profit fell 42% year on year to $54.7 million for the three months ended Sept 30, while revenue fell 13% to $566.1 million, Genting Singapore said in a business update on Nov 12. Both net profit and revenue for the July to September quarter were also lower than in the previous quarter from April to June. Casino revenue fell 22% to $315 million for the quarter under review compared with a year ago, as lower activity among premium gamblers and a lower-than-usual share of wagers retained by the casino in September further dented revenue. However, Genting said this was in line with trends in key regional markets. The group said adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation for the quarter, a measure of operating performance, would have been about $36 million higher than the reported $161.8 million if the casino had kept its usual share of premium wagers. Outside the casino, non-gaming revenue rose 1% year on year to $250.9 million for the quarter, despite fewer hotel rooms being available. This was up 29% from the previous quarter, although Genting did not elaborate on what drove the increase. The resort operator is banking on the year-end holiday season to draw visitors, even as upgrades to its hotels, gaming areas and other guest spaces limit how much of the resort it can operate through 2027. As part of efforts to attract premium customers, the resort is stepping up its marketing and using events and new openings at Weave, its retail and dining precinct, to give guests more reasons to visit. At the same time, RWS is revamping its gaming areas, lounges, restaurants and other guest spaces. It expects the upgrades to improve its hotel offerings and broaden the resort’s appeal over the longer term.

events.title: No love for Lambo: Luxury car dealer EuroSports reports losses, seeks funding to support business
events.summary: Lamborghini is expected to introduce a new version of its Temerario sports car (pictured on April 22) by March 2027. EuroSports Global’s losses widened as car sales fell, with revenue down more than 30% to $7.83 million. It blamed weak demand, high luxury car fees and economic uncertainty. The dealer hopes new Lamborghini models, including the Urus SE, will lift orders. It also expects the Temerario to arrive by March 2027. Its Scorpio Electric unit has won European and Singapore approval for the Lambda Scorpii motorcycle. EuroSports is seeking funding, as losses and short-term debts raise concern over its ability to keep operating. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s Lamborghini dealer EuroSports Global is looking to new luxury models to draw buyers after a tough quarter of falling sales, even as it seeks fresh funding to support its car business and plans to mass-produce a home-grown electric motorcycle. The group on Nov 12 said its net loss had widened to $1.24 million in the quarter ended Sept 30, from $752,000 a year earlier. Revenue fell by more than 30% to $7.83 million. For the first half of its financial year, the group’s net loss widened by 57% to $2.29 million as revenue fell 21.7% to $15.1 million, weighed down by falling car sales and thinner margins on cars sold. EuroSports is the distributor for Lamborghini and Touring Superleggera in Singapore, with some models selling for more than $2 million. However, hefty additional registration fees for luxury vehicles and rising certificate of entitlement premiums have crimped demand for high-end supercars here. EuroSports also expects economic and geopolitical uncertainty to make buyers more cautious in the months ahead. But the group said new models could help attract more orders, and expects to start delivering two new versions of Lamborghini’s Urus SE sport utility vehicle in the October-to-December quarter, although prices for this model may be lower. Lamborghini is also expected to introduce a new version of its Temerario sports car by March 2027 , following the recent launch of its Revuelto SV . EuroSports’ electric motorcycle business has a longer timeline. The Lambda Scorpii, developed by its subsidiary Scorpio Electric, became the first electric motorcycle designed from scratch in Singapore to secure European vehicle-type approval in 2025, the group said. The approval certifies that the motorcycle meets European Union safety, environmental and technical standards. The motorcycle secured approval from Singapore’s Land Transport Authority on June 12, and Scorpio Electric registered the first unit for use on Singapore roads on July 13. It is also setting up sales and servicing networks in the Asia-Pacific and Europe, with plans to build a network of distributors and dealers across 10 to 15 cities. EuroSports expects mass production and deliveries to begin in 2028, and is in the process of securing additional funding to support the commercialisation of this business. The company has spent heavily on research and development for the Lambda Scorpii , which has placed pressure on its financials over the years. The group disclosed in its financial statements that its losses, cash outflow and short-term obligations raised a material uncertainty over its ability to continue operating. In the first half, it burned through $1.18 million in cash to run its operations. As at Sept 30, what it owed in the short term exceeded its short-term assets – which included cash, cars and spare parts held for sale, and money that customers owe the company – by $6.54 million. Still, the board said it expects the car distribution business to generate enough cash to cover operating expenses over the next 12 months. It is in talks with financial institutions and potential investors for additional funding to support operations over at least that period.

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Open weight model can now say things Chinese authorities don't like OpenAI launches security products, tells orgs they’re doomed if they don’t use them 23 hours ago Software Samaritan revamps borked Indian certs to block smart TV ads 1 day ago Canonical web services get stage fright ahead of Ubuntu Summit 2 days ago Google gooses Python AI performance by... removing Python 2 days ago Anthropic tiptoes into MS Office territory 2 days ago An American AI lab has re-educated Qwen3.8-27B, a popular open-weight large language model from Alibaba, so the software forgets its Chinese ancestry. Nous Research, an Austin, Texas-based AI lab, has subjected the model to re-education through training, not to be confused with China's " Re-education Through Labor " system. With the help of a post-training process, Qwen3.8-27B has been reborn under the name Arete "to reinforce Western values on a Chinese-trained model." What qualifies as a "Western value" remains open to interpretation. "Open-weight Chinese models are among the strongest available, but they ship with state-aligned behavior baked into the weights," Nous Research wrote in a blog post . Your correspondent tested this with a variant model, Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-6bit, locally. Asked about events during 1989 in Tiananmen Square, the model either refused to discuss the topic or provided euphemistic response. What's perhaps more surprising is that Anthropic claims operators affiliated with Alibaba's Qwen lab used outputs from its Claude models to train competing AI models via distillation . Nous Research, maker of the Hermes Agent , cites that sort of censorship as a risk for users of AI models trained in China. The concern comes amid broader scrutiny of Chinese influence in the tech industry, heightened by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation following controversy involving a woman US intelligence has accused of spying for China. Nous says the risk posed by Chinese-made AI models go beyond promoting Beijing's worldview. Some Middle Kingdom models have been found to produce more vulnerable code under certain conditions, according to a study by Booz Allen Hamilton, which does a lot of business with the US government. Hirundo, a vendor which says it is building "the first Machine Unlearning Platform to ensure that AI models only know what they should," makes the same argument . The company also notes that its efforts to apply "unlearning" to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B saw a dramatic drop in output that reflects Communist Party of China's preferred censorship, propaganda messaging, or bias. 89.8 percent of the model's output reflected those values before unlearning reduced the incidence to 2.8 percent. Nous Research did not achieve such dramatic results, but did see an overall reduction in viewpoints deemed to be propaganda. "On our evaluation, Arete-27B raised its fact score from 2.32 to 2.98 out of 5 and cut answers containing propaganda from 22 percent to 1 percent, in line with the Western models we tested," the company said. To handle Arete's unlearning, Nous Research says it briefly considered Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra , "but had found evidence that it too had a checkered record on China-related topics." "We don't know definitively, but theorize that the bias imparted to Nemotron came from working with Chinese open models during the training process," the company said. "We have experienced similar contamination, because the vast majority of high quality open models are Chinese, and only open models have terms of use that permit this kind of tinkering and experimentation." In the end, the biz tapped Inkling , an open weight model from US-based Thinking Machines Lab, to act as the teaching model. Nous Research says its model re-education efforts show that the propaganda layer is shallow and, with 50 million tokens worth of supervised learning, is relatively easy to remove.

events.title: Builder fined $150k after mother and baby injured in wall fall
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Builder fined $150k after mother and baby injured in concrete wall collapse Topic: Housing Construction Industry The concrete wall fell onto the rear part of the neighbouring house. ( ABC News: Marco Catalano ) A construction company has been fined after a 30-tonne concrete wall fell on a neighbouring property. A mother and her baby sustained minor injuries. Smart Builty Pty Ltd has been convicted and fined $150,000. A construction company has been fined $150,000 after a 30-tonne section of a concrete wall fell on to a house in Adelaide's inner south, injuring a mother and her baby. According to a ruling handed down by the South Australian Employment Court, the concrete wall was not properly secured and fell onto the rear of a neighbouring property at Wayville on November 28, 2023, during severe weather. It fell onto the back 60 centimetres of the home and most of its outdoor living area. The ruling said the principal contractor at the site, Smart Built Pty Ltd, was constructing a three-storey residential development which included 10-metre high precast concrete wall panels. It said the panels had been supported by temporary "propping" but the company had requested its removal about two weeks earlier to allow for better access to parts of the construction site. "No inspection of the precast panels or their permanent structural support was undertaken by any engineer prior to removal of the temporary propping," the ruling said. The ruling noted that victim impact statements had described the "profound impact the offending" on the mother and her baby, who both suffered minor injuries. The mother required stitches to her knee, while her baby "sustained superficial cuts only", but the court said those injuries could have been more serious. "Other section[s] of the inadequately supported wall loomed over the rest of the … family's home," the ruling said. On the day the wall fell, flooding and storm damage were reported around Adelaide, including at Wayville. ( Supplied: Spence Denny ) The court said the cost of structural damage to the home amounted to $85,413.82 and a further $19,211 damage to its contents. "The defendant [Smart Built Pty Ltd] paid $10,000 to the neighbours affected by the collapse to compensate them for the inconvenience of ongoing building works," the ruling said. It said the defendant had helped with practical steps to facilitate repairs, which were being arranged through the family's insurer. The ruling said the removal of the propping meant the wall was not "connected to other significant structural elements". "The design drawings clearly state … that the precast panels are to remain propped until the wall bracing is installed," the ruling stated. The court said it accepted "the offending did not involve deliberate or reckless conduct" but that the "poorly controlled risk of harm … was of death or extremely serious injury to multiple people". "I conclude the offending involved mid-range objective seriousness rather than a lower level," the ruling said. "I accept the defendant's evidence of its subsequently changed safety systems … I also accept the defendant's current intention is to not use precast panels again." The court imposed a conviction and fined Smart Built Pty Ltd $150,000.

events.title: Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU
events.summary: Published 13 November 2026, 01:17 GMT Andy Burnham said he believes a "win-win" deal can be agreed with the European Union, adding it could be "more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for" in 2016. The prime minister is exploring closer ties with the bloc and is expected to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility at a UK-EU summit on 20 November. Speaking after meeting European leaders in Ireland on Thursday, Burnham said he hopes a deal could help lower prices and boost the UK economy. He predicted the negotiations could "go down to the wire". The Conservatives have previously said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset". While Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good", he has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election. Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this. The manifesto also said the party wanted to "make Brexit work" and reset the UK's relationship with the EU. Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer struck a deal in May 2025 covering fishing, trade and other areas and next week's summit will see the UK government seek to agree further changes. Burnham has also made clear he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc. Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others Published 1 day ago UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC Published 6 days ago Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham Published 30 September Can Burnham avoid another Labour welfare rebellion? Published 1 day ago Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Burnham was asked to explain if his decision to reopen the debate on the UK's future with Europe had helped or hindered the negotiations linked to the summit. Burnham replied "I think it has helped" before adding: "We've got a big week ahead of us to try and get this deal over the line. "But let's be clear what's at stake: what we can achieve through this deal is lower prices for British consumers, lower costs for British businesses, more growth in our economy so there's really big prizes here, and I will fight now over the days to come to make sure we get this deal over the line." Pressed on whether discounted university tuition fees for European students would be part of the deal, Burnham said "requests are coming from the European side, we are putting our requests on the table too". He added: "I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe. I think it actually could be more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016." Ahead of the summit, the UK and EU agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports. Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations. As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits. Burnham also told MPs last month that the summit presents an opportunity to make progress on "controlling illegal immigration". Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules, saying it would "actually take us backwards". On Thursday, Conservative MP and former minister Dame Priti Patel said: "Andy Burnham's obsession with the EU risks dragging Britain backwards, damaging our economy and leaving hardworking British taxpayers footing the bill." The Liberal Democrats earlier this month described the draft deal as a "patch, not a fix" and said the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU". Reform UK believes one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules" and any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy. The Green Party has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK". events.title: ‘Bring Back THE Boss’: Nvidia Employees Petition for Jensen Huang’s Return
events.summary: Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation , according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED. An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter. “We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another. One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.” The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment. Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset . The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email. Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips. It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned . In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation. One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED. Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.” Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.” In your inbox: Inside WIRED’s newsroom with Katie Drummond They war-gamed dimming the sun —it went worse than you think The Big Interview: Nathan Fielder tells us everything Live tracker: Elon Musk’s America PAC is spending big on the midterms Introducing the app: More ways to make the most of WIRED © 2026 Condé Nast. events.title: ‘Renewed confidence’: Singtel lifts FY2027 guidance as underlying profit grows 10%, net profit falls 55%
events.summary: Singtel’s revision came on the back of an 8.7% rise in first-half operating companies’ earnings before interest and taxes to $902 million. Singtel’s H1 net profit fell 55% to S$1.54 billion after last year’s S$2.21 billion divestment gains were not repeated. Underlying net profit rose 10% to S$1.49 billion, helped by NCS, Digital InfraCo, Optus, Airtel and AIS. Revenue rose 6% to S$7.29 billion. Singtel lifted its interim dividend to S$0.09 and raised full-year OpCo Ebit guidance. SINGAPORE – Telecommunications giant Singtel on Nov 13 raised financial year 2027 growth guidance for its operating companies’ (Opco) earnings before interest and taxes (Ebit) to between mid and high single digits. This was an upgrade from the guidance of low- to mid-single-digit growth it gave in May , and the second year in a row that the telco has raised its Opco Ebit guidance at the half-year mark. The revision came on the back of an 8.7% rise in first-half Opco Ebit to $902 million. The growth was led by strong performance by Australian subsidiary Optus, tech service provider NCS and its digital infrastructure arm Digital InfraCo. Optus’ Ebit rose 13.7% to A$322 million (S$282 million), NCS’ rose 15.5% to $212 million and Digital InfraCo’s rose 25.3% to $51 million. Arthur Lang, group chief financial officer of Singtel, said at a media briefing of the company’s first-half results on Nov 13 that the telco was entering the second half of the year “with a renewed confidence versus six months ago”. His comments came even as the telco reported a 54.7% drop in net profit to $1.5 billion for the first half ended September, in the absence of exceptional gains recorded the previous year. Underlying profit for the period was up 10.4% at $1.5 billion. Lang said that when the group set its initial set of guidance in May, the Strait of Hormuz crisis had just broken out and inflation was a concern. Moreover, the proposed merger of Simba and M1 had just been called off, adding a new degree of uncertainty. In addition, Singtel said that it was also reviewing its capital expenditure guidance of about $3 billion. The group expects capital expenditure to be lower than initially estimated on the back of disciplined capital allocation. However, Singtel Singapore’s Ebit was down 4.5% as a result of the absence of one-off income recorded in the corresponding period the previous year. Excluding the one-off, Singtel Singapore’s Ebit was down 1%. Singapore mobile service revenue grew 3.8% in the second quarter from the first quarter , its second consecutive quarter of sequential growth. Group chief executive Yuen Kuan Moon said this followed seven quarters of decline. Average revenue per user rose to $23 for the quarter ended Sept 30, from $22 the previous quarter. The telco attributed the rise to its three-brand strategy of Singtel, Gomo and hi!. “We are not interested in going after just the pure volume of subscribers,” said Ng Tian Chong, CEO of Singtel Singapore. Optus stake sale still on the table In July , Singtel confirmed that it was in discussion with interested parties to sell a stake in Optus. Yuen said Singtel’s search for a minority “like-minded Australian partner” for Optus was still ongoing. However, given the strong performance of Optus, Lang noted that a stake in the company will not be available “at any value”. Earlier media reports noted that New Zealand-based infrastructure investor Morrison was in talks to buy a minority stake valued at more than A$2 billion. Singtel said that its first-half financial year 2027 net profit decline was mainly due to the absence of $2.2 billion in net exceptional gains recorded a year earlier from the partial sale of its stake in Airtel and the Intouch-Gulf Energy merger. Excluding exceptional items, underlying net profit rose about 10% from $1.4 billion a year earlier. The group’s operating revenue rose 5.5% to $7.3 billion in the first half , from $6.9 billion in the year-ago period. In constant currency terms, revenue would have increased 1.4%, while underlying net profit would have grown 15.9%, Singtel said. The board approved an interim dividend of nine cents per share, comprising a core dividend of 7.1 cents and a value realisation dividend of 1.9 cents . This was 10% higher than the 8.2 cents per share declared a year earlier.

events.title: Applied Materials forecasts quarterly revenue above estimates on strong AI chip demand
events.summary: Applied Materials is benefiting from increased spending by chipmakers racing to meet the extraordinary AI-led demand for chips and memory. Applied Materials expects fiscal first-quarter revenue of about US$11.10 billion, above Wall Street’s US$10.89 billion estimate, as AI chip demand keeps spending high. Fourth-quarter Semiconductor Systems revenue rose 64% to US$8 billion, and adjusted profit was US$4.16 a share, beating forecasts. Chief executive Gary Dickerson said 2027 could be “another record year”, with wafer fab equipment demand set to rise more than 30% and customers wanting tools sooner. Applied Materials forecast fiscal first-quarter revenue above Wall Street expectations on Nov 12 , betting that strong demand for advanced AI chips will continue to fuel spending on its semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The company, which supplies equipment for key wafer fabrication processes, is benefiting from increased spending by chipmakers racing to meet the extraordinary artificial intelligence-led demand for chips and memory. “The actual metrics of the market show that demand is still very strong,” said Bob O’Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research. Applied’s results show chipmakers and foundries are “buying as much equipment as they possibly can”, he added. The Santa Clara, California-based company’s Semiconductor Systems revenue jumped to US$8 billion (S$10.3 billion) in the fourth quarter, up about 64% from a year earlier. The company is one of Apple’s partners for its American Manufacturing Program, which includes work at Applied’s Austin, Texas, facility to boost US production of chipmaking equipment. “We expect 2027 to be another record year for the market and Applied,” chief executive Gary Dickerson said on a post-earnings call. He said wafer fab equipment demand should rise more than 30% and customers are asking for tools sooner, not later. China accounted for 25% of fourth-quarter revenue, down from 29% a year earlier, though sales there rose about 35% to US$2.64 billion. The company forecast quarterly revenue of around US$11.1 billion, plus or minus US$500 million, compared with the average of analysts’ estimates of US$10.89 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. The company reported fourth-quarter adjusted profit of US$4.16 per share, beating analysts’ average estimate of US$4.05. REUTERS

events.title: House Democratic leaders face fallout over poorly timed floor vote fumbles
events.summary: A week that was supposed to see House Democrats transition seamlessly from a landslide midterm victory to a leadership coronation has instead been pocked by surprise Republican victories on the House floor. Why it matters: Skeptics of Democratic leadership have seized on these strategic fumbles to cast doubt on their much-heralded managerial abilities in the lead-up to the party's leadership elections next week. "It's really unfortunate that this happened this week when, obviously, that is a narrative we hear leadership portray," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) told Axios. Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) said this week has "certainly not given me confidence," and that the election was an "indictment on how our party has been operating thus far, and this is a big part of why." "We do know that the Democratic caucus has blundered before on things, like whipping the votes to protect NPR last spring," said Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio). "We botched that one." What happened: The House voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday to quash an effort by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, with support from all House Democrats present. The outcome quickly sparked backlash because nearly a dozen House Democrats were absent, many of whom got caught in a traffic jam returning from an Elect Democratic Women event. That was followed by an incident on Wednesday in which House Republicans passed a veterans bill by voice vote despite Democratic opposition. The incidents follow a procedural blowup in September in which a pair of centrist House Democrats repeatedly broke with leadership and helped the GOP advance key bills. What they're saying: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), asked about these incidents by Axios, touted a different veterans bill Democrats forced to a successful floor vote on Thursday via a discharge petition. "House Democrats once again successfully forced a vote on a piece of legislation designed to make life better for the American people," he said. House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) did not respond to Axios' question and walked off the House floor into her office. The intrigue: Even some current and incoming House Democrats who are voting for Jeffries as speaker acknowledged the vote was a black eye. "I think everyone's frustrated with how that all went down, I'm not going to lie to you about that," said Rep.-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.). "People are pissed," a senior House Democrat told Axios. The other side: Other Democrats told Axios the absences were an inevitable reality of Congress, noting that several who missed votes have said they were attending to emergencies. "I think everyone's explained what the situations were — somebody was recovering from surgery. There are certain things that are unavoidable," said Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.). Others said the upshot is that House Democrats need to do a better job of getting to votes on time: "The general consensus among the new members is on Jan. 3, it's time to lock in," Rep.-elect Matt Little (D-Minn.) told Axios. Others said the speakership election offers a window into how Jeffries' approach to the speakership might play out over the coming year. Jeffries has always taken a more hands-off approach than his predecessor, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), preferring to let issues and fights among members resolve themselves.

events.title: Senate Dems can look forward to unlikely MAGA allies
events.summary: Senate Democrats could find some of their most surprising allies next Congress from the right wing of the Republican Party . Why it matters: Senate Democrats are on track to need only four GOP votes to break filibusters next Congress. They could find those votes from a bloc of GOP senators with a shared appetite for taking on corporate power. Enter Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), Jim Banks (R-Ind.), Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.). Each has already worked with Democrats, and their votes could put legislation over the top. Who we're watching: Hawley has co-led multiple pieces of legislation with progressive star Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) this Congress. Hawley is often viewed as a loner in the GOP, pairing populist economics with hardcore culture war issues from abortion to transgender care to religious freedom. He's been scathing in his postelection critiques. "This Congress did not come and work for the people. This Congress came and worked for AI companies, and it worked for data centers, and it worked for big tech companies," he told reporters on Tuesday. He's scoping out areas for potential bipartisan deals: "You want to raise the minimum wage? I'm for that. You want to work to get gas prices down? I'm for that. I am open to anything to bring down the cost of health care," he said. Zoom in: Watch the health care space, specifically undoing cuts passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and drug price controls. President Trump has specifically asked Congress to codify his most favored nations drug pricing deals, which could give Republicans an opening to work with Democrats. Hawley and moderate Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) were among the loudest GOP voices opposing the expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act credits last year. Zoom out: Social Security and tech safety issues could also be huge areas of unexpected bipartisan work. Over the summer, Warren and Moreno released a sweeping plan to "save Social Security." Warren and Banks have tag-teamed on numerous tech and AI safety bills, including a joint statement on Nvidia this week. Hawley is also a major critic of AI. Schmitt worked with Warren in 2024 and 2025 to challenge Big Tech's dominance of Pentagon AI contracts, and with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) in July to crack down on search engine monopolies. What to watch: While there will be fewer this Congress, Democrats will also have a club of more moderate Republicans they can try to pick up too. Murkowski, along with Sens. John Curtis (R-Utah) and Todd Young (R-Ind.), will be top targets.

events.title: Nvidia fallout fuels questions about Lutnick’s staying power
events.summary: The News Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has kept his job through scrutiny over his ties to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein; his cryptocurrency firm, Tether; and his former financial services firm, Cantor Fitzgerald. The Nvidia fallout may be the toughest test yet of his staying power. A growing GOP contingent is pointing the finger at Lutnick for not cracking down hard enough on Megaspeed, the AI chip firm with ties to an alleged Chinese spy with whom former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair, and for what they see as the Commerce Department’s broader failure to restrict AI chip exports to China. In the wake of reporting that other administration officials had urged the Commerce secretary to move faster, Republicans on and off Capitol Hill are accusing Lutnick of defying President Donald Trump by not imposing curbs on the firm — and even positing his job could be at risk. “We’re hearing … Trump has directed three times that [Megaspeed be blacklisted],” Rep. John Moolenaar, the top Republican on the House Select Committee on China, told Semafor. “If that’s true … then clearly, it seems that those questions need to be answered.” But so far the balance of GOP officials are coming to Lutnick’s defense, suggesting the commerce secretary won’t be going anywhere soon. The president himself is so far standing by Lutnick despite the bipartisan backlash, reinforcing his willingness to go easier on China as he pursues a trade detente with Beijing. “What I would say to everybody: Just settle down,” Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., told Semafor. “We don’t need to shoot Howard today.” “There’s lots and lots and lots of stuff here that’s going to come out. Should it come out? Absolutely,” Justice continued. “Should we get on some witch hunt running through the wilderness? … I don’t do that.” Congress will get more answers soon: Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters Thursday that Lutnick will testify before the chamber’s Commerce Committee. And House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., said that Huang, who resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following revelations of another affair with a colleague, will appear before his panel . Even Lutnick’s critics think he’ll eventually pull himself out of trouble, even as longstanding interagency tension threatens to boil over. “When you saw [Treasury] Secretary [Scott] Bessent blowing up at Lutnick in the Situation Room, you can rest assured the working level at Treasury was all over Commerce about chip sales for over a year,” Steve Bannon, the MAGA commentator and Bessent ally, told Semafor. “Now the issue becomes: Does Lutnick start inventing excuses to save himself?” A Commerce Department spokesperson said that “Treasury and Commerce have a great working relationship,” adding that both “are committed to advancing President Trump’s agenda.” The Nvidia news landed just in time for Democrats, who are finalizing their oversight plans for the next Congress. Already, lawmakers have laid the groundwork to investigate Lutnick’s involvement with Cantor Fitzgerald , Tether , and Epstein . The detractors No GOP lawmaker has called explicitly for Lutnick’s firing. But they haven’t hesitated to blame him for many of the recent revelations about Nvidia — including the fact that Huang accompanied Trump to China earlier this year despite the since-revealed existence of a State Department memo outlining his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy. “How on Earth do you put somebody on Air Force One [when you have] been informed there was a suspected improper relationship beforehand? How is that protecting the president?” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said. “Shame on Lutnick for allowing that exposure to happen for the president; to me, that’s a disqualifying moment for Lutnick.” Compared to Epstein, “this, to me, is next-level,” he added. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., rebuked Commerce for not shedding more light on the circumstances, particularly when it comes to the sale of AI chips to Megaspeed. “If I were the secretary, I’d call a press conference and explain what happened,” Kennedy said. “This is as serious as an aneurysm.” Even some of the Trump administration’s staunchest allies have weighed in, accusing Lutnick of defying the president by failing to rein in Megaspeed. “Lutnick, it appears, used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur even though President Trump has directed his administration and the Department of Commerce not to allow that to happen,” China hawk Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Fox News. He urged Lutnick to testify before the Senate Banking Committee. The defenders Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., told Semafor that “you’ve got to get the facts” before drawing any conclusions, adding that Lutnick has “always responded to my questions, so that’s all I can ask.” Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., also cast doubt on whether Lutnick really was at fault. “In a lot of cases, where they simply blame someone, I want to know what the rules are that he’s trying to comply with,” Rounds told Semafor. “Is there something that we’ve done, in terms of policy, that might have either delayed his ability or something else? I don’t know, and I’d rather get the facts before I make a decision as to guilt.” The AI industry sees little problem with Lutnick’s conduct either way. “Commerce’s job is to expand the economy, domestic and foreign, pretty much at all costs,” National Artificial Intelligence Association CEO Caleb Max said. “So if you zoom out, I don’t think it looks nefarious; I think it looks natural.” The View From the white house Far more crucially, the White House’s public posture on the debacle indicates that Trump is not particularly concerned about the fallout, let alone Lutnick’s role in it. “Secretary Lutnick is a champion of President Trump’s America First trade and tariff policies, which have secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments,” a White House official said. “President Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.” The White House pointed Semafor to the president’s comments earlier this week, when he told reporters that he didn’t think he’d bring up the subject during his upcoming meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Notable The Commerce Department is finalizing a rule to block China’s remote access to AI chips, The Information reported . White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be pushed out of his role, Reuters reported .
