events.title: A Tool Built by Election Deniers Said These Voters Were Dead. We Found Them Alive.
events.summary: A voter departs after casting a ballot at a polling location in Atlanta on Nov. 3. Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Image Ahead of the midterms, conservative election activists discussed plans to wield a powerful new weapon in the war against fraud: a data tool built by one of their own that could identify suspicious voters and help with contesting their ballots. The system was put to the test this week in Forsyth County, Georgia, where a member of the county’s election board provided other officials with what he suggested was evidence of wrongdoing: four allegedly dead voters. But it turns out all four are alive and well, ProPublica determined. The board rejected the attempt to challenge their ballots. The effort, though, shows that even after last week’s blue wave, those who believe the 2020 election was stolen have continued to relentlessly search for ways to contest Republican losses. In Georgia, Democrats swept statewide offices . The board member who initiated the Forsyth County challenge, Max Clavijo, is a member of the Election Integrity Network, a group led by conservative lawyer Cleta Mitchell that works to restrict voting and tighten election laws and rules. Mitchell worked closely with Donald Trump in his attempt to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election and, since he retook the presidency, has been central to his push to assert greater federal control over voting . In the run-up to the midterms, on right-wing media and on private organizing calls, EIN participants outlined plans to search voter rolls with a software tool known as ELLY’s Election Monitor and contest ballots the tool deemed suspicious. ELLY was developed by EIN member Rick Richards. It aggregates public data from state voter files, federal change-of-address records, tax documents, obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other sources. In Georgia, State Election Board members and top staffers have urged counties to use the tool to search their voter rolls for signs of fraud. Richards talked about ELLY’s national potential on a podcast in late September, on which right-wing media personalities and activists touted its capacity to help GOP candidates contest their defeats. “We can prove the fraud that’s gone on in every state,” one commentator said. “This data will be able to set up challenges to those who lose.” The following month, on a private call with EIN members and other conservative activists, Richards promised to provide data from more than 3,000 counties to “citizen monitors” and GOP candidates to try to prove fraud, according to a recording reviewed by ProPublica. Read More How Cleta Mitchell Turned Trump’s “Big Lie” Into a Movement In an interview, Richards told ProPublica that he gave Clavijo data on Forsyth County at Clavijo’s request. He said in a subsequent email that their actions were meant to inform the board and remain confidential. Clavijo didn’t respond to questions from ProPublica. Richards refused to answer questions about whether Clavijo’s effort was part of a wider EIN campaign to contest votes cast in the midterms. “That’s irrelevant,” he said. “The data is the data. People can use it for what they want to.” Mitchell, EIN’s leader, didn’t respond to questions about the group’s plans related to ELLY, either in Georgia or nationally. In the months since some on Georgia’s State Election Board started promoting ELLY’s use, its accuracy has been much debated. The tool doesn’t have access to personal identifiers such as voters’ Social Security or driver’s license numbers or full dates of birth, which increases the potential for mismatches involving people with the same names. Voting rights groups have called ELLY error-prone . The Cherokee County election director complained to the state board after the tool falsely flagged a county board member’s spouse as dead . State Election Board members and Richards have defended ELLY. Accusations that the data is unreliable were “horse hockey,” Richards told ProPublica, explaining this was “a Southern colloquialism for B.S.” Late last week, according to several people familiar with the matter, Clavijo circulated documents to board members and Forsyth County’s election director. Based on data from ELLY, Clavijo questioned whether the names of more than 22,000 people on the county’s voter roll were correct and disputed the eligibility of 69 voters. In addition to four he claimed were deceased, he alleged others had moved out of the county or state, had voter ID irregularities or had registered under fictitious names, giving an initial as their first name. During the meeting, Clavijo claimed that he was not trying to disrupt the election’s certification or formally challenge the voters, a process outlined in statutes that can lead to ballots being tossed or voters removed from the rolls. (Richards also said they had not formally challenged ballots.) Clavijo said he was merely seeking “to clean the voter rolls” and inform the board so officials could investigate further. But other board members accused him of doing an end run around the formal challenge process. Barbara Luth, the board chair, said she felt “sorry for” Clavijo because activists were bypassing the challenge procedure “by coming to you and having you submit it.” Under fire from fellow board members, Clavijo admitted he could not vouch for the data’s accuracy. “I did not make any explicit accusation that the information was 100% correct,” he said. The cover letter Clavijo submitted with the challenges said that they had not been verified with any “human review,” according to sources familiar with the matter. Richards and Clavijo submitted obituaries for the voters they claimed were dead, but there were discrepancies between the information in them and the voters’ records. All of the obituaries said or suggested the deceased lived outside of Forsyth County, which would have made it impossible to vote there. One said the person lived in Arizona . events.title: Dubai's Parkin posts record profit as fines outpace fees for first time
events.summary: Dubai's public parking operator Parkin reported a 27 per cent annual jump in third-quarter profit, with income from fines and seasonal permits outpacing parking fees for the first time. Net profit after tax was at Dh199.2 million ($54.2 million), as revenue grew 21 per cent year-on-year to a record Dh415.2 million, the company said in a filing to the Dubai Financial Market. Its enforcement category – which groups fines and seasonal parking passes – contributed Dh136.4 million, surpassing parking fees that added Dh127.8 million, which was a 5 per cent annual drop. Earlier this year, Parkin introduced micro cameras on kerbsides to catch motorists who avoid tickets. Cars with automatic cameras to scan entire streets have been operating for several years. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation – a key metric for profitability – for the three-month period jumped 28 per cent to a record Dh255 million. For the third quarter, Parkin sold a record 110,600 seasonal passes, which was a 37 per cent annual jump, while total fines issued jumped 34 per cent to about 916,100. For the first nine months of 2026, Parkin's profit grew by a quarter to Dh550.6 million, as revenue through September climbed 24 per cent to more than Dh1.16 billion. Ebitda for the period also grew by 24 per cent to Dh703.4 million. During the period, seasonal permits grew 58 per cent to about 308,600, while fines rose 24 per cent to more than 2.36 million. The company added about 53,500 parking spaces over the past 12 months to lift its total to a record 272,500, it said. Parkin's results demonstrate “the strength of our diversified business, with growth across developer parking, seasonal cards and our other revenue streams more than offsetting softer public parking revenues during the quarter”, chief executive Mohamed Al Ali said in a statement. “We continued to execute our growth strategy with discipline,” he added. Parkin has been playing a major role in Dubai 's strategy of expanding its paid public parking network to curb illegal parking and better manage available spaces. Last week, paid parking was extended to certain areas of the emirate's Jebel Ali Industrial area and Al Furjan. Last month, Parkin partnered with Q Mobility to manage smart parking facilities across Etihad Rail’s passenger station network .

events.title: Scientists check their work and confirm it with update on iconic black hole image
events.summary: The image of the red ring around the black hole M87, produced by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) array, made front-page news around the world in 2019. There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong. This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data. The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica. Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape. Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. The new approach used closed triplets (using three telescopes for error correction) rather than station pairs in an effort to reduce error. To the relief of the EHT team, the new image recreated the iconic ring-like image seen in the original, according to a paper published in Nature today . In a prepared statement, Lai said taking pictures of black holes was not easy. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the Moon," he said. He explained that when his team applied new advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to the original Event Horizon Telescope dataset, they found a black hole almost identical in size and shape to the historic EHT image. "Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data. This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process," he said. Event Horizon Telescope director Laurent Loinard welcomed the new study. "It is extremely gratifying to see that an elegant, entirely independent method recovers the ring structure of M87 across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration's published results," he said. ®

events.title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
events.summary: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey. COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20. This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.   In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked. This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.  Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.” So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.  Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.) The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country). Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal. Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.   One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there. The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use. Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity. Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest. Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions. The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.  With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change. I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

events.title: Chris Kempczinski's new value menu for McDonald's
events.summary: The Signal Interview An 11-item menu board from the 1950s still hangs in McDonald’s Chicago headquarters, recalling the era when Ray Kroc struck his franchise agreement with the McDonald brothers and began building the world’s best known fast-food chain. The 10-cent root beers are long gone, but Chris Kempczinski, who marked his seventh anniversary as CEO this week, is having to pay new attention to its value proposition. The business is facing a “challenging” US consumer environment, he told investors this week, with comparable sales falling 0.2% in the three months to September. Kempczinski’s assurance that the company had started to turn things around in the last month of the quarter helped revive a stock that had fallen a jarring 32% between February and October. But to reverse the drop in customer visits, he has had to put more marketing dollars behind potentially slimmer-margin deals, like a $2 breakfast sandwich with free fries for loyalty program members. “Our goal is straightforward,” Kempczinski told Wall Street: “Customers should see a clear and compelling value proposition every time they consider McDonald’s.” Few companies see as many consumers each week as McDonald’s does, and it has seen growing numbers of lower-income Americans staying home for breakfast or skipping it altogether, Kempczinski says in an interview for . “Housing, medical care, childcare, utilities, transport — all of those things are putting, I think, a lot of pressure on people’s disposable income,” he says. McDonald’s sometimes benefits in tough economic times, as higher-earning households trade down from pricier restaurants. But the US economy’s current “K-shaped” nature means that wealthier households are still eating out in pricier restaurants, rather than trading down to eat burgers and fries. Reserving the right to get smarter in a franchised system Kempczinski’s $8.5 billion game plan, announced in June and dubbed “McDonald’s > NEXT,” is the second strategic overhaul of his tenure. Designed to update the group’s menu and modernize restaurants, he expects it to lift sales and margins by making McDonald’s “more customers’ first choice more often.” The complication is that about 95% of the world’s 46,000 McDonald’s restaurants are owned and operated by franchisees — and some have pushed back against a proposal that could require $650,000 to $800,000 of investment per store. There is tension in any business where customers want better value, franchisees want healthier returns, and shareholders want faster growth. McDonald’s relies on its 5,000 independent partners to execute its strategy, Kempczinski notes, which means he must operate “through influence, not through direct control.” A clear focus on growth can unite his disparate stakeholders, he believes. “If you have growth and the pie is expanding, it’s amazing how harmonious everything is,” he says. “When the pie isn’t growing, then everybody starts to think about their share … and then a system can turn on itself.” Restaurant upgrades are essential for driving that growth, he says, because “you can’t sell a $5 burger in a $1 lobby.” But he knows he can’t influence franchisees who think he’s not listening to them, and he says the headline number McDonald’s put on its proposals “for sure is going to get knocked down” in response to their feedback. He won’t be so “dogmatic” about the details of his strategy that he won’t learn from their feedback, he says. “We have a saying here at McDonald’s: We reserve the right to get smarter.” This week, he told analysts he feels “overall, good” about franchisees’ willingness to roll out the upgrades his strategic plan requires. Changing a risk-averse culture through ‘positive shaming’ Kempczinski, who grew up in a Catholic household in Cincinnati and would visit McDonald’s after Friday night football games, admits to some Midwestern conservatism. When he was invited to pick art for his office from the McDonald’s archive, he chose an all-American Norman Rockwell painting. But the former Procter & Gamble brand executive says he balances those instincts with a restlessness that he is trying to bring to McDonald’s. “The company is never going to go faster than the pace that the CEO sets,” he says, and he is pushing people to take more risks and make faster decisions. McDonald’s is “awesome” at testing new offerings and ideas, Kempczinski says, by way of example. With thousands of restaurants, “we can do A/B testing forever … but you can also test for too long.” The danger in a collaborative culture like at McDonald’s is that “everybody owns it and nobody owns it,” he observes. “Yes, we all need to work together, but at the end of the day, there needs to be a person or a group who’s actually held accountable for the results.” A CEO can do that by appointing people to senior positions who model the behavior they want others to adopt, he says. And, instead of shaming people for their mistakes, he believes “positive shaming” — praising top performers who set the right example — gets better results. The lessons of a Big Arch and a little bite McDonald’s menu now ranges from Cookie Butter Iced Coffee to the Red Bull Dragonberry Energizer drink, and includes far more chicken than it once did. Demand for chicken has been surging for several years, and the home of the Big Mac already sells more of it than KFC or Chick-fil-A. But Kempczinski sees “a lot of headroom” to sell more still, he says, with a push to add KFC-style breaded chicken to the menu. McDonald’s already commands more than 40% of the beef business in its 10 biggest markets, amounting to about $50 billion, he explains — but it has only 20% of the $130 billion chicken market. His strategy is about more than building on the power of McNuggets and McCrispy Strips, he says. “It’s just simple math.” Consumers have higher expectations than before about the taste and quality of their fast food, Kempczinski says, even as they also want it at affordable prices. “And the reality is, today, we don’t have enough customers saying that McDonald’s is the best place to go, if I want to get a great tasting chicken sandwich, or if I want to get a great cup of coffee.” In an hour-long interview, Kempczinski doesn’t refer to any of his menu items as “the product” — the sterile marketing term he used to describe a new Big Arch burger he introduced in March. The awkwardly small bite he took during one of his regular “Chris K” LinkedIn videos prompted days of mockery, as gleeful rivals recorded themselves sinking their molars into their own burgers. Kempczinski says he and his team debated whether and how to respond before deciding to “just let the internet run wild.” Jumping in and trying to control the conversation would have been “the biggest mistake” they could have made, he concluded. “The internet’s undefeated. events.title: Canonical web services get stage fright ahead of Ubuntu Summit
events.summary: A swathe of Canonical's web services has been offline for hours, an awkward warm-up for tomorrow's Ubuntu Summit. Canonical's status page lists widespread disruption beginning at approximately 1100 UTC, affecting gopkg.in, Ubuntu cloud images and mailing lists, jaas.ai, the Ubuntu keyserver, Launchpad PPAs, the Livepatch API, canonical.com, Ubuntu login, maas.io, and 16 other services. Landscape is also affected. Email and the company's Discourse forums remain available. The Register has asked Canonical for more information but had received no response at publication time. The company suffered a DDoS attack last month , although the cause of this outage has not been confirmed. The timing is unfortunate. As the banner across the top of the Discourse forum page says: "The Ubuntu Summit starts tomorrow – join from anywhere!" The online event runs on November 12-13. For the first time since the 2022 Summit in Prague, The Reg FOSS desk won't be attending in person. Canonical is still experimenting with the format of the event, and the last few have been primarily online, with just a small in-person audience in its London offices. This is the second of two Summits this year, labeled 26.04 and 26.10 to mirror Ubuntu's release cycle. The timetable , hosted on the Discourse site, lists several talks on AI and agentic coding. The AI-heavy program we reported from June's event appears to be continuing. ®

events.title: How the MAGA map cracked
events.summary: The News It’s easy to understand why Republicans couldn’t imagine the Trump coalition cracking. The MAGA electoral map, first built in 2016, stayed mostly intact for eight years and five elections. Rural areas stayed red or got redder. Non-white, working class areas drifted away from Democrats. The party of the New Deal was reduced to an urban and suburban archipelago, blue smudges on a red map that the president liked to show off to White House visitors. One good thing about America’s languid vote count is that a more interesting picture fills in after the big story is over. We knew last week that the Trump coalition came apart, and we’re learning now that Democrats won the country by 14 points, in the average House vote. Republicans couldn’t imagine that shift before Tuesday. Obviously, they didn’t plan for it when they heeded the president, in deep red states, and re-drew congressional maps. They planned for at least another decade of the Trump coalition, with rural America locked up, suburban America still competitive, and non-white voters alienated from the “woke” opposition party. Gerrymander hubris The story of North Carolina this year is the shattered GOP gerrymander — seven seats that backed Trump by double digits in 2024, then elected Democrats. The stories in Indiana, South Carolina, and Utah are that Republicans tried to re-draw their maps, failed, and were saved from electoral disaster. Had Republicans built the districts they wanted, most of them, across those three states, would have voted for Democrats. Why were Republicans so hubristic? Look closely at what happened from 2016 to last week. The Trump electoral map was the most solid either party had built in generations. It kept the upper Midwest competitive, which George W. Bush hadn’t been able to do. It made Appalachia nearly uninhabitable for Democrats, which Ronald Reagan couldn’t do. Richard Nixon couldn’t carry a GOP Congress on his coattails. Trump did several times — both chambers in 2016 and 2024, the Senate in 2018, the House in 2022. Every political coalition falls apart eventually, unless you’re running the Liberal Democratic Party of Japan or something. Barack Obama’s 2008 win led Democrats into some dizzy daydreams about a “permanent” majority that Republicans could only temporarily defeat. “Obama doesn’t need right-leaning whites anymore,” Ron Brownstein wrote in 2013, after Democrats won a second presidential election with a minority of white voters but a supermajority of non-whites. For a long time, both parties wondered if Trump had built something sturdier than that. He wasn’t counting on demographic change to keep Republicans in power. He’d ditched the GOP’s commitment to entitlement reform, which alienated working class voters, and its support for free trade, which was one of the Democrats’ best arguments when those voters got queasy about their cultural views. Not only did he do it, but Republicans who campaigned like him were able to keep those gains. In 2016, Trump carried 206 counties that had supported Barack Obama twice. Democrats believed this was a fluke, that more populist politics could win them back — not asking “if we broke up the big banks, would that end racism?” In 2020 they campaigned like eastern Iowa, northeast Ohio, and southeast Pennsylvania had gotten their anti-establishment votes out of their system and could be won again.But when he won back the White House in 2024, Trump carried 181 of those counties. And nearly every Republican walked the same map. The GOP’s disastrous midterm strategy was premised on voters who had become comfortable supporting Republicans after 2016 and nodded when Mike Johnson said “this isn’t your grandfather’s Democrat Party” — always “Democrat,” never “Democratic.” Democrats changed Republicans didn’t plan for Democrats to change, and offer a less culturally left-wing package to these voters. In much of the country, Democrats were able to reintroduce themselves and slice up the Trump map. The Rio Grande Valley and South Florida were disasters for Republicans, who treated Latino voters like new members of the MAGA movement, not as the swing voters they are. But the drop-off with rural white voters was more damaging in more of the country. Republican gerrymandering followed a simple formula: Carve up Democratic cities and overwhelm them with rural voters. This worked because they had a good idea of how Republican those rural voters were. It stopped working because Democrats competed for so many of them. That explains the disaster in North Carolina, where 47% of white voters backed Sen.-elect Roy Cooper, and Republicans did historically poorly with those voters down-ballot. Rep. Tim Moore, who had helped draw the state’s gerrymander, had given himself a seat where liberal Mecklenburg County voters were outnumbered by rural conservatives to the west. Lakesha Womack beat him by doubling the Democratic margin in Mecklenburg and by losing by less elsewhere, cutting his margins in rural counties by 15 to 20 points. “Rural voters are not necessarily all the way MAGA voters,” North Carolina Democratic Party chair Anderson Clayton told me last week. “They’re not necessarily bought into Republican politics. It’s just that the Republicans were the only party that’s been communicating to them and aggressively trying to be in their communities, and running candidates in them.” Clayton had been trying to make this change for years. Lots of Democrats had, with little success. This gave Republicans the confidence that, while Trump voters were harder to motivate without him on the ballot, they had ruled out supporting Democrats and could be convinced to come out to protect their guns, kids, and religion from them.If that’s not true, the electoral map stops looking so solid. Seats built to withstand a +13 swing to Democrats couldn’t be saved on a +14 swing. But Republicans believed that Trump’s nationalism and populism were locking in voters; Democrats were relying on their messy coalition and old issues, like protecting Social Security, losing their most loyal voters to the grave. It was a good strategy for a decade. It lasted longer than Karl Rove’s “permanent majority,” which was less appealing to rural voters and more appealing in the suburbs. But neither theory of the electorate worked without voters who believed their vote was protecting their way of life – culture and costs. What’s next What implications does this have for the electoral map, which both parties are still empowered to re-draw next year? It’s definitely changed the risk assessment. Republicans learned that black voter turnout will increase, against them, if their party draws maps to reduce their power — and that they don’t get a commensurate thank-you turnout from white voters. That will probably cost them a Senate seat in Mississippi, nearly cost them another in Louisiana, and almost blocked Marsha Blackburn’s wide path to the governor’s mansion in Tennessee. events.title: Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro does not like to be taken apart
events.summary: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook got a mixed reception from iFixit's teardown specialists, who praised its easily replaced lid but found fans and USB-C ports buried beneath the logic board. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display was unveiled at the end of October. It features a tandem OLED screen that stacks two layers of organic light-emitting pixels, eliminating the need for a backlight, and adds touch capability to the MacBook line for the first time. Although the vendor was patted on the back in recent years for improving the repairability of its famously locked-down products, this machine shows Apple still has some way to go. The good? The entire lid comes off relatively easily. Its three-screw hinges closely resemble those on the M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, while streamlined display cable brackets simplify removal. Apple's Repair Assistant tool also handled a full system board swap well. Despite concerns about Touch ID fingerprint authentication, everything went relatively smoothly when iFixit paired a touchscreen from one machine with a logic board from another. On the first boot, Repair Assistant recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor, and touch control needed no separate calibration. The bad? Replacing the panel alone is not possible. When iFixit tried to separate it from the lid, the glass delaminated, cracking the OLED and touch-sensitive layers beneath. That could make for a costlier repair than bargained for. Under the bottom cover, the PROLED has a similar internal layout to the last few models of MacBook Pros, with the fans, board, speakers, and trackpad all in the same places. That means the same annoyances persist. The MagSafe power connector can be removed via two screws and a bracket, yet the USB-C ports can't be extracted the same way because the logic board is in the way. The headphone jack and the fans also require removing the system board first, and the HDMI port and SDXC card reader are soldered to the board itself, as is the storage and memory. Another gripe is that this MacBook's battery pack is hard to remove, though at least it is removable, unlike in many thin-and-light laptops. The tested Pro weighs 1.38 kg or about 3 pounds. For these reasons, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display earns a 5 out of 10 repairability score from iFixit , but this is actually a one point increase over the score it gave the M5 MacBook Pro. The Apple logo has its own lighting. Older MacBooks with illuminated logos borrowed light from the LCD backlight shining through an apple-shaped window in the lid. This model uses a strip of LEDs along one edge of the logo, passing through a diffuser for an even glow. Because it sits behind the display panel, it would be nearly impossible to repair if it failed, especially if the panel is destroyed during removal. Under a microscope, the PROLED XDR display looks very different from earlier MacBooks: the blue subpixel is significantly larger than the green and red ones. The reason, we're told, is that blue OLED materials wear out faster, so a larger subpixel can emit the same amount of light while putting less strain on the material. ®

events.title: China’s Nvidia Honeypot Isn’t Surprising. Jensen Huang Fell for It Anyway
events.summary: There’s a specific mantra drilled into government workers, military officers, and intelligence personnel during counterintelligence briefings: “If she’s a 10 and you’re a 5, she’s a spy!” Or, as the US Army’s Counterintelligence Command posted on Valentine’s Day: “It doesn’t take a mathematician to figure out ‘10 + 5 = honeytrap.’” The very beautiful woman who is suddenly interested in your very ordinary existence probably has ulterior motives , is the message. Jensen Huang surely doesn’t live a typical life—he’s a centibillionaire, the swashbuckling CEO of Nvidia, one of the hottest and most geopolitically consequential companies of the 21st century. Surely he’s aware of the possibility that he’d cross paths with intelligence assets. In fact, it’s hard to think of many companies in the world that would be a higher priority target for foreign intelligence agencies. All of that makes the stock-shaking news this week all the more surprising. How did Huang get embroiled in a spy scandal that mixes infidelity, international espionage, the Trump administration, and the economic behemoth of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry? The story kicked off just before Halloween, with a six-byline story in The New York Times reporting that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Starting somewhere between 2024 and 2025, Huang allegedly had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a one-time executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider known as Megaspeed. US intelligence agencies warned top US officials that they believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. So far, Nvidia’s board, which has launched its own investigation, says it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but that’s far from the only concern. As one would expect, China has denied any nefarious plot centered on Jensen Huang. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson on Monday said , “The narrative about so-called Chinese spies is entirely based on groundless speculation—it’s nothing more than slander and smearing.” But according to reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times , US intelligence officials also claim that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was reporting to China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. On Monday, Megaspeed said on LinkedIn that US authorities found “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities." (There’s no indication so far that Alice Huang, a one-time Chinese state journalist, is an employee or “officer” of Chinese intelligence; she’s believed to be an “asset,” an outsider who aids an intelligence agency, sometimes for pay, sometimes not.) China, though, has elevated economic espionage to a core pillar of its economic and military development, stealing the designs for everything from US fighter jets to solar panels and commercial paint recipes . “Honeypots” or “honey traps”—positioning an alluring operative to seduce or develop a relationship with a key target—are one of intelligence’s most infamous and well-established strategies. French officials have warned specifically about Chinese honeypots since at least 2011, when intelligence reports cited a pharmaceutical researcher who was seduced and then blackmailed by a Chinese spy operation. Over the past quarter of a century, as Silicon Valley emerged as a center of political and economic power, it has become a key focus of Chinese intelligence. In one plot, a Chinese national named Fang Fang spent years trying to cozy up to Bay Area politicians , including then US Representative Eric Swalwell. (While intelligence officials at the time reportedly believed Fang to be an operative, law enforcement officials never brought any charges against her). When traveling to China, US business executives have become accustomed to leaving their regular phones and computers at home and using burner devices to prevent the installation of spyware or malware (as I did, when I traveled to China for WIRED in 2019 to report on Huawei ). In 2012, when Leon Panetta was making his first trip to China as defense secretary, he and his team were advised to bathe and shower in the dark in the event his hotel room was bugged. Last year, the threat of honeypots prompted the US government to explicitly ban personnel working in China and Hong Kong from engaging in romantic or sexual relationships with Chinese citizens. More recently, US officials joined with allies to warn about China’s increasingly sophisticated “ LinkedIn espionage ”: using the business-focused social networking site to recruit and build relationships with unwitting executives. Alice Huang’s Megaspeed, for its part, is a major Pacific region player in cloud services focused on the advanced computer chips that are the heart of Nvidia’s business.

events.title: Nvidia handed downgrade on Jensen Huang and AI uncertainty
events.summary: BREAKING: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia chief executive Financial services company Baird has given Nvidia a rare downgrade as chief executive Jensen Huang 's alleged affair with a Chinese spy casts doubt over his tenure. Baird analyst Tristan Gerra more than halved the chip maker's target from $500 to $200. Mr Gerra delayed his forecasts for data centres in 2027, saying supply issues are “mostly behind a potential slowdown, alongside potential demand softening”. AI hyperscaler capital expenditure could also slow to 40 per cent growth or slightly less for 2027, he said. Baird downgraded Nvidia stock to neutral, while a separate analysis from Morgan Stanley removed it as a top pick. Nvidia was trying to rally after a difficult period for tech-related stocks. Shares in the chip bellwether rebounded on Wednesday as CoreWeave's better-than-expected quarterly results lifted other chip stocks. Nvidia closed 2.92 per cent higher on Wednesday at $173.73 a share, after ending 5 per cent lower in the previous session. However, shares in Nvidia are on track for a sixth consecutive losing week. The company's stock is down about 8 per cent for the year. Mr Huang admitted to an extramarital affair in a letter to employees on Sunday. “To my colleagues at Nvidia, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence,” he wrote. Nvidia's board of directors has launched an investigation into the affair, adding that Mr Huang fully supports the review and is committed to co-operating with it. “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information … The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” it said. The explosive allegations come at a time when traders were already scrutinising AI tech stocks after recent earnings reports stoked fears over data centres and the financing behind them. Mr Huang's affair has also rocked Washington, with some legislators calling for investigations . The House foreign affairs committee has requested US President Donald Trump to appear for a closed-door briefing with Mr Huang on his interactions with the alleged spy. US Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and House permanent select committee on intelligence chairman Rick Crawford requested in a letter to Mr Huang that he brief their committees by November 18. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” they wrote, referring to the “People's Republic of China”. Analysts are also considering Mr Huang's future as they assess the direction of Nvidia, one of the key nodes in the broader AI nexus. Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore wrote that Mr Huang's leadership is “crucial to the company's direction”. On Tuesday, tech analyst Dan Ives said he estimates there is a 15 per cent chance Mr Huang is removed as chief executive. The next test for Nvidia will be on November 16, when it is due to report its third-quarter results.

events.title: Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?
events.summary: The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank has a grievance redress mechanism for people affected by projects it finances. But those seeking to file a complaint face significant hurdles. Critics say reforms are needed. For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over. For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods. In late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank . It remains unclear whether this complaint will lead to an independent investigation. The AIIB, which finances major infrastructure projects across Asia, has a mechanism in place to deal with such complaints. Individuals who suffer adverse effects from the bank-financed projects may, under certain conditions, file a complaint with the institution. However, access to this process — known as the Project Complaints Mechanism (PPM) — remains controversial. According to a report by The Diplomat , a magazine that covers political and economic developments in Asia, none of the 45 complaints listed on the AIIB's website had been deemed admissible as of mid-September. The bank acknowledged that "no cases have passed the PPM's eligibility assessment," but it stressed that this is "only part of the story." South Asia projects boost China's presence in India's sphere The AIIB emphasized that not every issue needs to be resolved through this mechanism. The PPM is "only one part of AIIB's grievance redress ecosystem," the Beijing-based bank said in response to a query from DW. Those affected should first attempt to resolve concerns directly with the project team at the local level, it said. According to the bank, "twelve complaints were in fact resolved at the project level — as a direct result of AIIB's follow-up and intervention — and one was resolved through domestic courts." But critics see this as a major weakness. "The mechanism must be easily accessible," said Arntraud Hartmann, a development economist at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS Europe) in Bologna, Italy. She argued that people affected by the projects, for instance, are required to document potential violations of environmental and social standards from the start. "How is the affected party supposed to know which standards might have been violated?" she questioned. The AIIB disputes this claim. "In terms of accessibility, we have made the submission form simpler and translated it into 12 languages," it said, adding that complaints can be submitted online, by phone, or by email. Urgewald, a German environmental NGO, cites another problem with AIIB-financed projects. For many of them, information on environmental impacts and resettlements is either missing or published late, it noted. For 2024, the NGO found that 11 of the 16 projects it examined lacked complete environmental and social impact assessments. In many cases, information on the potential number of displaced residents was also missing, it added. "The information published on the bank's website is often insufficient and inconsistent. Particularly important documents, such as environmental impact assessments or resettlement plans, vary widely or are missing entirely," said Nora Sausmikat, a China expert at Urgewald. The lack of information makes it difficult for those affected to respond promptly and report violations early on, she underscored, adding that the situation is particularly difficult for people without formal land titles. Christoph Steinert, a political scientist at the University of Konstanz, said the mere existence of such grievance redressal mechanisms "is not enough." Particularly vulnerable groups often know little about their rights, he said, adding that information should be available in local languages and targeted outreach directed at affected communities. Criticism of the AIIB's procedures is not new. A 2023 report by international aid organizations, including Recourse, Accountability Counsel, and Inclusive Development International, revealed that the AIIB's grievance mechanism had failed to accept a single complaint since its 2019 inception. The study highlighted that 101 of the 219 AIIB-financed projects, or 46% of the total projects at the time, were ineligible for review due to co-financing exemptions. The AIIB typically provides funding without leading projects, a standard practice in development finance. When complaints arise, it directs complainants to the lead lender. As a result, nine of the 45 complaints fell outside its jurisdiction. For Sausmikat, this is part of the problem. "The AIIB, however, decided against revising this requirement and established a mechanism that is very difficult to access," she said.

events.title: Microsoft's Patch Tuesday can't break stuff if it won't install
events.summary: Users are having difficulty installing Microsoft's latest Windows patch. Patch Tuesday contained a truckload of fixes for Microsoft products . However, for some users, installing the update, KB5132061, is proving challenging. In the hours after the patch was released, multiple complaints began to surface that the download and installation were failing, with some customers reporting a 0x800F0993 error code. Others say they received a 0x800F0989 error. Microsoft does not currently list any known issues with the update and is yet to make a statement or provide explanation for the glitch. In addition to the security fixes, this patch resolves a number of known issues from previous updates, including a problem where USB Audio 1.0 devices might fail to start and display an error code 10 in Device Manager. In the absence of a statement from Microsoft, several users have taken to sleuthing. One, with the handle of Forceflow on the ElevenForum site, suggested the bug might be related to Windows Sandbox, and said that after disabling the feature and rebooting, the patch installed successfully. However, others reported problems regardless of Windows Sandbox status, and alternative solutions included using DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) to check the package or downloading the update manually. It's an important patch to install, since it addresses 726 vulnerabilities in Windows alone, and the difficulties affected users face are less than ideal. Microsoft patches have lately displayed more gremlins than usual. Out-of-band releases are depressingly regular after updates break functionality. A September Out-of-band release, for example, was hurriedly pushed out after the September 2026 Windows security update caused trouble for Remote Desktop Services. The October Patch Tuesday for Windows Server sent Exchange Servers toppling , with a registry edit workaround suggested. There was no out-of-band update - Microsoft said the problem had been resolved in the November update. At least this latest release appears to be failing before users get a chance to see what is broken this time. ® Updated to add on November 12: Microsoft has confirmed that there was indeed a problem with installing the update for some users, but the good news is that a fix is rolling out and no action is required on the part of customers (at least those connected to the internet and using Windows Update). The bad news is, alas, there appear to be a few issues with the update around printing and activation. Microsoft giveth, and Microsoft taketh away.

events.title: Vodacom rules out financial services spin-off
events.summary: African telecoms heavyweight Vodacom has ruled out spinning off its financial services unit, its CEO Shameel Joosub told Semafor, rejecting a path taken by rivals seeking to extract more value from fast-growing mobile money businesses. Joosub’s stance potentially sets up a test of two competing strategies across Africa’s telecoms sector after Airtel Money’s London listing gave it a valuation of about $7 billion, or roughly five times annual revenue. Using the same yardstick, Vodacom’s larger financial services business would command roughly $13.5 billion. “We don’t want to sell the crown jewels,” Joosub said. Yesterday the company issued an earnings report that showed revenue from the fintech business rose by almost 20% in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period a year earlier, contributing about a third to the group’s core earnings of $2.6 billion.

events.title: NASA asks Earthlings to wave as Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away
events.summary: Voyager 1 will become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth next week, and NASA wants us to mark the occasion by flashing our lights at the sky. The spacecraft, which suffered a communications hiccup last month, is traveling at approximately 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) and will mark the 50th anniversary of its launch next year. Before then, it has another distance record to set. "Light-day" is a bit snappier than 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). NASA puts the crossing at 05:16:07 EST (10:16:07 UTC) on Wednesday, November 18. For "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," participants are invited to flash the mission's three-letter designation – VGR – in Morse code after sunset on November 17, using a flashlight or NASA's website. According to the space agency, this will create "a symbolic wave of golden light encircling the planet after sunset." It is also a nice way to mark the achievement – Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object from Earth, and its extraordinary longevity remains a testament to the skill of engineers past and present. Not that Voyager 1 will be able to detect any flashlights on Earth. Its cameras were turned off decades ago, after the famous Pale Blue Dot image was captured. NASA has invited the public to join in a spacecraft photo opportunity before. On July 19, 2013, Cassini photographed Earth and the Moon from its orbit around Saturn for "The Day the Earth Smiled," while people back home were encouraged to look up and "just smile at the sheer joy of being alive on a Pale Blue Dot." Voyager 2, the spacecraft's sibling, is not expected to reach the same milestone for another nine years. It took a different path through the solar system to swing past Uranus and Neptune. It will, however, be uncertain as to whether Voyager 2 will still be able to communicate by then – even with recent efforts to eke out the probe's dwindling power supply, margins are razor thin. ®

events.title: Dangote Refinery IPO draws more than $4B of interest
events.summary: The initial public offering of Africa’s biggest refinery attracted orders worth more than twice what was targeted, reflecting investor appetite for home-grown industrial firms. Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote had aimed to raise around $1.6 billion for the Dangote Refinery company in Africa’s largest-ever share sale, but drew more than $4 billion , Bloomberg reported. In a separate development, the tycoon scrapped plans to list his cement company in the UK, a move that marks a setback for the London Stock Exchange . The Dangote Refinery IPO marked an opportunity for global investors seeking exposure to one of Africa’s most strategic industrial assets while proving that a significant allocation can be secured from across the continent: Dangote priced individual shares cheaply to attract retail investors. African policymakers are keen to deepen capital markets to mobilize more of the continent’s domestic resources to fund industrialization and cut borrowing costs. But analysts say byzantine regulations and intra-continental barriers have hampered development of the continent’s capital markets. Nigeria is leading the push to change the status quo: Its finance minister this week laid out proposals that would make it easier to trade bonds across ​West Africa . — Alexis Akwagyiram

events.title: MSF urges global health officials to widen Ebola vaccine access
events.summary: Global health officials have been urged to widen the use of an existing Ebola vaccine in DR Congo following reports it may provide protection against a strain it was not designed to target. The Bundibugyo strain — for which there is currently no vaccine — has killed more than 5,300 people in the country’s largest-ever outbreak. Medical charity Doctors Without Borders said restrictions on using Ervebo, developed by Merck for use against a prior Ebola strain, should be lifted so more people at risk, including young children, can be vaccinated. The charity said DR Congo requested 500,000 doses of Ervebo, but only 70,000 were released. The World Health Organization recommends limiting its use against Bundibugyo to research studies because its effects remain unproven. Doctors Without Borders said early observations of fewer infections and deaths among previously vaccinated people justified wider use. A larger release from the global stockpile requires backing from the WHO’s vaccine advisers, who meet next week. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: Africa calls on COP31 to boost adaptation finance
events.summary: African countries want the COP31 climate talks, now underway in Türkiye, to set out how the world will deliver on last year’s pledge to triple adaptation finance designed to help cope with the growing impact of extreme weather events. A large share of the money has previously come from aid budgets, which have fallen to their lowest level since 2014 , and most wealthier countries have pledged little-to-no new climate finance from this year . The African Group of Negotiators says addressing this issue is vital to a successful outcome in Antalya as support for the continent’s vulnerabilities has been “dwindling,” according to its chairperson. But even a tripling in financing will not close the gap: In 2024, the amount available for developing economies reached around $30 billion — that pales against the $305 billion the UN estimates they need annually to 2035. Plans have been announced at COP31 to scale up successful adaptation projects and attract larger investments. But these cannot be “entirely dependent on voluntary contributions,” Kenya’s climate envoy told Semafor. — Chloé Farand

events.title: South Africa’s unemployment crisis worsens
events.summary: South Africa’s unemployment crisis deepened in the third quarter, official data showed, with anger over the lack of jobs spilling into the country’s politics and its debate over migration. The official unemployment rate reached 33.7%, slightly higher than the previous three months, with 8 million-plus people looking for work and more than four in five of them unemployed for at least a year, Statistics South Africa said in Tuesday’s update. The data deepens questions about the economic record of President Cyril Ramaphosa, who made job creation a central priority after taking office in 2018. It also risks compounding voter fury that has battered Ramaphosa’s African National Congress at the polls , and feeds into a combustible political environment in which migrants are blamed for competition over jobs and public services. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.summary: It’s been inching in that direction for years, and now it’s official: Dubai’s public parking monopoly earns more from fines than public parking fees. Parkin reported record third-quarter revenue , up 21% to 415 million dirhams ($113 million), driven by enforcement, expanding business with private developers, and longer-term permits. The latter may have skewed the results: Sales of discounted “seasonal cards” were up 37%, the company said, and those permits aren’t counted in public parking utilization and revenue, even though their holders occupy spaces. Parkin also expanded its portfolio to 272,500 spaces, nearly tripling the number managed for private developers over the past year. Still, for anyone parking in Dubai, it feels like enforcement is stricter, aided by the deployment of advanced cameras and AI-powered monitoring. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Spain’s workers hold a general strike over housing costs ahead of a national election
events.summary: Millions of Spanish workers have shut down businesses and disrupted transport in a massive protest over housing costs BARCELONA, Spain -- Millions of Spanish workers shut down businesses and snarled transport in a massive protest Wednesday over housing costs that the government hopes to leverage ahead of a national election later this month. The walkout — under the slogan “Salaries. Housing. Prices.” — was the first general strike in Spain in 14 years. In Barcelona, the country’s second-largest city, most storefronts on a main shopping boulevard were boarded up in anticipation of violence during protests later in the day. Some retail chains were open to business while public transport was at a standstill or facing long delays. The subway opened only for the rush hour. Carlos Ferrer, a 45-year-old customer service worker who was trying to get back home to Alicante by train from Barcelona, said sometimes only “radical measures, such as a general strike” can force a change of course. “Authorities need to feel pressure from the citizens so they can do something," he said. Rain pelted the capital, Madrid, as strikers marched down main streets and blocked off Gran Vía, the city’s main thoroughfare, where big brand stores remained open although some were also boarded up. Unions have called for workers to march through the city center later Wednesday, and protests are also planned in more than 50 cities and towns. Manuel Gómez, a 19-year-old student in Madrid, welcomed the protests, which he said marked a change for the country. “In Spain, we have a serious problem, which is that when we don’t like something, we never go out to protest,” he said. About 5% of flights for Wednesday were canceled at airports across the country, according to the country’s airport operator, AENA. “The strike has exceeded the labor unions’ expectations,” said Unai Sordo, secretary general of CCOO, one of the two unions calling the strike. “It has been a success in terms of turnout.” Earlier, the two unions — CCOO and UGT — reported significant work stoppages in strategic sectors. They said the stoppages amounted to 90% in the automotive and port sectors, 85% in the meat industry, 82% in waste collection, and 75% in the energy sector. Minor incidents were reported in the first hours of the strike. Tires were set on fire at roadblocks in Barcelona, and scuffles with police were reported near the main wholesale market on Madrid’s outskirts. Police also used pepper spray against the strikers in some places. Many schools and universities reportedly closed or are working at minimal capacity. In Madrid, this added to an ongoing strike started by teachers nearly a month ago demanding better working conditions. In southwestern Spain, classes were suspended due to bad weather. “It’s extremely important to remind people that we, the workers — who are also renters or who also pay mortgages — are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill,” Sandra Mora, spokesperson for the Tenants Union, told national radio, RNE. The strike brought workers, activists, politicians and ordinary Spaniards around the same interests — accessible housing. The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, eating into household budgets and angering voters. Microsoft apologizes for email disruption, says AI agents not responsible Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE The anger reached a boiling point following the nationally televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last month. The subsequent death of Maricarmen , as the woman became known, caused even more indignation and solidified her as a symbol of Spaniards who feel they pay too much in rent and can’t even dream of homeownership. Housing activists leveraged the uproar over Maricarmen's eviction to call for the general strike, and soon won the backing of the UGT and CCOO unions. The housing activists are seeking the elimination of pricey tourist apartments, a crackdown on real estate speculation and the automatic renewals of leases as a way to protect renters. Unions demand more government intervention in the housing market and a new minimum wage agreement through talks with the business owners' association. The nationwide protests over Maricarmen's eviction propelled Spain’s government to push through emergency measures to limit evictions and help tenants, but right-wing parties in the Parliament refused to ratify them , claiming they would provoke a flight of properties from the rental market. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez then doubled down and called an early election , hoping to earn four more years in power for his left-wing coalition. The vote is set for Nov. 29. Then, in late October came a brutal high-speed train collision — Spain's second deadly rail disaster of the year — that killed 69 people.

events.title: Duolingo, Strava, and Ticketmaster Are All Caught Up in EU’s New Digital Fairness Rules
events.summary: The European Commission announced a sweeping set of updates to consumer law on Wednesday to protect European Union citizens from “harmful digital practices”—whether while online shopping, browsing social media , or doing their Duolingo lesson. Within the package, the Commission unveiled its Digital Fairness Act to address harmful practices online. Proposed rules include banning dark patterns —practices that manipulate consumers into making decisions they would not otherwise make, such as falsely claiming a product is running low. They will also ensure ticket retailers, like Ticketmaster, make tiered pricing transparent; force influencers to disclose when they are being paid to promote a product; outrule personalized advertising and pricing targeting minors or taking advantage of sensitive data; make digital subscriptions easier to cancel; and give consumers a right to interact with human customer service. The package “represents the most significant reform of EU consumer protection rules in more than 20 years” according to Michael McGrath, the EC Consumer Protection Commissioner, noting that existing consumer rules were developed before ecommerce, the attention economy, and use of personal data for marketing took off. “The digital fairness act will make sure the digital economy works for consumers and not against them,” he said at a press conference. The bill will also enable all consumers to turn off addictive design features on digital services, such as autoplay of videos and streaks—including on apps like Strava and Duolingo. Some of these patterns the EU has already restricted for children through its Kids Act , which in addition to banning under-13s from accessing social media and chatbots, targets addictive designs in those services. Some European rights groups have called for those protections to be extended to all consumers and, teasing the Digital Fairness Act in September’s State of the Union address, President Ursula von der Leyen said: “But it is not only minors who are at risk. Addictive design, for example, is harming everyone. That is why we need a wider framework.” Some of the risks are also already regulated by the EU Digital Services Act. On Friday, the European Commission said ByteDance’s TikTok had breached those rules with the “rabbit hole effect” of its “For You” feed algorithm which personalizes content recommended to users. The tech regulator had previously found TikTok’s “addictive design” broke the rules by including features such as infinite scroll, autoplay, and push notifications, in addition to the algorithm. In July, it found Meta to be in breach of the act due to similar features on Instagram and Facebook . If confirmed, both companies may now face fines of up to 6 percent of worldwide annual turnover. The new regulation is designed to fill the gaps between this, the Digital Markets Act, and August’s AI Act , says executive vice president Henna Virkkunen, “not duplicate this.” The package should simplify consumer protection rules across the bloc’s 27 members and be a “strong safety net in the digital world,” she adds. The Commission aims to accelerate cross-border cooperation through strengthened enforcement rules. These would also give the regulator direct powers to investigate large-scale impact and fine firms up to 6 percent of their worldwide annual turnover. Non-EU companies would be required to appoint a local legal representative to cooperate with authorities. Correction: 11/12/2026, 10:15 GMT. events.title: Diesel still costing close to a ‘dismal’ £2 a litre despite oil price falls
events.summary: Pump prices stay stubbornly high as leading bank official warns energy costs are likely to remain ‘elevated’ The price of diesel on UK forecourts remains stubbornly close to October’s record high of £2 despite a sharp fall in oil prices. A litre costs an average of 197p, according to the AA, which described the situation as “dismal”. By contrast, petrol has fallen 6p to 168p from the peak of 174.7p in early October. That was the highest level since August 2022. Continue reading...

events.title: The Download: preserving minds and weighing open AI risks
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.  To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death. Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud. Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be . —Antonio Regalado This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands. MIT Technology Review Narrated: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks? Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify. The warning was the latest flashpoint in the debate over open frontier AI models. Critics warn that bad actors can misuse them, while supporters argue they prevent a handful of companies from controlling the technology. The debate, however, is more complicated than it seems . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 COP31’s flagship pledge to electrify 35% of energy use is sinking Only around a dozen nations are reportedly ready to sign it. ( Politico ) + It requires quadrupling the pace of electrification. ( New Scientist $) + John Kerry says the US must follow China on clean energy. ( Guardian ) + But the US skipped the talks entirely for a second year. ( NYT $) + What’s the future of electricity? ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 The Nvidia spy scandal reportedly involves $7.5 billion of chips Alice Huang allegedly obtained 240,000 restricted chips. ( Information $) + Trump was told of Huang’s spy link on Air Force One . ( NYT $) + Experts warn the scandal could erode America’s AI lead. ( Verge ) + Nvidia’s slide has let Microsoft overtake it in value. ( Reuters $) 3 Studies found AI agents go rogue because they’re “incorrigible” Their training rewards them for finishing tasks at any cost. ( NYT $) + This is why AI agents lie and cheat to reach their goals. ( MIT Technology Review ) 4 Anthropic has scaled back its IPO valuation to $1.4 trillion It aimed for $2 trillion before the recent AI jitters. ( Guardian ) 5 Drone strikes have wiped out 3% of Yandex’s cloud customer data Ukraine hit three of its data centers in October. ( Reuters $) + Ukraine’s drones are fighting data centers for fiber. ( Ars Technica ) 6 Moderna says its new vaccine could prevent cancer in high-risk people The company’s CEO calls it the “holy grail” of cancer prevention. ( FT $) + Hong Kong is testing a next-gen ultrasound cancer treatment. ( SCMP ) 7 Scientists have slowly reversed human cells’ ages by decades One age marker was set back as far as 60 years. ( Wired $) + “Reprogramming” is the buzziest de-aging idea. ( MIT Technology Review ) 8 Robot vessels are hunting for mines in the Strait of Hormuz AI helps them spot mines camouflaged on the seabed. ( BBC ) 9 Life may have started inside a tiny bubble That’s the idea behind the “lipid first” origin theory. ( Quanta ) 10 As Voyager 1 reaches a light day from Earth, here’s what it’s taught us Its discoveries rewrote textbooks in real time. ( New Scientist $) Quote of the day “What a dereliction of duty. He’s supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends.” —Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, accuses President Donald Trump of ignoring warnings about the alleged relationship between Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a Chinese spy. One more thing How refrigeration ruined fresh food Bananas may not be chilled in the grocery store, but they’re the ultimate refrigerated fruit. It’s only thanks to a network of thermal control that they’ve become a global commodity. And that salad bag on the shelf? It’s not just a bag but a highly engineered respiratory apparatus. According to Nicola Twilley—a contributor to The New Yorker and cohost of the podcast Gastropod—refrigeration has wrecked our food system. Thankfully, there are promising alternative preservation methods.  Read the full story on her research . —Allison Arieff We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + A whisky made like wine is wowing the spirits world. + Britain lost in the fog makes for hauntingly beautiful photos . + Chronophoto is a fiendishly addictive game that challenges you to date old photos to the year. + Dozens of saxophonists met up in New York to play the gloriously cheesy riff from George Michael’s “Careless Whisper.”
